title: Auditing Emergent LLM-Agent Collaboration through Cooperation-Obligation Coupling
summary: LLM-agent systems can solve complex tasks through dynamic self-organization and emergent cooperation. Auditing this process is essential because plausible intermediate or final outputs can conceal incomplete or unsupported work and poorly allocated responsibility, ultimately compromising response quality. While existing approaches may record messages, tool calls, provenance, or task dependencies, an auditability gap exists as they do not jointly represent what work remains, who is responsible for it, and what evidence justifies each work-state transition. We address this auditability gap by proposing \emph{Integrated Cooperation-Obligation REpresentation} (iCORE). It creates a unified encoding $X=(G,Q,Π)$ integrating observable interactions as a cooperation graph $G$, evolving work and assignments as an obligation graph $Q$, and the audit map $Π$ linking them with verifiable properties and evidence. This iCORE representation enables the auditor to certify two complementary properties: {Work soundness}, where every active decision-relevant work assertion must have a finite justification through $G$ and $Π$; and {Agent-assignment stability}, which requires that no feasible alternative agent improve the declared contribution value for an evaluated obligation by more than $ε$. We establish local-to-global soundness and assignment-regret guarantees and a performance bound under stated conditions. iCORE is an instrumentation layer over workflows. Numerical results show that the full coupled state exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects in two execution modes and that, relative to passive full-state observation, iCORE-Audit yields absolute trajectory-quality improvements of $11.5\%$ and $26.4\%$ in controlled and real-LLM execution, respectively, with corresponding absolute terminal-performance improvements of $15.1\%$ and $31.0\%$.

AI.tldr: iCORE proposes a unified representation integrating cooperation, obligation, and audit maps to enable formal auditing of LLM-agent systems, guaranteeing work soundness and agent-assignment stability with demonstrated quality improvements of 11.5–31.0%.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent systems exhibit emergent cooperation and self-organization, but plausible outputs can hide incomplete work, unsupported reasoning, or misallocated responsibility. Existing auditing methods (message logs, provenance tracking, task dependency graphs) fail to jointly capture what work remains, who is responsible, and what evidence justifies each work-state transition — creating an auditability gap that iCORE aims to fill.
AI.method: iCORE encodes the system as a triple X=(G, Q, Π): a cooperation graph G capturing observable interactions, an obligation graph Q tracking evolving work and agent assignments, and an audit map Π linking both with verifiable properties and evidence. The framework certifies two properties: (1) Work soundness — every decision-relevant work assertion has finite justification through G and Π; (2) Agent-assignment stability — no alternative agent can improve declared contribution by more than ε. Local-to-global soundness, assignment-regret guarantees, and performance bounds are established under stated conditions.
AI.result: Numerical results show that iCORE's full coupled state exactly reconstructs soundness and assignment defects across two execution modes. iCORE-Audit yields absolute trajectory-quality improvements of 11.5% (controlled) and 26.4% (real-LLM execution), with terminal-performance improvements of 15.1% and 31.0%, respectively, relative to passive full-state observation.
AI.conclusion: iCORE provides a principled instrumentation layer that makes LLM-agent workflows auditable by unifying cooperation, obligation, and evidence into a single verifiable representation, enabling formal guarantees and empirically significant quality improvements.

title: Stop Shipping AI Agents on Faith: Capability Is Not Production Readiness
summary: AI agents are moving into production workflows where they retrieve information, call tools, maintain state, and act on behalf of users or organizations, but many release decisions still rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that do not show whether an agent is ready to operate under production constraints. Capability is therefore not production readiness. This paper introduces the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index for AI agents. PAI combines four dimensions of deployment evidence: Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance. Evaluation measures observed behavior, Context measures the operating environment that shapes that behavior, Compliance measures alignment with applicable rules and controls, and Governance measures whether the organization can authorize, monitor, audit, and control the agent during operation. PAI is implemented inside ProofAgent Harness, an open source infrastructure for auditable AI agent evaluation and governance. Validation across two heavily regulated domains, healthcare and finance, shows that PAI carries held out readiness signal and separates higher risk from lower risk configurations. The results show that context engineering strongly changes reliability, capability improves behavior but does not determine readiness, and governance evidence must remain visible rather than averaged away. PAI reframes agent release from a faith based deployment decision into an auditable readiness decision.

AI.tldr: The ProofAgent Index (PAI) is a governance readiness index for AI agents that evaluates production readiness across four dimensions—Evaluation, Context, Compliance, and Governance—rather than relying on capability signals alone. Implemented in the open-source ProofAgent Harness, PAI was validated in healthcare and finance, showing that governance evidence must remain visible and that capability does not equate to production readiness.
AI.motivation: AI agent deployment decisions currently rely on capability signals, demos, or behavioral tests that fail to capture whether an agent is ready for production constraints. There is a gap between demonstrating capability and proving production readiness, leading to faith-based rather than auditable deployment decisions.
AI.method: The authors propose the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness index structured around four dimensions: (1) Evaluation — observed behavior; (2) Context — the operating environment shaping behavior; (3) Compliance — alignment with applicable rules and controls; (4) Governance — organizational ability to authorize, monitor, audit, and control the agent. PAI is implemented in ProofAgent Harness, an open-source auditable evaluation and governance infrastructure. Validation is conducted across two heavily regulated domains: healthcare and finance.
AI.result: PAI carries a held-out readiness signal and successfully separates higher-risk from lower-risk agent configurations. Three key findings: (1) context engineering strongly impacts reliability; (2) improved capability enhances behavior but does not determine readiness; (3) governance evidence must remain visible rather than being averaged away.
AI.conclusion: PAI reframes AI agent release from a faith-based deployment decision into an auditable readiness decision, asserting that capability is not production readiness and that governance evidence visibility is essential for safe agent deployment.

title: Scaling LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Systems: Design Principles and Architectural Scalability Analysis
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems have the potential to enable collective intelligence and scale toward solving highly complex tasks through coordinated ensembles of specialized agents. However, despite their theoretical potential, the architectural design space remains largely non-systematized and lacks broadly established design principles. Furthermore, the scalability characteristics of such systems are only partially understood so far. This paper makes two contributions. We first distill four design principles for scalable MAS architectures from a structured analysis of prior work: simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, and summary-based communication. We operationalize these principles in a reference architecture whose topology is formalized as a constrained directed workflow graph, and we evaluate four configurations of increasing complexity on a standardized benchmark of terminal-based system engineering tasks using two LLMs of differing capability. Our findings show that scaling yields measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when the underlying LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity, then degrades due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. In addition, persistent consistency issues emerge as a central challenge across all scaling levels. These results provide concrete design guidance for practitioners and highlight consistency and evaluation standardization as key targets for future research.

AI.tldr: The paper distills four design principles for scalable LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), proposes a reference architecture based on constrained directed workflow graphs, and evaluates scaling behavior. Key findings: scaling yields accuracy gains with near-linear cost growth only when the LLM exceeds a capability threshold; performance peaks at intermediate complexity then degrades; and consistency issues persist across all scaling levels.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems hold promise for solving complex tasks through coordinated ensembles, but the architectural design space lacks systematization, design principles are not well established, and scalability characteristics remain poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors (1) distill four design principles (simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows with optional loops, summary-based communication) through structured analysis of prior work; (2) operationalize these in a reference architecture formalized as a constrained directed workflow graph; and (3) evaluate four configurations of increasing complexity on a standardized terminal-based system engineering benchmark using two LLMs of differing capability.
AI.result: Scaling yields measurable accuracy improvements with approximately linear cost growth, but only when the underlying LLM exceeds a minimum capability threshold. Performance peaks at intermediate complexity, then degrades due to timeouts and evaluation limitations. Persistent consistency issues emerge as a central challenge across all scaling levels.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides concrete design guidance for practitioners building LLM-based MAS and identifies consistency and evaluation standardization as critical targets for future research.

title: Argonaut: Interactive Visual Exploration for Distributed Optimization
comment: 6 pages, 8 figures. Accepted in ACSOS 2026 [artifacts track]
summary: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings is often hard to explore and navigate: disentangling what other agents choose, how their choices are interdependent, and how they collectively reach a global objective quickly becomes intractable as the system scales. The major limitation is observability of the search process. Existing methods are largely centralized and offer limited support, visualizing only the final solution or providing algorithm backends over a fixed dataset, so how a solution is reached stays a black box. We present Argonaut, a lightweight, containerized optimization dashboard that enables interactive, visual exploration of the entire search process for multi-agent discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings. Users upload datasets, construct agents and options, modify the decision space and its parameters on the fly, and run multiple algorithm backends to inspect how each configuration shapes local agent decisions and the resulting global objective. By uniting system construction, optimization, and analysis in one interactive loop, the first of its kind, Argonaut makes distributed discrete-choice optimization a human-in-the-loop process rather than a one-shot, black-box computation. We evaluate Argonaut on real-world household-electricity, shared-mobility, and sensor-data-exchange datasets scaling to 5600 agents and up to 1M solutions under brute force. Built on a Node.js interface with extensible Java and Python optimization backends, it maintains a typical runtime of 200 agents over 100 decision attributes in under 30 seconds.

AI.tldr: Argonaut is an interactive, containerized dashboard that enables visual exploration of the entire multi-agent discrete-choice optimization process in decentralized settings, transforming a traditionally black-box computation into a human-in-the-loop workflow.
AI.motivation: Distributed discrete-choice optimization in decentralized settings suffers from poor observability — understanding how agents make interdependent choices and collectively converge on a global objective is intractable as systems scale. Existing tools are centralized, visualize only final solutions, or operate over fixed datasets, leaving the search process opaque.
AI.method: Argonaut provides a lightweight, containerized Node.js dashboard where users can upload datasets, construct agents and options, modify decision-space parameters on the fly, and run multiple extensible algorithm backends (Java and Python). It unifies system construction, optimization, and analysis in a single interactive loop for visual exploration of the entire search process.
AI.result: Evaluated on household-electricity, shared-mobility, and sensor-data-exchange datasets scaling to 5,600 agents and up to 1 million solutions under brute force. Typical runtime with 200 agents over 100 decision attributes completes in under 30 seconds.
AI.conclusion: Argonaut demonstrates that making distributed discrete-choice optimization interactive and visually explorable — rather than a one-shot black box — is both feasible and scalable, enabling deeper human insight into decentralized multi-agent decision processes.

title: OwlPath: Lossless Knowledge Compression for LLM Bug Repair
summary:
LLM-based software engineering agents are constrained by limited context windows: roughly 100K tokens must store structurally relevant code  subsets to resolve bugs. Standard retrieval models treat code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop dependencies including subclass  chains, transitive callers and interface implementations through slow trial and error. We tackle this limitation with lossless knowledge  compression, encoding source code into an OWL2 ontology to answer structural queries using minimal relevant code fragments.
  We present OwlPath, an OWL2 reasoning layer atop CodeGraph, a widely used code intelligence platform with 500K+ GitHub stars, offering a unified  CLI for structural code retrieval. Powered by tree-sitter parsing, OwlPath supports multi-language repositories (Python, JavaScript,  TypeScript, Go, etc.) and encodes language-specific semantics into a unified OWL2 ontology. It adopts two complementary modules. First, a  transitive-closure engine fetches all structurally linked symbols via single SPARQL property-path queries, capturing multi-hop relations missed  by string matching. Second, the OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM) precomputes a compact 3KB summary with module trees, core APIs and  issue-related symbols, directing agents to target modules in the first query.
  Evaluated on 18 SWE-bench Pro instances, OwlPath obtains a 68.4% strict-apply rate versus 66.7% for the CodeGraph baseline, cutting token usage  by 28.8% and runtime by 39.5%. In offline retrieval tests over 67 instances, OwlPath improves recall 2.06 times (0.464 vs 0.226) and reaches  88.1% hit rate compared to CodeGraph's 59.7%. On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark, recall rises from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69-80%  accuracy on transitive caller and interface tasks.

AI.tldr: OwlPath compresses source code into an OWL2 ontology to enable efficient structural retrieval for LLM-based software engineering agents, improving recall (2.06×), hit rate (88.1% vs 59.7%), and reducing token usage (28.8%) and runtime (39.5%) compared to a CodeGraph baseline.
AI.motivation: LLM-based SE agents are bottlenecked by ~100K token context windows. Standard retrieval treats code as plain text, forcing agents to resolve multi-hop structural dependencies (subclass chains, transitive callers, interface implementations) via costly trial-and-error. A more efficient, structure-aware retrieval mechanism is needed.
AI.method: OwlPath builds an OWL2 reasoning layer on top of the CodeGraph platform, using tree-sitter parsing for multi-language support (Python, JS, TS, Go, etc.). It employs two modules: (1) a transitive-closure engine using SPARQL property-path queries to capture multi-hop structural relations in a single query, and (2) an OWL Software Knowledge Map (OWL-SKM) that precomputes a compact 3KB summary (module trees, core APIs, issue-related symbols) for targeted first-query routing.
AI.result: On 18 SWE-bench Pro instances: 68.4% strict-apply rate (vs 66.7% baseline), 28.8% token reduction, 39.5% runtime reduction. On 67-instance offline retrieval: recall improved 2.06× (0.464 vs 0.226), hit rate 88.1% (vs 59.7%). On a 37-question structural retrieval benchmark: recall rose from 4.4% to 28.8%, with 69–80% accuracy on transitive caller and interface implementation tasks.
AI.conclusion: Lossless knowledge compression via OWL2 ontologies significantly outperforms text-based retrieval for structural code queries, enabling more efficient LLM-based program repair with lower token costs and faster execution. The approach is practical, integrating with a widely-adopted code intelligence platform.

title: OneShot: Index-in-Ranking with Neural Scoring for Large-Scale Retrieval
summary: In modern recommendation systems, retrieval serves as a primary stage responsible for filtering billions of candidate items down to thousands prior to refined ranking. To make this massive search effective and efficient, the system relies on ranking accuracy and indexing efficiency. However, these two objectives are traditionally misaligned: while the former optimizes for the alignment between ranking predictions and user behavior, the latter optimizes for a structural grouping of item representations which enables fast search among billions of candidates. Thus, despite extensive efforts to scale up interaction modeling for retrieval, they remain fundamentally limited by the structural misalignment between the ranking objectives and the proximity-learned index. In this work, we address this long-standing dichotomy by proposing a new holistic retrieval framework, OneShot. It is an end-to-end, in-model index learning framework that natively aligns index learning with ranking objectives. Using this joint learning as a structural foundation, OneShot pushes the boundaries of retrieval expressiveness by scaling interaction modeling with neural scoring beyond the persistent dot-product bottleneck. OneShot is fully deployed in Instagram's industrial short-video recommendation system, driving significant wins in user daily sessions, engagement, and time-spent. Additionally, OneShot achieves a $20\%$ recall gain at the operational ranking volume and a 10x efficiency improvement at an equivalent recall level.

AI.tldr: OneShot is an end-to-end retrieval framework that jointly learns index structure and ranking objectives, overcoming the traditional misalignment between ranking accuracy and indexing efficiency. It scales neural interaction modeling beyond the dot-product bottleneck and delivers significant gains when deployed in Instagram's short-video recommendation system.
AI.motivation: Retrieval systems face a fundamental dichotomy: ranking objectives optimize for prediction-user alignment, while indexing optimizes for structural grouping of item representations to enable fast search. This misalignment limits the effectiveness of scaling interaction modeling. The authors aim to unify these two objectives in a single, holistic framework.
AI.method: OneShot is an end-to-end, in-model index learning framework that natively aligns index learning with ranking objectives through joint optimization. It scales interaction modeling via neural scoring, breaking through the conventional dot-product bottleneck that constrains retrieval expressiveness.
AI.result: Fully deployed in Instagram's short-video recommendation system, OneShot drives significant improvements in user daily sessions, engagement, and time-spent. It achieves a 20% recall gain at operational ranking volume and a 10x efficiency improvement at equivalent recall levels.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning the index and ranking model resolves the long-standing structural misalignment in retrieval systems, enabling both higher recall and greater efficiency at industrial scale.

title: Digital Harf: A Clinically Integrated Multimodal AI System for Pervasive Arabic Speech and Language Therapy
summary: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Arabic-speaking countries face compounded barriers to effective speech and language therapy: a shortage of qualified specialists, limited service reach beyond urban centers, and a near-total absence of culturally grounded digital therapy materials. We present Digital Harf, a pervasive, multimodal AI platform that extends clinician-led speech and language therapy into the home. The system integrates three therapeutic modules - language therapy, speech intelligibility, and picture description - within a unified workflow that adapts to each child's performance over time. To address the critical shortage of Arabic therapy content, we introduce an Agentic Synthetic Data Engine (ASDE) that automatically generates culturally relevant images, prompts, and language tasks guided by explicit therapeutic and cultural criteria. Expert evaluation with 13 licensed Speech-Language Pathologists yielded a 90.1% clinical acceptance rate for ASDE-generated content without any manual curation or selection, and strong ratings for cultural and linguistic alignment across the full platform. Digital Harf demonstrates that AI-driven therapeutic systems can be built from the ground up for underrepresented linguistic settings, treating cultural grounding as core infrastructure rather than an adaptation afterthought.

AI.tldr: Digital Harf is an AI-powered speech and language therapy platform for Arabic-speaking children with autism, featuring an Agentic Synthetic Data Engine that auto-generates culturally relevant therapy content, achieving 90.1% clinical acceptance from 13 speech-language pathologists.
AI.motivation: Arabic-speaking children with Autism Spectrum Disorder face severe barriers: shortages of qualified speech-language pathologists, limited access beyond urban areas, and a near-complete lack of culturally grounded digital therapy materials. Existing solutions are either not in Arabic or lack cultural/linguistic relevance.
AI.method: The authors developed Digital Harf, a pervasive multimodal AI platform with three integrated therapeutic modules (language therapy, speech intelligibility, picture description) that adapt to individual child performance. The core innovation is an Agentic Synthetic Data Engine (ASDE) that automatically generates culturally relevant images, prompts, and language tasks using explicit therapeutic and cultural criteria. The system was evaluated by 13 licensed Speech-Language Pathologists.
AI.result: ASDE-generated content achieved a 90.1% clinical acceptance rate without any manual curation or selection. Strong ratings were also obtained for cultural and linguistic alignment across the entire platform.
AI.conclusion: AI-driven therapeutic systems can be purpose-built for underrepresented linguistic settings, with cultural grounding treated as foundational infrastructure rather than a post-hoc adaptation. Digital Harf demonstrates the feasibility of extending clinician-led therapy into home settings for Arabic-speaking populations.

title: FAVA: Formal Authorization for Verified Agents with Evidence-Backed Permission Graphs
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents autonomously interleave semantic reasoning with complex system operations. In these dynamic environments, static tool-level permissions are fundamentally insufficient; safe authorization is highly context-dependent and heavily reliant on evolving runtime states and data flows. We present FAVA (Formal Authorization for Verified Agents), a permission-carrying authorization framework for agent execution. FAVA utilizes an LLM-guided Permission Intermediate Representation (IR) to translate ambiguous natural-language tasks into structured constraints. A deterministic lowering pass then converts this IR into an evidence-backed permission graph that explicitly tracks data flows, dependencies, and contextual labels. To provide strict security guarantees, a Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) authorizer mathematically verifies the current graph against security policies before any effectful action executes. A runtime gateway then enforces the solver's result, either authorizing the execution or intercepting it with a precise counterexample. We evaluate FAVA across OpenAgentSafety, OctoBench, and ActPlane scenarios. Our evaluation demonstrates that FAVA achieves a 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate (DCR) over the aggregate dataset, successfully intercepting dynamic violating traces in the evaluated trace-conditioned scenarios.

AI.tldr: FAVA is a permission-carrying authorization framework for LLM agents that uses an LLM-guided Permission IR, a deterministic lowering pass to an evidence-backed permission graph, and an SMT-based authorizer to mathematically verify actions against security policies at runtime, achieving 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Static tool-level permissions are fundamentally insufficient for LLM agents operating in dynamic environments, where safe authorization is highly context-dependent and reliant on evolving runtime states and data flows. There is a need for a formal, verifiable authorization mechanism that adapts to these conditions.
AI.method: FAVA operates in three stages: (1) an LLM-guided Permission Intermediate Representation (IR) translates ambiguous natural-language tasks into structured constraints; (2) a deterministic lowering pass converts the IR into an evidence-backed permission graph that explicitly tracks data flows, dependencies, and contextual labels; (3) a Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) authorizer mathematically verifies the permission graph against security policies before any effectful action executes. A runtime gateway enforces the solver's verdict, either authorizing execution or intercepting it with a precise counterexample.
AI.result: FAVA achieves a 90.5% Decision Compliance Rate (DCR) over an aggregate dataset drawn from OpenAgentSafety, OctoBench, and ActPlane scenarios, successfully intercepting dynamic violating traces in trace-conditioned evaluations.
AI.conclusion: FAVA demonstrates that combining LLM-guided semantic extraction with formal SMT-based verification provides a viable path toward provably safe authorization for autonomous LLM agents, bridging the gap between natural-language task ambiguity and rigorous, context-aware runtime enforcement.

title: Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability
summary: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates recursive weight-sharing transformer architectures as efficient surrogate models for small-data engineering design tasks, finding they offer an effective trade-off between accuracy, parameter count, and computational cost compared to over-parameterized conventional transformers.
AI.motivation: Conventional transformers are over-parameterized for low-dimensional engineering surrogate modeling where simulation data is scarce and expensive. Excess parameters cause overfitting and waste memory/compute, motivating a shift toward architectures that invest in additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters.
AI.method: The authors conduct a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms — a Tiny Recursive Model, a proposed Depth Recursive Transformer, and a simple recursive transformer — on two low-dimensional tasks: (1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages using FEA data, and (2) a Laplace PDE iterative solver for capacitance fields. Architectures are compared on Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank, parameter count, and FLOPs.
AI.result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers demonstrate a generalizable trade-off between predictive performance, parameter efficiency, and computational cost, outperforming conventional over-parameterized transformers on small engineering datasets.
AI.conclusion: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective, generalizable surrogate modeling approach for resource-constrained engineering design, offering practical design guidelines for architecture selection under limited data regimes.

title: Prompt Chaining in Practice: A Case Study in Automated Scholarly Report Generation
comment: This is the version of the article accepted for publication in SUMMA 2025 after peer review. The final, published version is available at IEEE Xplore: https://doi.org/10.1109/SUMMA68668.2025.11302303
summary: The exponential growth of scholarly publications requires automated tools for effective information synthesis. However, simple, single-shot prompting methods often lack the reliability and quality required for complex synthesis tasks. This paper introduces and empirically evaluates a multi-stage prompt chaining methodology as a more reliable architectural pattern for such tasks. This approach is implemented in our system, AI SciBrief, which automatically generates scholarly digests. We conducted a comparative experiment, measuring the performance of our prompt chaining method against a carefully optimized single-shot baseline. Both systems were evaluated against a human-authored "gold standard" report for the "Education" domain. The results demonstrate a significant difference in reliability: our prompt chaining method achieved a 100% success rate, whereas the optimized baseline failed in 50% of its runs. In terms of quality, the proposed method also demonstrated a clear advantage, achieving a superior ROUGE-L F1-score (0.507 vs. 0.486), driven primarily by higher precision. We conclude that prompt chaining is a more dependable and effective engineering approach for complex, multi-step generative tasks, significantly mitigating the risks of failure and inconsistency inherent in monolithic prompts.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-stage prompt chaining methodology for automated scholarly digest generation (AI SciBrief), demonstrating 100% success rate vs. 50% failure for single-shot prompting, with higher ROUGE-L F1 (0.507 vs. 0.486).
AI.motivation: Exponential growth of scholarly publications demands automated synthesis tools, but single-shot prompting methods suffer from reliability and quality issues for complex synthesis tasks.
AI.method: The authors implemented a multi-stage prompt chaining methodology in a system called AI SciBrief, compared against an optimized single-shot baseline. Both were evaluated against a human-authored gold-standard report in the Education domain, using success rate and ROUGE-L F1-score as metrics.
AI.result: Prompt chaining achieved 100% success rate (vs. 50% failure rate for baseline) and higher ROUGE-L F1-score (0.507 vs. 0.486), driven primarily by improved precision.
AI.conclusion: Prompt chaining is a more dependable and effective engineering approach for complex, multi-step generative tasks, significantly reducing failure and inconsistency risks inherent in monolithic prompts.

title: Multi-Head Attention Residuals
summary: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

AI.tldr: Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR) replaces the single shared query in attention residuals with per-subspace heads, each learning its own softmax over depth history. This resolves the forced compromise where different feature subspaces must read the same depth distribution, improving validation loss at 100M–1B scales with negligible parameter/compute cost.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformers use a single additive residual stream, meaning each sublayer only reads the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by allowing learned softmax attention over depth, but use one shared query across the entire model width. As model width grows, different feature subspaces increasingly disagree about which prior layers to attend to, creating a forced compromise that harms representational capacity.
AI.method: MHAR reshapes the routing query into H per-subspace heads, each with its own independent softmax over the depth history. This produces a block-diagonal read pattern with zero added parameters. H=1 recovers standard attention residuals exactly. Fused Triton kernels are introduced to improve throughput from 0.2–0.5× to 0.55–0.88× of baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion via delta attention residuals enables 8B mid-training.
AI.result: Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based corpus (quality-filtered, STEM/code-heavy), MHAR improves validation loss at 100M (-0.061), 350M (-0.149), and 1B (-0.140) parameters over a standard Transformer. It achieves best results among four compared methods at every scale. Validation loss is U-shaped w.r.t. head count H, with a flat optimum at H=4 or H=8; H=16 gives back gains. Probe analysis confirms subspace disagreement as the underlying driver. At 8B mid-training, gains of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA are observed.
AI.conclusion: MHAR provides a simple, parameter-free architectural improvement that addresses a fundamental tension between model width and depth-history routing. The head count H is a genuine design axis with a U-shaped optimum, not merely a free hyperparameter. The method scales well to larger models and supports efficient mid-training conversion of existing checkpoints.

title: $Σ$-Mem: An Online Reliability Memory for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Memory is central to long-horizon LLM agents, yet existing memory systems primarily preserve interaction content rather than modeling which agents can be trusted and under what conditions. This limitation is particularly important in multi-agent systems, where a central model may be unable to directly verify plausible or correlated peer responses. We introduce $Σ$-Mem, an online reliability memory that records historical competence evidence for individual peers and peer relationship evidence across the peer set. Both forms of evidence are maintained as real symmetric states and updated from post-decision correctness feedback. By Weyl's inequality, the spectral change caused by each event-level update is bounded, enabling stable online adaptation without retraining the underlying models. $Σ$-Mem provides a general write-and-read interface: the same memory can be used for residual steering of a central model, response-free peer routing, or reliability-weighted voting. Across five Qwen-family models, $Σ$-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts and generalizes to unseen peers and task domains. Direct memory readouts also outperform majority voting and the best fixed peer over the full OOD evaluation set. Moreover, performance improves consistently as more correctness feedback becomes available, indicating that $Σ$-Mem progressively accumulates actionable reliability information. These results establish reliability memory as a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems.

AI.tldr: Σ-Mem introduces an online reliability memory system for multi-agent LLMs that tracks peer trustworthiness via spectral updates, enabling adaptive coordination without retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing memory systems for LLM agents preserve interaction content but fail to model agent trustworthiness and reliability conditions. In multi-agent settings, a central model cannot directly verify peer responses, especially when they are plausible or correlated, creating a need for systematic reliability tracking.
AI.method: Σ-Mem maintains two forms of real symmetric evidence states: individual peer competence and peer relationship evidence. Both are updated online from post-decision correctness feedback. Using Weyl's inequality, event-level spectral changes are bounded, ensuring stable adaptation without retraining. The memory supports three readout modes: residual steering, peer routing, and reliability-weighted voting.
AI.result: Across five Qwen-family models, Σ-Mem adapts to counterfactual reliability shifts, generalizes to unseen peers and tasks, and outperforms majority voting and the best fixed peer on OOD evaluation. Performance improves monotonically with more correctness feedback.
AI.conclusion: Reliability memory serves as a reusable foundation for adaptive coordination in LLM-based multi-agent systems, enabling progressive accumulation of actionable trust information.

title: Do Context Files Help Coding Agents? A Two-Agent Ablation Study on Real Repositories
summary: Persistent context files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) are standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet evidence for their effectiveness is contradictory. We present a controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), 17 real tasks from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), and 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent (bounded to <=10-15pp via equivalence testing). A failure-mode triage reveals why: agents fail on implementation skill---feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring---not missing repository knowledge that a context file could supply; a manipulation probe confirms the real AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass on either agent. We further show that borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman rho=0.75), offering a candidate explanation for prior contradictions: single-agent studies draw tasks from different agents' informative bands. We release all code, data, and analysis.

AI.tldr: A controlled study ablating persistent context file strategies (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md) across two frontier coding agents (Claude Code, Codex) on 17 real tasks finds context injection does not measurably improve correctness. Failures stem from implementation skill deficits, not missing repository knowledge. Agent-specific task difficulty bands may explain contradictory prior findings.
AI.motivation: Persistent context files like AGENTS.md are widely adopted as standard practice for guiding AI coding agents, yet prior evidence on their effectiveness is contradictory. The authors seek to resolve this contradiction through a rigorous, controlled ablation study.
AI.method: Controlled ablation of context-injection strategy across two frontier agents (Claude Code and Codex), using 17 real-world tasks drawn from 3 repositories (15 shared + 2 Codex-only), totaling 288 evaluated runs with gold-test evaluation. Equivalence testing bounds effects to ≤10–15 percentage points. A failure-mode triage categorizes error types, and a manipulation probe tests whether AGENTS.md converts near-misses to passes.
AI.result: Context strategy does not measurably move correctness on either agent. Failures are attributed to implementation skill deficits — feature design, pattern selection, exact wiring — not missing repository knowledge. The manipulation probe confirms AGENTS.md never converts a near-miss to a pass. Additionally, borderline task difficulty is agent-specific (Spearman ρ = 0.75), suggesting single-agent studies may sample tasks from different informative difficulty bands.
AI.conclusion: Persistent context files do not reliably improve coding agent performance; failures are rooted in implementation capability rather than knowledge gaps. Agent-specific difficulty bands provide a candidate explanation for contradictory findings in prior single-agent studies. All code, data, and analysis are released.

title: Hierarchical Reranking for Scalable Financial RAG System
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Accepted at FinLLM @ IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: Analyzing financial documents such as 10-K filings, tabular disclosures, and macroeconomic reports demands expert reasoning and extensive time. However, existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation systems often struggle to process hybrid text-table structures or the massive scale of financial documents. To address these challenges, we propose Hierarchical Reranker, a RAG framework designed to improve retrieval performance and generative reliability across large-scale financial datasets. The system integrates three key innovations: Pre-Retrieval Optimization, enhancing query clarity and search efficiency through normalization, keyword expansion, and table transformation; Hierarchical Reranker Architecture, improving retrieval precision through a two-stage ranking mechanism; and Long-Context Management, preserving reasoning accuracy through adaptive input partitioning and fusion under extensive contexts. Across multiple benchmarks, including FinQA, FinanceBench, and ConvFinQA, the proposed system achieved an NDCG@20 score of 0.7918 and demonstrated superior factual consistency. Its robustness was further validated by achieving second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge. This work presents a deployable, domain-optimized RAG pipeline that enhances both the accuracy and scalability of financial reasoning, paving the way for automated audit reporting and quantitative investment analysis. The source code will be made publicly available on GitHub upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: A Hierarchical Reranker RAG framework is proposed to improve retrieval and generation for large-scale financial documents, featuring pre-retrieval optimization, a two-stage ranking mechanism, and long-context management, achieving strong NDCG@20 scores and second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge.
AI.motivation: Financial document analysis (10-K filings, tabular disclosures, macroeconomic reports) requires expert reasoning and is time-consuming. Existing RAG systems struggle with hybrid text-table structures and the massive scale of financial documents, motivating the need for a domain-optimized retrieval pipeline.
AI.method: The proposed Hierarchical Reranker RAG framework integrates three innovations: (1) Pre-Retrieval Optimization via normalization, keyword expansion, and table transformation to enhance query clarity; (2) a two-stage Hierarchical Reranker Architecture for improved retrieval precision; and (3) Long-Context Management using adaptive input partitioning and fusion to preserve reasoning accuracy under extensive contexts.
AI.result: The system achieved an NDCG@20 score of 0.7918 across FinQA, FinanceBench, and ConvFinQA benchmarks, demonstrated superior factual consistency, and secured second place in the ACM-ICAIF '24 FinanceRAG Challenge.
AI.conclusion: The work presents a deployable, domain-optimized RAG pipeline that enhances accuracy and scalability of financial reasoning, with potential applications in automated audit reporting and quantitative investment analysis. Source code will be open-sourced on GitHub.

title: Evaluating the Vergence-Accommodation Conflict in Gaze-Based 3D Target Selection
summary: State-of-the-art head-mounted displays (HMDs) enable gaze-based selection in virtual environments. Yet, these HMDs suffer from the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC), which is known to affect interaction performance. The VAC might influence gaze-based selection performance because it directly affects eye-movement behavior. Thus, in this paper, we investigate how the VAC influences gaze-based 3D target selection across varying depth conditions. Our results show that as the (visual) depth increases, user performance significantly decreases with gaze-based selection. Moreover, a previously suggested Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model captured this performance change better relative to a linear model. These findings provide evidence that gaze-based pointing is negatively affected by the VAC and highlight the importance of accounting for depth-dependent factors when designing gaze-based interaction in 3D environments.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC) in head-mounted displays affects gaze-based 3D target selection performance, finding that increased visual depth significantly degrades selection accuracy and efficiency, and that a Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model better captures this performance decline than a linear model.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art HMDs enable gaze-based selection but suffer from the vergence-accommodation conflict (VAC), which directly impacts eye-movement behavior. Despite this, no prior work had systematically examined how VAC influences gaze-based 3D pointing performance across depth conditions — a critical gap given the growing use of gaze interaction in immersive environments.
AI.method: The authors conducted a controlled experiment with participants performing gaze-based 3D target selection tasks across varying visual depth conditions in an HMD. Performance was evaluated using standard metrics (e.g., throughput, error rate, movement time) and modeled using both a conventional linear Fitts' law formulation and a Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model, comparing model fit quality across depth conditions.
AI.result: As visual depth increased, user performance with gaze-based selection significantly decreased. The Variation in Diopter Fitts' law model — which accounts for depth-dependent perceptual effects — captured this performance degradation better than the standard linear Fitts' law model, demonstrating that VAC-induced changes in eye-movement behavior translate to measurable pointing performance costs.
AI.conclusion: Gaze-based pointing is negatively affected by the VAC, and depth-dependent factors must be accounted for when designing gaze-based interaction techniques in 3D environments. The Diopter-based Fitts' law variant provides a more accurate predictive model for gaze-based selection across depth.

title: Open Security Benchmark: Towards Autonomous Enterprise Cyber Defense
comment: 14 pages, 3 tables. Code: https://github.com/OpenSecurityAI/osb ; datasets: https://huggingface.co/OpenSecurityAI
summary: Enterprises are moving toward autonomous cyber defense: agentic AI that builds situational awareness of an organization's security state and reasons from it to assessments, decisions, and actions. This rests on a holistic view of the enterprise's security state, the continuous, cross-vendor picture of identities, cloud and infrastructure, data, applications, and their configurations that security posture management assembles. As agents take on this work, what matters is not whether an agent can produce an answer but whether it should be trusted to. The field cannot yet answer this question. Real enterprise environments are private, cross-vendor, and deeply correlated, and none is exposed publicly as a shared, queryable target for evaluating such agents end to end. We call this the environment data gap. We present Open Security Benchmark (OSB), a framework that benchmarks agentic AI on this work. OSB surfaces a curated enterprise environment - a frozen, holistic view of the security state - and evaluates posture investigation across two modalities: text-to-SQL over a relational snapshot and each vendor's native API over a served instance of the same environment. Freezing the environment pins the target state as an immutable snapshot and anchors answers to a closed-form ground truth. OSB is built from five components: a data layer, a task and evaluation-set layer, a multi-dimensional scoring layer, a minimal auditable harness, and a bring-your-own path that serves public comparison and private tenant evaluation from one substrate. We instantiate the framework with two identity-security packs and a family of synthetic-organization environment datasets spanning multiple scales, and chart its extension to further posture subdomains, investigation modalities, and defense stages from assessment toward remediation.

AI.tldr: OSB introduces a framework for benchmarking autonomous AI agents in enterprise security posture management, addressing the "environment data gap" where no shared, queryable enterprise environments exist for evaluation. It freezes a holistic security state snapshot, evaluates agents via text-to-SQL and native API modalities against ground-truth answers, and supports both public comparison and private tenant evaluation.
AI.motivation: Enterprises are adopting agentic AI for cyber defense, but there is currently no way to evaluate whether such agents can be trusted. The core problem, termed the "environment data gap," is that real enterprise environments are private, cross-vendor, deeply correlated, and none is publicly available as a shared benchmark target for end-to-end evaluation of security posture investigation agents.
AI.method: OSB is built from five components: (1) a data layer providing a frozen, holistic security-state snapshot; (2) a task and evaluation-set layer; (3) a multi-dimensional scoring layer; (4) a minimal auditable harness; and (5) a bring-your-own path enabling both public comparison and private tenant evaluation. It evaluates posture investigation across two modalities: text-to-SQL over a relational snapshot, and native API queries against a served instance of the same environment. Freezing the environment pins the target state immutably, anchoring answers to closed-form ground truth. The framework is instantiated with identity-security packs and synthetic-organization datasets at multiple scales.
AI.result: OSB provides a reproducible, ground-truth-anchored benchmark for agentic AI in security posture management. The instantiation with identity-security packs and multi-scale synthetic environments demonstrates feasibility, with a clear path to extend the framework to additional posture subdomains, investigation modalities, and defense stages from assessment toward remediation.
AI.conclusion: OSB fills a critical evaluation gap in autonomous cyber defense by providing the first framework for benchmarking agentic AI against a frozen, holistic enterprise security state with verifiable ground truth, enabling both public benchmarking and private organizational assessment from a single substrate.

title: Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning
summary: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) — the instability of individual modality contributions across incremental tasks — as a key overlooked factor in multimodal continual learning. The authors propose CMCDR, a regularization method with both replay-based and replay-free variants that preserves modality contribution structures from previous tasks, validated on class-incremental learning and visual QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal continual learning (MMCL) methods focus on cross-modal alignment and semantic similarity to mitigate forgetting, but neglect whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across tasks. This "Modality Contribution Drift" (MCD) at the decision level causes catastrophic forgetting that existing approaches cannot reliably address.
AI.method: The authors first quantify MCD with a score combining contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled modality-subset interventions. They then propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves modality contribution structures from prior tasks. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, comparing contribution profiles between current and frozen previous models, and constraining changes in modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses without exemplars.
AI.result: Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering demonstrate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR. Theoretical and empirical analyses confirm that existing MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate MCD.
AI.conclusion: Modality Contribution Drift is a critical but previously overlooked source of forgetting in MMCL. CMCDR effectively addresses this drift across both replay-based and replay-free settings, offering a general and effective solution validated on diverse multimodal continual learning benchmarks.

title: AI-assisted pre-review of open-source software submissions: an experience report from BOSC 2026
summary: Most conferences rely on peer-review of submissions, but as generative AI makes it easier than ever to prepare submission materials, some conferences are seeing an overwhelming surge of submissions. We wanted to see if generative AI could help our conference's volunteer reviewers by pre-reviewing abstracts for certain criteria. The Bioinformatics Open Source Conference (BOSC) was well-positioned to experiment with this, as we already had a detailed rubric used by reviewers to evaluate submitted abstracts on multiple criteria, including openness (public availability of the code or other content associated with the project), valid open source license, and "runnability" (how easy it is to download, build, and run the project - an important measure of reusability). For BOSC 2026, we built bosc-pre-review, an agentic skill that assessed six review criteria, and Runabilly, which builds and tests each project in a disposable Docker container for safety. The AI only gathered evidence to present to the reviewers; humans made every decision regarding the acceptance of the abstracts. After the review period, we surveyed the reviewers to determine how useful they found the pre-review. Most of those who responded said they found it useful, but they preferred to check the AI's conclusions against their own, rather than accepting the AI results unquestioningly.

AI.tldr: BOSC 2026 experimented with AI-assisted pre-review of conference abstracts using an agentic tool (bosc-pre-review) and a container-based build tester (Runabilly). The AI gathered evidence on six criteria (openness, licensing, runnability, etc.) for human reviewers, who retained full decision-making authority. Survey results showed reviewers found the pre-review useful but preferred to verify AI conclusions independently rather than accepting them blindly.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has made it easier to produce submission materials, leading to an overwhelming surge of submissions at academic conferences. The authors sought to explore whether generative AI could assist volunteer reviewers by pre-screening abstracts against established rubric criteria, thereby reducing reviewer burden while preserving human judgment in acceptance decisions.
AI.method: The authors developed two tools: (1) bosc-pre-review, an agentic skill that evaluates submitted abstracts against six criteria from BOSC's existing review rubric (including openness, valid open source license, and runnability); and (2) Runabilly, which automatically builds and tests each submitted project inside a disposable Docker container to assess reusability. The AI only gathered and presented evidence; humans made all final acceptance decisions. A post-review survey assessed reviewer perceptions of the pre-review system's usefulness.
AI.result: Most survey respondents reported finding the AI pre-review useful. However, reviewers expressed a strong preference for cross-checking the AI's conclusions against their own judgment rather than accepting the AI-generated assessments unquestioningly.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted pre-review can be a valuable aid for human reviewers facing high submission volumes, but it functions best as an evidence-gathering assistant rather than an autonomous evaluator. Human oversight remains essential to the integrity of the peer-review process.

title: KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/flagos-ai/KernelGenBench
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

AI.tldr: KernelGenBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-generated and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware. It reveals that agent-based methods outperform pure LLM sampling, cuBLAS operators are hardest to generate, cross-platform performance degrades severely, and autonomous kernel generation remains extremely token-costly.
AI.motivation: LLMs drive demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development is highly specialized and labor-intensive. While LLMs and agentic frameworks promise automatic kernel generation, no comprehensive benchmark exists to evaluate generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms.
AI.method: The authors introduce KernelGenBench with two sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three distinct sources beyond PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. A large-scale evaluation consuming over 15 billion tokens was conducted, comparing agent-based methods against pure LLM sampling methods.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling, with cuBLAS operators being the most challenging across all methods. (2) Generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms; kernel-specialized agents suffer severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E). (3) Autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive — specialized agents average 5.11M tokens per successful operator, orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling.
AI.conclusion: KernelGenBench establishes a unified evaluation framework that exposes critical gaps in current LLM-based kernel generation: cross-platform portability remains poor, certain operator categories (cuBLAS) are persistently difficult, and the token cost of agent-based generation is prohibitively high for practical deployment.

title: VISA: A Structured Description Protocol for Agent-Based Simulation Models Towards Machine Reproducibility
summary: Agent-based models (ABMs) are difficult to reproduce: their behavior is spread across prose narratives, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, so that two readers routinely reconstruct different models from the same documentation. We present VISA, a structured, symbol-based description protocol that specifies a model in eight interconnected tables---four at the agent level (Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function) and four at the model level (Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation)---under the principle of minimality with completeness. VISA makes a model machine-parseable and unambiguous via two artifacts: nineteen executable consistency rules that turn model validity into a checkable property, and three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, and code generation) that operationalize the full author--check--code--reproduce loop. We validate the protocol on three external, independently authored ABMs spanning three platforms: we reproduce two cross-language (NetLogo to Python) directly from their VISA specifications, and we capture a third, an industrial AnyLogic model, in eight tables (passing all nineteen rules) while honestly demarcating where reproduction is blocked by a proprietary movement library and unavailable data---itself a transparency contribution. VISA moves the reproduction barrier from the model, where it is invisible, to a named, localized dependency, where it is actionable.

AI.tldr: VISA is a structured, symbol-based description protocol that uses eight tables and nineteen consistency rules to make agent-based models machine-parseable, unambiguous, and reproducible, validated across three external models spanning NetLogo, Python, and AnyLogic platforms.
AI.motivation: Agent-based models (ABMs) suffer from a reproducibility crisis: their behavior is scattered across prose, platform-specific code, and implicit assumptions, causing different readers to reconstruct different models from identical documentation. The authors aim to move the reproduction barrier from invisible model-level ambiguity to named, localized, and actionable dependencies.
AI.method: The authors propose VISA, a structured description protocol built on eight interconnected tables (four agent-level: Agent, Variable, Sensing, Internal Function; four model-level: Associated Data, Input/Output, Schedule, Validation). VISA is operationalized through two artifacts: (1) nineteen executable consistency rules that make model validity a checkable property, and (2) three reusable LLM-executable skills (authoring, checking, and code generation) that implement the full author–check–code–reproduce loop. The protocol adheres to a principle of minimality with completeness.
AI.result: The protocol was validated on three independently authored ABMs across three platforms. Two models were successfully reproduced cross-language (NetLogo to Python) directly from their VISA specifications. A third industrial AnyLogic model was fully captured in the eight tables (passing all nineteen rules) with honest demarcation of where reproduction was blocked by a proprietary movement library and unavailable data, itself framed as a transparency contribution.
AI.conclusion: VISA shifts the reproduction barrier from invisible, model-internal ambiguity to named, localized dependencies where it becomes actionable. The protocol demonstrates that structured, symbol-based specification with machine-checkable consistency can materially improve ABM reproducibility across languages and platforms.

title: AgentS4D: Benchmarking Runtime Risks across the Execution Lifecycle of LLM-Based Workspace Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based workspace agents execute stateful, multi-step workflows across heterogeneous resources, external tools, and persistent state. Their safety must therefore be assessed from actions, side effects, and state changes throughout execution. Although recent benchmarks have advanced executable safety testing and trajectory-aware verification, they rarely provide a unified account of where risks enter, how they elicit unsafe behavior, which harms they target, and where supporting evidence appears during execution. We introduce AgentS4D, a sandboxed benchmark for lifecycle-wide runtime safety evaluation. Its four-dimensional runtime-safety framework uses six risk-entry sources, six induction strategies, and nine target harms to guide case construction, while seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. AgentS4D contains 328 risk-injected cases. We evaluate all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, and Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, and Qwen3.7-Plus) on these cases, yielding 6,560 runs. Overall, 4,461 runs (68.0%) trigger prespecified unsafe signals. Across the 20 configurations, the observed safety of an agent system varies with both its harness-LLM pairing and how risk is introduced. Agent systems exhibit markedly different safety behavior when the same induction strategy reaches them through different risk carriers. They also respond differently to the same target harm when it is realized through different carriers and strategies. Moreover, 4,344 runs (66.22% overall) are unsafe yet complete. Thus, task completion cannot establish runtime safety, and testing only one form of a risk can conceal important weaknesses. Evaluations should examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions and retain evidence throughout execution.

AI.tldr: AgentS4D introduces a 4D runtime-safety benchmark with 328 risk-injected cases, evaluated across 20 harness-LLM combinations (6,560 runs). Results show 68% trigger unsafe signals, safety varies significantly by harness-LLM pairing and risk introduction method, and 66.22% of runs are unsafe yet complete, demonstrating that task completion does not imply safety.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based workspace agents lack a unified account of where risks enter, how unsafe behavior is elicited, which harms are targeted, and where evidence appears during execution. Current approaches fail to examine complete agent configurations across diverse risk conditions holistically.
AI.method: AgentS4D is a sandboxed benchmark built on a four-dimensional runtime-safety framework: (1) six risk-entry sources, (2) six induction strategies, (3) nine target harms guide case construction, and (4) seven lifecycle checkpoints organize post-run evidence. The benchmark contains 328 risk-injected cases tested across all 20 combinations of four harnesses (Hermes, OpenClaw, Claude Code, Codex) and five LLM backends (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiniMax-M3, Qwen3.7-Plus), yielding 6,560 total runs.
AI.result: 4,461 of 6,560 runs (68.0%) triggered prespecified unsafe signals. Safety behavior varies substantially with harness-LLM pairings and how risk is introduced. Identical induction strategies produce markedly different safety outcomes when delivered through different risk carriers. Similarly, the same target harm yields different responses when realized through different carriers and strategies. Crucially, 4,344 runs (66.22%) were unsafe yet completed successfully, demonstrating that task completion cannot serve as a proxy for runtime safety.
AI.conclusion: Runtime safety evaluation must examine complete agent configurations (harness + LLM) across diverse risk conditions, retaining evidence throughout the entire execution lifecycle. Testing only one form of a risk can conceal critical vulnerabilities, and task completion alone is insufficient to establish safety.

title: Heterogeneous Ranking in Industrial-Scale Recommender Systems: A Case Study
comment: Accepted to ACM RecSys Industry Track 2026
summary:
Heterogeneous recommendation feeds present complex challenges that extend beyond those found in highly homogeneous environments (e.g., music-only or video-only closed-ecosystem platforms). In Google Discover, a unified feed integrates diverse content sourced from the decentralized open web, including web articles, long-form and short-form videos, user-generated content (UGC), and beyond. Different content types exhibit distinct feature densities and user interaction patterns. Building a unified ranking model that sustains high performance across such heterogeneity, while avoiding negative transfer or majority bias, remains a significant industrial challenge.
  This paper presents an end-to-end case study on the industrial-scale multi-task ranking of heterogeneous feeds, grounded in real-world deployment. We introduce HA-MoE, a heterogeneity-adaptive multi-gated mixture-of-experts architecture that incorporates explicit heterogeneity context into both gating networks and expert representations. This approach enables effective specialization without significantly increasing operational overhead. To support reliable deployment, we introduce LENS, a lightweight observability framework that provides interpretable diagnostics of expert specialization and tracks this functional heterogeneity across continuous retraining. We evaluate our method using Dual-Level AUC (DL-AUC), a heterogeneity-aware evaluation metric that combines global ranking performance with cross-segment ranking correctness. Offline evaluations on a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline models. Furthermore, online A/B testing confirms gains in feed activity and exploration metrics. Together, offline and online results validate the effectiveness of our approach for managing heterogeneity in industrial-scale recommender systems.

AI.tldr: Google presents HA-MoE, a heterogeneity-adaptive mixture-of-experts architecture for unified multi-task ranking of diverse content feeds (articles, videos, UGC) in Google Discover. It introduces explicit heterogeneity context into gating and expert representations, a lightweight observability framework (LENS) for monitoring expert specialization, and a Dual-Level AUC metric, achieving offline and online gains.
AI.motivation: Unified recommendation feeds like Google Discover aggregate heterogeneous content types (web articles, short/long-form videos, UGC) from the open web. These content types have distinct feature densities and user interaction patterns. Building a single ranking model that performs well across all types without negative transfer or majority bias is a major industrial challenge.
AI.method: The authors propose HA-MoE (Heterogeneity-Adaptive Multi-gated Mixture-of-Experts), which injects explicit heterogeneity context (content type signals) into both gating networks and expert representations, enabling type-aware specialization with minimal overhead. They also introduce LENS, a lightweight observability framework that diagnoses expert specialization and tracks functional heterogeneity across retraining iterations. For evaluation, they propose DL-AUC (Dual-Level AUC), which combines global ranking AUC with cross-segment ranking correctness.
AI.result: Offline experiments on large-scale industrial data show consistent improvements over baselines. Online A/B testing demonstrates significant gains in feed activity and exploration metrics.
AI.conclusion: The HA-MoE architecture effectively handles heterogeneous content ranking in industrial-scale systems. The combination of LENS for observability and DL-AUC for evaluation provides a robust framework for deploying and monitoring such models, with both offline and online results validating the approach.

title: DP-LENS: A Density-Aware Polyfocal Lens with Topology-Driven Auto-Routing for Occlusion Management in Immersive 3D Analytics
comment: Accepted to IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR) 2026, to appear in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics (TVCG). 11 pages
summary: Immersive environments, e.g., virtual reality (VR), offer a unique approach to exploring complex 3D datasets, where data is often heavily occluded and exploration incurs a high cognitive load. We propose DP-LENS, a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens equipped with topology-driven auto-routing. While preserving peripheral context through geometric deformation and 3D perspective techniques, it enables users to explore 3D data with a lower cognitive load. To facilitate hands-free macro-navigation, we integrate a Large Language Model (LLM) to serve as a supplementary voice-based target selection tool that initiates the auto-routing algorithm. Two user studies with 34 participants investigate the potential benefits of this system. Our first study (N=18) compared the manual DP-LENS against two industry-standard baselines (i.e., World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing) in heavily occluded 3D datasets. The results show that DP-LENS significantly reduced cognitive load, decreased completion time, and improved user preference. The second study (N=16) compared the topology-driven auto-routing system (initiated via voice commands) with a fully manual DP-LENS. The results show that the auto-routing system improved task efficiency, further reduced cognitive load, and garnered higher user preference. Furthermore, the auto-routing partially decoupled exploration efficiency from the physical dimensions of the data and mitigated physical fatigue to some extent. Based on the findings, we proposed design implications to inform the development of more spatially scalable and low-fatigue interactions for future 3D visual analytics systems.

AI.tldr: DP-LENS is a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens with LLM-driven voice-controlled auto-routing for exploring heavily occluded 3D datasets in immersive environments. It reduces cognitive load, improves task efficiency, and outperforms standard baselines (World-in-Miniature, volumetric slicing) across two user studies (N=34).
