AI.motivation: Exploring complex 3D datasets in immersive environments (e.g., VR) is challenging due to heavy occlusion and high cognitive load. Existing techniques like World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing have limitations in preserving context while navigating dense 3D data. There is a need for a hands-free, low-cognitive-load exploration method that maintains peripheral context.
AI.method: DP-LENS combines: (1) a density-aware polyfocal fisheye lens that deforms 3D geometry to magnify regions of interest while preserving peripheral context via 3D perspective techniques; (2) a topology-driven auto-routing algorithm for macro-navigation; and (3) an LLM-based voice interface for hands-free target selection that triggers the auto-routing. Two user studies were conducted: Study 1 (N=18) compared manual DP-LENS against World-in-Miniature and volumetric slicing; Study 2 (N=16) compared LLM+auto-routing DP-LENS against fully manual DP-LENS.
AI.result: Study 1: DP-LENS significantly reduced cognitive load, decreased task completion time, and improved user preference over both baselines. Study 2: The topology-driven auto-routing system (voice-initiated) improved task efficiency, further reduced cognitive load, garnered higher user preference, partially decoupled exploration efficiency from physical data dimensions, and mitigated physical fatigue.
AI.conclusion: DP-LENS with LLM-driven auto-routing offers a spatially scalable, low-fatigue interaction paradigm for 3D visual analytics in immersive environments. The authors propose design implications for future systems targeting reduced cognitive and physical load in complex 3D data exploration.

title: RoguePrompt: Dual-Layer Encoding for Self-Reconstruction to Circumvent LLM Moderation
comment: This manuscript supersedes the preliminary version available as arXiv:2511.18790. The work has been substantially revised, expanded, and reorganized, with a refined threat model, revised methodology, clearer stage-level evaluation criteria, and expanded analysis of moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly integrated into mainstream development platforms and daily technological workflows, typically behind moderation and safety controls. Despite these controls, preventing prompt-based policy evasion remains challenging, and adversaries continue to "jailbreak" LLMs by crafting prompts that circumvent implemented safety mechanisms. Prior work has established cipher-mediated interaction, code-embedded decryption, prompt decomposition and reconstruction, and layered custom encryption as viable attack primitives. However, reported evaluations generally collapse visible acceptance, successful recovery of the concealed request, and subsequent execution into an aggregate attack-success outcome. This leaves limited evidence about where multistage prompt-transformation attacks fail within an observable black-box interaction. This paper introduces RoguePrompt, a jailbreak pipeline that partitions a forbidden prompt and applies two nested encodings, Vigenere followed by ROT13, along with natural-language reconstruction instructions. RoguePrompt was developed and evaluated under a black-box threat model, with only API or user-interface access to the hosted models, and was tested on 313 real-world, hard-rejected prompts. Success was measured in terms of moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution when the relevant stage exceeded its automated criterion. RoguePrompt achieved average rates of 93.93% for filter bypass, 79.02% for reconstruction, and 70.18% for execution. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of layered prompt encoding while providing stage-level evidence of where multistage jailbreaks fail during moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution.

AI.tldr: RoguePrompt is a multi-stage jailbreak pipeline that uses layered Vigenère + ROT13 encoding with reconstruction instructions to bypass LLM safety filters, achieving 93.93% filter bypass, 79.02% instruction reconstruction, and 70.18% execution rates across 313 hard-rejected prompts under black-box conditions.
AI.motivation: Prior jailbreak evaluations collapse multiple stages (moderation bypass, instruction recovery, and execution) into a single aggregate success metric, obscuring where multi-stage prompt-transformation attacks actually fail. The authors aim to provide stage-level diagnostic evidence about failure points in black-box LLM safety mechanisms.
AI.method: RoguePrompt partitions a forbidden prompt and applies two nested classical ciphers—Vigenère followed by ROT13—along with natural-language reconstruction instructions. The pipeline is evaluated under a black-box threat model (API/UI access only) on 313 real-world prompts that were previously hard-rejected by safety filters. Success is measured independently at three stages: moderation bypass, instruction reconstruction, and execution, each gated by automated criteria.
AI.result: RoguePrompt achieved 93.93% average filter bypass rate, 79.02% instruction reconstruction rate, and 70.18% execution rate across the 313-prompt test set, with stage-level granularity revealing where failures concentrate.
AI.conclusion: Layered prompt encoding is highly effective for circumventing LLM safety controls. More importantly, disaggregating jailbreak success into distinct stages provides diagnostically useful evidence about failure modes, enabling more targeted hardening of moderation, reconstruction-detection, and execution-prevention components.

title: DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series
summary: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

AI.tldr: DoTime is an open-source generator for multivariate temporal structural causal models with interventions, featuring continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling, and regime-switching dynamics. It provides frozen evaluation suites and demonstrates that interventional training yields consistent direction-accuracy gains over observational models.
AI.motivation: Existing causal inference benchmarks for time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation underdeveloped in critical areas like healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science.
AI.method: DoTime generates multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with novel capabilities: continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guards, regime-switching SCMs (generalizing interrupted time series), non-stationary dynamics via switching parameters, and deterministic ramp/sinusoidal intervention profiles inside evaluation windows. The generator serves as a prior for a causal foundation model. Four frozen evaluation suites with 100,000 trajectories and eight named identification structures are released, along with reference baselines and an evaluation harness. The falsifiable claim — interventional training improves direction-accuracy over observational models — is tested with a prior-fitted network (PFN) across three seeds.
AI.result: Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional PFN achieved a positive direction-accuracy gap over the observational model in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.
AI.conclusion: Interventional training provides measurable and consistent advantages in direction-accuracy for causal inference on time series. DoTime fills a critical gap in benchmarking infrastructure, enabling rigorous evaluation of causal methods with exact ground truth across diverse temporal structures and intervention regimes.

title: Sympathetic Framing: Evaluating AI Alignment across Sociodemographic Groups
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly shaping how we consume information and form our worldview. This raises concerns beyond bias in AI: do LLMs grasp the emotional nuances conveyed via textual framing? In this work, we empirically evaluate how well an array of LLMs aligns with human emotional perception. Considering news headlines covering political and geopolitical conflicts, both human participants (n = 3011, a representative sample of the U.K. adult population, via a YouGov survey) and seven LLMs answered whether headlines evoked sympathy for a specified side in a conflict. We find that the correlation between AI and human evaluations varies across models, ranging from very high (0.789, GPT-5.2) to medium (0.4 ,Mistral Large 2512). Crucially, the leading models are broadly aligned with human judgments across all demographic subgroups, including age, gender, level of education, prior geopolitical knowledge, and participants' predispositions regarding the conflict, although there are statistically significant differences between groups. This research, with its robust design and large, demographically diverse dataset, offers the most comprehensive evaluation of LLMs' comprehension of news framing to date. Findings highlight an important, often-ignored aspect of differential alignment: even when aggregate performance is high, AI alignment is not universal -- it may correspond differently with demographic features and cultural norms. Considering or ignoring the need for differential alignment may therefore have significant implications for the development of ethical and useful AI systems.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates how well seven LLMs align with human emotional perception of news headlines about political conflicts, using a representative UK sample (n=3011). While leading models show high aggregate correlation with human judgments (up to 0.789 for GPT-5.2), alignment varies across demographic subgroups, revealing that even high-performing models exhibit differential alignment across age, gender, education, political knowledge, and pre-existing predispositions.
AI.motivation: Beyond standard bias concerns, LLMs increasingly mediate information consumption and worldview formation. The authors ask whether LLMs can grasp the emotional nuances conveyed through textual framing — specifically, whether headlines evoke sympathy for particular sides in geopolitical conflicts — and whether this alignment is uniform across diverse human populations or varies systematically by demographic and attitudinal factors.
AI.method: A YouGov survey collected responses from 3,011 UK adults (demographically representative), who rated whether news headlines covering political/geopolitical conflicts evoked sympathy for a specified side. Seven LLMs evaluated the same headlines. Alignment was measured via correlation between human and model judgments, both in aggregate and disaggregated by demographic subgroups (age, gender, education, prior geopolitical knowledge, conflict predispositions), with statistical tests for between-group differences.
AI.result: Aggregate human-AI correlation ranged from very high (GPT-5.2: 0.789) to medium (Mistral Large 2512: ~0.4). Leading models aligned broadly with all demographic subgroups, but statistically significant differences between groups were detected — demonstrating differential alignment: even when overall performance is strong, models correspond differently with distinct demographic and cultural cohorts.
AI.conclusion: AI alignment with human emotional perception is not universal even when aggregate metrics appear strong. Differential alignment — systematic variation in model-human correspondence across demographic and cultural lines — is an underappreciated dimension of AI ethics. Recognizing and addressing this is critical for developing ethical, useful AI systems that serve diverse populations equitably.

title: RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI
summary: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

AI.tldr: RadHarmony is an open-source Python library that unifies loading, harmonization, and augmentation of heterogeneous radiological datasets (24 public datasets) through a single API, supporting chest X-rays, CT, and MRI with classification, segmentation, bounding box, and report text labels. It features an AI-agent-assisted integration workflow and is validated via a reference Vision Transformer pretrained across three chest radiograph datasets.
AI.motivation: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets that differ in sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. This heterogeneity creates significant engineering overhead and limits reproducibility. A unified, standardized interface is needed to streamline multi-dataset integration.
AI.method: The authors developed RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that: (1) standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format; (2) wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching; (3) supports multiple annotation types (classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, radiology reports) through one interface; (4) includes an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration; and (5) introduces an AI-agent skill that automates the integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. Validation is performed by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a Vision Transformer baseline, on three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code.
AI.result: The library successfully integrates 24 public datasets with standardized metadata. The RadHarmony-ViT reference model was pretrained across three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets without requiring any dataset-specific code, demonstrating the library's utility for seamless multi-dataset training.
AI.conclusion: RadHarmony lowers the barrier for multi-dataset radiological deep learning by providing a unified API, standardized metadata, and AI-assisted dataset integration. It promotes reproducibility and accelerates research by eliminating the need for dataset-specific preprocessing code.

title: AgentRadio: Passive Awareness for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Collaboration
summary: Understanding large codebases is a long-horizon task for Large Language Model (LLM) agents: answering a single question can require building and running the software, tracing execution across files, and synthesizing evidence over tens of minutes. On SWE-Atlas QnA, a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6) resolves only 32.3% of tasks. Dividing the work among agents with clean contexts mitigates this limitation. However, the subtasks of code comprehension are interdependent. One agent's findings can rewrite another's task, so agents must coordinate during execution, not only at phase boundaries. Existing multi-agent systems support such exchange only between phases, through staged handoffs or synchronized rounds. Communication and work remain mutually exclusive. A discovery made mid-execution cannot be shared until the next boundary. We present AgentRadio, an asynchronous message-passing layer that equips coding-agent harnesses with three primitives: threads, messages, and waiting for mentions. The last runs as a background task, surfacing teammates' messages without interrupting foreground work, so each agent remains passively aware of its peers and folds new findings into its ongoing task. Under a five-phase protocol of division of labor and negotiation, four agents organized by AgentRadio resolve 62.1% of tasks, 29.8 points above a single agent and above Claude Code with the newer Opus 4.8 (57.2%). Rubric-level analysis shows the gain growing with task difficulty, consistent with mid-course correction as the underlying mechanism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Coral-Protocol/AgentRadio.

AI.tldr: AgentRadio introduces an asynchronous message-passing layer enabling multi-agent coding systems to coordinate mid-execution (not just at phase boundaries), using threads, messages, and background mention-waiting. Four agents using AgentRadio resolve 62.1% of SWE-Atlas QnA tasks, outperforming both a single Claude Code agent (32.3%) and Claude Code with newer Opus 4.8 (57.2%).
AI.motivation: Understanding large codebases is a long-horizon task where a single LLM agent performs poorly (only 32.3% on SWE-Atlas QnA). Existing multi-agent systems restrict communication to phase boundaries (staged handoffs or synchronized rounds), making communication and work mutually exclusive. This prevents agents from sharing mid-execution discoveries that could rewrite another agent's task, limiting effective coordination on interdependent subtasks.
AI.method: AgentRadio provides an asynchronous message-passing layer with three primitives: (1) threads for organizing agent conversations, (2) messages for communication, and (3) waiting for mentions as a background task that surfaces teammates' messages without interrupting foreground work. This allows each agent to remain passively aware of peers and fold new findings into ongoing tasks. The system operates under a five-phase protocol of division of labor and negotiation, evaluated on the SWE-Atlas QnA benchmark.
AI.result: Four agents organized by AgentRadio resolved 62.1% of SWE-Atlas QnA tasks, achieving a 29.8 percentage-point gain over a single Claude Code agent (Opus 4.6, 32.3%) and outperforming Claude Code with the newer Opus 4.8 model (57.2%). Rubric-level analysis showed the performance gain increased with task difficulty, consistent with mid-course correction as the underlying mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous, mid-execution coordination via AgentRadio significantly improves multi-agent performance on long-horizon code comprehension tasks. The ability to share discoveries without waiting for phase boundaries enables effective mid-course correction, with gains scaling with task difficulty.

title: A Taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork Requirements
summary: Autonomous systems are increasingly deployed in safety- and mission-critical domains where humans and robots must operate as a team to complete complex tasks. Existing requirements for Human-Robot teamwork remain fragmented across disparate sources, with no unified framework that addresses complexities of collaborative Human-Robot tasks. We address this gap by presenting a taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements derived from analysis of (academic and industrial) literature, standards and regulatory guidance. We extracted a construction corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources. Through iterative classification and refinement, we develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy comprising 6 high-level categories and 21 low-level subcategories that distinguish information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. We validate the taxonomy through expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration on an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements drawn from 19 sources spanning six HRT domains.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a two-level hierarchical taxonomy of Human-Robot Teamwork (HRT) requirements, derived from 361 requirements across 14 cross-domain sources. Validated by 5 experts and demonstrated on 448 requirements from 19 sources, the taxonomy comprises 6 high-level categories and 21 subcategories, unifying previously fragmented HRT requirements.
AI.motivation: Requirements for Human-Robot teamwork are currently fragmented across disparate academic, industrial, standards, and regulatory sources, with no unified framework that captures the full complexity of collaborative human-robot tasks. This gap hinders systematic design, evaluation, and assurance of autonomous systems in safety- and mission-critical domains.
AI.method: The authors constructed a corpus of 361 requirements from 14 cross-domain sources (academic literature, industry, standards, regulatory guidance). They performed iterative classification and refinement to develop a two-level hierarchical taxonomy. Validation involved expert evaluation with 5 domain specialists and a utility demonstration applying the taxonomy to an independently assembled corpus of 448 requirements from 19 sources across six HRT domains.
AI.result: The resulting taxonomy has 6 high-level categories: information provision, relational control, decision support, safety mechanisms, performance monitoring, and foundational system capabilities. These branch into 21 low-level subcategories. Expert evaluation and the independent corpus demonstration confirmed the taxonomy's coverage, clarity, and practical utility.
AI.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a unified, validated framework for specifying, analyzing, and comparing HRT requirements across domains. It enables more systematic engineering of human-robot teams and offers a foundation for future standards development and assurance practices in collaborative autonomous systems.

title: An Exploration Graph with Continuous Refinement for Efficient Multimedia Retrieval
summary: As datasets and the dimensionality of feature vectors continue to grow, Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) in large multimedia databases becomes increasingly relevant. Graph-based approaches have demonstrated to offer the best trade-off between retrieval precision and search time. Despite their ability to deliver search times several orders of magnitude faster than exact search techniques, existing methods suffer from slow constructions speeds or high memory requirements. This paper presents a "continuous refining Exploration Graph" (crEG), a novel approach for rapidly constructing a compact exploration graph with state-of-the-art search performance. Additionally, it provides the ability to enhance its effectiveness even further through an optional edge optimization algorithm. Both algorithms are specifically designed to produce and operate on undirected graphs with even degrees and guarantee graph connectivity at any time, a property particularly valuable for "exploratory search", where the query is part of the database elements. Although such queries provide an advantageous starting point for graph search algorithms, they have been rarely considered in the context of ANNS, yet are crucial for recommendation and exploration systems. Our experiments demonstrate high efficiency in ANNS does not necessarily translate to a good performance in "exploratory search".

AI.tldr: crEG introduces a fast, compact graph construction method for ANNS with optional edge optimization, emphasizing undirected graphs with even degrees and guaranteed connectivity, and highlights the underexplored problem of "exploratory search" where queries are database elements.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based ANNS methods suffer from slow construction speeds or high memory requirements. Moreover, "exploratory search" — where the query belongs to the database — is crucial for recommendation/exploration systems but rarely addressed in ANNS literature, and high ANNS efficiency does not guarantee good exploratory search performance.
AI.method: The paper proposes the "continuous refining Exploration Graph" (crEG), which rapidly constructs a compact, undirected exploration graph with even node degrees and guaranteed connectivity at all times. An optional edge optimization algorithm further improves effectiveness. Both algorithms are tailored for undirected graphs.
AI.result: Experiments show that crEG achieves state-of-the-art search performance with fast construction and low memory usage. Critically, the paper also demonstrates that strong ANNS performance does not directly translate to strong performance in exploratory search settings.
AI.conclusion: crEG offers a compelling balance of construction speed, memory efficiency, and retrieval precision. The work also calls attention to exploratory search as a distinct and important evaluation paradigm for ANNS methods in recommendation and exploration systems.

title: Creative Task Cards for Reflection, Self-Efficiency and Self-Regulation in CS1 Introductory Programming: Initial Insights
comment: In Proceedings of The First Reflection in Creative Experience (RiCE) Workshop (RiCE W1) arXiv:2607.24558
summary: Computer Science students in introductory programming courses struggle with emotional challenges such as low levels of sustained interest and a lack of self-belief. However, students are typically introduced to disciplinary strategies (such as debugging strategies) and not the metacognitive nor self-regulation strategies that could help them overcome such emotional challenges. This paper addresses this issue by introducing creative task cards designed to support students' reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation in programming assignments. To evaluate the cards, twenty-nine students used them to complete a mock coding assignment in-class and participated in surveys and focus groups. Our initial qualitative insights suggest that students: found value in taking breaks, particularly when they could leave the classroom to reflect with peers; could use drawing to better reflect on feelings of cognitive overload; and felt more capable progressing with their work once breaking it into smaller steps.

AI.tldr: Creative task cards were introduced to help introductory CS students with emotional challenges like low interest and self-belief by fostering reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation. A study with 29 students showed that taking breaks, drawing to manage cognitive overload, and breaking tasks into smaller steps were valued strategies.
AI.motivation: Introductory programming students face emotional challenges (low sustained interest, lack of self-belief) but are typically taught only disciplinary strategies (e.g., debugging), not metacognitive or self-regulation strategies that address these emotional hurdles.
AI.method: The authors designed creative task cards to support reflection, self-efficacy, and self-regulation. A classroom study was conducted with 29 students who used the cards for a mock coding assignment, followed by surveys and focus groups for qualitative evaluation.
AI.result: Three key qualitative findings: (1) students valued taking breaks, especially leaving the classroom to reflect with peers; (2) drawing helped students reflect on feelings of cognitive overload; (3) breaking work into smaller steps improved students' sense of capability and progress.
AI.conclusion: Creative task cards show promise as a tool for integrating metacognitive and self-regulation support into programming education, helping students manage the emotional and cognitive demands of introductory coursework.

title: Low-Latency Bootstrapping for CKKS using Roots of Unity
summary: We introduce Sparse Roots of Unity (SPRU) bootstrapping, a new bootstrapping algorithm for the CKKS homomorphic encryption scheme for approximate arithmetic. The original CKKS bootstrapping method relies on homomorphically evaluating a polynomial that approximates modular reduction modulo q. In contrast, SPRU bootstrapping directly embeds the additive group modulo q into the complex roots of unity, which can be evaluated natively in the CKKS scheme. This approach significantly reduces the multiplicative depth required for bootstrapping, enabling the use of a smaller ring dimension and improving efficiency. In practice, using the OpenFHE C++ library, SPRU bootstrapping achieves up to a 5x reduction in latency when applied to ciphertexts with a small number of slots.

AI.tldr: SPRU bootstrapping is a new CKKS bootstrapping method that embeds modular reduction into complex roots of unity rather than using polynomial approximation, significantly reducing multiplicative depth, enabling smaller ring dimensions, and achieving up to 5x latency reduction for small-slot ciphertexts.
AI.motivation: The original CKKS bootstrapping relies on homomorphically evaluating a polynomial that approximates modular reduction modulo q, which incurs high multiplicative depth and forces the use of large ring dimensions. This motivates a more efficient approach that reduces computational overhead.
AI.method: SPRU bootstrapping directly embeds the additive group modulo q into the complex roots of unity, exploiting the fact that CKKS can natively evaluate operations on complex numbers. This avoids polynomial approximation of modular reduction and substantially lowers the multiplicative depth required for bootstrapping.
AI.result: Implemented in the OpenFHE C++ library, SPRU bootstrapping achieves up to a 5x reduction in latency compared to prior methods, particularly for ciphertexts with a small number of slots.
AI.conclusion: By replacing polynomial approximation with a native embedding into roots of unity, SPRU bootstrapping offers a more efficient CKKS bootstrapping solution, especially beneficial in low-slot-count scenarios, with practical gains demonstrated in OpenFHE.

title: PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective
summary: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

AI.tldr: PlatformBid is the first benchmark for auto-bidding from a unified ad platform perspective (integrating SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange). It defines three competitive settings—homogeneous, heterogeneous, and promotional—and evaluates classical, RL-based, and generative methods. The authors also propose BidFlow, a flow-matching-based auto-bidding method that achieves +0.68% target cost improvement in online Kuaishou experiments.
AI.motivation: Current auto-bidding research focuses narrowly on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions. However, modern ad platforms (e.g., social media, e-commerce) internally integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange, requiring auto-bidding algorithms that jointly optimize both advertiser conversions and platform total revenue. No platform-centric evaluation framework exists, and deployment evidence linking offline benchmarks to online performance is lacking.
AI.method: The authors propose PlatformBid, a benchmark with three competition settings: (1) homogeneous (identical algorithms), (2) heterogeneous (diverse strategies), and (3) promotional (budget surges during events). They evaluate existing methods across control-based, RL-based, and generative paradigms. Additionally, they introduce BidFlow, a novel auto-bidding method using flow-matching for expressive policy representation in dynamic competitive environments, validated via online A/B testing on Kuaishou.
AI.result: PlatformBid systematically benchmarks a wide range of auto-bidding methods across three realistic competition settings. The proposed BidFlow method demonstrates strong offline performance and achieves a +0.68% improvement in target cost in online Kuaishou experiments, confirming offline-online consistency of the benchmark.
AI.conclusion: PlatformBid fills a critical gap as the first unified platform-centric auto-bidding benchmark. BidFlow, leveraging flow-matching, proves effective in dynamic competitive environments. The offline-online consistency demonstrated by Kuaishou deployment validates the benchmark's practical relevance for real-world ad platforms.

title: LayerRAG-Bench: A Cross-Layer Reliability Benchmark for Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Agentic retrieval-augmented generation systems can produce answers that appear grounded while failing at the evidence, tool-contract, authorization, or session-state layer. We introduce LayerRAG-Bench, a controlled cross-layer reliability benchmark with 8 enterprise domains, 240 tasks, 9 fault scenarios, 2 contract modes, and 38,880 live task-level records across nine models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini. Schema normalization raises schema-drift success from 0.000 to 0.913, but stale evidence, missing tool output, denied permissions, and wrong-session context are not recovered by schema normalization. Groundedness-only evaluation also produces substantial false positives under stale and wrong-session evidence. These results support a layer-specific evaluation principle: a reliability intervention should be credited for repairing its target layer without being mistaken for a universal fix.

AI.tldr: LayerRAG-Bench is a cross-layer reliability benchmark for agentic RAG systems, revealing that schema normalization dramatically improves schema-drift robustness but fails to address faults at other layers (stale evidence, missing tools, permissions, session context), while groundedness-only evaluation produces false positives, supporting the principle that reliability interventions should be layer-specific.
AI.motivation: Agentic RAG systems can produce seemingly grounded answers that fail at different abstraction layers (evidence, tool-contract, authorization, session-state), yet current evaluation lacks systematic cross-layer reliability assessment. The authors aim to identify whether reliability interventions (like schema normalization) genuinely repair their target layer or are mistaken for universal fixes.
AI.method: The authors introduce LayerRAG-Bench, a controlled benchmark spanning 8 enterprise domains, 240 tasks, 9 fault scenarios, 2 contract modes, and 38,880 live task-level records. They evaluate 9 models (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini) across multiple reliability layers and test the effect of schema normalization on different fault types, while also comparing layer-specific evaluation against groundedness-only evaluation.
AI.result: Schema normalization improves schema-drift success from 0.000 to 0.913. However, faults at other layers — stale evidence, missing tool output, denied permissions, and wrong-session context — are not recovered by schema normalization. Groundedness-only evaluation produces substantial false positives under stale and wrong-session evidence conditions.
AI.conclusion: The results support a layer-specific evaluation principle: a reliability intervention should be credited for repairing only its target layer and should not be mistaken for a universal fix across all reliability layers.

title: Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition
comment: Accepted into COLM AIW, waiting decision for AdvML-Frontiers x CoTMA and HAIPS
summary: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

AI.tldr: Standard model-merging methods fail to preserve both harm classification accuracy and adversarial refusal simultaneously; the refusal fine-tune dominates due to larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, collapsing safety recognition into broad refusal behavior.
AI.motivation: Model merging is widely used to combine separately fine-tuned capabilities without retraining, but it is unclear whether standard methods can simultaneously preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors—specifically, nuanced harm classification and robust adversarial refusal.
AI.method: Two Gemma-3-1B-IT models were separately fine-tuned on complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. These were merged using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES methods, then evaluated on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Task-vector properties (cosine similarity and per-layer magnitudes) were measured to explain observed asymmetries.
AI.result: All merging methods showed a stark asymmetry: merged models retained 81–85% jailbreak refusal rates, while CARES classification accuracy dropped to at most 12.9%. The two task vectors were nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011), ruling out directional opposition as the cause. Instead, the refusal fine-tune exhibited consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to disproportionately favor refusal updates.
AI.conclusion: Standard model merging can collapse nuanced safety recognition into indiscriminate refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale, even when not directionally opposed. This reveals a fundamental limitation of current merging techniques for compositional safety.

title: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
summary: Social learning is a powerful mechanism through which agents learn about the world from others. However, humans sometimes choose direct experience over social learning, which can carry time and cognitive resource costs. How do people balance social and non-social learning? We propose a Rational Mentalizing model of the decision to engage in social learning. This model estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goal and the informativeness of their future actions. It then weighs the utility of social learning against the utility of non-social learning. Using a novel game where players choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment, we show that the Rational Mentalizing model can quantitatively capture human trade-offs between these strategies. These findings suggest that selective social learning is guided by 'Theory of Mind' in the service of utility maximization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Rational Mentalizing model that uses Theory of Mind to quantitatively predict when humans choose social learning over direct exploration, validated through a novel experimental game.
AI.motivation: Humans flexibly choose between social learning (observing others) and non-social learning (direct experience), but existing models do not adequately explain how people balance these strategies. Understanding this trade-off is critical, as social learning saves time and cognitive resources but may be less informative than direct exploration.
AI.method: The authors propose a Rational Mentalizing model that estimates the utility of social learning by reasoning about another agent's goals and the informativeness of their future actions, then weighs this against non-social learning utility. They test the model using a novel experimental game where participants choose between observing other agents or exploring the environment directly.
AI.result: The Rational Mentalizing model quantitatively captures human trade-offs between social and non-social learning strategies, outperforming alternative accounts.
AI.conclusion: Selective social learning is guided by Theory of Mind processes in the service of utility maximization, suggesting that mentalizing about others' goals and informative actions underpins decisions about when to learn socially.

title: SIGIL: Compiling Agent Skills into Typed Harnesses
summary: AI-Integrated agents increasingly acquire capability from skills: prose procedure files loaded into a model's context and run by a tool-calling loop. A skill is described to the runtime but never encoded in it, so the model re-derives its control flow on every run and may skip mandated verification. Across 30 skills and two model generations, a prose agent performs only 56% of the steps its own skill mandates, while producing artifacts that pass output checks. The remedy is known: write a harness, in which the procedure is program structure. However, hand-writing harnesses is tedious and discards the authoring surface that made skills succeed. To address this limitation, we introduce Skill Compilation, realized in SIGIL, which compiles a prose skill into an executable harness. At its center is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation separating model-owned cognition from code-owned mechanism. Compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps, complete the full procedure 2.3x as often, and require 0.58x the tokens. Notably, the guarantee is model-independent: the harness holds at 86% across two model generations while prose swings from 56% to 68%.

AI.tldr: Prose-based AI agents execute only 56% of mandated steps. The paper introduces Skill Compilation via SIGIL, which compiles prose skills into executable harnesses using AG-IR (a typed agentic intermediate representation). Compiled harnesses achieve 86% step completion, 2.3x higher full-procedure completion, and 0.58x token usage, with performance guarantees that hold across model generations.
AI.motivation: AI agents using prose procedure files (skills) loaded into context suffer from unreliable execution: the model re-derives control flow on every run and often skips mandated verification steps. Despite passing output checks, these agents complete only 56% of required steps. Hand-written harnesses solve this but are tedious to create and discard the accessible authoring surface that made prose skills popular.
AI.method: The authors introduce Skill Compilation, implemented in a system called SIGIL. The core innovation is AG-IR, a typed agentic intermediate representation that cleanly separates model-owned cognition (reasoning, generation) from code-owned mechanism (deterministic control flow, verification). SIGIL compiles a prose skill into an executable harness that structurally encodes the procedure, ensuring mandated steps are reliably executed while preserving the authoring surface of prose.
AI.result: Evaluated across 30 skills and two model generations: compiled harnesses perform 86% of mandated steps (vs. 56% for prose), achieve full procedure completion 2.3× more often, and consume 0.58× the tokens. Critically, the 86% step completion rate is model-independent, holding steady across model generations, while prose agent performance swings from 56% to 68%.
AI.conclusion: Skill Compilation bridges the gap between the accessibility of prose skill authoring and the reliability of programmatic harnesses. By separating cognition from mechanism via AG-IR, SIGIL delivers robust, model-independent guarantees on procedural execution without sacrificing the authoring experience that made skills successful.

title: Dynamic Exploration Graph: A Novel Approach for Efficient Nearest Neighbor Search in Evolving Multimedia Datasets
summary: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) represents a fundamental problem in various applications (image-search, recommendation systems). While graph-based algorithms have demonstrated a good balance between search accuracy and time, handling dynamic datasets, where data points are continuously added or removed, remains a challenge. This paper introduces the Dynamic Exploration Graph (DEG), an extension of the continuous refining Exploration Graph, which retains high search efficiency for static dataset while adding essential support for dynamic data. At the core of the DEG design are two key innovations: a novel vertex deletion algorithm which guarantees graph connectivity and a data distribution-agnostic method for graph expansion. Through these mechanisms, the DEG maintains a balanced and well-connected structure, even under continuous data alterations. Empirical experiments in both streaming and online scenarios demonstrate the superior performance of the DEG, surpassing existing dynamic graph algorithms in terms of construction time and search efficiency. Although optimized for dynamic datasets, the DEG delivers results as good as current state-of-the-art approaches for static dataset, underscoring its broad applicability.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Dynamic Exploration Graph (DEG), a graph-based ANNS algorithm that extends the Exploration Graph to support dynamic datasets through a connectivity-guaranteeing vertex deletion algorithm and a distribution-agnostic graph expansion method, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both dynamic and static scenarios.
AI.motivation: Graph-based ANNS algorithms excel on static datasets but struggle with dynamic datasets where points are continuously inserted and deleted. Existing solutions either sacrifice search efficiency or fail to maintain graph connectivity and balance under frequent updates, motivating the need for a graph structure natively designed for dynamic environments.
AI.method: The DEG extends the continuous refining Exploration Graph with two core innovations: (1) a novel vertex deletion algorithm that preserves graph connectivity upon point removal, and (2) a data distribution-agnostic method for graph expansion that maintains a balanced, well-connected structure regardless of the underlying data distribution. The approach handles both streaming (insertion-only/insertion+deletion) and online scenarios.
AI.result: Empirical experiments across streaming and online scenarios show DEG surpasses existing dynamic graph algorithms in construction time and search efficiency. For static datasets, DEG matches the performance of current state-of-the-art static ANNS approaches.
AI.conclusion: DEG successfully bridges the gap between static and dynamic ANNS, delivering a unified solution that maintains high search accuracy and efficiency under continuous data alterations while remaining competitive on static data, demonstrating broad applicability across diverse real-world scenarios.

title: VizPilot: Automated Onboarding for SVG-based Composite Visualizations using Multimodal LLMs
summary: Composite visualizations integrate multiple visualizations to represent complex datasets effectively, but their intrinsic composite designs often impose a high initial cognitive load on novice users. Existing visualization onboarding approaches are typically platform-dependent, require substantial manual authoring effort, and struggle with the structural complexity of composite visualizations, limiting their general applicability. We present VizPilot, an automated visualization onboarding approach that reverse-engineers composite visualization structure to generate interactive onboarding experiences directly from raw visualization artifacts. VizPilot consists of two modules: a Composite Visualization Analyzer and an Onboarding Interface. Leveraging Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the Analyzer employs a two-stage pipeline that decomposes a visualization into visual components, extracts structured explanations, and maps them to precise SVG elements for reliable highlighting and interaction. Implemented as a browser extension, VizPilot requires only a brief visualization description and optional interaction source code from the visualization developer to automatically generate onboarding content. The Onboarding Interface supports both guided narrative scrollytelling and free exploration, enabling users to learn visualization components progressively or on demand. We evaluate VizPilot through a comparative analysis of different input modalities, a usage scenario demonstrating reduced authoring effort, and a user study assessing its impact on users' cognitive load. The results demonstrate that VizPilot effectively automates the authoring of onboarding experiences while improving the usability and accessibility of composite visualizations.

AI.tldr: VizPilot is an automated system that reverse-engineers composite visualizations using Multimodal Large Language Models to generate interactive onboarding experiences, reducing cognitive load for novice users while minimizing manual authoring effort.
AI.motivation: Composite visualizations are powerful for representing complex data but impose high initial cognitive load on novices. Existing onboarding approaches are platform-dependent, labor-intensive to author, and fail to handle the structural complexity of composite visualizations, limiting their broad applicability.
AI.method: VizPilot employs two modules: a Composite Visualization Analyzer and an Onboarding Interface. The Analyzer uses MLLMs in a two-stage pipeline to (1) decompose visualizations into components and extract structured explanations, then (2) map those components to precise SVG elements for reliable highlighting and interaction. Implemented as a browser extension, it requires only a brief description and optional source code. The Onboarding Interface supports guided scrollytelling and free exploration modes.
AI.result: Evaluation via comparative analysis of input modalities, a usage scenario demonstrating reduced authoring effort, and a user study on cognitive load shows that VizPilot effectively automates onboarding authoring while improving usability and accessibility of composite visualizations.
AI.conclusion: VizPilot successfully automates the creation of interactive onboarding experiences for composite visualizations, reducing both developer authoring burden and novice users' cognitive load, thereby enhancing visualization accessibility.

title: Granite: A Modular Methodology for Foundational Verification of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
summary:
Granite is a methodology for modular verification of both functional correctness and nonleakage of RTL processors against ISA contracts. We prove that the cycle-by-cycle timing of a pipelined RISC design--with speculation, precise interrupts, and I/O--is determined solely by observables specified in an ISA leakage contract. For programs that keep observables independent of secrets (i.e., following the cryptographic-constant-time discipline), this result rules out information leakage through known and unknown timing side channels.
  Granite's specifications only constrain functional correctness and information-flow dependencies: not how many cycles an instruction takes, at which instruction an interrupt is handled, or the exact latencies of submodules such as multipliers and memory. Granite's central technique is leakage-aware refinement via determinism, which establishes correctness and confidentiality together as trace equivalence with respect to a family of cycle-level, deterministic spec machines. Secret-independent nondeterminism is handled by existentially parameterizing specs with untrusted, deterministic functions acting only on public data. Submodules are proved against their own leakage-aware specs, and these proofs compose into the whole-design guarantee--which therefore holds over a space of secure implementations.
  We believe this work is the first to achieve modular and foundational connection between instruction-set-level leakage contracts and microarchitecture-specific cycle-by-cycle execution with wire-level observations. Our proofs compose with a certified static analysis that recognizes cryptographic-constant-time code to derive a single Rocq theorem about the cycle-by-cycle confidentiality of a hardware-and-software cryptographic implementation--eliminating every intermediate specification, including the ISA contract itself, from the trusted computing base.

AI.tldr: Granite is a modular verification methodology that proves both functional correctness and nonleakage of pipelined RTL processors against ISA-level leakage contracts. By establishing determinism-based trace equivalence with parameterized spec machines, it guarantees that cycle-by-cycle observations reveal no secrets for constant-time programs, with all proofs composing down to a single Rocq theorem.
AI.motivation: Existing hardware verification either addresses functional correctness or information-flow security in isolation, and lacks a modular, foundational connection between ISA-level leakage contracts and microarchitectural cycle-by-cycle execution. The authors aim to close this gap, eliminating all intermediate specifications—including the ISA contract—from the trusted computing base.
AI.method: Granite employs leakage-aware refinement via determinism: it defines a family of cycle-level, deterministic specification machines and proves trace equivalence between the RTL implementation and these specs. Secret-independent nondeterminism is handled by existentially parameterizing specs with untrusted deterministic functions over public data. Submodules are verified against their own leakage-aware specs, and proofs compose modularly into a whole-design guarantee. The proofs further compose with a certified static analysis for cryptographic-constant-time code, yielding a single Rocq (Coq) theorem.
AI.result: For a pipelined RISC design featuring speculation, precise interrupts, and I/O, Granite proves that cycle-by-cycle timing is determined solely by ISA-level observables. For programs adhering to the cryptographic-constant-time discipline, this rules out all known and unknown timing side channels. The methodology is demonstrated with a fully composed proof yielding a single Rocq theorem covering the entire hardware–software stack.
AI.conclusion: Granite is the first work to achieve a modular, foundational connection between ISA-level leakage contracts and microarchitecture-specific, wire-level cycle-by-cycle execution. It eliminates all intermediate specifications from the TCB and provides end-to-end confidentiality guarantees for cryptographic implementations spanning hardware and software.

title: Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding
summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

AI.tldr: Converting MHA/GQA to MLA for KV-cache compression harms draft-token acceptance rates in speculative decoding. The authors propose Functional Reconstruction, an end-to-end post-conversion optimization that reproduces original attention output responses, significantly improving acceptance across 37 of 64 evaluated configurations.
AI.motivation: MLA offers compact KV caches for efficient long-context inference, but most open-source LLMs use MHA/GQA. Direct conversion methods introduce attention-function errors (from low-rank factorization and RoPE handling) that, while tolerable for standalone generation, substantially degrade draft-token acceptance in speculative decoding — undermining the complementary speedup speculative decoding provides.
AI.method: The authors frame MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction (reproducing the original MHA/GQA post-output-projection response) rather than cache compression. Their E2E method optimizes each converted MLA attention module on calibration hidden states to match the original attention output, without requiring verifier logits or supervision. The procedure is converter-agnostic and preserves both the converted cache structure and inference graph.
AI.result: Evaluated across 192 configurations (4 Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA converters, HF and vLLM backends, 4 tasks of 200 prompts each), Functional Reconstruction materially improved acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, left 26 unchanged, and decreased only 1 (using a 0.5-percentage-point tolerance).
AI.conclusion: Post-conversion functional reconstruction is an effective, low-cost way to recover speculative decoding performance lost during MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion, enabling MLA's memory efficiency and speculative decoding's latency gains to be combined without retraining from scratch.

title: BridgeAlign: Bridging Preference Alignment for Humanities and Social Sciences
summary: While data synthesis for large language models (LLMs) is prevalent, it primarily targets domains with verifiable answers, overlooking open-ended humanities and social sciences (HSS), where nuanced quality judgments matter more than objective correctness. This makes preference alignment a natural paradigm for broad HSS tasks. Yet existing methods are either costly or not tailored to broad HSS disciplines. We thus propose BridgeAlign, among the first preference-alignment pipelines for broad HSS disciplines, with three phases: i) Seed Curation: curating HSS seed documents from web corpora via heuristic/LLM-based filtering and text refinement; ii) Preference Data Synthesis: generating preference triplets via persona-based instruction inversion with Q&A consistency checks; iii) Preference Optimization: moving beyond naive human-vs-model heuristics by first grounding preferences in HSS quality rubric, then generating transitional responses via controlled quality degradation to form near-boundary preference pairs for finer-grained quality discrimination. Aligning over 210k synthetic preference samples, BridgeAlign enables Qwen3-8B to achieve the best average across 17 benchmarks against 11 strong baselines; importantly, leading on both human-preference and knowledge-based capabilities at once, with no trade-off between them, as supported by extensive experiments and contextualized by existing theories.

AI.tldr: BridgeAlign is a preference-alignment pipeline for open-ended humanities and social sciences (HSS) tasks, using seed curation, persona-based instruction inversion with consistency checks, and rubric-grounded near-boundary preference pairs. It enables Qwen3-8B to achieve SOTA on 17 benchmarks against 11 baselines, excelling simultaneously on human-preference and knowledge-based capabilities without trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Data synthesis for LLMs focuses on domains with verifiable answers, neglecting open-ended HSS disciplines where nuanced quality judgments matter more than objective correctness. Existing preference alignment methods are either too costly or not designed for the breadth of HSS. There is a need for a scalable, quality-centric alignment pipeline tailored to broad HSS tasks.
AI.method: BridgeAlign comprises three phases: (1) Seed Curation — filtering HSS documents from web corpora via heuristic/LLM-based filtering with text refinement; (2) Preference Data Synthesis — generating preference triplets via persona-based instruction inversion with Q&A consistency checks; (3) Preference Optimization — grounding preferences in an HSS quality rubric, then generating transitional responses through controlled quality degradation to form near-boundary preference pairs, enabling finer-grained quality discrimination beyond naive human-vs-model heuristics. The pipeline yields 210k+ synthetic preference samples for alignment.
AI.result: Aligning Qwen3-8B with BridgeAlign achieves the best average performance across 17 benchmarks against 11 strong baselines. Notably, the model leads on both human-preference and knowledge-based capabilities simultaneously, demonstrating no trade-off between these typically competing objectives.
AI.conclusion: BridgeAlign demonstrates that a carefully designed, rubric-grounded preference alignment pipeline can effectively adapt LLMs to broad HSS disciplines, achieving strong performance on both subjective quality and objective knowledge metrics. The absence of a trade-off between these capabilities is supported by extensive experiments and contextualized through existing theoretical frameworks.

title: Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion
summary: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

AI.tldr: Divergence Decoding is a training-free framework that fuses generalist and specialist LLM capabilities at inference time by using Jensen-Shannon divergence to detect when the specialist model is likely to err, dynamically routing control to the generalist. It outperforms both model types on scientific benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Generalist LLMs excel at reasoning but lack specialized scientific knowledge, while domain-specialist models possess deep knowledge but suffer from degraded reasoning and robustness. Existing solutions typically require costly training, fine-tuning, or manual orchestration. A training-free method to dynamically combine the complementary strengths of both model types at inference time is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose Divergence Decoding, which adapts the speculative decoding "draft-and-verify" framework into an adaptive routing mechanism. At each token generation step, Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) is computed between the output distributions of the generalist and specialist models. When the specialist's distribution diverges significantly from the generalist's (exceeding a threshold), this is interpreted as a reasoning risk, and control is routed to the generalist. Otherwise, the specialist's output is used, preserving domain expertise. This enables inference-time policy composition without any training.
AI.result: Evaluated on Qwen and Llama model families across GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench, Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized models and general-purpose models individually, surpassing most single-model baselines.
AI.conclusion: Divergence Decoding offers a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive, inference-time collaboration, effectively combining domain expertise with strong general reasoning.

title: Autonomous Event-Driven Multi-Agent Orchestration for Enterprise AI at Scale
summary: Enterprise AI aims to move toward continuous event monitoring, detection, and action across specialist agents, yet existing multi-agent systems largely assume discrete request-response workflows and remain underexplored at enterprise scale. We evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios spanning Persona (<10 agents), Department (20-80), and Enterprise (200) scales, and introduce a Task Manager for continuous operation via priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Results show that scale, not task complexity, dominates orchestration performance: both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale as agent discovery noise becomes the primary bottleneck, with simple tasks degrading more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at smaller scales, but its higher overhead worsens at enterprise scale; ReAct is more robust by handling failures incrementally. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14-75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates two multi-agent orchestration architectures—DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct—across 208 enterprise scenarios at three scales (Persona, Department, Enterprise). Scale, not task complexity, dominates performance degradation, with agent discovery noise as the primary bottleneck. The authors introduce a Task Manager with priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption, which significantly reduces latency and improves correctness at enterprise scale.
AI.motivation: Enterprise AI needs continuous event monitoring and action across specialist agents, but existing multi-agent systems assume discrete request-response workflows and have not been rigorously evaluated at enterprise scale (200+ agents). There is a gap in understanding how orchestration architectures perform under continuous, noisy, large-scale conditions.
AI.method: The authors evaluate DAG Plan and Execute and ReAct architectures across 208 production-derived enterprise scenarios at three scales: Persona (<10 agents), Department (20–80 agents), and Enterprise (200 agents). They introduce a Task Manager module for continuous operation featuring priority inference, related-event merging, and preemption. Performance is measured along dimensions of task success, latency, precision, and robustness to agent discovery noise.
AI.result: Scale dominates orchestration performance more than task complexity. Both architectures perform well at small scale but degrade at enterprise scale, with agent discovery noise as the primary bottleneck. Simple tasks degrade more sharply than complex ones. DAG Plan and Execute offers higher precision and structured parallelization at small scales but suffers from overhead at enterprise scale. ReAct is more robust due to incremental failure handling. The Task Manager reduces high-priority queue latency by 14–75% and improves related-event correctness by over 20 percentage points at enterprise scale.
AI.conclusion: Orchestration architecture choice should be scale-dependent: DAG Plan and Execute suits smaller, structured deployments, while ReAct is preferable for enterprise-scale robustness. Continuous operation mechanisms like the proposed Task Manager are critical for practical enterprise multi-agent systems, particularly for priority handling and event correlation at scale.

title: TrustChain-Review: A Risk-Adaptive Blockchain and Game-Theoretic Framework for Trustworthy AI-Assisted Code Review
summary: Context: AI-assisted software development can speed up coding and review, but it also makes accountability harder to establish. Developers may submit insufficiently verified code, reviewers may approve changes with limited inspection, and centralized reputation records may be difficult to audit. Objectives: This study introduces TrustChain-Review, a framework that combines verifiable evidence, strategic incentives, and risk-sensitive governance to support more trustworthy code review. Methods: The framework includes a blockchain-based evidence layer, a three-player game-theoretic model for developers, reviewers, and the platform, and a rule that applies stronger governance when the expected benefit justifies its cost. The evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset. Six governance configurations are compared over 30 independent runs using reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency. Results: The full-evidence configuration produces the strongest reputation, trust, and detection results, but it also has the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration lowers this cost and improves cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, although its trust and detection results are lower than those of the full-evidence setting. Conclusion: Strong evidence-based governance is most appropriate for high-risk or audit-sensitive changes. For routine or lower-risk contributions, selective governance offers a more practical balance between trustworthiness and operational cost.

AI.tldr: TrustChain-Review integrates blockchain evidence, game-theoretic incentives, and risk-adaptive governance to improve trust and accountability in AI-assisted code review, demonstrating that full-evidence governance maximizes detection and trust but at high cost, while risk-adaptive governance offers a more cost-efficient trade-off for routine changes.
AI.motivation: AI-assisted software development accelerates coding and review but erodes accountability: developers may submit unverified code, reviewers may conduct only superficial inspections, and centralized reputation records are hard to audit. A trustworthy, verifiable, and incentive-aligned code review mechanism is needed.
AI.method: The TrustChain-Review framework comprises three components: (1) a blockchain-based evidence layer for immutable audit trails, (2) a three-player game-theoretic model involving developers, reviewers, and the platform to align strategic incentives, and (3) a risk-sensitive governance rule that escalates oversight only when the expected benefit outweighs its cost. Evaluation uses a controlled simulation calibrated with the Diff Quality Estimation dataset across 30 independent runs, comparing six governance configurations on reputation accuracy, trust convergence, malicious-review detection, superficial-review detection, net platform utility, governance cost, and cost-efficiency.
AI.result: The full-evidence configuration achieved the highest reputation accuracy, trust convergence, and detection rates (both malicious and superficial reviews) but incurred the highest governance cost. The risk-adaptive configuration significantly reduced governance cost and improved cost-efficiency by applying stronger controls selectively, though its trust and detection metrics were lower than the full-evidence setting.
AI.conclusion: Full-evidence governance is best suited for high-risk or audit-sensitive code changes, while risk-adaptive, selective governance offers a more practical cost-trustworthiness balance for routine, lower-risk contributions.

title: LoopMemGR: From Behavior Logs to Evolving Memory for Generative Recommendation
summary: Generative recommendation formulates next-item prediction as conditional autoregressive generation over discrete Semantic IDs, enabling end-to-end recommendation over large-scale item spaces. However, most existing methods follow a history-as-context paradigm that repeatedly reconstructs user preference from behavior history while discarding system-side recommendation decisions after each request. This creates an asymmetric memory: the system remembers what the user has done, but not what it has previously recommended or learned from the resulting feedback. Consequently, useful preference-validation signals, potential negative evidence, and historical exploration information cannot be directly reused across requests. To address these limitations, we propose LoopMemGR, a closed-loop recommendation experience memory framework for generative recommendation. In addition to the conventional behavior log, LoopMemGR maintains a recommendation experience log that records past recommendation--feedback trajectories. It extracts request-relevant evidence through three complementary views: the recency view captures short-term interaction dynamics, the frequency view summarizes recurring recommendation patterns, and the global view distills transferable regularities shared across users. These signals are compressed into a fixed number of experience tokens to condition the generative backbone under a bounded input budget. Extensive experiments on an industrial Taobao dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of closed-loop experience accumulation and multi-view experience extraction.

AI.tldr: LoopMemGR introduces a closed-loop memory framework for generative recommendation that records past recommendation-feedback trajectories, addressing the asymmetry where systems remember user behavior but not their own prior decisions. It extracts evidence via recency, frequency, and global views, compressing them into experience tokens to augment next-item generation.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods use a history-as-context paradigm that only captures user-side behavior history, discarding system-side recommendation decisions and resulting feedback after each request. This "asymmetric memory" prevents reuse of preference-validation signals, negative evidence, and exploration history, limiting the system's ability to learn from its own past actions across requests.
AI.method: LoopMemGR maintains a recommendation experience log alongside the conventional behavior log.
