It employs three complementary views for evidence extraction: (1) a recency view for short-term interaction dynamics, (2) a frequency view for recurring recommendation patterns, and (3) a global view for transferable cross-user regularities. These signals are compressed into a fixed number of experience tokens to condition the generative backbone within a bounded input budget.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on an industrial Taobao dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of closed-loop experience accumulation and multi-view experience extraction for generative recommendation.
AI.conclusion: Closed-loop recommendation experience memory significantly improves generative recommendation by enabling the system to retain and reuse its own prior recommendation-feedback trajectories. The multi-view extraction strategy effectively balances short-term, recurring, and global patterns within constrained input budgets.

title: Investigating Effective Uncertainty Visualizations for Ordinal Crowdsourced Data of Crowding Conditions
summary: Commuters often encounter crowding in railway systems, particularly in queues where passenger density varies throughout the day. This introduces uncertainty in crowdedness, making it difficult for individuals to anticipate conditions and plan their trips effectively. Crowdsourcing has been a valuable method for collecting localized user data. But the unpredictability of crowds and the uncertainty of crowdsourced information pose new challenges for decision-making. However, we know little about how to effectively visualize uncertainty in crowdedness to support informed commuting decisions, particularly when using crowdsourced ordinal data. Here, we investigated different uncertainty visualizations and their effectiveness in representing the variability and reliability of crowdsourced crowding data. They were evaluated through an online study, and we found that cluster visualization is best suited to reduce cognitive load while maximizing user confidence and trust. On the other hand, participants showed higher accuracy in determining crowd levels when using bubble treemaps.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how to effectively visualize uncertainty in crowdsourced railway crowding data to support commuter decision-making, finding that cluster visualization reduces cognitive load and boosts confidence/trust, while bubble treemaps yield higher accuracy in determining crowd levels.
AI.motivation: Railway commuters face unpredictable crowding that varies throughout the day, and while crowdsourcing offers a way to collect localized data, the inherent uncertainty of such information poses challenges. There is a knowledge gap regarding how to visualize uncertainty in ordinal crowdsourced crowding data to support informed commuting decisions.
AI.method: The authors designed and compared multiple uncertainty visualization techniques for representing variability and reliability in crowdsourced ordinal crowding data. These visualizations were evaluated through an online user study measuring accuracy, cognitive load, user confidence, and trust.
AI.result: Cluster visualization was best for reducing cognitive load while maximizing user confidence and trust. Bubble treemaps led to higher accuracy in determining crowd levels. Different visualization techniques exhibited distinct trade-offs across the measured dimensions.
AI.conclusion: No single visualization excels on all metrics; cluster visualizations and bubble treemaps each offer distinct advantages for communicating uncertainty in crowdsourced crowding data. Designers should select visualization types based on the priority of accuracy versus cognitive ease and user trust.

title: Flock: Fast Proving for Batch Boolean Computations
comment: See eprint https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1329 for up to date version
summary:
For many applications of SNARKs, a key bottleneck is proving large batches of standard cryptographic hash evaluations, such as SHA-256, Keccak, or BLAKE3. We introduce Flock, a hash-based SNARK for extremely fast proving of such batched Boolean computations. Flock proves batches of the same R1CS circuit (plus input/output relations between them), can prove hash-chains and Merkle path openings, and in principle can be extended to full-fledged hash-based signature verification. At its core, Flock combines new optimizations for the lincheck and zerocheck protocols with an aggressively optimized proof-of-concept implementation co-designed by coding agents.
  On a single core of an M4 Max processor, Flock proves 82k evaluations of the BLAKE3 compression function, 42k SHA-256 compressions, and 30k Keccak permutations per second --- less than a $250\times$ overhead over native execution. On ten cores, throughput exceeds 660k BLAKE3 compressions per second; in proving SHA-256, Flock is more than $9\times$ faster than Binius64, the prior state of the art, and more than $500\times$ faster than the fastest elliptic curve-based SNARK we measured against.

AI.tldr: Flock is a hash-based SNARK that achieves extremely fast proving of batched Boolean computations, reaching up to 82k BLAKE3 compressions per second on a single M4 Max core — less than 250× overhead over native execution — and outperforming prior work by 9× over Binius64 and 500× over elliptic-curve-based SNARKs.
AI.motivation: Many SNARK applications are bottlenecked by proving large batches of standard cryptographic hash evaluations (SHA-256, Keccak, BLAKE3). Existing solutions are significantly slower than native execution, creating a need for a high-throughput proving system specialized for batched Boolean hash computations.
AI.method: Flock combines novel optimizations for the lincheck and zerocheck sub-protocols within a hash-based SNARK framework. It supports proving batches of identical R1CS circuits with input/output relations, hash-chains, and Merkle path openings. The implementation is co-designed and aggressively optimized with the aid of coding agents.
AI.result: On a single M4 Max core: 82k BLAKE3 compressions/sec, 42k SHA-256 compressions/sec, and 30k Keccak permutations/sec (all under 250× native overhead). On 10 cores, throughput exceeds 660k BLAKE3 compressions/sec. Flock is 9× faster than Binius64 (prior SOTA) and 500× faster than the fastest elliptic-curve-based SNARK tested for SHA-256 proving.
AI.conclusion: Flock demonstrates that hash-based SNARKs with optimized lincheck/zerocheck protocols can achieve near-native-throughput proving for batched hash computations, dramatically narrowing the gap between native execution and ZK-proving overhead for this critical workload class.

title: RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation
summary: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

AI.tldr: RLPF introduces a staged reinforcement learning reward that orders failed programs by execution progress and ranks correct programs by relative runtime improvement, fine-tuning Qwen3-32B to significantly boost both correctness (11.1%→54.6%) and efficiency (8.1%→38.6%) on PerfCodeBench.
AI.motivation: Existing code models are trained primarily for correctness via execution feedback, ignoring runtime performance. Two correct programs can pass the same tests yet differ vastly in efficiency. The authors argue that code agents should be trained to prefer faster correct implementations, treating efficiency as a training objective rather than merely an evaluation metric.
AI.method: RLPF (Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback) structures execution outcomes into a staged composite reward: (1) for failed programs, ordering is based on execution progress (e.g., compilation success, partial test passes); (2) for correct programs, ranking uses relative improvement from a baseline toward an expert reference runtime. This provides meaningful gradients both before and after correctness is achieved, unlike naive runtime rewards that are fragile and task-dependent. The method is applied to fine-tune Qwen3-32B on PerfCodeBench.
AI.result: Fine-tuning with RLPF raises the rate of correct-and-runnable solutions from 11.1% to 54.6% and relative efficiency from 8.1% to 38.6%. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems and shows modest transfer of optimization behavior to EffiBench-X. Ablations reveal that model-generated references provide weaker but still useful supervision, and the full composite reward outperforms correctness-only and runtime-only baselines in reliability.
AI.conclusion: Code agents can be trained to not only pass tests but also optimize the programs they write. RLPF demonstrates that carefully structuring runtime feedback into a staged reward — with progress-based ranking before correctness and efficiency-based ranking after — enables effective reinforcement learning for both correctness and performance.

title: HSS-Synth: Humanities and Social Sciences Data Synthesis for LLMs
summary: High-quality, diverse data are vital for large language models (LLMs) but remain scarce and costly. Data synthesis is a viable alternative and succeeds on closed tasks, yet the humanities and social sciences (HSS) are overlooked, and their open-ended nature makes synthesis challenging. Moving beyond prior capability-centric, fragmented attempts, we adopt a subject-centric paradigm, define the first HSS domain system covering 14 mainstream fields, and introduce HSS-Synth, the first data synthesis pipeline for HSS. HSS-Synth comprises: (1) constructing seed documents from web corpora via multi-step filtering and text refinement evaluated by a judge; (2) specifying "requirements + persona" to backtranslate seed documents into diverse yet faithful instructions with a strict Q&A alignment check; and (3) breaking LLM response limits via teacher-forced Answering that feeds seed documents during response generation to anchor semantics, reduce hallucinations, and preserve tone and integrity. HSS-Synth yields 237k high-quality, diverse instruction-tuning samples that outperform 14 leading baselines on 16 benchmarks. The fine-tuned Qwen3-8B-Base sets a new SOTA and approaches the official Qwen3-8B, improving both human preference and knowledge capabilities without performance seesaws. Extensive experiments demonstrate HSS-Synth's robustness and transferability. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/pengr/HSS-Synth.

AI.tldr: HSS-Synth introduces a subject-centric data synthesis pipeline for humanities and social sciences, producing 237k high-quality instruction-tuning samples that set new SOTA on 16 benchmarks when fine-tuning Qwen3-8B-Base.
AI.motivation: High-quality, diverse data for LLM training is scarce and expensive. While data synthesis works for closed tasks, the open-ended nature of humanities and social sciences (HSS) poses unique challenges that prior capability-centric, fragmented approaches fail to address. A dedicated HSS synthesis pipeline is lacking.
AI.method: HSS-Synth proposes a three-stage subject-centric pipeline: (1) Seed Document Construction — multi-step filtering and text refinement of web corpora, evaluated by a judge model; (2) Instruction Backtranslation — using "requirements + persona" specifications to convert seed documents into diverse, faithful instructions with strict Q&A alignment checks; (3) Teacher-Forced Answering — feeding seed documents during response generation to anchor semantics, reduce hallucinations, and preserve tone and integrity, overcoming LLM response length limitations. The pipeline covers 14 mainstream HSS fields within a newly defined domain system.
AI.result: HSS-Synth generates 237k instruction-tuning samples that outperform 14 leading baselines across 16 benchmarks. Fine-tuned Qwen3-8B-Base achieves new SOTA, approaching the official Qwen3-8B, and improves both human preference and knowledge capabilities without performance seesaws. Robustness and transferability are demonstrated through extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: A subject-centric synthesis paradigm effectively addresses the open-ended nature of HSS data generation. HSS-Synth provides a scalable, high-quality solution for enriching LLM training data in humanities and social sciences, with strong empirical validation and publicly available code.

title: PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction
summary: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

AI.tldr: This paper presents PIE-Abducer and PIE-APT, a unified framework for reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs using Description Logic. It addresses incomplete knowledge via incremental direct-derivation abduction (avoiding Minimal Hitting Set enumeration) and employs a Generate-and-Test architecture combining backward-chaining A* search with abduction and forward-chaining validation. Evaluation on four OWL benchmarks demonstrates qualitative and quantitative superiority over classical planners and MHS-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing action formalisms for Dynamic Knowledge Graphs suffer from decidability issues, the Ramification Problem, and the prohibitive combinatorial search required by structural abduction (specifically Minimal Hitting Set enumeration) for handling incomplete knowledge in open-world environments. The authors aim to provide a unified, decidable framework that natively operates on expressive Description Logics without external modal operators.
AI.method: The framework comprises two modules: (1) PIE-Abducer, an incremental direct-derivation abduction mechanism that injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences, bypassing MHS enumeration; (2) PIE-APT, which uses a recursive Generate-and-Test architecture interleaving backward-chaining A* search with PIE-Abducer (up to a bounded causal depth) and validates plans via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. State transitions are modeled as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories along a linear timeline, with actions represented natively in OWL.
AI.result: Evaluation on four OWL benchmarks—testing parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting—shows qualitative superiority over classical planners. Quantitatively, the direct-derivation abduction approach outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.
AI.conclusion: The unified PIE framework successfully integrates incremental direct-derivation abduction with abductive temporal planning in expressive Description Logics, preserving decidability while efficiently handling incomplete knowledge. The direct-derivation approach proves both qualitatively and quantitatively superior to classical planning methods and traditional MHS-based abduction.

title: Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents
summary: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

AI.tldr: Language agents exhibit a systematic "Reasoning Backroom" gap: what they say they used (attributed skill use) diverges from what actually changed their decisions (causal reliance). Intervention-based evaluation with BACKTRACE/BACKROOMBench reveals pervasive provenance failures — silent uptake, performative use, and phantom attributions — across models, domains, and multi-agent settings.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluators infer skill use from visible reasoning traces or agent self-attribution, which capture apparent use rather than actual causal influence. The authors hypothesize a systematic gap — the "Reasoning Backroom" — between stated skill use and intervention-measured impact, representing a fundamental AI provenance problem that cannot be resolved through observation alone.
AI.method: BACKTRACE framework: pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual. It intervenes on five dimensions (skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment) and elicits attribution only after answer commitment. Instantiated as BACKROOMBench spanning controlled logic, competition mathematics, single/multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Employs observational detectors (direct claims, text mentions, trace similarity, LLM judge) as baselines against causal measurement.
AI.result: Pervasive provenance failure demonstrated: stated skill use remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity. Stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. No observational detector reliably identifies causally skill-dependent decisions. In multi-agent systems, skill influence survives communication after source loss, while no-skill teams still name non-existent skills and sources.
AI.conclusion: The Reasoning Backroom constitutes a general AI provenance problem requiring intervention-based audit. Observational methods are insufficient for determining whether agents actually rely on skills versus merely appearing to use them.

title: PROGRESS: Property-Guided Regression Search for Semantic Falsification
summary:
Search-based regression-test generation effectively explores complex program structures, yielding high structural coverage, but its oracles are derived from the system under test: faults already present are recorded as expected behavior rather than exposed. Property-based testing offers independent semantic oracles, but depends on high-quality properties and gives little guidance for reaching deep states or satisfying selective preconditions.
  We present PROGRESS (PROperty-Guided REgression Search for Semantic Falsification), integrating intent-driven properties into coverage-guided, search-based evolutionary test generation to reach deep program states and detect violations of intended behavior. PROGRESS (1) extracts intent-bearing code context and uses a language-model pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while limiting implementation leakage; (2) extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with a search objective and property-aware fitness function per property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions; and (3) binds property parameters and uses jqwik-provided generators to connect quantified inputs to evolving test sequences, steering generation toward coverage and bug-detection goals.
  We evaluate PROGRESS on 25 large-scale Java systems against regression-test generation, standalone property-based testing, and context ablations. PROGRESS detects 328/562 current-version bugs (58%) versus none for regression-test generation, and satisfies all preconditions for 70/150 hard-to-reach properties versus 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablations show documentation and caller/callee context are key to generating valid executable properties. PROGRESS preserves structural exploration while exposing faults missed by regression-derived assertions; we release a comprehensive artifact package.

AI.tldr: PROGRESS combines property-based testing with search-based regression test generation. It uses LLMs to generate executable jqwik properties from code context, then extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA with property-aware fitness functions to steer test generation toward satisfying preconditions and detecting property violations. It finds 58% of current-version bugs vs. 0% for pure regression testing.
AI.motivation: Two complementary testing paradigms have opposite weaknesses: search-based regression test generation (e.g., EvoSuite) achieves high structural coverage but suffers from the oracle problem—faults already present are silently encoded as expected behavior. Property-based testing provides independent semantic oracles but struggles to reach deep program states and satisfy complex preconditions. The authors aim to unify both paradigms to leverage their strengths while mitigating their weaknesses.
AI.method: PROGRESS operates in three stages: (1) It extracts intent-bearing code context (Javadoc, method signatures, caller/callee relationships) and uses an LLM pipeline to generate executable jqwik properties while minimizing implementation leakage. (2) It extends EvoSuite's DynaMOSA algorithm with a new search objective and property-aware fitness function for each property, rewarding progress through preconditions and prioritizing falsifying executions. (3) It binds property parameters using jqwik-provided generators, connecting quantified inputs to evolving test sequences so that generation is steered toward both coverage and bug-detection goals.
AI.result: On 25 large-scale Java systems, PROGRESS detected 328 out of 562 current-version bugs (58%), compared to zero for regression-test generation alone. It satisfied all preconditions for 70 out of 150 hard-to-reach properties versus only 18 for standalone jqwik. Ablation studies revealed that documentation and caller/callee context are critical for generating valid executable properties.
AI.conclusion: PROGRESS successfully integrates property-based oracles into search-based test generation, preserving structural exploration while exposing faults that regression-derived assertions miss. The approach demonstrates that intent-driven properties can effectively guide evolutionary search toward both deep coverage and semantic bug detection.

title: Restoring Collaborative Signals in Semantic-ID Generative Recommendation via Personalized Natural Language
summary: Making LLM-based generative recommendation models stronger and more personalized through natural language and explicit reasoning is a widely anticipated yet still unsolved goal. Such models cast recommendation as autoregressively generating an item's semantic-ID (SID), a short tuple of discrete codes, so that recommending well reduces to emitting the right SID. In this setting the model verbalizes its knowledge poorly, and text and SID tokens live in misaligned embedding spaces. Deep reasoning therefore rarely turns into a correct SID, and enabling explicit "thinking" often gives no gain or even hurts. The deeper cause is that a compact SID cannot hold content and collaborative signal at once: the two compete, and collaboration loses. Because a mis-predicted SID is a wrong recommendation, this caps accuracy directly. Costly multi-round training barely helps, and few methods try to supply the missing signal at inference time. What is missing is a reliable channel that carries collaborative signal into SID generation. We therefore propose a framework, guided by personalized natural language, that adds hierarchical collaborative cues as the model generates, without altering the backbone or retraining the SIDs. Rather than mapping language onto SIDs directly, it uses language to attach analyzable links between collaborative patterns and their audiences, restoring the collaborative signal that SIDs miss. The result is consistent gains in recommendation accuracy, grounding generation in collaborative structure at inference time rather than relying on explicit reasoning or retraining.

AI.tldr: LLM-based generative recommenders using semantic IDs (SIDs) suffer from misaligned embedding spaces where collaborative signals are lost, making explicit reasoning ineffective. The authors propose an inference-time framework that uses personalized natural language to inject hierarchical collaborative cues into SID generation, restoring the missing collaborative signal without retraining, yielding consistent accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: LLM-based generative recommendation models cast recommendation as autoregressive SID generation, but compact SIDs cannot simultaneously encode both content and collaborative signals—collaboration loses out. This causes poor verbalization of knowledge, misaligned text/SID embedding spaces, and explicit reasoning that rarely translates into correct SIDs. Multi-round training is costly and inadequate, and few methods address the missing collaborative signal at inference time.
AI.method: The proposed framework operates at inference time without altering the backbone model or retraining SIDs. It uses personalized natural language to attach analyzable links between collaborative patterns and their target audiences, injecting hierarchical collaborative cues as the model generates. Rather than directly mapping language onto SIDs, it channels collaborative signal through language-based guidance, effectively restoring what the SID representation inherently lacks.
AI.result: Consistent gains in recommendation accuracy, with generation grounded in collaborative structure at inference time, outperforming approaches that rely solely on explicit reasoning or retraining.
AI.conclusion: SIDs' inherent limitation—the competition between content and collaborative signals—is a fundamental bottleneck for LLM-based generative recommenders. The proposed inference-time, language-guided framework effectively resolves this by supplying missing collaborative cues without architectural changes, demonstrating that reliable collaborative signal injection during generation is key to unlocking stronger, more personalized recommendations.

title: A Mathematical Framework for Reading the Autopsias' Meta - Compositional System
summary: Background. New forms of music writing using computers have arisen in the past 20 years. Most of them use the capacities of digital manipulation of data like animation, algorithmic processing, cinematic view, and much more. These scores use dynamic musicography, and all of them share a problem. They have readability problems. We will argue that this problem can be addressed by mathematical tools. Aims. Take the Autopsias [Autopsies] meta-compositional system as a study case for starting the construction of a mathematical framework that can overview the readability for cynetic musicography. The Autopsias system is the process of transforming a musical score dynamically. Methodology. We will start to build a mathematical framework by taking a group of basic topological concepts, and applying them after a bridge between a printed score and a dynamic computational re-appropriation of it has taken place. We will observe the writing and the performing of the several performances of the Autopsias composition, and analyze them from a mathematical perspective, in order to get the ability to start constructing a new set of orthographical tools for the performance of dynamic musicography. Main Contribution. The performances of Autopsias show that mathematics, as with pitch-class sets, can be helpful for understanding music information, as well as its performance. Also show the necessity of augmenting the set of orthographic rules, in order to improve the dialog between composers and performers.

AI.tldr: Dynamic (cynetic) musicographic scores suffer from readability issues; this paper proposes using topological mathematical tools to analyze the Autopsias meta-compositional system and develop new orthographic conventions for dynamic score performance.
AI.motivation: New digital music writing forms using animation, algorithms, and cinematic views produce dynamic scores ("cynetic musicography") that share a common readability problem, hindering effective communication between composers and performers.
AI.method: The authors use the Autopsias meta-compositional system as a case study, building a mathematical framework with basic topological concepts. They bridge printed scores to dynamic computational re-appropriations, observe multiple performances, and analyze them mathematically to derive new orthographic tools.
AI.result: Performances of Autopsias demonstrate that mathematics (analogous to pitch-class set theory) can aid in understanding both musical information and its performance, while also revealing the need for expanded orthographic rules.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical frameworks, particularly topological approaches, show promise for addressing readability in dynamic musicography, and augmenting orthographic rule sets is necessary to improve composer-performer dialogue.

title: Send and Pretend: Exploiting Transcript Consistency Issues in End-to-End Encrypted Group Chats
comment: Accepted to USENIX Security 2026; Artifacts available at https://github.com/sbaresearch/transcript-consistency
summary: End-to-end encrypted (E2EE) messaging apps are widely praised for their security and thus also used for sensitive coordination in group chats (e.g., by political decision makers). After Threema and WhatsApp, also Signal and iMessage have recently introduced polls to aid agreement processes in groups. This implicitly sets the expectation that all participants see the same outcome and thus have the same view of the conversation. This property is commonly referred to as transcript consistency (TC). In this work, we demonstrate that today's major E2EE messengers do not guarantee any form of TC for group chats, allowing a malicious group member to selectively omit, reorder, or present altered content to different recipients without triggering warnings in their user interface. We systematically investigate the extent of the problem under a malicious-participant threat model that targets the integrity of the shared transcript, or inconsistent delivery across a user's linked devices. We identify multiple equivocation vectors that range from protocol fallback paths to deliberate use of pairwise delivery channels within groups. We demonstrate concrete exploitation scenarios such as social engineering, evading moderation, and, in particular, rigging polls. Beyond these cross-service design issues, we also uncover implementation-specific behaviors with privacy implications (e.g., device OS fingerprinting). Finally, we contextualize our findings within prior transcript-consistency research and outline practical low-overhead mitigations and UI signaling strategies that can be integrated into state-of-the-art E2EE group protocols.

AI.tldr: Major E2EE messengers (Signal, WhatsApp, Threema, iMessage) fail to guarantee transcript consistency in group chats, enabling malicious participants to manipulate what different members see — including rigging polls — without triggering warnings.
AI.motivation: E2EE messaging apps increasingly support group polls for decision-making (even among political actors), creating an implicit expectation that all participants see identical results. However, the actual transcript consistency guarantees in these protocols remain unexamined under a malicious-participant threat model.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze major E2EE messengers under a malicious-participant threat model targeting transcript integrity and multi-device delivery consistency. They identify equivocation vectors including protocol fallback paths and pairwise delivery channels, then construct concrete exploitation scenarios and uncover implementation-specific privacy leaks like device OS fingerprinting.
AI.result: All examined messengers lack transcript consistency guarantees. Attackers can selectively omit, reorder, or alter content per recipient. Concrete exploits include poll rigging, social engineering, and moderator evasion. Additional privacy issues such as OS fingerprinting via implementation quirks were also discovered.
AI.conclusion: The paper highlights a systemic gap in E2EE group protocol design and proposes practical, low-overhead mitigations and UI signaling strategies that can be integrated into existing protocols to enforce transcript consistency.

title: SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training
summary: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

AI.tldr: SDO is a plug-and-play data organization framework that uses frozen external embeddings and an exposure-driven feedback mechanism to dynamically organize mini-batch composition (via KNN-based locality-aware batching) and sample exposure (via exposure-balanced scheduling), accelerating LLM post-training convergence across SFT, DPO, and GRPO.
AI.motivation: Existing post-training efficiency methods treat data organization as a static preprocessing step using fixed embedding-based partitions, ignoring that sample optimization needs evolve during training. This leads to redundant updates for well-optimized samples and under-optimization of others, wasting compute.
AI.method: SDO has two components: (1) Locality-aware batching — within each epoch, mini-batches are formed via KNN neighborhood traversal on frozen external embeddings to ensure coherent gradient signals. (2) Exposure-balanced scheduling — across epochs, per-sample participation is tracked, and over-exposed samples have their sampling probability reduced to maintain long-term coverage. The method is plug-and-play and requires no model warm-up overhead.
AI.result: SDO accelerates convergence across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, with the largest gains in the early-to-mid training phase. It produces more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding any training samples.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, structure-aware data organization with exposure feedback significantly improves post-training efficiency for LLMs, outperforming static preprocessing approaches by adapting mini-batch composition and sample exposure to the evolving optimization landscape.

title: Same Facts, Different Diagnosis: Measuring and Mitigating Narrative Anchoring in Clinical Language Models
summary: Large language models used for clinical diagnostic reasoning are sensitive to sociolinguistic register, not just clinical content. We term this failure mode Narrative Anchoring: identical clinical facts expressed in different registers cause diagnostic outputs to diverge. Unlike prior demographic-bias work, which manipulates explicit identity tokens such as race or income, our benchmark isolates register as the sole channel of variation, with no demographic marker present in any form. We construct a dataset of 1,000 USMLE clinical vignettes, each rewritten into three sociolinguistically distinct personas under an independently audited fact-preservation guarantee, verified by a separate model that never sees the generation prompt. Across seven language models spanning three architecture families and scales, Narrative Anchoring is statistically significant under direct prompting in every model tested, with a Narrative Anchoring Gap of 0.064 to 0.151. Chain-of-thought reasoning and explicit debiasing instructions reduce the bias only partially, and their apparent gains are frequently confounded by accuracy collapse. We introduce NarrativeShield, a three-agent pipeline that structurally extracts and verifies clinical facts before diagnostic reasoning begins, reducing the Narrative Anchoring Gap to near-zero ($-0.004$ to $0.037$) and achieving the lowest rate of severely unstable decisions (DSS $<$ 0.8) of any method across all models, at a modest and mechanistically expected accuracy cost for most models. A stress test using a non-instruction-tuned base model shows that executing a debiasing intervention at all is gated by zero-shot instruction-following ability, not prompt content alone. We release our dataset, human-validated for fact preservation, as a standalone resource for studying register-based clinical bias.

AI.tldr: Large language models exhibit "Narrative Anchoring" — diagnostic outputs that diverge based on sociolinguistic register even when clinical facts are identical and no demographic markers are present. The authors introduce a fact-preserved benchmark of 1,000 USMLE vignettes across three registers, demonstrate the bias across seven models, and propose NarrativeShield, a three-agent pipeline that reduces the bias to near-zero.
AI.motivation: Prior work on bias in clinical LLMs has focused on explicit demographic markers (race, income, gender). This paper identifies a subtler failure mode — sociolinguistic register alone, independent of any identity tokens, causes diagnostic reasoning to shift. The motivation is to isolate, quantify, and mitigate this understudied channel of clinical bias.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of 1,000 USMLE vignettes, each rewritten into three sociolinguistically distinct "personas" under a fact-preservation guarantee independently audited by a separate verification model. Seven LLMs spanning three architectures are evaluated under direct prompting, chain-of-thought, and debiasing instructions. The proposed mitigation, NarrativeShield, is a three-agent pipeline: a FactExtractor structurally extracts clinical facts, a FactVerifier checks their fidelity against the original, and a Diagnostician reasons solely from verified facts — decoupling register from content before reasoning.
AI.result: Narrative Anchoring is statistically significant under direct prompting in every model tested, with a Narrative Anchoring Gap of 0.064–0.151. Chain-of-thought and debiasing instructions reduce bias only partially and often confound gains with accuracy collapse. NarrativeShield reduces the gap to near-zero (−0.004 to 0.037), achieves the lowest rate of severely unstable decisions (DSS < 0.8), with a modest accuracy cost. A stress test on a base (non-instruction-tuned) model shows that zero-shot instruction-following ability gates any debiasing intervention.
AI.conclusion: Sociolinguistic register is an independent and pervasive source of clinical reasoning bias in LLMs, distinct from demographic bias. Fact-structural disentanglement via NarrativeShield effectively mitigates this bias, though at a modest accuracy trade-off. The work underscores that debiasing methods contingent on instruction-following will fail on base models, and calls for register-aware evaluation in clinical AI.

title: PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments
summary: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

AI.tldr: PAUSE is a benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in realistic, stateful, service-integrated environments that require reasoning over persistent user state, authorization constraints, and multi-turn interactions. Even top proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion, revealing systematic failure patterns in stateful reasoning and configuration awareness.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for personal AI assistants fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, failing to capture the real-world challenges of persistent user state reasoning, user-specific configurations, permission constraints, and long-horizon interactions across multiple services. There is a need for a realistic, user-centric evaluation framework.
AI.method: The authors introduce PAUSE, a benchmark featuring stateful, service-integrated environments where agents must coordinate across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state and authorization constraints. It incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation and adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework: semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics for open-ended service management tasks, and deterministic state-based verification for constraint-intensive tasks. A user-centric synthesis pipeline enables scalable generation of coherent environments and annotated tasks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness. The benchmark reveals consistent and interpretable failure patterns across models.
AI.conclusion: PAUSE provides a principled, reproducible, and extensible framework for evaluating personal AI assistants under realistic service conditions, highlighting significant room for improvement in stateful reasoning and user-configuration awareness. The synthesis pipeline supports ongoing benchmark expansion and future research.

title: Belief Coevolution in a Social Network of Generalist and Specialist Large Language Models
comment: 33 pages (14 pages of main text), 7 figures, 14 tables
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments. However, the processes by which beliefs form and propagate among interacting LLMs remain poorly understood. We introduce CoevolveSim, a framework for studying belief diffusion within networked LLM populations. CoevolveSim allows us to isolate and study three factors: domain specialization, social-role assignment, and social network structure. Within this framework, generalist and specialist LLM agents exchange and revise beliefs. In each round, an LLM agent observes a summary of its neighbors' beliefs before updating its own. We run 1,280 controlled simulations spanning four scenarios, two network structures, and 20 medical-indication statements. We find that persona-style role assignment and network structure reshape individual belief revision but have minimal effect on population-level consensus. In contrast, introducing (finetuned) specialist LLMs more than doubles the shift in consensus and gives rise to consistent asymmetries in exerted influence. We further show that simple persistence-based opinion-dynamics models reproduce collective outcomes in all-generalist LLM populations, whereas heterogeneous LLM populations require population-level belief composition to reproduce consensus and agent identity to predict individual belief transitions. Our results indicate that realistic simulation of belief diffusion in multi-agent LLM systems requires a diverse set of underlying LLMs, not persona prompting alone.

AI.tldr: A framework called CoevolveSim is introduced to study belief diffusion among networked LLMs. Using 1,280 simulations, the study shows that while persona-style role assignment and network structure affect individual belief revision, only introducing finetuned specialist LLMs significantly shifts population-level consensus. Persistence-based models capture all-generalist populations, but heterogeneous populations require modeling belief composition and agent identity.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, yet the mechanisms of belief formation and propagation among interacting LLMs are poorly understood. The authors aim to systematically isolate factors driving belief diffusion in LLM populations.
AI.method: The authors propose CoevolveSim, a simulation framework where LLM agents exchange and revise beliefs over multiple rounds. Agents observe neighbor summaries before updating. The study runs 1,280 controlled simulations across four scenarios (varying domain specialization, social-role assignment, and network structure), two network topologies, and 20 medical-indication statements. Both generalist and specialist (finetuned) LLMs are used. Persistence-based opinion-dynamics models are tested for their ability to reproduce collective outcomes and individual belief transitions.
AI.result: Persona-style role assignment and network structure reshape individual belief revision but barely affect population-level consensus. Introducing finetuned specialist LLMs more than doubles the shift in consensus and produces consistent asymmetries in exerted influence. Simple persistence-based opinion-dynamics models reproduce collective outcomes in all-generalist populations. However, heterogeneous LLM populations require population-level belief composition to reproduce consensus and agent identity to predict individual belief transitions.
AI.conclusion: Realistic simulation of belief diffusion in multi-agent LLM systems requires a diverse set of underlying LLMs (e.g., finetuned specialists), not merely persona prompting alone. Heterogeneity in model capabilities fundamentally alters belief dynamics in ways that homogeneous prompting strategies cannot replicate.

title: From Backlog Items to Security Guidance: Towards Continuous Security Compliance
comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026), Industry Showcase track
summary: Continuous software engineering in regulated domains requires engineering teams to address security throughout the development lifecycle. Yet making security requirements explicit in backlog items is still problematic. Engineers must instead infer security relevance of backlog items from brief, free-form descriptions and often lack timely guidance on applicable requirements. We present an NLP-based backlog enrichment system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to relevant security requirements. The approach combines a security-relevance classifier with a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline over security requirements documents. The approach was developed and evaluated in the context of a large enterprise in highly regulated domains. We present three contributions. First, we release a dataset of 288 backlog items labeled for security relevance by nine security practitioners, with substantial agreement (Fleiss' $κ=0.787$). Second, a recall-oriented classifier achieving $F2=0.774$ in-distribution and mean zero-shot G-measure $\approx 0.65$ across five established benchmarks, matching or outperforming most published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. Third, we preliminarily evaluated a four-stage security requirements document-grounded RAG pipeline with two practitioners on industrial backlogs using company-internal security policies and CIS Benchmarks. Of the retrieved 24 clauses, 12 were rated at least 4/5 for relevance. Our findings provide first indicators that NLP-based product backlog enrichment can support engineers in identifying security requirements early in the development process. With this work we aim to facilitate continuous security compliance through proactive introduction of security requirements in continuous software engineering.

AI.tldr: An NLP system that detects security-relevant backlog items and links them to applicable security requirements using a classifier and a RAG pipeline, evaluated with industrial data and practitioners, showing promising results for early security compliance in regulated software engineering.
AI.motivation: In regulated software domains, engineering teams struggle to explicitly identify security requirements in backlog items. Descriptions are brief and free-form, and practitioners lack timely, context-specific guidance on which security requirements apply to a given backlog item.
AI.method: A two-part NLP system: (1) a recall-oriented security-relevance classifier trained to detect whether a backlog item has security implications; (2) a four-stage retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline grounded in security requirements documents (company-internal policies, CIS Benchmarks) that retrieves and presents relevant security clauses. Evaluation uses a newly released labeled dataset of 288 backlog items (annotated by 9 practitioners, Fleiss' κ=0.787) and five established benchmarks.
AI.result: The classifier achieves F2=0.774 in-distribution and a mean zero-shot G-measure of ~0.65 across five benchmarks, matching or surpassing published classical-ML and open-source GPT baselines. In a preliminary RAG evaluation with two practitioners on industrial backlogs, 12 of 24 retrieved security clauses were rated ≥4/5 for relevance.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that NLP-based backlog enrichment can help engineers identify security requirements early in development, supporting proactive continuous security compliance in regulated domains.

title: Measuring Alignment With Reader Highlights Net of Position and Length
comment: 15 pages, 7 tables. Analysis code and de-identified artifacts included as ancillary files; five of six scripts reproduce the paper's numbers from the shipped artifacts alone. Reports claims from our own prior work that this corpus does not reproduce, and lists twelve claims withdrawn during internal adversarial review in Appendix A
summary: Context compression discards most of a document before a language model reads it, and is normally evaluated by downstream task accuracy - which makes another model the judge of what mattered. Naturalistic social highlighting offers a non-circular reference: many people independently marking passages on the same page. But the obvious metric, the fraction of crowd-marked sentences a compressor keeps, is confounded twice: crowd marks are front-loaded and crowd-marked sentences are longer, so any method favouring early or long sentences scores well regardless of readers. We remove both by matching each marked sentence against unmarked sentences of the same document at equal relative depth and equal within-document length rank, and we calibrate every estimator on synthetic nulls built from position and length alone - a step that matters, since depth-only stratification returns a false positive on 20-36% of nulls containing no effect. On 120 web documents (at least 12 independent readers each), a language-model importance ranking keeps 38.4% of crowd-marked sentences against 19.9% of their matched neighbours: an enrichment of +0.196 [+0.148, +0.239], at p = 0.0005 under an exact randomization test that assumes nothing about clustering, and replicated cross-vendor. Naive truncation, whose keep rule is position, correctly falls to +0.003. To give the number a scale: scored identically, on the same budget, against a crowd label recomputed to exclude them, a single human reader reaches +0.182 - indistinguishable from GPT-5.4 (+0.002 [-0.081, +0.088]) and below Claude Opus 5. Classical methods are not null - Luhn's 1958 heuristic reaches +0.088 - so reader selection is partly recoverable by counting words; conditioning additionally on lexical centrality removes only 0.010, so the agreement is not centrality. We also report that a claim in our own prior work does not reproduce on this corpus.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates context compression methods using crowd-sourced social highlights as a non-circular ground truth, introduces a rigorous methodology to control for position and length confounds (matching and synthetic null calibration), and finds that LM-based importance ranking significantly enriches for crowd-marked sentences, performing comparably to a single human reader, while naive truncation and classical heuristics perform worse.
AI.motivation: Context compression is typically evaluated by downstream task accuracy, which circularly uses another model as judge. The authors leverage naturalistic social highlighting — independent reader annotations — as an external, non-circular reference. However, the naive metric (fraction of marked sentences kept) is confounded by position bias (marks cluster early) and length bias (marked sentences are longer). The work aims to develop de-confounded evaluation methodology for compression methods.
AI.method: The authors construct a matched-pair design: each crowd-marked sentence is paired with unmarked sentences from the same document matched on relative depth (position) and within-document length rank. They calibrate estimators using synthetic nulls built from position and length alone. Evaluation uses 120 web documents with ≥12 independent readers each. An exact randomization test (assumption-free about clustering) assesses statistical significance. Methods tested include LM importance ranking, naive truncation, Luhn's 1958 heuristic, and lexical centrality, benchmarked against single human readers and different LM vendors.
AI.result: LM importance ranking retains 38.4% of crowd-marked sentences vs. 19.9% of matched neighbors (+0.196 enrichment, CI [+0.148, +0.239], p=0.0005). Naive truncation yields only +0.003. A single human reader scores +0.182 — indistinguishable from GPT-5.4 (+0.002 difference) and below Claude Opus 5. Luhn's 1958 heuristic reaches +0.088, showing partial recoverability via word counting. Lexical centrality conditioning removes only 0.010, indicating agreement is not centrality-driven. A prior claim by the authors fails to reproduce on this corpus. Depth-only stratification produces false positives on 20-36% of nulls, validating the need for length matching.
AI.conclusion: LM-based importance ranking meaningfully captures reader-relevant content beyond position and length heuristics. Proper calibration against position-length nulls is essential — depth-only stratification inflates false positives. The agreement between LM ranking and crowd highlights is not explained by lexical centrality, and the method rivals single-human performance, establishing social highlighting as a viable non-circular evaluation framework for context compression.

title: Student Perceptions and Preferences Regarding AI-Generated Instructional Videos in Computing Education
summary: Students differ in how they prefer to engage with learning resources, with some favoring textual materials and others visual or video-based content. Recent advances in generative AI have led CS education research to focus on text-based AI tools for developing learning resources. However, advances in AI video models and the rapid proliferation of AI video generation tools have made it possible for instructors to create high-quality personalized educational videos efficiently and cost-effectively. Understanding students' perceptions of AI-generated videos is thus critical for helping CS instructors know when and how to use them purposefully. To address this gap, we conducted a descriptive post-test survey study in which 170 computing students at two U.S. institutions watched three 3-minute AI videos on the Markdown markup language created with Knowlify. Students then completed a survey about their perceptions of the Markdown videos and their broader views on the use of AI-generated videos in education. Students rated the Markdown videos as high-quality, accurate, and usable, with nearly half unable to determine whether the videos were AI-generated. At the same time, students expressed limited comfort with the widespread adoption of AI videos in the classroom. They preferred AI videos for simple, supplemental, and visual use cases, while expressing concerns about lower-quality or inaccurate content, reduced instructor interaction, and diminished educational value.

AI.tldr: A survey of 170 computing students found they rated AI-generated educational videos as high-quality and accurate, with nearly half unable to identify them as AI-generated. However, students expressed limited comfort with widespread classroom adoption, preferring AI videos for simple, supplemental, visual content while voicing concerns about inaccuracy and reduced instructor interaction.
AI.motivation: Prior CS education research on generative AI has focused on text-based tools, neglecting the emerging capabilities of AI video generation. With AI video models now enabling efficient, cost-effective creation of personalized educational videos, there is a critical need to understand student perceptions to guide instructors on when and how to deploy such resources purposefully.
AI.method: The authors conducted a descriptive post-test survey study with 170 computing students at two U.S. institutions. Participants watched three 3-minute AI-generated videos on the Markdown markup language (created with Knowlify) and subsequently completed a survey assessing their perceptions of the videos and their broader attitudes toward AI-generated educational content.
AI.result: Students rated the AI-generated Markdown videos as high-quality, accurate, and usable. Nearly half could not determine the videos were AI-generated. However, students expressed limited comfort with widespread classroom adoption, favoring AI videos only for simple, supplemental, and visually-oriented use cases. Concerns centered on potential for lower-quality/inaccurate content, diminished instructor interaction, and reduced educational value.
AI.conclusion: AI-generated educational videos hold promise as perceived by students, but their adoption should be strategic and limited to contexts where they complement rather than replace instructor-led instruction. Instructors should be mindful of student concerns regarding accuracy, interaction, and educational depth when integrating AI video content.

title: ThreatForest: Multi-Agent Attack Tree Generation with Pluggable TTP Framework Mapping
summary: Threat modeling is essential for secure software development, yet manual analysis of cloud-native architectures is slow and demands scarce security expertise. We present ThreatForest, a multi-agent system that generates structured attack trees from source code repositories, maps attack steps to adversary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) from a pluggable set of frameworks (MITRE ATT&CK, CAPEC, and cloud-specific threat matrices), and synthesizes actionable mitigations. ThreatForest decomposes threat modeling into a multi-stage agent pipeline -- repository analysis, context refinement, threat generation, parallel attack-tree construction with TTP mapping and mitigation synthesis, and report generation -- orchestrated as a directed graph with deterministic verification gates, bounded retries, and three human-in-the-loop validation points. A domain-specific sentence-transformer maps each attack step to candidate techniques by cosine similarity; we show empirically that this embedding stage, not the surrounding pipeline, is the dominant accuracy bottleneck. We evaluate ThreatForest across seven application domains on a sixteen-dimension rubric, scored by a panel of independent LLM raters with an adversarial verification pass and expert review. Panel-measured quality reaches 0.63-0.68 (on a 0-1 scale) for threat statements, attack trees, and mitigations, but only 0.29 for embedding-only TTP mapping -- a gap stable across all seven domains that isolates the binding constraint. A controlled single-call baseline on the same model more than doubles mapping defensibility, pinning the limitation on the embedding encoder rather than the multi-agent design. To our knowledge, ThreatForest is the first end-to-end system that turns a code repository into TTP-mapped attack trees with evidence-based mitigations across adversary frameworks, with a reusable framework for benchmarking such systems.

AI.tldr: ThreatForest is a multi-agent system that automatically generates TTP-mapped attack trees with mitigations from code repositories. Evaluated across seven domains, it achieves 0.63–0.68 quality scores for threats, trees, and mitigations, but only 0.29 for embedding-based TTP mapping, identifying the sentence-transformer encoder—not the multi-agent pipeline—as the primary accuracy bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Manual threat modeling for cloud-native architectures is slow and requires scarce security expertise. Existing approaches lack end-to-end automation that converts source code into structured, framework-mapped attack trees with actionable mitigations.
AI.method: A multi-agent pipeline: (1) repository analysis, (2) context refinement, (3) threat generation, (4) parallel attack-tree construction with TTP mapping via a domain-specific sentence-transformer using cosine similarity, plus mitigation synthesis, (5) report generation. Orchestrated as a directed graph with deterministic verification gates, bounded retries, and three human-in-the-loop validation points. A controlled single-call baseline ablates the multi-agent design.
AI.result: Panel-measured quality (0–1 scale): threat statements, attack trees, mitigations score 0.63–0.68; embedding-only TTP mapping scores 0.29. The gap is stable across all seven domains. A single-call baseline more than doubles mapping defensibility, isolating the embedding encoder as the binding constraint.
AI.conclusion: ThreatForest is the first end-to-end system turning code repositories into TTP-mapped attack trees with evidence-based mitigations across frameworks. The primary accuracy bottleneck is the embedding-based TTP mapping stage, not the multi-agent architecture, providing a clear target for future improvement.

title: Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision
summary: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

AI.tldr: BridgeMIL is a two-stage framework for EEG-based disease diagnosis that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision, avoiding the problematic assumption that all EEG segments inherit equally reliable diagnostic labels. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple datasets and backbones.
AI.motivation: Standard EEG diagnosis pipelines segment recordings into short instances and inherit the subject's label for every instance, incorrectly assuming all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. While Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) addresses this by treating subjects as bags, end-to-end MIL suffers from limited subject-level supervision due to far fewer subjects than instances. BridgeMIL is proposed to overcome this tension.
AI.method: BridgeMIL uses two stages: Stage 1 pretrains an encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags, using variance and covariance regularization to prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the pretrained encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject-level predictions, and constrains representation drift via feature retention.
AI.result: BridgeMIL achieved the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone combinations across three EEG disease datasets and five backbone architectures, with an overall mean accuracy of 76.57% — 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Analyses showed substantial variation in inherited-label reliability, greater sensitivity to subject scarcity than instance scarcity, and more structured representation spaces with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved class separation.
AI.conclusion: Aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while leveraging abundant EEG instances — without assigning disease labels to individual instances — is critical for EEG-based diagnosis. BridgeMIL demonstrates that decoupling representation learning from subject-level supervision yields stronger, more structured representations and robust diagnostic performance.

title: AHA-Memes: A Fine-Grained Multimodal Benchmark for Understanding Hate in Arabic Memes
summary: Hateful memes are a growing form of multimodal online harm, where hostile intent is often conveyed through the joint interpretation of images, text, cultural references, and implicit targets. While hateful meme detection has advanced in high-resource languages, Arabic remains underexplored, with existing meme resources focusing mainly on propaganda or coarse harmful-content labels. We introduce AHA-Memes (Arabic HAteful Memes), which is, to our knowledge, the first large-scale Arabic hateful meme benchmark with fine-grained, multi-label annotations. The dataset includes 5K manually annotated memes using a taxonomy that captures hate types, i.e., attack strategies. We further provide ~66K silver-labeled memes to support future studies. We benchmark text-only, image-only, and late-fusion multimodal models, as well as few-shot in-context learning (ICL) and open- and closed-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under zero-shot and fine-tuning settings. Our results establish strong baselines and highlight key challenges in culturally grounded Arabic hateful meme detection. We release the dataset, annotation guidelines, and evaluation scripts to support future research. WARNING: This paper contains examples that may be disturbing to readers.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AHA-Memes, the first large-scale Arabic hateful meme benchmark with 5K manually annotated memes using a fine-grained, multi-label taxonomy capturing hate types and attack strategies. It benchmarks diverse models (text-only, image-only, multimodal fusion, VLMs, ICL) to establish strong baselines and reveals key challenges in culturally grounded Arabic hateful meme detection.
AI.motivation: Arabic remains underexplored in hateful meme detection despite the growing prevalence of multimodal online harm. Existing Arabic meme resources focus mainly on propaganda or coarse harmful-content labels, lacking fine-grained, multi-label hate speech annotations tailored to culturally specific memes.
AI.method: Curated AHA-Memes: 5K manually annotated memes with a fine-grained taxonomy (hate types, attack strategies) plus ~66K silver-labeled memes. Benchmarked text-only, image-only, late-fusion multimodal models, few-shot ICL, and open/closed-weight VLMs in zero-shot and fine-tuning settings.
AI.result: Established strong baselines across model paradigms and identified key challenges in detecting culturally grounded Arabic hateful memes, particularly those requiring joint multimodal understanding and cultural contextualization.
AI.conclusion: Culturally grounded Arabic hateful meme detection remains challenging for current models. The AHA-Memes dataset, annotation guidelines, and evaluation scripts are publicly released to spur further research in this understudied area.

title: SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis
summary: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

AI.tldr: SkillMentor proposes learning blind-spot diagnosis as a distinct agent capability, training a Mentor policy via RL to discover failure modes and curate corrective skills, achieving 44.2% average executor improvement without updating executor weights or using human supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing agent self-evolution research focuses on learning how to act (execution improvement) while neglecting the capability of discovering what the agent does not know (blind-spot diagnosis). Current approaches treat failure discovery as given, rather than as a learnable skill. The authors aim to isolate diagnosis as a standalone capability, excluding executor adaptation and human supervision to force progress purely from diagnostic learning.
AI.method: SkillMentor trains a Mentor policy using reinforcement learning to perform three tasks: (1) generate diagnostic tasks that probe the executor's weaknesses, (2) identify recurrent failure modes from execution traces, and (3) curate discovered failure patterns into reusable corrective skills. Critically, the executor's weights remain frozen and no human-annotated examples are used, isolating diagnosis as the sole source of improvement.
AI.result: SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2% across two benchmarks: AppWorld and BFCLv3 (BFCL = Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard).
AI.conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability that can drive meaningful agent self-evolution independently of executor weight updates or human-curated data. This opens a new dimension for agent improvement beyond execution-focused learning.

title: Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation
summary: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone.
