While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

AI.tldr: Atomic Policy Optimization (APO) is an unsupervised alignment framework for flow-matching models that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. It uses a dual-reward mechanism — a structural mode reward via eigen-decomposition of sample similarities and a thermodynamic stability reward — to self-correct predictions. APO outperforms fully supervised baselines on crystal and antibody structure prediction, achieving state-of-the-art match rates and structural fidelity while improving inference efficiency.
AI.motivation: Flow-matching models like FlowDPO rely on supervised preference learning aligned with ground-truth coordinates, but obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive. This creates a bottleneck in data-scarce regimes, motivating an unsupervised alternative.
AI.method: APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments. It employs a dual-reward mechanism: (1) a structural mode reward that reinforces the policy's dominant latent modes via eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (2) a thermodynamic stability reward. The framework enables self-correction by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups, effectively straightening probability paths for improved inference efficiency.
AI.result: APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines on crystal and antibody structure prediction benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art match rates and structural fidelity. It also significantly improves inference efficiency via straightened probability paths.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching. APO demonstrates that unsupervised alignment via physical rewards is not only viable but can surpass supervised approaches in 3D atomic structure prediction.

title: Can Large Language Models Resolve Real Java Merge Conflicts? An Evaluation with a Calibrated LLM-as-Judge
summary: Merge conflicts are a recurring cost of collaborative software development, and the traditional structured and semi-structured merge tools that address them frequently abstain: when their heuristics do not apply, they leave the conflict unresolved. Large language models (LLMs) can instead produce a candidate resolution for almost any conflict, but measuring whether those resolutions are actually good at scale is hard, because obtaining human desirability judgments for every model output does not scale. We study both problems together on real Java merge conflicts from ConflictBench. We first build an LLM solver as a generate-validate-retry agent that uses only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks) and never sees the developer's answer. We then evaluate its resolutions with a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge implemented as a G-Eval metric and, crucially, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels before use, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. On a meta-evaluation of 292 human-labeled cases, the judge reaches 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall, so every acceptance is trustworthy and every downstream rate is a conservative lower bound. Under this validated judge, LLM solvers match the developer's own resolution on about 55% of true conflicts (conservative floor), and under a coverage-fair comparison the LLMs (55-59%) beat the strongest traditional tool (AutoMerge, 36.7%) by roughly 18-22 points; the edge comes almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy, since the tools abstain on 20-90% of conflicts while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Finally, the LLM judge accepted 4 of the 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check, evidence that structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an LLM-based merge conflict solver using a generate-validate-retry agent, evaluated with a calibrated LLM-as-judge metric and a deterministic structural-validity check. The LLM solver matches developer resolutions on ~55% of true conflicts, beating traditional tools (AutoMerge at 36.7%) by 18–22 points due to superior coverage. The calibrated judge achieves 100% precision at 64.6% recall. A key finding: structural correctness cannot be delegated to an LLM, as the judge accepted 4 of 5 structurally invalid resolutions.
AI.motivation: Merge conflicts are a persistent cost in collaborative development. Traditional structured/semi-structured merge tools frequently abstain when their heuristics fail, leaving conflicts unresolved. LLMs can propose resolutions for nearly any conflict, but evaluating output quality at scale is difficult because obtaining human desirability judgments for every candidate is infeasible. This paper addresses both the resolution and evaluation problems together.
AI.method: The authors build an LLM-based merge conflict solver as a generate-validate-retry agent using only inference-time signals (conflict markers, a Java parser, and duplicate-declaration checks), never seeing the developer's ground-truth answer. Evaluation uses a two-metric suite: (1) a developer-match LLM-as-judge based on G-Eval, calibrated against ConflictBench's human labels before deployment, and (2) a deterministic structural-validity check that uses no LLM. The judge is meta-evaluated on 292 human-labeled cases.
AI.result: The calibrated LLM judge achieves 100% precision (zero false accepts) at 64.6% recall on the meta-evaluation, meaning every acceptance is trustworthy and all downstream rates are conservative lower bounds. Under this judge, LLM solvers match the developer's resolution on ~55% of true conflicts (a conservative floor). In a coverage-fair comparison, LLMs (55–59%) outperform AutoMerge (36.7%) by roughly 18–22 percentage points. The advantage stems almost entirely from coverage, not raw accuracy: traditional tools abstain on 20–90% of conflicts, while the LLM under forced resolution abstains on none. Critically, the LLM judge accepted 4 of 5 resolutions that fail the deterministic structural check, demonstrating that structural correctness must not be delegated to an LLM.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based merge conflict resolution substantially outperforms traditional tools in coverage-fair comparisons, with the calibrated LLM judge providing trustworthy, conservative lower-bound evaluations. However, LLM judges cannot reliably assess structural validity, necessitating a hybrid evaluation approach that combines LLM-based semantic matching with deterministic structural checks. The paper demonstrates a practical path toward automated merge conflict resolution with rigorous, scalable evaluation.

title: Interpretable Representation via LLM-Driven Generative Disentanglement for Local-Life Service Recommendation
summary: While large language models (LLMs) have advanced ID-based recommendation through Semantic ID (SID) modeling, existing SID generation frameworks largely follow a single-representation-then-quantization paradigm. This design faces two bottlenecks: semantic entanglement mixes heterogeneous attributes, such as geography, brand, and category, causing information loss during quantization, low-quality SIDs, and severe collisions; moreover, black-box representation learning provides neither explicit attribute semantics nor clear geographic or semantic meanings for SID positions. These limitations weaken both retrieval reliability and the ability to diagnose or control SID generation. We propose Interpretable Representation via LLM-Driven Generative Disentanglement for Local-Life Service Recommendation (LGRID). LGRID introduces a generative disentanglement paradigm through an Encode -> Disentangle -> Align -> Quantize pipeline. It first uses joint LLM encoding to preserve cross-attribute geographic-semantic dependencies, rather than encoding fields independently. A Structured Disentangled Block then routes hidden states into attribute-aligned slots for geographic and semantic factors. Synergistic Alignment Learning makes these slots both generatively decodable and discriminative for retrieval, while Dual-Stream Residual Quantization separately discretizes the two streams into compact SIDs with explicit attribute correspondence. This design yields interpretable SIDs with positions grounded in item attributes and local-service semantics. Experiments on Kuaishou and Foursquare show that LGRID consistently outperforms strong SID baselines, achieving up to a 5.44 percent relative AUC gain. It also achieves over 99 percent attribute-decoding accuracy for coarse geographic fields and reduces the full-SID collision rate to 39.9 percent, compared with 97.0 percent for LGSID.

AI.tldr: LGRID proposes a generative disentanglement paradigm for SID-based recommendation, replacing single-representation-then-quantization with an Encode→Disentangle→Align→Quantize pipeline that produces interpretable, attribute-grounded Semantic IDs, achieving superior AUC, near-perfect attribute decoding, and dramatically reduced collision rates.
AI.motivation: Existing SID generation frameworks suffer from semantic entanglement (mixing heterogeneous attributes like geography, brand, category during quantization) causing information loss, low-quality SIDs, and high collision rates. Additionally, black-box representation learning offers no explicit attribute semantics or interpretable meanings for SID positions, undermining retrieval reliability and diagnosability.
AI.method: LGRID uses a four-stage pipeline: (1) joint LLM encoding to preserve cross-attribute geographic-semantic dependencies; (2) a Structured Disentangled Block that routes hidden states into attribute-aligned slots for geographic and semantic factors; (3) Synergistic Alignment Learning making slots both generatively decodable and discriminative; (4) Dual-Stream Residual Quantization that separately discretizes the two streams into compact, interpretable SIDs with explicit attribute correspondence.
AI.result: On Kuaishou and Foursquare, LGRID achieves up to 5.44% relative AUC gain over strong SID baselines, over 99% attribute-decoding accuracy for coarse geographic fields, and reduces the full-SID collision rate to 39.9% (vs. 97.0% for LGSID).
AI.conclusion: Interpretable SIDs grounded in explicit item attributes and local-service semantics significantly improve both retrieval performance and system transparency, enabling better diagnosis and control of SID generation.

title: Multi-Session User Experience Assessments of Computationally Optimized Automated Vehicle Functionality Visualizations
summary: Understanding automated vehicles (AVs) is crucial to improving their acceptance. Numerous approaches to visualizing relevant traffic information to passengers have been proposed and empirically evaluated. As this is time-consuming, costly, and reduces the possible design parameters, we employed multi-objective Bayesian optimization to optimize the design of visualizations in AVs. In particular, we evaluated multi-session aspects involving iterative optimization. We optimized the design for passenger trust and perceived safety while minimizing cognitive load. Results from an online study (N=74) show that this method effectively identifies visualization design parameter values that improve trust, safety, and predictability while making the design process more efficient and scalable. However, shortcomings of the computational approach when optimizing for subjective measurements are highlighted and discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper applies multi-objective Bayesian optimization to efficiently design in-vehicle visualizations for autonomous vehicles, optimizing for passenger trust, perceived safety, and low cognitive load. An online study (N=74) demonstrates the method's effectiveness but also reveals limitations when optimizing subjective measures.
AI.motivation: Traditional empirical evaluation of AV passenger visualizations is time-consuming, costly, and limits the exploration of design parameters. The authors seek a more efficient, scalable method to identify optimal visualization designs that enhance trust and safety without causing excessive cognitive load.
AI.method: The authors employed multi-objective Bayesian optimization — a sample-efficient computational approach — to iteratively optimize visualization design parameters across multiple sessions. An online study with 74 participants was conducted to evaluate the optimized designs on metrics of trust, perceived safety, predictability, and cognitive load.
AI.result: The multi-objective Bayesian optimization approach successfully identified visualization design parameters that improved trust, safety, and predictability. The method proved more efficient and scalable than traditional approaches. However, shortcomings were observed when the computational method was applied to subjective measurement optimization.
AI.conclusion: Multi-objective Bayesian optimization is a promising tool for efficient AV visualization design, offering improvements in both design quality and process scalability. Yet, its application to subjective measures requires caution, and the authors highlight the need for further refinement when computational optimization intersects with human-subjective evaluations.

title: Distributed Point Functions and Function Secret Sharing
summary:
A distributed point function (DPF) is a cryptographic primitive that enables compressed additive sharing of a secret weight-1 vector (equivalently, a point function) across two or more parties. The appealing lightweight structure of DPF constructions has enabled a wide range of applications. These include private information retrieval, anonymous messaging, secure computation with preprocessing, and pseudorandom correlation generators for expanding small correlated seeds into large pseudorandom instances of cryptographic correlations.
  In this article, we survey definitions, constructions, and applications of DPFs. We also discuss the extension of DPF to function secret sharing (FSS), which generalizes point functions to support richer function classes. Efficient FSS schemes yield a similar generalization for most of the applications of DPFs.

AI.tldr: A survey of distributed point functions (DPFs) — cryptographic primitives for compressed secret sharing of point functions — covering definitions, constructions, applications (PIR, anonymous messaging, secure computation, PCGs), and the generalization to function secret sharing (FSS) for richer function classes.
AI.motivation: DPFs offer a lightweight, communication-efficient method for additively sharing secret weight-1 vectors across multiple parties. Their structural simplicity has unlocked numerous privacy-preserving applications. This motivates a comprehensive survey to unify definitions, compare constructions, catalog applications, and highlight the natural extension to FSS.
AI.method: This is a survey article that systematically reviews, organizes, and synthesizes existing literature on DPFs and FSS. It covers formal definitions, known constructions (e.g., tree-based DPF from pseudorandom generators), and explores the design space, before surveying practical applications and the generalization from point functions to broader function classes via FSS.
AI.result: The survey documents that DPFs enable compact, information-theoretic or computational sharing of point functions with short keys (logarithmic in domain size). Applications span private information retrieval (PIR), anonymous messaging, secure multiparty computation with preprocessing, and pseudorandom correlation generators (PCGs). Efficient FSS schemes extend these benefits to richer function classes.
AI.conclusion: DPFs and their FSS generalizations form a foundational building block for efficient privacy-preserving protocols. Their lightweight key structure and broad applicability make them a critical primitive in modern cryptography, and ongoing work continues to expand the class of functions that can be efficiently shared.

title: TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification
summary: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

AI.tldr: TIER-MoE introduces a risk-guided mixture-of-experts framework that estimates per-sample modality reliability via out-of-fold prediction loss, enabling sparse modality-expert routing while preserving multimodal complementarity through a shared path. It outperforms SOTA on four biomedical datasets.
AI.motivation: Current multimodal fusion models cannot distinguish whether a modality's reduced influence stems from it being unreliable, redundant, or mismatched to a specialized expert. The paper aims to explicitly quantify modality reliability at the sample level to enable more informed and robust fusion decisions.
AI.method: TIER-MoE learns sample-specific modality risk as the expected prediction loss from unimodal predictors trained via out-of-fold cross-validation (so no sample sees its own training data). This risk is combined with expert-specific subspace compatibility scores for sparse modality-to-expert routing. An always-active shared pathway preserves cross-modal complementarity alongside the sparse expert pathways.
AI.result: TIER-MoE achieves superior predictive performance (Macro-F1) and probability calibration (Brier score) over state-of-the-art methods on four biomedical multimodal datasets (Alzheimer's disease, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification). It also demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling sample-level modality risk via out-of-fold loss estimation, combined with subspace-based sparse expert routing and a shared complementary path, yields both better accuracy and better-calibrated uncertainty in multimodal biomedical prediction tasks.

title: Models for minimalist RAG: B1ade 335M Embedding and 1B Parameter Small Language Models
summary: Language and embedding models used in RAG systems are conventionally assumed to require large-scale pretraining and explicit grounding supervision. We present B1ade, an efficient RAG architecture comprising two purpose-built components: a compact embedding model and a purpose-built SLM. B1ade-embed, a 335M parameter retrieval model constructed via parameter-free fusion of five pretrained encoders achieves top MTEB scores among sub-500M models with zero additional training, and B1ade-1B, an SLM trained on low-cost GPUs using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on 723M tokens (2.2M examples) of curated context-question pairs with rewards that optimize only answer similarity. Our central finding is emergent attribution: despite receiving no explicit supervision for source citation, B1ade-1B cites retrieved passages in 42.4% of responses, exceeding the attribution rate of its training distribution by 5.5 percentage points. This demonstrates that grounding behavior can emerge as an accuracy-maximizing strategy under RL training, without explicit reward engineering. On standard QA benchmarks, B1ade-1B achieves 81.82% on PopQA, 65.8% on PubMedQA, and 51.09% on FEVER. In end-to-end RAG evaluation, B1ade-1B achieves an average score of 0.654 across correctness, completeness, coherence, and faithfulness, a 10.8% improvement over the SFT, while closing the gap with models 1.5x its size. These results show that strategic model composition and reward design suffice for resource-efficient RAG, without large-scale pretraining.

AI.tldr: B1ade presents a resource-efficient RAG architecture with two components: a compact 335M embedding model (B1ade-embed) built via zero-training encoder fusion, and a 1B SLM (B1ade-1B) trained with GRPO on 723M tokens. The key finding is emergent attribution — the model learns to cite sources without explicit supervision, achieving 42.4% attribution rate. On QA benchmarks, it reaches 81.82% on PopQA, 65.8% on PubMedQA, and 51.09% on FEVER, with a 10.8% RAG improvement over SFT baselines.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the conventional assumption that RAG systems require large-scale pretraining and explicit grounding supervision. It aims to demonstrate that effective retrieval-augmented generation can be achieved through strategic model composition and reward design alone, without the computational burden of massive pretraining or explicit attribution rewards.
AI.method: B1ade consists of two components: (1) B1ade-embed, a 335M retrieval model created via parameter-free fusion of five pretrained encoders, achieving top MTEB scores among sub-500M models with zero additional training; (2) B1ade-1B, an SLM trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on 723M tokens (2.2M curated context-question examples), using rewards that optimize only answer similarity — deliberately excluding any explicit citation or attribution rewards.
AI.result: B1ade-1B achieves 81.82% on PopQA, 65.8% on PubMedQA, and 51.09% on FEVER. In end-to-end RAG evaluation, it scores 0.654 average across correctness, completeness, coherence, and faithfulness — a 10.8% improvement over SFT. Crucially, emergent attribution occurs: the model cites retrieved passages in 42.4% of responses, exceeding the training distribution's attribution rate by 5.5 percentage points, despite zero explicit citation supervision.
AI.conclusion: Grounding behavior can emerge as an accuracy-maximizing strategy under RL training without explicit reward engineering. Strategic model composition (encoder fusion + compact SLM) and reward design (answer similarity only) suffice for resource-efficient RAG, closing the gap with models 1.5x larger while avoiding large-scale pretraining.

title: Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems
summary: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Trajectory Graph Copilot, a framework that uses a Graph Neural Network to model historical agent trajectories as probabilistic graphs, enabling pre-action error diagnosis to prevent LLM agents from making compounding mistakes in long-horizon interactive tasks, achieving a 14.69% average improvement in pass ratio.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks (e.g., embodied AI) due to compounding errors — a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, exhausting limited step budgets on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. Existing solutions like fine-tuning are costly, motivating a more efficient diagnostic approach.
AI.method: The authors draw inspiration from software debugging and propose Trajectory Graph Copilot. Its core component, Graph Debugger, models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and employs a Graph Neural Network (GNN) to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. It functions as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, providing early warnings about potentially flawed actions before execution, prompting the agent to self-correct.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three different LLM agents demonstrate an average pass ratio improvement of 14.69%.
AI.conclusion: Pre-action error diagnosis via trajectory graph modeling effectively mitigates compounding errors in long-horizon LLM agent tasks without requiring costly fine-tuning, significantly enhancing task completion success rates.

title: A comparative analysis of automated techniques for security bug report identification
summary:
Timely identification of security-related bug reports is essential to minimize the window of vulnerabilities in software systems. Manually screening incoming bug reports to identify security-related issues is time-consuming, error-prone, and non-scalable for large-scale software systems. Thus, a variety of automatic techniques, including traditional machine learning (ML) techniques and large language models, have been proposed to facilitate this task. However, the literature remains fragmented. Most studies introduce or optimize a particular technique and evaluate it against a limited set of baselines, often under different experimental setups. As a result, it is difficult to compare their results and draw reliable conclusions about the effectiveness of existing approaches, leaving researchers and practitioners without clear guidance on which techniques are most suitable for the task.
  To address this gap, we conducted a comparative analysis of several promising automated techniques to identify security-related bug reports using benchmark datasets. We evaluated Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, OpenAI's GPT-5.2, BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework).
  Our results indicate that SetFit achieves the best overall performance, achieving an F1-score of 0.80 and outperforming other techniques on three of the four datasets. RoBERTa performs competitively and approaches SetFit in some projects, while traditional ML techniques, particularly Logistic Regression, remain a strong baseline in certain contexts. In contrast, GPT-5.2 performs poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. In addition, cross-project experiments demonstrate that transfer learning can improve performance for projects with limited data, but may degrade results for projects with strong project-specific characteristics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a comparative analysis of automated techniques (traditional ML, LLMs, and few-shot learning) for identifying security-related bug reports, finding that SetFit achieves the best overall F1-score of 0.80, while GPT-5.2 performs poorly.
AI.motivation: The literature on automated identification of security-related bug reports is fragmented: studies introduce or optimize individual techniques and evaluate them against limited baselines under inconsistent experimental setups. This makes cross-study comparison unreliable and leaves practitioners without clear guidance on which techniques are most effective.
AI.method: The authors conducted a comparative evaluation using benchmark datasets, testing seven techniques: Logistic Regression, SVM, Random Forest, GPT-5.2 (zero-shot and few-shot), BERT-base, RoBERTa, and SetFit (a state-of-the-art few-shot learning framework). They evaluated on four datasets and also performed cross-project transfer learning experiments.
AI.result: SetFit achieved the best overall performance (F1-score of 0.80), outperforming other techniques on three of four datasets. RoBERTa performed competitively, approaching SetFit on some projects. Traditional ML, especially Logistic Regression, remained a strong baseline in certain contexts. GPT-5.2 performed poorly in both zero-shot and few-shot settings. Cross-project transfer learning improved performance for data-limited projects but degraded results when projects had strong project-specific characteristics.
AI.conclusion: SetFit is the most effective technique for identifying security-related bug reports, while lightweight traditional ML methods like Logistic Regression still offer competitive baselines. Large language models like GPT-5.2 are not yet reliable for this task. Transfer learning is beneficial for data-scarce projects but must be applied cautiously when projects exhibit distinct characteristics.

title: VIG-RL: Learning to Search and Insert for Verified Image Grounding
summary: In knowledge-intensive scenarios, providing reliable interleaved text-image responses requires Verified Image Grounding (VIG): the precise integration of retrieved authentic visual evidence. Existing retrieval-augmented frameworks predominantly rely on decoupled, static pipelines, inherently failing to dynamically reason about when external knowledge is required and where visual assets should be contextually inserted. To bridge this gap, we propose VIG-RL, an autonomous agentic framework that formulates the search-selection-insertion workflow as an active decision-making process. Operating within a dynamic ReAct-style loop, VIG-RL is optimized via reinforcement learning, guided by a composite reward system that holistically evaluates the agent's step-by-step tool execution and final multimodal alignment. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that VIG-RL establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing static baselines.

AI.tldr: VIG-RL is a reinforcement learning-based agentic framework that dynamically decides when and where to insert verified images into text responses, outperforming static retrieval-augmented baselines on Verified Image Grounding (VIG) tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented frameworks for multimodal responses use decoupled, static pipelines that cannot dynamically reason about when external visual evidence is needed or where it should be inserted. This limits their effectiveness in knowledge-intensive scenarios requiring reliable, verified interleaved text-image outputs.
AI.method: The authors propose VIG-RL, an autonomous agentic framework that treats the search-selection-insertion workflow as an active decision-making process. It operates in a ReAct-style loop and is optimized via reinforcement learning with a composite reward system that evaluates both step-by-step tool execution and final multimodal alignment holistically.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show that VIG-RL establishes new state-of-the-art performance, significantly surpassing existing static baselines for Verified Image Grounding.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, RL-optimized agentic frameworks like VIG-RL are superior to static retrieval pipelines for multimodal knowledge grounding, as they can adaptively decide when and where to integrate verified visual evidence.

title: CrossAtlas: Evaluating Projection Techniques for Spatial Referencing in Cross-Reality Collaboration
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, Accepted to IEEE ISMAR 2026 (TVCG journal track)
summary: Cross-reality collaboration increasingly connects immersive and desktop users within synchronized workspaces, yet little is known about how bidirectional projection techniques between immersive 3D layouts and desktop 2D views influence communication. Spatial referencing depends on shared spatial understanding, but different mappings preserve and distort geometric relationships in different ways, altering perceived adjacency, orientation, and coverage across collaborators' views. We present CrossAtlas, a synchronized PC-VR collaboration platform that integrates multiple bidirectional projection techniques, including three planar projection variants and equirectangular, a spherical projection variant, across layouts of varying curvature. In a controlled study with 24 dyads, collaborators completed spatial referencing tasks under different projection-layout conditions while we collected performance and subjective measures. Our results show that projection choice strongly shaped collaboration, with the spherical variant often outperforming planar projections and remaining robust across object layouts.

AI.tldr: CrossAtlas introduces bidirectional projection techniques for cross-reality collaboration between VR and desktop users. A controlled study with 24 dyads reveals that spherical (equirectangular) projection often outperforms planar variants for spatial referencing tasks, showing robustness across different object layouts.
AI.motivation: Cross-reality collaboration between immersive (VR) and desktop users is increasingly common, but little is known about how bidirectional projection techniques—mapping between immersive 3D layouts and desktop 2D views—affect communication. Spatial referencing depends on shared spatial understanding, and different projection mappings may preserve or distort geometric relationships (adjacency, orientation, coverage) in ways that impact collaboration quality.
AI.method: The authors developed CrossAtlas, a synchronized PC-VR collaboration platform integrating multiple bidirectional projection techniques: three planar projection variants and one spherical (equirectangular) variant, tested across layouts of varying curvature. A controlled study was conducted with 24 dyads performing spatial referencing tasks under different projection-layout conditions, collecting both performance metrics and subjective measures.
AI.result: Projection choice strongly influenced collaboration outcomes. The spherical (equirectangular) projection variant frequently outperformed planar projections and demonstrated greater robustness across diverse object layouts, indicating that spherical mappings better preserve the geometric relationships necessary for effective spatial referencing in cross-reality settings.
AI.conclusion: Bidirectional projection techniques are a critical design factor in cross-reality collaboration systems. Spherical projections like equirectangular offer superior support for spatial referencing compared to planar alternatives, and their robustness across layouts makes them a promising default choice for synchronized PC-VR workspaces.

title: CHARGE: Leveraging CWE Hierarchies for Hardware Security SystemVerilog Assertion Generation
comment: This paper is an extended version of the paper accepted to the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: This paper presents CHARGE, an automated framework for generating security properties for unverified RTL modules using CWEs and large language models (LLMs). The hallmark is a reasoning process that leverages the hierarchical nature of CWE entries to improve accuracy when identifying security-critical assets in unverified RTL modules. As a result, the approach can infer expected security behaviors and generate properties from identified assets and CWE semantics, avoiding the need for trusted design specifications and reducing manual engineering effort. We evaluate the framework on the Hack@DAC18, 19, and 21 open source SoC designs using OpenAI's GPT-4.1. CHARGE detects 27 of 42 known bugs in these designs. For Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC, 89% of the generated SVAs run in Cadence JasperGold FPV, and 92.2% are non-vacuous. We compare to an open-source, manually written set of properties for these designs and find that CHARGE correctly writes properties for three bugs in which the manually written properties were incorrect. In addition, CHARGE-generated properties identify a new bug in the Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC that was not previously identified.

AI.tldr: CHARGE is an automated framework that uses CWEs and LLMs to generate security properties for unverified RTL modules. By leveraging the hierarchical structure of CWE entries and GPT-4.1, it identifies security-critical assets, infers expected behaviors, and generates SystemVerilog assertions without requiring trusted specifications. It found 27/42 known bugs, generated 89% runnable and 92.2% non-vacuous SVAs on OpenPiton, corrected three manually-written property errors, and discovered one previously unknown bug.
AI.motivation: Manual generation of security properties for hardware RTL modules is labor-intensive and requires trusted design specifications, which are often unavailable or incomplete. Existing automated approaches struggle to accurately identify security-critical assets and map them to appropriate security properties. The paper addresses the need for a specification-free, automated method to generate high-quality security assertions that can detect hardware security bugs.
AI.method: CHARGE employs a multi-stage reasoning framework: (1) it analyzes unverified RTL using an LLM to identify security-critical assets; (2) it leverages the hierarchical structure of Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) entries to improve asset identification accuracy; (3) it maps identified assets to CWE semantics to infer expected security behaviors; and (4) it automatically generates SystemVerilog Assertions (SVAs) encoding these behaviors. The system uses OpenAI's GPT-4.1 as the underlying LLM.
AI.result: Evaluated on Hack@DAC18, 19, and 21 SoC designs, CHARGE detected 27 out of 42 known bugs. On Hack@DAC21 OpenPiton SoC, 89% of generated SVAs ran successfully in Cadence JasperGold Formal Property Verification, with 92.2% being non-vacuous. Compared to manually written open-source properties, CHARGE correctly wrote properties for three bugs where manual properties were incorrect, and discovered one previously unknown bug in OpenPiton.
AI.conclusion: CHARGE demonstrates that LLMs combined with structured CWE knowledge can effectively automate hardware security property generation, achieving high rates of runnable and non-vacuous assertions while reducing reliance on trusted specifications. The approach not only matches but in some cases exceeds manual property-writing efforts, suggesting a viable path toward scalable, specification-free hardware security verification.

title: EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis
summary: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

AI.tldr: EvoCause uses LLMs to iteratively refine causal graphs for root cause analysis of alarm cascades, guided by expert incident labels. The refined graph alone (no LLM at inference) improves RCA accuracy on both synthetic data and a new real-world benchmark, TeleRCA.
AI.motivation: Existing RCA methods learn a static causal graph from observational alarm logs but cannot incorporate expert diagnoses of historical incidents to improve the graph. The gap is that expert labels indicate which alarms should be root causes but do not specify the structural edits needed to satisfy those constraints.
AI.method: EvoCause operates in a closed loop: expert labels constrain which nodes should be sources (zero-in-degree), an LLM proposes semantically plausible graph edits (edge additions/deletions), deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity, and the best refined graph is selected based on a labeled alignment set. At test time, RCA predictions use only the refined graph with no LLM involvement.
AI.result: On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with PC causal discovery improves Node F1 by +11.59, Case EM by +9.40, and Graph F1 by +4.59 percentage points over unrefined PC, while reducing nSHD by 0.2379. On the new TeleRCA benchmark (485,681 alarm events, 194 alarm types, 5,621 resources), anonymizing alarm titles lowers Node F1 by 6.12 and Case EM by 8.04 points, confirming that semantic alarm-name information aids graph refinement.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between causal graph learning and expert incident diagnosis via LLM-driven graph refinement yields significant RCA improvements. The approach is transparent at inference and leverages semantic information embedded in alarm names. The TeleRCA benchmark enables further research on real-world alarm RCA.

title: VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Agent implementations: https://github.com/veris-ai/riley-agent
summary: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

AI.tldr: VAmoS Bench is a voice agent simulation benchmark that evaluates complete end-to-end voice-agent systems in a stateful customer-support task, measuring "containment" — whether the agent correctly resolves (or appropriately refuses/redirects) phone calls without human handoff — using 100 scenarios with a simulated caller, a PostgreSQL backend, and binary assertion grading that verifies both conversational correctness and actual database state changes.
AI.motivation: Existing voice-agent benchmarks focus on component-level metrics (WER, latency, naturalness, turn-taking) but rarely measure whether an agent correctly handles a complete phone call end-to-end. The authors identify a gap around "containment" — the share of calls resolved autonomously without human escalation. They argue that correct outcomes may include refusals or redirects, not just task completion, and that current evaluation fails to catch agents that say they performed an action without actually updating backend systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce VAmoS Bench, featuring a credit-card support agent named Riley for a fictional bank. The benchmark comprises 100 scenarios, each with a simulated caller holding a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. An isolated simulation is spun up per scenario, with the caller interacting with Riley over audio (~1/3 of scenarios include adversarial pressure). Riley has access to five tools executing real SQL. Each scenario defines binary assertions, and a grader evaluates the complete trace — including conversation, tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows — against these assertions. This dual verification catches both agents that misrepresent actions and those that perform correct actions but leak protected information.
AI.result: The paper presents the first version of VAmoS Bench, focused on financial services (credit-card support: freeze, cancel, replace, activate). The evaluation protocol is designed to support an evolving leaderboard, where additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version while later versions expand tasks and scenarios.
AI.conclusion: VAmoS Bench fills a critical evaluation gap by measuring end-to-end containment in voice-agent systems through stateful simulation with ground-truth database verification. Its design — combining conversational assessment with backend state checking and supporting adversarial scenarios — provides a more rigorous and realistic measure of voice-agent reliability than component-level metrics alone.

title: The Case for Vibe Modeling: A Missing Step in AI-Based Trustworthy Software Development
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software artifacts from natural language prompts. While this enables rapid prototyping and lowers the barrier to software creation, it also introduces challenges related to understanding, validation, traceability, and trust. In this paper, we argue that current AI-based development practices focus too heavily on the direct generation of code and insufficiently on intermediate representations that preserve human intent and support reasoning about system behavior. We argue for vibe modeling as a lightweight intermediate abstraction between natural language interaction and code generation. To explore its potential, we present a student survey study that examines perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios. Our results are intended to inform future studies for trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering via vibe modeling.

AI.tldr: The paper critiques the current LLM-driven code generation paradigm for over-prioritizing direct code output over human-understandable intermediate representations. It proposes "vibe modeling" as a lightweight abstraction layer between natural language prompts and code generation and presents a student survey study examining perceptions of LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the usefulness of vibe modeling.
AI.motivation: LLM-based code generation from natural language enables rapid prototyping but creates significant challenges in understanding, validation, traceability, and trust. The authors argue that current practices focus excessively on direct code generation while neglecting intermediate representations that preserve human intent and facilitate reasoning about system behavior.
AI.method: The paper introduces the concept of "vibe modeling" as a lightweight intermediate abstraction situated between natural language interaction and code generation. It then conducts a student survey study to assess perceptions across multiple dimensions: understanding of LLM outputs, validation effort required, levels of trust, and the perceived usefulness of vibe modeling in various AI-assisted development scenarios.
AI.result: Results from the student survey study are presented to explore perceptions regarding LLM output understanding, validation effort, trust, and the perceived utility of vibe modeling across several AI-assisted development scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The findings are intended to inform future research directions toward trustworthy and explainable AI-based software engineering, with vibe modeling proposed as a promising intermediate representation approach to bridge the gap between natural language intent and generated code.

title: CCFormer: Efficient Cross-Field Interaction and Hierarchical Sequence Compression for Industrial Recommendation at Tencent
summary: Recent studies in industrial recommendation systems have demonstrated that sequential recommendation models built upon self-attention can benefit from predictable scaling laws by increasing sequence length and model capacity. However, practical recommender systems impose strict latency and resource constraints, making it challenging to balance computational overhead with fine-grained feature interaction. In this paper, we propose CCFormer, an efficient Transformer backbone that unifies cross-field feature interaction and compressed long-sequence modeling for industrial recommendation. Specifically, CCFormer combines feature-field separated cross attention with long-sequence subspace token mixing to exploit long-term preference signals across heterogeneous feature domains. A hierarchical sequence compression strategy with progressively expanded receptive fields enables efficient long-sequence modeling with reduced information loss. Extensive experiments on two public benchmarks and a large-scale industrial dataset demonstrate that CCFormer consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Online A/B tests in a video recommendation scenario and an advertising ranking scenario at Tencent further validate its industrial practicality, yielding a 3.57% CTR gain and a 1.71% advertising revenue lift, respectively, while accelerating model training by 2.21x over the strong HSTU baseline. CCFormer has been fully deployed in Tencent's production recommendation system, serving the main traffic of both scenarios.

AI.tldr: CCFormer is an efficient Transformer for industrial recommendation that unifies cross-field feature interaction and compressed long-sequence modeling, achieving significant CTR and revenue gains at Tencent while accelerating training.
AI.motivation: Sequential recommendation models based on self-attention benefit from longer sequences and larger capacity (scaling laws), but industrial systems face strict latency and resource constraints. There is a need to balance computational efficiency with fine-grained feature interaction across heterogeneous feature domains.
AI.method: CCFormer combines (1) feature-field separated cross attention for cross-field interaction, (2) long-sequence subspace token mixing for capturing long-term preferences, and (3) a hierarchical sequence compression strategy with progressively expanded receptive fields to reduce sequence length while minimizing information loss.
AI.result: On two public benchmarks and one large-scale industrial dataset, CCFormer outperforms SOTA baselines. Online A/B tests at Tencent show: 3.57% CTR gain in video recommendation, 1.71% advertising revenue lift in ad ranking, and 2.21x training speedup over HSTU.
AI.conclusion: CCFormer effectively balances efficiency and expressiveness, making it suitable for real-world industrial deployment. It has been fully deployed in Tencent's production recommendation system, serving main traffic for both video recommendation and advertising ranking scenarios.

title: FADEx: Feature Attribution and Distortion-based Explanation of Dimensionality Reduction
comment: 18 pages, 17 figures, to be published in IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) is a fundamental tool for high-dimensional data exploration, reducing the complexity of latent spaces of machine learning models, and assisting in the explanation of complex opaque models. However, non-linear DR techniques often function as opaque transformations themselves, making it challenging to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. This lack of transparency complicates the analysis and interpretation of structural patterns, hindering the ability to reason about the organization of high-dimensional data based on the projected layout. In order to address this challenge, dimensionality reduction explanation methods have shown promise in improving the understanding of the observed groups and cluster structures. Unfortunately, existing DR explanation approaches tend to suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific dimensionality reduction methods, which hinder their use. In this work, we propose FADEx, a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. FADEx computes the local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method, while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, we demonstrate FADEx's effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing the behavior of DR methods. The results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

AI.tldr: FADEx is a novel, DR-agnostic local feature attribution method that explains dimensionality reduction projections using first-order Taylor expansion and SVD-based weighted least squares, outperforming existing explanation methods in robustness and reliability.
AI.motivation: Non-linear dimensionality reduction techniques are opaque, making it difficult to understand how individual features influence point positions in reduced spaces. Existing DR explanation methods suffer from multiple attributions per feature and are restricted to specific DR methods, limiting their practical utility for interpretation and analysis.
AI.method: FADEx leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition. It computes local linear models using weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping. This design makes it agnostic to the underlying DR method while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis.
AI.result: Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, FADEx demonstrated effectiveness and versatility. It yielded robust and reliable explanations and outperformed existing approaches in several aspects.
AI.conclusion: FADEx provides a versatile, DR-agnostic explanation framework that overcomes key limitations of prior methods—namely multiple attributions and restricted DR applicability—offering both feature attributions and distortion analysis to aid in understanding high-dimensional data organization.

title: Adaptive Security at the Edge for 6G-Enabled Healthcare IoT
comment: 2 pages, 2 figures, 2026 Joint European Conference on Networks and Communications & 6G Summit (EuCNC/6G Summit), extended abstract
summary: Healthcare IoT services increasingly rely on edge gateways to relay routine telemetry and deliver rare but timecritical alarms. Even short traffic bursts can inflate worstcase delay and interfere with urgent messages. We present NANOEDGEGUARD, a kernel-plane closed-loop controller that observes per-source traffic intensity at the edge and enforces an auditable, multi-tier rate policy using in-kernel traffic-control hooks. Unlike static firewall rules or user-space control loops, our design prioritizes fast actuation and explicit recovery through hysteresis, and it records policy transitions for auditability. Using a Raspberry Pi gateway hosting an MQTT broker and two ESP32 endpoints generating vitals, alarms, and a timed burst, we show that adaptive kernel-plane rate control reduces the 99th-percentile alarm RTT by 13.3% compared to a user-space firewall baseline while maintaining no-enforcement-level RTT, and it reduces excess admitted burst traffic by 46% compared to no enforcement. These early results indicate that adaptive, auditable enforcement at the gateway can improve resilience for healthcare IoT, and it can be extended toward on-demand policy deployment in future edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: NANOEDGEGUARD is a kernel-plane rate controller for healthcare IoT edge gateways that enforces multi-tier traffic policies with hysteresis-based recovery, reducing 99th-percentile alarm RTT by 13.3% and excess burst traffic by 46% compared to baselines.
AI.motivation: Healthcare IoT edge gateways must handle both routine telemetry and time-critical alarms. Even brief traffic bursts can inflate worst-case delay and disrupt urgent message delivery. Existing approaches (static firewall rules, user-space control loops) lack the speed and adaptability needed for precise, auditable rate enforcement under bursty conditions.
AI.method: NANOEDGEGUARD is a kernel-plane closed-loop controller that monitors per-source traffic intensity and applies multi-tier rate policies via in-kernel traffic-control hooks (tc). It employs hysteresis for explicit, stable recovery and logs all policy transitions for auditability. Evaluation uses a Raspberry Pi gateway running an MQTT broker with two ESP32 endpoints generating vitals, alarms, and timed bursts, comparing adaptive kernel-plane control against a user-space firewall baseline and no-enforcement conditions.
AI.result: Adaptive kernel-plane rate control reduced 99th-percentile alarm round-trip time by 13.3% versus the user-space firewall baseline while matching no-enforcement RTT levels. It also reduced excess admitted burst traffic by 46% compared to no enforcement.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, auditable kernel-plane enforcement at the edge gateway improves resilience for healthcare IoT traffic. The approach is extensible toward on-demand policy deployment in future edge intelligence systems.

title: THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model
summary: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

AI.tldr: THGFM is a dual-path temporal heterogeneous graph transformer that combines parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization via a non-competitive gated fusion mechanism, and incorporates relative time directly into attention scores using rotary temporal attention.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal heterogeneous graph models struggle with two key limitations: (1) difficulty reconciling parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and (2) time is typically injected only as additive features outside the attention kernel rather than being integrated directly into the attention computation.
AI.method: THGFM employs a dual-path architecture: (1) a Shared-Space Temporal Attention branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer, (2) a Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention branch for relation-aware specialization. These are fused via Dual-Path Relational–Shared Fusion using Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion, which assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to each branch without zero-sum competition. Additionally, Rotary Temporal Attention rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching to directly incorporate temporal information into attention scores.
AI.result: THGFM achieves a +3.25% six-task mean gain over baseline graph transformers. Peak relative gains include +12.37% on OAG-CS PV, +4.87% on PF-L2, +1.18% on PF-L1, and improvements of +4.24%, +3.73%, and +4.61% on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.
AI.conclusion: The dual-path architecture with non-competitive gated fusion and rotary temporal attention effectively addresses the core challenges in temporal heterogeneous graph learning, enabling scalable web-scale modeling with consistent performance improvements across diverse academic graph benchmarks.

title: Training Skills Like Parameters via Self-Supervised Semantic Diffusion
summary: While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable general instruction-following capabilities, they often fall short of human experts in highly specialized, open-ended domains such as creative screenwriting. Prior approaches typically adopt post-training, yet both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning require weight access that closed-source frontier models do not offer, and demand heavy compute. Moreover, what is learned is tied to a single checkpoint and cannot be inspected by humans. Recent advancements in agentic continual learning instead attempt to bridge this gap by accumulating external textual skills. However, these methods heavily rely on costly human expert annotations or unreliable LLM-as-a-judge feedback for reflection. To overcome this bottleneck, we propose a novel, unsupervised self-evolving agent framework inspired by the corruption-and-reconstruction paradigm of diffusion models. Instead of relying on explicit external scoring, we leverage existing high-quality human artifacts to construct self-supervised signals. Training then follows the familiar loop of neural network training, forward, loss, and backward, with the loss coming from contrasting the agent's reconstruction against the human original. What is updated is not model weights but an external library of textual skills. We evaluate our framework on the challenging task of short drama screenwriting. Experimental results demonstrate that our method enables the agent to autonomously extract and internalize highly generalizable skills, significantly enhancing its domain-specific generation capabilities. Furthermore, this self-contrastive reflection paradigm offers a scalable pathway for agents to teach themselves the production of complex, high-quality human artifacts, without requiring external supervision.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an unsupervised self-evolving agent framework that uses a self-supervised, contrastive reconstruction paradigm (inspired by diffusion models) to enable agents to autonomously learn domain-specific skills from human artifacts, demonstrated on short drama screenwriting.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle in specialized open-ended domains like screenwriting. Existing solutions (SFT, RLHF) require weight access and heavy compute, while agentic continual learning methods depend on costly human annotations or unreliable LLM-as-judge feedback. There is a need for a scalable, unsupervised approach that works with closed-source models.
AI.method: A corruption-and-reconstruction framework inspired by diffusion models: high-quality human artifacts are corrupted, and the agent must reconstruct them. The reconstruction is contrasted against the original human artifact to produce a self-supervised loss signal (forward-loss-backward loop). Updates are applied not to model weights but to an external library of textual skills, enabling model-agnostic, inspectable skill accumulation.
AI.result: The framework enables autonomous extraction and internalization of highly generalizable skills. On short drama screenwriting, the agent significantly enhances domain-specific generation capabilities without external supervision.
AI.conclusion: The self-contrastive reflection paradigm offers a scalable pathway for agents to teach themselves complex, high-quality human artifact production without requiring weight access, external supervision, or costly human annotations — pointing toward more autonomous and accessible domain adaptation.

title: Specification-Guided Synthesis of Deadlock-Free Communication Protocol Refinements with Large Language Models
summary: Ensuring behavioural correctness in communication protocols is a central challenge in distributed software systems, as subtle inconsistencies can lead to deadlocks. In such settings, protocol refinement - the safe substitution of a protocol that preserves correctness and compatibility with other components - is essential. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and program synthesis, yet lack mechanisms to reliably produce outputs with correct behaviour. Formal specification approaches, such as multiparty session types (MPST), offer rigorous guarantees, including deadlock freedom, but provide limited support for automatically constructing protocol refinements. In this paper, we present Syntropy, a framework for synthesising protocol refinements guided by MPST specifications and LLMs. It incorporates refinement constraints directly into the generation process, ensuring the generated variants satisfy these guarantees. Our comprehensive evaluation indicates that Syntropy achieves 95.6%-99.5% validity while maintaining high syntactic correctness, and produces diverse, non-trivial refinements across multiple LLMs.

AI.tldr: Syntropy is a framework that combines multiparty session types (MPST) with LLMs to automatically synthesize protocol refinements that are guaranteed to be deadlock-free and behaviourally correct, achieving 95.6%–99.5% validity in evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLMs excel at code generation but lack mechanisms to ensure behavioural correctness (e.g., deadlock freedom) in distributed communication protocols. Conversely, formal methods like MPST provide rigorous correctness guarantees but offer limited automation for constructing protocol refinements. There is a gap between LLM fluency and formal verifiability that Syntropy aims to bridge.
AI.method: Syntropy is a framework that guides LLM-based generation using MPST specifications. It injects refinement constraints directly into the synthesis process, ensuring that generated protocol variants satisfy formal guarantees such as deadlock freedom. The approach leverages the structure of multiparty session types to constrain the LLM's output space to only valid refinements.
AI.result: The framework achieves 95.6%–99.5% validity across multiple LLMs while maintaining high syntactic correctness. It also produces diverse, non-trivial protocol refinements, demonstrating both reliability and expressiveness.
AI.conclusion: Syntropy successfully integrates formal MPST-based constraints with LLM-driven synthesis, enabling the automatic generation of protocol refinements that are both behaviourally correct and practically useful. This bridges a critical gap between formal verification and neural code generation for distributed systems.

title: TCA-SIR: Learning Target-Conditioned Abstractions for Scientific Inspiration Retrieval
summary: Scientific hypothesis generation for AI for Science typically involves Scientific Inspiration Retrieval (SIR) followed by hypothesis composition. Existing SIR methods rank papers by topical similarity and do not explicitly represent how a candidate inspiration transfers to a target problem. This is especially limiting for remote inspirations, whose value often lies in reusable problem-solving principles rather than topical overlap. Motivated by how humans abstract transferable aspects of a source and remap them to a new target, we reformulate SIR as target-conditioned abstraction (TCA). The retrieval object is a transferable abstract principle extracted from a candidate specifically for the target. We present TCA-SIR, which learns to generate target-conditioned abstractions and uses their representations to predict transferability. On ResearchBench, TCA-SIR outperforms prior SIR methods and direct LLM retrieval, improving HitRate@top4% over MOOSE-Chem by more than 10 percentage points. Learned abstractions also recover target-relevant mechanisms more clearly than an untrained TCA prompt, yielding both stronger retrieval and an interpretable rationale for scientific inspiration.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates Scientific Inspiration Retrieval (SIR) as target-conditioned abstraction (TCA), where transferable principles are extracted from candidate papers specifically for a target problem, improving retrieval of remote inspirations and outperforming prior methods on ResearchBench.
AI.motivation: Existing SIR methods rely on topical similarity, which fails to capture the value of remote inspirations — these often contribute reusable problem-solving principles rather than surface-level topical overlap. The authors are motivated by how humans abstract and remap transferable aspects from a source to a new target.
AI.method: The authors propose TCA-SIR, which reformulates SIR as target-conditioned abstraction. Rather than retrieving papers by topical similarity, the method learns to generate a transferable abstract principle from each candidate paper explicitly conditioned on the target problem, then uses the representation of that abstraction to predict transferability for downstream hypothesis generation.
AI.result: On ResearchBench, TCA-SIR outperforms prior SIR methods and direct LLM retrieval, improving HitRate@top4% over MOOSE-Chem by more than 10 percentage points. Learned abstractions also recover target-relevant mechanisms more clearly than an untrained TCA prompt.
AI.conclusion: Target-conditioned abstraction yields both stronger retrieval performance and an interpretable rationale for scientific inspiration, demonstrating that explicitly modeling transferable principles conditioned on the target problem is more effective than topical similarity for scientific inspiration retrieval.

title: A Montage-Agnostic Encoder for Calibration-Light Cross-User Gesture Recognition from Surface Electromyography
summary: Pattern-recognition control promises a myoelectric prosthesis that responds to many intended gestures rather than one or two, but the promise has stayed in the laboratory. A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A montage-agnostic encoder is introduced that reads each electrode with shared weights and locates it by its physical coordinate rather than its index, so one architecture ingests any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users, it exceeds a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, and falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation study. A controlled subject-count sweep shows the margin is close to flat from nine training subjects to thirty-nine, so the training pool binds only as a stability floor below which cross-user training fails to converge; what tracks the direction of the comparison across the three databases is instead the strength of the per-user baseline, which signal fidelity sets. Comparing against an LDA baseline depends on budget spent training models and on how good that baseline is, and self-supervised pretraining had no benefits once a supervised model was adequately trained.

AI.tldr: A montage-agnostic encoder for myoelectric pattern recognition uses shared-weight electrode reading and physical coordinate localization, enabling cross-user generalization without per-user calibration. It outperforms per-user baselines on two databases, with three key components each contributing substantially in ablation. Performance gaps correlate with per-user baseline strength and signal fidelity rather than training pool size beyond a stability floor of nine subjects.
AI.motivation: Myoelectric pattern-recognition prostheses remain confined to labs because recognizers fail to transfer across users, requiring costly per-user labeled calibration. The authors aim to overcome this by enabling cross-user generalization without montage-specific retraining.
AI.method: A montage-agnostic encoder processes each electrode via shared weights and identifies it by physical coordinates rather than index, accepting arbitrary channel counts. The architecture is trained across multiple users. Ablation studies isolate three key components, and subject-count sweeps assess training pool size effects. Comparisons use macro-F1 against per-user Hudgins features + LDA, evaluated on DB1, DB2, and DB5. Self-supervised pretraining is also tested.
AI.result: The encoder surpasses per-user Hudgins+LDA by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 (every held-out subject) and 0.108 on DB2, but falls below on DB5. Each of three key components accounts for >50% of 3-shot macro-F1 in ablation. The margin remains near-flat from 9 to 39 training subjects. Performance direction across databases tracks per-user baseline strength (signal fidelity), not training pool size. Self-supervised pretraining yields no benefit once supervised training is adequate.
AI.conclusion: Cross-user myoelectric control is feasible with a coordinate-aware, montage-agnostic encoder. Success hinges on signal fidelity of the per-user baseline rather than number of training subjects (beyond a modest stability floor). Self-supervised pretraining adds no value when sufficient supervised data exists.

title: Don't Trust the AI Ecosystem: Analyzing Privacy Leakage in Compromised Open-Source Components
summary: Existing model inversion (MI) attacks predominantly rely on post-training optimization to recover private data from model outputs. However, these methods are fundamentally constrained by the target model's generalization bottleneck, often yielding generic features rather than specific identities, particularly on high-dimensional datasets. In this paper, we introduce GradLock, a novel training-time injection attack that stealthily injects sensitive training data directly into the model parameters. Operating within a compromised supply chain context, GradLock leverages stateless deterministic indexing to establish isolated data vaults and employs dynamic gradient locking to prevent payload degradation during the optimization process. This mechanism allows the adversary to extract pixel-perfect data from the final model without retaining access to the training environment. Extensive experiments on MNIST, Imagenette, and CelebA demonstrate that GradLock achieves near-lossless reconstruction (SSIM ~ 1.0) and instant extraction (< 1.0s).
