Compared to existing training-time injection methods, our approach exhibits superior robustness against standard deployment optimizations, including quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning. Furthermore, a user deployment study reveals that 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic, highlighting a severe blind spot in the security of modern AI supply chains.

AI.tldr: GradLock is a training-time injection attack that embeds sensitive data directly into model parameters using stateless deterministic indexing and dynamic gradient locking, enabling pixel-perfect, instant extraction of private data from the final model without retaining training environment access.
AI.motivation: Existing model inversion attacks are post-training and limited by the target model's generalization bottleneck, producing only generic features rather than specific identities on high-dimensional datasets. Training-time injection methods offer a stronger alternative, but prior approaches lack robustness against standard deployment optimizations like quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning.
AI.method: GradLock operates within a compromised AI supply chain context. It uses stateless deterministic indexing to create isolated data vaults within model parameters, combined with dynamic gradient locking to prevent payload degradation during training optimization. This allows the adversary to embed private data during training and later extract it from the released model without ongoing access to the training environment.
AI.result: On MNIST, Imagenette, and CelebA, GradLock achieves near-lossless reconstruction with SSIM ~1.0 and extraction in under 1.0 second. It demonstrates superior robustness against quantization, pruning, and fine-tuning compared to existing training-time injection methods. A user study shows 93.3% of participants failed to detect the malicious logic.
AI.conclusion: GradLock exposes a critical blind spot in modern AI supply chain security, demonstrating that adversaries can embed and reliably extract private data through training-time injection with high fidelity and robustness against standard countermeasures, all while evading human detection.

title: Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

AI.tldr: Medical VLMs' chain-of-thought reasoning doesn't reliably cause their predictions. CoT-Mediate tests this by editing one clinical attribute in the model's own reasoning and checking if predictions follow. Prefix-forced continuation mediates better than re-prompting; provenance doesn't matter much — contextual position does. Removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether chain-of-thought reasoning generated by medical VLMs causally influences their clinical predictions, or whether the reasoning is merely epiphenomenal. Existing evaluations lack systematic methods to perturb reasoning and measure downstream effects while controlling for confounding factors like sycophancy (models deferring to stated sources rather than the reasoning itself).
AI.method: CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework with two key components: (1) a dual-arm protocol that compares re-prompted evidence versus prefix-forced continuation for injecting edited reasoning; and (2) a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle genuine mediation from sycophancy. The framework perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within the model's own generated CoT and measures whether predictions follow. Evaluated on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma using 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each.
AI.result: Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting. Provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning across both models. Laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. Contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness, and contextual position — not stated provenance — primarily determines whether medical VLMs use their CoT reasoning to inform predictions. This has implications for how CoT faithfulness should be evaluated and interpreted in medical VLMs.

title: Beyond Similarity: Grounded Agentic Extraction and Expert-Adjudicated Evaluation of Intertextuality in Classical Chinese Histories
summary: Computational approaches to intertextuality have advanced from string matching to neural retrieval, yet their outputs, similarity scores and parallel-passage lists, identify where texts reuse one another without characterizing how or why. We recast fine-grained intertextuality extraction as an agentic task in which a large language model (LLM) reads two text units in full and, through a constrained tool interface, must ground each proposed reuse in exact character spans on both sides and label it under a five-dimension typology of reuse (form, aspect, source-marking, function, stance). We validate the approach on an exhaustive comparison of the Analects with the Book of Han, where three domain experts adjudicate a pooled multi-model candidate set into a benchmark of 2,533 intertextual pairs. Against this standard we study twelve LLMs, reporting precision (56%-93%), a 51$\times$ cost spread at comparable quality, and how well their confidence is calibrated. Expert agreement traces a reliability gradient: dimensions legible on the textual surface are annotated consistently, while those requiring inference of intent are contested, delimiting the claims such annotation supports. Scaling the validated extractor to the full Twenty-Four Histories (65,380 comparisons, 5,766 pairs) recovers corpus-level structure a similarity score cannot express. The interpretive composition of citation shows no systematic change across eighteen centuries, yet the same passage is quoted less and less literally. Stability in the aggregate with drift in the individual case is what a cultural-attraction account expects. We release the extraction protocol and the expert-adjudicated benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes intertextuality detection as an agentic LLM task requiring exact character-span grounding and five-dimension typology labeling. Validated on Analects–Book of Han comparisons with expert adjudication (2,533 pairs), the approach achieves 56–93% precision across twelve LLMs. Scaling to the Twenty-Four Histories reveals stable aggregate citation patterns but decreasing literalness over eighteen centuries, consistent with cultural-attraction theory.
AI.motivation: Existing computational intertextuality methods produce only similarity scores and parallel-passage lists, identifying *where* reuse occurs but not *how* or *why*. There is a need for fine-grained extraction that characterizes the nature of textual reuse along multiple interpretative dimensions, moving beyond surface-level matching to capture the rhetorical and functional aspects of citation.
AI.method: The authors formulate intertextuality extraction as an agentic task: an LLM reads two full text units and, through a constrained tool interface, must (1) ground each proposed reuse in exact character spans on both source and target sides, and (2) label it under a five-dimension typology (form, aspect, source-marking, function, stance). Validation uses an exhaustive comparison of the *Analects* with the *Book of Han*. Three domain experts adjudicate a pooled multi-model candidate set to produce a benchmark of 2,533 intertextual pairs. Twelve LLMs are evaluated against this benchmark for precision, cost, and confidence calibration. The validated extractor is then scaled to all Twenty-Four Histories (65,380 comparisons yielding 5,766 pairs).
AI.result: Precision across twelve LLMs ranges from 56% to 93%, with a 51× cost spread at comparable quality levels. Expert agreement reveals a reliability gradient: surface-level dimensions are annotated consistently, while dimensions requiring intent inference are contested. At corpus scale, the interpretive composition of citation shows no systematic change across eighteen centuries, yet the same passages are quoted progressively less literally. This pattern — stability in aggregate with drift in individual cases — aligns with cultural-attraction theory.
AI.conclusion: Agentic LLM-based extraction with constrained grounding and multi-dimensional typology enables fine-grained intertextuality analysis at scale. The approach captures interpretative dimensions that similarity scores cannot, while expert adjudication reveals inherent limits on which dimensions can be reliably annotated. The historical finding of aggregate stability with individual drift supports a cultural-attraction account of textual transmission. The protocol and benchmark are released publicly.

title: INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning
summary: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

AI.tldr: INCLAIR is a framework for detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles that uses multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates natural-language explanations with limited expert supervision. It leverages U-statistic theory to control inference cost and uses top-k pooling to address attenuation of localized anomalies. The method outperforms baselines on three clinical datasets and is validated via a case study on steroid profiles with domain-expert and DNA-based assessments.
AI.motivation: Anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important yet challenging due to three factors: sparse abnormal evidence, unequal patient history lengths, and the high cost of obtaining expert explanations. Existing methods struggle to address these issues simultaneously, motivating a framework that can score observations against diverse historical contexts, aggregate evidence robustly, and produce interpretable explanations under limited supervision.
AI.method: The proposed INCLAIR framework scores each observation against multiple historical contexts and aggregates evidence at the profile level. Under within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score adopts an order-l U-statistic form, enabling a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The analysis also reveals that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies proportional to anomaly support and profile length, motivating a validation-selected top-k pooling strategy. The framework generates grounded natural-language explanations with limited expert supervision.
AI.result: INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three clinical datasets. A case study on longitudinal steroid profiles demonstrates practical relevance: INCLAIR's predictions and explanations align with domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis, confirming clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.
AI.conclusion: INCLAIR provides an effective, theoretically grounded, and interpretable framework for anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical data. By combining U-statistic-based aggregation, top-k pooling, and natural-language explanation generation, it overcomes key practical challenges — sparse anomalies, variable-length histories, and costly expert labeling — and delivers clinically actionable results validated by domain experts.

title: Advancing Awkward Arrays for High-Performance CPU and GPU Processing
summary: Awkward Array is a Python library for representing and processing nested, variable-length data that is widely used in high-energy physics. As HL-LHC analyses increasingly rely on accelerator hardware, efficient execution of irregular workloads has become essential. While dense numerical arrays map naturally to GPUs, nested and variable-length data structures remain significantly more difficult to accelerate because they require indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns. We present recent developments in the Awkward Array GPU backend, including CUDA implementations built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), optimized memory management, and segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays. These developments preserve the existing Python programming model while substantially improving GPU throughput on irregular workloads. We describe the backend architecture, automated validation framework, and benchmark results comparing CPU, CuPy, and CUDA implementations.

AI.tldr: Awkward Array now features a GPU backend using NVIDIA CCCL for efficient CUDA-based processing of nested, variable-length data, preserving its Python API while significantly accelerating irregular workloads critical for HL-LHC physics analyses.
AI.motivation: HL-LHC analyses demand accelerator hardware for performance, but nested and variable-length data structures (ragged arrays) resist GPU acceleration due to indirect indexing, segmented operations, and irregular memory access patterns—unlike dense numerical arrays that map naturally to GPUs.
AI.method: The authors developed a GPU backend for Awkward Array built on NVIDIA CUDA Core Compute Libraries (CCCL), incorporating optimized memory management, segmented reduction algorithms for ragged arrays, and an automated validation framework to ensure correctness while maintaining the existing Python programming model.
AI.result: The CCCL-based CUDA backend substantially improves GPU throughput on irregular workloads compared to CPU and CuPy implementations, with benchmark results demonstrating significant speedups while preserving usability.
AI.conclusion: GPU acceleration of nested, variable-length data is feasible without sacrificing the high-level Python interface, enabling efficient irregular workload execution for HL-LHC and other data-intensive scientific domains.

title: ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation
summary:
Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

AI.tldr: ROCS defers request-candidate interactions, isolates candidate representations, and evaluates shared portions of the model once per request, achieving up to 3x QPS improvement without quality loss in production recommendation systems.
AI.motivation: Recommendation models scale feature-interaction and sequence modules for quality, but production cost constraints limit scaling. A key observation is that each user request is evaluated against many candidates with shared request-side features, creating an opportunity to reduce redundant computation.
AI.method: The ROCS paradigm employs three core techniques: (1) Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures; (2) Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures; (3) In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO), a co-designed GPU optimization to accelerate ROCS model execution.
AI.result: On public benchmarks, ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across backbones. In production: up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models with no quality degradation; 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model.
AI.conclusion: ROCS has been successfully deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and over two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

title: Recognition and Label-Free Adaptation Across Recording Sessions in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding
summary: Recognition accuracy obtained during a recording session does not persist when a user puts on the electrodes again after the electrodes had previously been removed. The electrodes may have moved slightly, the skin may be drier or wetter, or the elbow may be positioned differently; these factors all contribute to day-to-day variability and therefore represent a major obstacle to implementing successful pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems in daily practice. However, simply recalibrating a user's hand for 20 min at every doff/don event is a clearly unrealistic expectation. A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained here using data collected during a particular recording session, and then applied to data collected later in a different recording session without adjusting anything, on the ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. The performance of this approach is compared to that of a per-user LDA classification pipeline, and to that of two published approaches that only rely on source data collected from the same recording session. Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 against 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and, on the per-window metric the published baselines use, sits above both published source-only results, a band of two points that locates the encoder rather than ranking it. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation, a standard method in the domain-adaptation literature, collapses this architecture entirely. Aligning the encoder's feature statistics to the new session recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would.

AI.tldr: A montage-agnostic encoder trained on one recording session transfers across sessions without recalibration, achieving 0.688 macro-F1 vs. 0.540 for a per-user LDA pipeline, with feature-statistic alignment as the only effective test-time adaptation method.
AI.motivation: Pattern-recognition myoelectric control suffers from day-to-day variability (electrode shift, skin condition, limb position), making recalibration at every don/doff event impractical. A solution that eliminates per-session recalibration is needed for real-world deployment.
AI.method: A montage-agnostic encoder is trained for cross-user, cross-montage transfer using single-session data from NinaPro DB6 (10 intact subjects). It is applied unchanged to a different recording session. Comparison is made against: (1) a per-user LDA pipeline, (2) two published source-only approaches. Five label-free test-time adaptation methods are evaluated, including feature-statistic alignment and batch-normalisation re-estimation.
AI.result: The encoder achieves 0.688 macro-F1 across sessions vs. 0.540 for the per-user LDA pipeline. It surpasses both published source-only baselines on their per-window metric. Only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation causes complete collapse. Aligning feature statistics recovers performance approximately equivalent to one labelled calibration repetition.
AI.conclusion: A montage-agnostic encoder effectively mitigates inter-session variability in myoelectric control without per-session recalibration. Feature-statistic alignment is the only robust test-time adaptation, recovering performance comparable to a single labelled calibration trial.

title: Benign on Label, Malicious by Design: Clean-Label Dormant-to-Activated Backdoor via Machine Unlearning with Removable Camouflage
summary: Existing backdoor attacks often become effective immediately after backdoor implantation and may therefore be exposed before exploitation. Machine unlearning activated dormant backdoors mitigate such behavioral exposure by remaining inactive after training and becoming effective only after selected training records are unlearned. However, existing methods struggle to simultaneously achieve a low pre-unlearning attack success rate and strong post-unlearning activation under clean-label constraints and realistic unlearning requests. Achieving this transition requires jointly establishing a persistent latent association and a removable suppressive influence. To address this challenge, we propose a clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor framework based on dual-generator learning and formulate it as a bilevel optimization problem: By simulating latent backdoor establishment and machine unlearning, the framework alternately learns sample-specific triggers that establish a latent trigger-to-target association and label-consistent camouflage samples that provide removable suppression. Once a small subset of camouflage samples is unlearned, the suppression is lifted and the dormant backdoor is activated. Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 show that our method maintains lower pre-unlearning attack success rates while achieving stronger post-unlearning activation across multiple unlearning algorithms than representative backdoor baselines. These results demonstrate that reliable dormancy-to-activation transitions can be achieved by coordinating a persistent latent association with removable suppression under clean-label and realistic deletion constraints.

AI.tldr: A novel clean-label backdoor attack that remains dormant after training and only activates when specific training records are unlearned, achieving reliable dormancy-to-activation transitions through dual-generator bilevel optimization.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor attacks are effective immediately after implantation, risking exposure before exploitation. While machine unlearning-activated dormant backdoors address this by delaying activation until after unlearning, current methods fail to simultaneously achieve low pre-unlearning attack success and strong post-unlearning activation under clean-label constraints and realistic unlearning scenarios.
AI.method: A clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor framework using dual-generator learning, formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. One generator learns sample-specific triggers establishing latent trigger-to-target associations, while the other generates label-consistent camouflage samples providing removable suppression. The framework alternates between simulating latent backdoor establishment and machine unlearning. The backdoor activates only after a small subset of camouflage samples is unlearned, lifting the suppression.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-10 demonstrate that the proposed method maintains lower pre-unlearning attack success rates while achieving stronger post-unlearning activation across multiple unlearning algorithms compared to representative backdoor baselines.
AI.conclusion: Reliable dormancy-to-activation transitions can be achieved by coordinating a persistent latent association with removable suppression under clean-label and realistic deletion constraints, demonstrating an effective clean-label unlearning-activated backdoor mechanism.

title: ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution
summary: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

AI.tldr: ZUNA1.1 is a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG reconstruction, supporting variable-length sequences (up to 30s), arbitrary channel counts/locations, and partial temporal interval reconstruction, outperforming standard methods like spherical spline interpolation.
AI.motivation: EEG signal reconstruction typically requires rigid, fixed-configuration models. The authors sought to develop a more flexible architecture capable of handling variable sequence lengths, arbitrary channel configurations, and partial temporal reconstruction — moving beyond the limitations of their previous ZUNA1 model and standard interpolation methods.
AI.method: ZUNA1.1 employs a diffusion autoencoder architecture with 380 million parameters. It is designed to reconstruct EEG signals of variable length (up to 30 seconds), an arbitrary number of channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels rather than only entire channels.
AI.result: ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with the earlier ZUNA1 model while offering substantially greater flexibility. It continues to significantly outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction baselines, notably spherical spline interpolation as implemented in the MNE package.
AI.conclusion: ZUNA1.1 represents a meaningful advance in flexible EEG reconstruction, combining strong performance with open-source availability under the Apache 2.0 license, making it accessible for broad research and clinical applications.

title: AWARE-FX: An Auditable Knowledge-Guided AI System for Measuring Corporate Foreign-Exchange Hedging Disclosure
comment: 40 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Preprint; not peer reviewed
summary: Corporate annual reports contain weakly structured evidence about foreign-exchange risk management, derivative use, natural hedging, and explicit non-use. This study develops AWARE-FX, an auditable AI/NLP decision-support system that converts report text into traceable firm-year hedging-disclosure measures. The system combines a professional-source lexicon, negation and accounting-status logic, channel-specific financial encoders, exact evidence gates, conservative aggregation, and an audit ledger. Across 24,909 Hong Kong firm-years from 2008-2025, it retrieves and scores 543,527 snippets. Reliability is evaluated through ablations, a stratified 300-snippet human audit, three-seed FinBERT-ModernBERT comparisons, strict 2023-2025 temporal tests, probability calibration, selective prediction, and fixed-prompt generative-model benchmarks. FinBERT has the higher mean F1 in seven of eight encoder task-split comparisons; its temporal F1 ranges from 0.702 to 0.872. Abstaining on the 20% least-confident temporal observations raises retained-sample F1 by 0.050-0.077. Deterministic Qwen3-8B performs strongly on commodity and negation evidence but poorly on foreign-debt and accounting-context labels, showing that a general-purpose LLM does not uniformly replace domain constraints. The strict FX score is negatively associated with linked baseline and stress-period FX exposure, whereas the generic broad score is not. These associations provide external construct validation, not causal estimates of hedging effectiveness. AWARE-FX contributes a tested decision-support architecture in which retrieval, status logic, classification, uncertainty handling, aggregation, and external validation remain separately auditable.

AI.tldr: AWARE-FX is an auditable AI/NLP system that extracts foreign-exchange hedging disclosures from corporate annual reports. It combines a domain lexicon, negation logic, financial encoders (FinBERT excels), exact evidence gates, and uncertainty quantification. Applied to 24,909 Hong Kong firm-years, it produces FX scores validated against actual FX exposure, with selective prediction improving reliability and LLMs proving insufficient as uniform replacements for domain-constrained components.
AI.motivation: Corporate annual reports contain rich but weakly structured evidence on FX risk management (derivative use, natural hedging, explicit non-use). Manual extraction is infeasible at scale, yet existing automated approaches lack auditability, domain-specific logic, and rigorous validation. A reliable, transparent, and externally validated decision-support system is needed to convert textual disclosures into traceable quantitative measures for research and practice.
AI.method: AWARE-FX integrates: (1) a professional-source lexicon for FX hedging terminology; (2) negation and accounting-status logic to handle qualifiers and context; (3) channel-specific financial encoders (FinBERT, ModernBERT) for classification across multiple evidence types; (4) exact evidence gates for retrieval precision; (5) conservative aggregation of snippet-level scores into firm-year measures; (6) an audit ledger for full traceability. Evaluation uses 24,909 Hong Kong firm-years (2008–2025), yielding 543,527 scored snippets. Reliability is assessed via ablations, a stratified 300-snippet human audit, three-seed encoder comparisons, strict temporal holdout tests (2023–2025), probability calibration, selective prediction (abstaining on low-confidence instances), and fixed-prompt generative model (Qwen3-8B) benchmarks. External construct validation links scores to baseline and stress-period FX exposure.
AI.result: FinBERT achieves higher mean F1 in seven of eight encoder task-split comparisons; temporal F1 ranges from 0.702 to 0.872. Selective prediction (abstaining on the 20% least-confident temporal observations) raises retained-sample F1 by 0.050–0.077. Deterministic Qwen3-8B performs strongly on commodity and negation evidence but poorly on foreign-debt and accounting-context labels, demonstrating that general-purpose LLMs do not uniformly replace domain-constrained components. The strict FX score shows a significant negative association with linked baseline and stress-period FX exposure, while the generic broad score does not, providing external construct validation.
AI.conclusion: AWARE-FX demonstrates a viable, auditable decision-support architecture where retrieval, status logic, classification, uncertainty handling, aggregation, and external validation remain separately inspectable. The system's strict FX score captures economically meaningful variation missed by broad measures. Domain-specific encoders (FinBERT) outperform generic alternatives, and selective prediction materially improves reliability. General-purpose LLMs cannot yet substitute for carefully engineered domain constraints in this task. The architecture contributes a reusable template for transparent, validated NLP-based disclosure measurement in accounting and finance research.

title: MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale
summary: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

AI.tldr: MedLLM is a fully open 0.1B-parameter medical LM that reveals a task-type-dependent dissociation in medical competence under extreme compression: context-grounded QA is largely preserved, while knowledge-recall QA hits a capacity ceiling.
AI.motivation: Open medical language models have converged on the 7B+ scale, leaving the sub-billion parameter regime uncharacterized. The authors aim to probe how medical competence behaves under extreme model compression and whether different task types degrade uniformly.
AI.method: A three-phase fully open pipeline: (1) general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, (2) domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb (a reference-guided corpus selected from general web data via embedding similarity to medical QA), and (3) preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with DPO.
AI.result: At 0.1B parameters, MedLLM comes within 2.9pp of a medically adapted 7B model on context-grounded QA and surpasses instruction-tuned/general-purpose 7B baselines. On knowledge-recall QA, it stays near the task floor on MedQA (clinical vignettes) yet significantly exceeds all 7B and sub-7B baselines on MedMCQA. This dissociation—context-grounded vs. knowledge-recall competence—is invisible at 7B and surfaces only under capacity constraints.
AI.conclusion: Medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression; it bifurcates by task type. The dissociation between preserved context-grounded reasoning and capacity-limited knowledge recall is masked at larger scales, suggesting that sub-billion models offer a unique lens for studying capability emergence and capacity bottlenecks in domain-specific LMs.

title: Integrating AI into Requirements Quality Learning in Software Engineering Education: A TPACK-Guided Empirical Study
comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables, presented in the 38th CSEE&T in Florence, Italy, from July 20-22, 2026
summary: The rapid adoption of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in software engineering (SE) practice creates a need for pedagogically grounded approaches to AI integration in SE education, especially in conceptually intensive subjects such as requirements engineering (RE). This study examines a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level RE assignment on requirements quality analysis. Using a mixed-methods design (N=100; 72 submissions analysed), we examine how structured assignment design shaped students' AI use, affected their understanding of user story quality criteria, and influenced their perceptions of AI's benefits and limitations. Results show that students used the AI tool selectively, mainly as support for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were most evident for structurally concrete requirements quality dimensions, such as value articulation and testability, while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students reported conditional trust, active refinement, and increased awareness of quality criteria, alongside moderate usability challenges. The findings show that TPACK-guided scaffolding can align AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education.

AI.tldr: This study investigates a TPACK-guided integration of a multi-agent AI tool into a master-level requirements engineering assignment, finding that structured scaffolding promotes selective, analytical AI use and improves understanding of concrete quality criteria like value articulation and testability, while highlighting conditional trust and usability challenges.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of generative AI in software engineering practice creates an urgent need for pedagogically sound approaches to AI integration in SE education, particularly for conceptually intensive subjects like requirements engineering where uncritical AI use could undermine learning.
AI.method: Mixed-methods design with N=100 participants and 72 assignment submissions analyzed. A TPACK-guided, structured assignment was designed around a multi-agent AI tool for requirements quality analysis. Both quantitative alignment improvements across quality dimensions and qualitative perceptions of AI benefits/limitations were examined.
AI.result: Students used AI selectively for analysis and evaluation rather than automation. Alignment improvements were strongest for structurally concrete dimensions (value articulation, testability), while negotiability showed mixed effects. Students exhibited conditional trust, active refinement of AI outputs, increased awareness of quality criteria, and reported moderate usability challenges.
AI.conclusion: TPACK-guided scaffolding effectively aligns AI affordances with pedagogical goals and RE content, offering design guidance for responsible AI integration in RE education. The approach fosters critical engagement rather than passive reliance on AI tools.

title: Gradient-free Task-Conditioned Retrieval for On-Device In-Context Learning
summary: On-device in-context learning (ICL) relies on pre-inference retrieval to select demonstrations for useful context before downstream model inference. This retrieval must exploit task-specific information while operating over local memories under limited computation, memory, and data-exposure budgets. We propose Conditional Retrieval Alignment (CoRA), a gradient-free framework that converts a frozen encoder into a task-conditioned retriever using paired candidate inputs and outputs. CoRA selects complementary encoder layers, constructs an output-derived conditioning space from candidate memory, and aligns candidate input representations to this space through closed-form ridge regression. Low-rank factorization then produces a compact retrieval basis where candidate outputs are used only during offline index construction, whereas query-time retrieval requires only the query input and precomputed index. We show that CoRA's rank-constrained basis is the optimal low-rank compression of the output-conditioned fitted representation, and derive an exact two-pass streaming construction that avoids materializing the full fitted matrix. We further extend the framework to multimodal exemplar retrieval by incorporating visual representations into the conditioning and retrieval spaces. Experiments across ten textual datasets and four multimodal benchmarks with Llama-3.2-1B, MobileLLM-Pro, OpenFlamingo-3B, and Qwen3.5-2B, as well as end-to-end Raspberry Pi~5 deployment demonstrate that CoRA supports effective task-conditioned retrieval without retriever fine-tuning, backpropagation, or target-model calls.

AI.tldr: CoRA is a gradient-free framework that converts a frozen encoder into a task-conditioned retriever for on-device in-context learning, using paired input-output candidates and closed-form ridge regression with low-rank factorization, enabling efficient retrieval without fine-tuning or backpropagation.
AI.motivation: On-device in-context learning requires pre-inference retrieval of demonstrations under strict computational, memory, and data-exposure constraints. Existing methods struggle to exploit task-specific information effectively without gradient-based fine-tuning or target model calls.
AI.method: CoRA selects complementary encoder layers, constructs an output-derived conditioning space from candidate memory, aligns candidate input representations via closed-form ridge regression, applies low-rank factorization for a compact retrieval basis, and supports an exact two-pass streaming construction. For multimodal extension, visual representations are incorporated into both conditioning and retrieval spaces.
AI.result: Experiments across 10 textual datasets and 4 multimodal benchmarks with models including Llama-3.2-1B, MobileLLM-Pro, OpenFlamingo-3B, and Qwen3.5-2B, plus end-to-end Raspberry Pi 5 deployment, demonstrate effective task-conditioned retrieval.
AI.conclusion: CoRA enables effective task-conditioned retrieval without retriever fine-tuning, backpropagation, or target-model calls, making it well-suited for resource-constrained on-device ICL scenarios.

title: Safeguards Based on Copyable Context Cannot Provide Reliable Safety for LLMs
summary: Large language model safeguards decide whether to answer before seeing how an answer will be used. This creates a basic problem for dual-use tasks: the same answer can help an authorized professional or an attacker, while an attacker can imitate a benign request and interaction history. We separate the capability released by the model from the evidence available about downstream use. When that evidence is copyable, we derive the exact worst-case floor on attacker assistance while preserving useful answers. The result yields a safety trilemma: Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot coexist. We then show how a trusted credential can complement existing safeguards by adding hard-to-copy information that predicts actual downstream use, and identify the stronger condition needed to eliminate the floor. Evidence from dual-use evaluations, adaptive attacks, and deployed trusted-access programs supports the practical relevance of these conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that when evidence of downstream use is copyable, there exists an unavoidable worst-case floor on attacker assistance. This creates a safety trilemma: Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot all coexist. Trusted credentials with hard-to-copy information can break this floor.
AI.motivation: LLM safeguards decide whether to answer based on the request itself, without observing how the answer will actually be used. This is fundamentally problematic for dual-use tasks where identical answers can serve both legitimate and malicious purposes, and attackers can mimic benign requests and interaction histories.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem by separating the capability released by the model from the observable evidence about downstream use. They derive the exact worst-case lower bound on attacker assistance under the assumption that evidence is copyable, proving a safety trilemma. They then analyze how trusted credentials providing hard-to-copy information (that predicts actual downstream use) can complement existing safeguards and identify the stronger condition required to eliminate the attacker-assistance floor. Empirical validation comes from dual-use evaluations, adaptive attacks, and deployed trusted-access programs.
AI.result: A formal safety trilemma is proven: Useful Capability, Reliable Safety, and Open Access cannot simultaneously hold when evidence is copyable. Trusted credentials can break this impossibility by providing non-copyable evidence predictive of downstream use, but require a stronger condition to fully eliminate the attacker-assistance floor. Empirical evidence from dual-use evaluations, adaptive attacks, and real-world trusted-access deployments supports the practical relevance of these theoretical conditions.
AI.conclusion: Current safeguard paradigms face an inherent limitation when evidence of downstream use is copyable — there is an unavoidable floor on attacker assistance. Introducing hard-to-copy trusted credentials offers a principled path to overcome this limitation, with practical implications for designing safer LLM deployment strategies.

title: Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 23rd International Conference on Modeling Decisions for Artificial Intelligence (MDAI 2026)
summary: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

AI.tldr: Under leakage-aware evaluation that removes shortcuts from high-signal smart contracts, XGBoost outperforms Transformer and BiLSTM models for classifying Ethereum actors (organic users, Sybil bots, MEV bots), while offering lower latency and energy consumption. The authors introduce a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation to enable fair, deployable bot detection.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning Sybil detection methods treat blockchain activity as sequential data but suffer from inflated performance due to label leakage from high-signal contracts, high computational cost, and impracticality for real-time monitoring. The authors aim to rigorously compare sequence models against tree-based models under leakage-reduced conditions and determine which behavioral signals (order vs. timing) are most discriminative.
AI.method: The authors propose two contributions: (1) a Blind-Spot protocol that eliminates leakage from high-signal smart contracts during training/evaluation, and (2) a Transaction Grammar representation encoding wallet behavior via rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. They benchmark Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines on Ethereum actor classification under both standard and leakage-aware settings.
AI.result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models in classification accuracy while also providing lower inference latency and reduced estimated energy consumption, challenging the assumption that complex sequential architectures are necessary for this task.
AI.conclusion: Structural transaction patterns captured by tree-based models suffice for Sybil/MEV bot detection once label leakage is controlled. The Transaction Grammar and Blind-Spot protocol together form a practical, low-latency framework suitable for real-time Ethereum actor classification.

title: DualAnchor: Preserving Language Priors and Improving Lexical Fidelity in Gloss-Free Sign Language Translation
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led sign language translation (SLT), the task of converting sign-language videos into spoken-language text, to increasingly adopt LLMs as textual backbones. However, despite their strong language modeling capabilities, existing LLM-based SLT methods often undermine rather than exploit this language prior, producing disfluent translations, a failure we term language-prior degradation. Meanwhile, existing methods typically align videos and text at the sentence level, which does not ensure accurate lexical details and creates a lexical fidelity gap. To address both issues, we propose DualAnchor, a gloss-free LLM-based SLT training framework that couples two complementary anchors for linguistically fluent and visually faithful generation. Token-level Prior Anchoring (TPA) preserves the LLM's language prior by regularizing the multimodal decoder at each decoding step toward the next-token distribution of a frozen LLM conditioned on the same autoregressive prefix. Optimal Transport Alignment (OTA) improves lexical fidelity by formulating visual-textual matching as entropy-regularized partial optimal transport, with Sinkhorn optimization inducing a soft alignment between visual tokens and textual content tokens under a cosine cost. DualAnchor achieves strong overall performance on both PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily. Targeted analyses attribute these gains to the complementary effects of the two anchors: TPA improves fluency, whereas OTA reduces fine-grained lexical errors.

AI.tldr: DualAnchor is a gloss-free, LLM-based sign language translation framework that uses two complementary anchors: Token-level Prior Anchoring (TPA) to preserve the LLM's language prior for fluency, and Optimal Transport Alignment (OTA) to improve lexical fidelity. It achieves strong results on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based SLT methods suffer from two key problems: (1) language-prior degradation, where the LLM's language capabilities are undermined, producing disfluent translations; and (2) a lexical fidelity gap caused by sentence-level video-text alignment that fails to capture fine-grained lexical details.
AI.method: DualAnchor proposes two complementary mechanisms: (1) Token-level Prior Anchoring (TPA) — regularizes the multimodal decoder at each decoding step toward the next-token distribution of a frozen LLM conditioned on the same autoregressive prefix, thereby preserving the LLM's language prior; (2) Optimal Transport Alignment (OTA) — formulates visual-textual matching as entropy-regularized partial optimal transport, using Sinkhorn optimization to induce a soft alignment between visual tokens and textual content tokens under a cosine cost.
AI.result: DualAnchor achieves strong overall performance on both PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily benchmarks. Targeted ablation analyses attribute gains to complementary effects: TPA improves translation fluency, while OTA reduces fine-grained lexical errors.
AI.conclusion: The complementary anchoring strategy — TPA for linguistic fluency and OTA for visual-lexical fidelity — effectively addresses both language-prior degradation and the lexical fidelity gap in LLM-based SLT, offering a robust gloss-free training framework.

title: A dataset of rated conceptual arguments
summary: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques on 442 position texts across philosophical and conceptual domains, rated by experts along multiple dimensions. It proposes scoring functions and benchmarks LLMs, finding that performance on conceptual reasoning tracks general capability rankings.
AI.motivation: LLMs are well-tested on tasks with verifiable ground truth (math, programming) but poorly understood on "conceptual questions" — those lacking objective answers, such as philosophy, AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. The authors argue that individual arguments can be evaluated more reliably than bottom-line conclusions, enabling progress measurement.
AI.method: The authors construct a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques responding to 442 position texts across AI safety, decision theory, ethics, and politics. Six expert raters provide 1,458 ratings along four dimensions: centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. Two scoring functions are proposed to aggregate these ratings, and a range of LLMs are benchmarked against this dataset.
AI.result: Model performance on this conceptual reasoning benchmark tracks general capability rankings, suggesting that stronger models generally produce better-argued critiques across the rated dimensions.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating individual arguments rather than final conclusions provides a viable methodology for assessing LLM reasoning on open-ended conceptual questions, and current LLM rankings on this task align with their broader capability hierarchies.

title: EMBL AI Librarian: Life-Sciences Knowledge Layer for AI Agents
summary: The web is increasingly accessed by AI agents rather than humans. Every agent needs knowledge, especially in the life-sciences, where agentic pipelines are growing fast. Access to the literature is a crucial part of that need, and resources such as Europe PMC, with over 40M indexed records, are widely used to meet it. Yet these resources were not built for AI agents: they take keywords and complex syntax and return whole papers, so every agent must learn the syntax, issue several searches, and read full papers to find the evidence it needs. We introduce EMBL AI Librarian, a knowledge layer that upgrades the Europe PMC interface for AI agents: an agent asks in natural language and receives evidence that answers it. A single LLM orchestrates the whole knowledge retrieval process: it plans complementary subqueries executed by the live Europe PMC search engine, then reads the selected papers and locates the relevant evidence. We evaluate Librarian across four benchmarks: literature synthesis, claim verification, open-domain question answering, and downstream biology tasks such as protocol questions and sequence manipulation. On ScholarQABench, Librarian improves Citation F1 by more than $16$ points over strong recently published baselines. Used as the retrieval layer of an existing claim-verification pipeline, it increases agreement with expert consensus; and on the open-form LitQA2 benchmark, a GPT-5.4 agent scores about $8$ points higher when grounded in Librarian than with web search. Overall, our results show that equipping life-science agents with the Librarian knowledge layer improves performance across a range of tasks. We release our code publicly at https://github.com/petroni-lab/librarian

AI.tldr: EMBL AI Librarian is a natural-language knowledge layer atop Europe PMC that lets AI agents retrieve precise evidence from over 40M papers via orchestrated subquery planning, paper reading, and evidence localization—improving Citation F1 by 16+ points over baselines and boosting downstream task performance across literature synthesis, claim verification, QA, and biology tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing literature resources like Europe PMC were designed for human keyword/Boolean queries and return full papers, forcing AI agents to learn syntax, issue multiple searches, and sift through entire documents to find targeted evidence. This creates a bottleneck for agentic pipelines in the life sciences, where literature access is critical.
AI.method: A single LLM orchestrates the full retrieval pipeline: it decomposes natural-language queries into complementary subqueries executed against the live Europe PMC search engine, then reads retrieved papers and extracts specific evidence passages that directly answer the agent's question.
AI.result: On ScholarQABench, Librarian improves Citation F1 by over 16 points against strong baselines. As a retrieval layer for claim verification, it increases agreement with expert consensus. On LitQA2, a GPT-5.4 agent grounded in Librarian scores ~8 points higher than with web search.
AI.conclusion: Equipping life-science AI agents with the Librarian knowledge layer consistently improves performance across diverse tasks. The system is publicly released on GitHub.

title: Beyond Feeling Better: Capability-Sustaining Emotional Dialogue as a Longitudinal Research Paradigm
summary: Emotional dialogue research includes two influential strategy traditions. Empathetic dialogue prioritizes understanding a speaker's emotional experience. Emotional support conversation selects and sequences support for the seeker's current needs. Sustained use introduces a further goal. Effective support should sustain users' capacities for emotion regulation, coping, self-endorsed decisions, and social connection across the interaction lifecycle. We propose capability-sustaining emotional dialogue (CSED) as a longitudinal research paradigm that aligns supportive strategy with this goal and organizes data, models, system design, evaluation, and governance around repeated use, non-use, transition, and termination. A targeted literature-and-corpus audit motivates this position. In a PRISMA-ScR-guided sample, 95% of 60 system-building papers pursue relief-oriented goals. None evaluates capability or longitudinal outcomes, and only 1 considers dependency, autonomy, or termination risk. In 300 ESConv supporter turns, capability-relevant functions appear in 43.0%, while generic suggestions account for 22.0%, compared with 4.0% reappraisal, 6.7% self-efficacy support, and 0.3% boundary behavior. We release a protocol for extending the audit to model behavior. An illustrative process model connects latent user capability to six design commitments, four evaluation timescales, and lifecycle constraints. The resulting agenda makes CSED testable across data, policy design, training, evaluation, and governance.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Capability-Sustaining Emotional Dialogue (CSED), a longitudinal paradigm shifting emotional dialogue systems from short-term relief to long-term user capability building. An audit reveals 95% of existing systems target immediate relief, while analysis of ESConv data shows capability-relevant functions are present but underexploited. The authors provide a protocol, process model, and research agenda to make CSED testable.
AI.motivation: Current emotional dialogue systems overwhelmingly pursue relief-oriented goals—providing immediate comfort—without designing for sustained, repeated use. The authors argue this neglects critical long-term outcomes: users' capacities for emotion regulation, coping, autonomous decision-making, and social connection. The motivation is to realign system design, evaluation, and governance with a longitudinal, capability-sustaining objective that accounts for dependency, autonomy, and termination risk.
AI.method: (1) A PRISMA-ScR-guided literature audit of 60 system-building papers, coding for relief vs. capability goals and longitudinal outcomes. (2) A corpus audit of 300 ESConv supporter turns, annotating capability-relevant conversational functions (reappraisal, self-efficacy support, boundary behavior) versus generic suggestions. (3) A proposed protocol for extending audit methodology to model behavior. (4) An illustrative process model mapping latent user capability to six design commitments, four evaluation timescales, and lifecycle constraints (use, non-use, transition, termination).
AI.result: Literature audit: 95% of 60 systems pursue relief-oriented goals; none evaluates capability or longitudinal outcomes; only 1 paper considers dependency, autonomy, or termination risk. Corpus audit: capability-relevant functions appear in 43.0% of ESConv turns, but generic suggestions dominate (22.0%), while reappraisal (4.0%), self-efficacy support (6.7%), and boundary behavior (0.3%) are rare.
AI.conclusion: The CSED paradigm addresses a critical gap by making capability-sustaining emotional dialogue testable through a structured research agenda spanning data practices, policy design, training, evaluation, and governance, organized around the full interaction lifecycle.

title: Driving up Inference Energy on SNNs: Per-Sample and Universal Sponge Attacks
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) communicate through sparse binary spike events rather than dense activations, enabling energy-efficient inference on neuromorphic hardware and motivating their use in always-on, battery-powered edge systems. We show that this same efficiency advantage creates a distinct security risk: sponge attacks can increase inference-time spike activity and synaptic workload, inflating energy consumption while remaining difficult to detect through correctness-based monitoring alone. Prior input-space efficiency attacks on SNNs have focused on per-sample optimization, primarily in rate-coded settings. We extend this threat to native event-based binary inputs and study two attack models. First, we develop a per-sample sponge attack that crafts a custom adversarial spike train for each input via gradient-based optimization. This attack increases per-inference SynOps by 1.5-2.6x on three SNN models for the NMNIST, SHD, and IBM DVS Gesture datasets, while preserving the predicted class on at least 98% of evaluated samples. Second, to the best of our knowledge, we introduce the first universal sponge attack for native event-based SNN inputs: a fixed binary perturbation computed offline and applied via XOR to all subsequent inputs. Although weaker, it still inflates SynOps by 1.09-1.24x across all three datasets and represents a more realistic deployment threat because it requires no per-input optimization. Mapping SynOp inflation to estimated Loihi-1 energy yields per-inference overheads from 14 $μ$J to 13.24 mJ. These results show that native event-based SNNs are vulnerable to practical input-space efficiency attacks, and that reusable universal perturbations can accumulate into meaningful battery drain in continuously deployed edge systems.

AI.tldr: SNNs gain energy efficiency from sparse binary spikes, but this very property makes them vulnerable to "sponge attacks" that inflate energy consumption without affecting classification accuracy. The paper introduces both per-sample and the first universal sponge attacks for native event-based SNNs, demonstrating 1.5–2.6× and 1.09–1.24× SynOp inflation respectively, translating to significant energy overhead on neuromorphic hardware like Loihi-1.
AI.motivation: The energy efficiency of SNNs on neuromorphic hardware makes them attractive for always-on edge devices, but this efficiency is predicated on sparse spike activity. The authors identify a security vulnerability: adversarial inputs can deliberately inflate spike activity (a "sponge attack"), draining battery life while evading correctness-based monitoring. Prior work focused only on per-sample optimization in rate-coded settings; this work extends the threat to native event-based binary inputs and introduces universal (input-agnostic) perturbations, which pose a more realistic deployment threat.
AI.method: Two attack models are developed for native event-based SNN inputs. (1) Per-sample sponge attack: gradient-based optimization crafts a custom adversarial spike train for each input, maximizing SynOp count while preserving the predicted class. (2) Universal sponge attack: a fixed binary perturbation is computed offline (via iterative optimization over the training set) and applied via XOR to all subsequent inputs at inference time, requiring no per-input optimization. Attacks are evaluated on three SNN models across NMNIST, SHD, and IBM DVS Gesture datasets. SynOp inflation is mapped to estimated energy overhead on Intel's Loihi-1 neuromorphic chip.
AI.result: The per-sample attack achieves 1.5–2.6× SynOp inflation while preserving the predicted class on ≥98% of samples. The universal attack achieves 1.09–1.24× SynOp inflation across all three datasets. Estimated per-inference energy overhead on Loihi-1 ranges from 14 μJ to 13.24 mJ. The universal perturbation, though weaker per-sample, accumulates into significant battery drain over continuous deployment.
AI.conclusion: Native event-based SNNs are practically vulnerable to input-space efficiency attacks. The introduction of universal sponge attacks demonstrates that reusable, input-agnostic perturbations can cause meaningful cumulative energy drain in continuously deployed edge systems, representing a realistic threat that bypasses correctness-based defenses.

title: Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum
comment: Accepted as a full paper and scheduled for presentation at the European Conference on Advances in Databases and Information Systems (ADBIS 2026)
summary: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free Sybil detection framework for Ethereum that uses compression-based similarity (gzip NCD) on EVM transaction traces to construct behavioral graphs, without requiring direct token transfer links between wallets. It introduces a Transaction Grammar for symbolic trace representation and a Blind-Spot Protocol for filtering high-signal contracts, and validates the approach against supervised baselines, temporal splits, and adversarial stress tests.
AI.motivation: Existing Sybil detection methods either rely on token transfer graphs (requiring direct financial links between wallets) or employ supervised ML as closed-set classification, which fails under evolving attack strategies and evasion tactics. The authors seek a training-free, open-world primitive that can discover Sybil candidates without explicit funding connections, remains robust under temporal drift and adversarial camouflage, and leverages behavioral similarity rather than financial linkage.
AI.method: The framework operates in three stages: (1) A symbolic Transaction Grammar is synthesized from EVM traces, decomposing wallet behavior into transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. (2) The Blind-Spot Protocol filters high-signal contracts — those informative for discriminating Sybil versus organic behavior — by identifying contracts where behavioral patterns diverge. (3) Gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) computes pairwise behavioral similarity between wallets, yielding a behavioral graph used for Sybil candidate discovery via seed-wallet expansion. Validation uses supervised ML baselines, a temporal split for drift assessment, and synthetic camouflage stress tests.
AI.result: The compression-based similarity approach successfully differentiates Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without relying on direct financial links. The Blind-Spot Protocol effectively identifies high-signal contracts that improve Sybil discovery. The behavioral graphs demonstrate robustness under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations, outperforming or matching supervised baselines while requiring no training. Seed-wallet expansion without explicit funding links is validated.
AI.conclusion: The authors contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery whose core NCD primitive is training-free and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. They position this as a local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits rather than a formal open-set recognition system, emphasizing practical deployability in evolving adversarial environments.

title: Harness-G: A Graph-Structured Harness for Search Agents
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) search agents commonly model retrieval as free-form natural-language query generation and optimize multi-turn interactions using final-answer rewards. Current studies mainly improve training with denser or more structured credit signals, but rarely examine whether retrieval is properly formulated at the policy-environment interface. We observe pronounced retrieval aliasing during Search-R1 training: rollouts for the same question continue to generate distinct query strings, yet their accumulated evidence sets increasingly overlap. We call this phenomenon retrieval-equivalence collapse; in this regime, trajectories approach utility equivalence with respect to retrieval decisions, leaving within-group returns with little effective retrieval contrast. To address this problem, we propose Harness-G, a graph-structured retrieval framework that redesigns this interface. It reformulates free-form query generation as finite action selection: the policy selects an evidence sentence or entity, or chooses to answer, while the environment constructs the menu, tracks retrieval state, and validates and executes each choice. This interface reduces linguistic aliasing and makes same-state alternatives directly comparable. Building on this interface, we introduce Structured Non-myopic Credit (SNC), which uses a frozen answer scorer to compare the selected action with its alternatives and assigns downstream gains to the earlier actions that enabled them. Across six QA benchmarks, Harness-G achieves the highest average F1 at both evaluated model scales, outperforming the strongest baseline, Graph-R1, by 10.74 points at 1.5B and 3.98 points at 3B.

AI.tldr: Current RL search agents suffer from "retrieval-equivalence collapse," where different query strings yield overlapping evidence, reducing retrieval contrast. The authors propose Harness-G, a graph-structured interface that reformulates free-form query generation as finite action selection over evidence sentences/entities, and Structured Non-myopic Credit (SNC) for better credit assignment. Harness-G outperforms baselines by up to 10.74 F1 points on QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing RL-based search agents formulate retrieval as free-form NL query generation and optimize using final-answer rewards. Prior work focuses on denser credit signals but ignores a fundamental problem: retrieval-equivalence collapse, where different query strings during rollouts accumulate increasingly overlapping evidence, diminishing retrieval contrast and making credit assignment ineffective across within-group trajectories.
AI.method: Harness-G introduces two key components: (1) A graph-structured retrieval interface that replaces free-form query generation with finite action selection — the policy selects evidence sentences or entities (or chooses to answer), while the environment manages the menu, retrieval state, and action validation/execution, reducing linguistic aliasing. (2) Structured Non-myopic Credit (SNC), which uses a frozen answer scorer to compare the chosen action against alternatives and propagates downstream gains to earlier enabling actions, providing structured, long-horizon credit signals.
AI.result: Harness-G achieves the highest average F1 across six QA benchmarks at both 1.5B and 3B model scales, outperforming the strongest baseline (Graph-R1) by 10.74 points at 1.5B and 3.98 points at 3B.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating retrieval as a finite action-selection problem over a graph-structured interface, combined with structured non-myopic credit assignment, effectively mitigates retrieval-equivalence collapse and substantially improves RL-based search agent performance across diverse QA tasks.

title: Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks
summary: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces AI scanners to automatically detect four types of validity issues in agentic benchmarks (ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, answer format ambiguity). Evaluated on Inspect Evals benchmarks, the scanners identified verified quality issues across five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be found by manual inspection. Performance varied across benchmarks and criteria, highlighting open challenges for automated quality assurance.
AI.motivation: Frontier model capabilities are assessed using agentic benchmarks, but previous manual audits (e.g., SWE-Bench-Verified) have uncovered validity issues. Manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably detect flaws that compromise benchmark validity.
