AI.method: The authors developed AI scanners targeting four validity issue types: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. They created grading rubrics for each issue type to guide human labeling, then evaluated scanner performance against human labels on a held-out test set from Inspect Evals benchmarks.
AI.result: The scanners identified verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. However, not all issues were detected, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria, and models used.
AI.conclusion: The results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality at scale. The authors highlight open challenges including broader standardization gaps in evaluation that degrade scanner performance, suggesting future work needed for stronger quality assurance claims.

title: Agentic Method for Deterministic Validation of Legacy Code Migration
summary: Migration of legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing to ensure correct functionality. This effort is often complicated by the lack of test data and the difficulty of validating all corner cases. In this paper we propose a novel agentic test-synthesis method, the "Locksmith Loop," which is initiated by preparing two runtime environments: the COBOL source and the generated Java target are each instrumented with mocks and executed off-mainframe on commodity hardware, then an iterative agentic loop performs Witness Search over input mocks to penetrate program branches, followed by parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries are reached, an analyzer identifies a Locked Paragraph: a condition preventing deeper exploration. Across three COBOL-Java case studies, spanning two open-source programs and one internal production-like COBOL program and ranging from 430 to 4,114 source lines, Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus, reaching nearly complete coverage on the two open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the internal production-like COBOL program. The generated Java matched the COBOL reference under deterministic parity checks in all accepted test cases. Through these findings we demonstrate, to the best of our knowledge, a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle.

AI.tldr: Locksmith Loop is an agentic test-synthesis method that iteratively generates tests for COBOL-to-Java migration by combining Witness Search over input mocks with parity-preserving mutations, achieving high branch coverage (up to ~100% on open-source, 91.9% on production code) with deterministic correctness validation.
AI.motivation: Migrating legacy COBOL programs to Java requires extensive testing, but this is hindered by scarce test data and the difficulty of validating corner cases. Existing approaches struggle to penetrate deep program branches and lack deterministic oracles for correctness.
AI.method: The proposed "Locksmith Loop" runs both COBOL source and generated Java target off-mainframe on commodity hardware, each instrumented with mocks. An iterative agentic loop performs (1) Witness Search — exploring input mock configurations to penetrate program branches — and (2) parity-preserving mutations. When routing boundaries block progress, an analyzer identifies a "Locked Paragraph" (a condition preventing deeper exploration) to guide further search. Deterministic parity checks between COBOL and Java outputs serve as a correctness oracle.
AI.result: Across three case studies (two open-source, one production-like COBOL program; 430–4,114 LOC), Locksmith consistently improved coverage beyond input-search plateaus. It achieved near-complete coverage on open-source programs and 91.90% branch coverage on the production-like program. All accepted test cases passed deterministic parity checks, confirming behavioral equivalence.
AI.conclusion: The Locksmith Loop demonstrates a novel approach for validating agentic coding output using a deterministic oracle, effectively addressing the testing bottleneck in COBOL-to-Java migration and significantly improving branch coverage beyond what input-space search alone can achieve.

title: GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a GLM-based retriever for RAG over knowledge graphs and systematically compares GLM-based, GNN-based, and vector-search-based retrievers across single-hop, multi-hop, and out-of-domain settings. GLM retrievers achieve SOTA on out-of-domain multi-hop benchmarks and scale well, while GNN retrievers offer efficient graph coverage and vector search excels at single-hop tasks.
AI.motivation: RAG over knowledge graphs demands retrievers that capture both graph topology and semantics. While GNN-based retrievers model graph structure for multi-hop reasoning and GLMs integrate graph reasoning with language model semantics, no prior work has systematically compared these retriever paradigms, particularly regarding their transferability to unseen domains.
AI.method: The authors propose a GLM-based retriever and conduct a comparative evaluation against GNN-based retrievers and traditional vector-search-based retrievers. The analysis spans single-hop and multi-hop RAG settings, with controlled experiments measuring in-domain performance, out-of-domain generalization (transferability), graph coverage, parameter scaling behavior, and training efficiency across two multi-hop QA benchmarks.
AI.result: Finetuned GLM retrievers achieve state-of-the-art on two out-of-domain multi-hop benchmarks, demonstrating superior generalization. In-domain, GLM retrievers remain comparable to prior work and show promising scaling with increased parameters and subgraph coverage. GNN-based retrievers attain higher graph coverage with more efficient training. The vector-search baseline performs best on single-hop datasets.
AI.conclusion: No single retriever paradigm dominates all settings. GLM-based retrievers are preferable for out-of-domain multi-hop generalization, GNN-based retrievers for efficient graph coverage, and vector search for single-hop retrieval. The choice of retriever should be guided by the specific RAG task requirements, particularly domain transfer needs and hop complexity.

title: AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications
summary: System prompts are instructions configured by developers to govern the behaviors of foundation models in AI applications. They are used throughout commercial AI products, but are rarely disclosed to the public or regulators, creating a serious trust and accountability gap in the wide deployment of AI systems. In this paper, we introduce Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance (AISPA), a user-centric framework for systematically auditing system prompts in AI systems. AISPA examines specific parts of a system prompt and evaluates them along eight dimensions that matter to users. We then use this framework to review 3,249 instructions from system prompts in 88 commercial AI products, classifying each instruction as either protective (of users) or problematic. Our audit surfaces four core findings. First, system prompt design varies substantially across products and developers, with some organizations averaging over 60 protective instructions per product while others average fewer than 5. Second, protective instructions are widely adopted but shallow in scope: 98.9% of products contain at least one, yet only 24% cover all eight dimensions of the AISPA taxonomy. Third, system prompts have grown steadily longer and more protective of users, suggesting that user protection is becoming a more visible concern in commercial prompt design. Fourth, despite this progress, problematic instructions remain pervasive: roughly 40% of products contain at least one instruction that works against user interests, and protective and problematic instructions frequently coexist within the same prompt. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight for system prompts in commercial AI products.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AISPA, a framework for auditing system prompts in AI systems. An audit of 3,249 instructions from 88 commercial AI products reveals that while protective instructions are common (98.9% of products), they are shallow in scope, problematic instructions persist in ~40% of products, and system prompt design varies widely across developers.
AI.motivation: System prompts govern foundation model behavior in commercial AI products but are rarely disclosed, creating a trust and accountability gap. There is no systematic framework for auditing these prompts from a user-centric perspective.
AI.method: The authors propose AISPA (Artificial Intelligence System Prompt Assurance), a user-centric audit framework that evaluates system prompts along eight dimensions. They apply this framework to classify 3,249 instructions from system prompts across 88 commercial AI products, categorizing each as either protective (benefiting users) or problematic (working against user interests).
AI.result: Four core findings: (1) system prompt design varies dramatically across developers (some average 60+ protective instructions, others fewer than 5); (2) 98.9% of products contain protective instructions, but only 24% cover all eight AISPA dimensions; (3) system prompts have grown longer and more protective over time; (4) ~40% of products contain at least one problematic instruction, and protective/problematic instructions often coexist in the same prompt.
AI.conclusion: The findings underscore the need for greater transparency, standardization, and independent oversight of system prompts in commercial AI systems, given the coexistence of protective and problematic instructions and the wide variability in prompt design practices.

title: Temporal Poisoning: Clean-Label Backdoors via Event Redistribution in SNNs
summary: Backdoor attacks on Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) have primarily assumed dirty-label poisoning, in which triggered training samples are relabeled to an attacker-selected class. We study clean-label temporal poisoning, where a fixed timestamp transformation is applied only to the target-class training streams, leaving their labels unchanged. The transformation preserves the per-pixel, per-polarity event count exactly, making clean and triggered samples identical after temporal aggregation while altering the sequence processed by the SNN. Across three neuromorphic datasets and both convolutional and transformer-based victims, the attack reaches an ASR of 1.00 in the strongest configurations. We analyze the attack through poison-budget and trigger-shape ablations and evaluate established backdoor defenses adapted to spiking models. Defenses that collapse the time axis before inspection are blind by construction, while feature-space methods detect the poison only in selected settings. Our model-free detector, based on per-step event mass, detects the evaluated temporal transformations, demonstrating both the limitation of rate-collapsed defenses and the boundary of the attack's stealth. To our knowledge, this is the first clean-label backdoor attack evaluated on SNNs and neuromorphic event data.

AI.tldr: First clean-label backdoor attack on Spiking Neural Networks using temporal poisoning: a fixed timestamp transformation applied only to target-class streams, preserving event counts while altering temporal structure. Achieves ASR of 1.00 across datasets and architectures. Rate-collapsed defenses are blind; a per-step event mass detector exposes the attack, revealing stealth limitations.
AI.motivation: Prior SNN backdoor attacks rely on dirty-label poisoning (relabeling triggered samples). This work investigates whether clean-label attacks—where labels remain correct—are feasible in the neuromorphic domain, exploiting the temporal dimension unique to SNNs that rate-based defenses ignore.
AI.method: The attack applies a fixed timestamp transformation exclusively to target-class training streams, preserving per-pixel, per-polarity event counts so that temporally aggregated statistics are identical for clean and poisoned samples. Only the event sequence is altered. The authors evaluate across three neuromorphic datasets with convolutional and transformer SNN architectures, perform poison-budget and trigger-shape ablations, and test defenses including rate-collapsed (blind by design) and feature-space methods. They also propose a model-free detector based on per-step event mass.
AI.result: The clean-label temporal attack achieves ASR of 1.00 in strongest configurations. Defenses collapsing the time axis are blind by construction. Feature-space defenses detect poisoning only in limited settings. The proposed per-step event mass detector successfully identifies the temporal transformations, exposing the attack's stealth boundary.
AI.conclusion: Clean-label temporal backdoor attacks pose a credible threat to SNNs that existing rate-collapsed defenses cannot address. However, the attack's stealth is imperfect, as temporal-aware detection methods can expose the manipulation. This establishes a new attack-defense axis in neuromorphic security research.

title: Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation
summary: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Explorative Modeling (XM), a new paradigm that shifts factorization from the generation procedure to the training loop. By exploring K candidate matches between generated outputs and data, then training on the best match, XMs force predictions to commit to modes rather than blurring them. This approach serves both as a third pretraining axis (scaling exploration improves performance beyond scaling data/parameters) and as a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, achieving strong results across images, video, and language.
AI.motivation: Despite the success of end-to-end training in deep learning, generative modeling remains an exception—existing scalable approaches factor the generation procedure to handle multi-modal distributions, which prevents true end-to-end generation. The authors aim to resolve this by rethinking where factorization occurs: moving it from generation to training.
AI.method: Explorative Models (XMs) factor the training loop rather than the generation process. During training, the model explores K candidate matches between its generated outputs and the data distribution, selecting the best match for optimization. This forces the model to commit to specific modes instead of producing blurred averages across modes. The approach is evaluated across continuous and discrete domains (images, video, language) and tested as both an add-on pretraining axis for existing models and as a standalone end-to-end generative framework.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) Scaling exploration yields monotonic performance improvements—gains increase from 7% to 36% as data scales, 13% to 23% as models grow, and efficiency gains more than double at 3x compute. (2) Exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, and parameter efficiency by 47%. (3) Achieves near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet-128 without guidance. (4) XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion model performance on control tasks with 16–256x fewer inference steps.
AI.conclusion: XMs establish a fundamentally new axis for scaling generative models—beyond data and parameters—and simultaneously offer a viable end-to-end generative modeling paradigm. The results demonstrate that factoring the training loop rather than the generation process is both theoretically sound and practically impactful across modalities.

title: From Single- to Cross-Document: Benchmarking Multi-Granularity Event Analysis of Large Language Models
comment: 9 pages. Published in the Proceedings of the 49th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR 2026)
summary: Event analysis is an essential and fundamental direction of information extraction, involving various event-centric tasks at different granularity of documents. While large language models (LLMs) have preliminarily achieved promising performance in part of these tasks individually, their capability in event analysis still lacks comprehensive understanding due to restricted document granularity, task designs, and data source of existing benchmarks. To address these limitations, we introduce MiGUE-Bench, a systematic benchmark for assessing the performance of LLMs in multi-granularity event analysis. To support large-scale evaluation, we first develop an LLM-driven self-correcting annotation framework called MiGUE-Pipeline, enabling scalable acquisition of high-quality source data of events with automatic labels. Then, we design four core tasks in our benchmark, i.e., event detection, relation reasoning, structure induction, and future prediction, to probe model competence at different levels, from atomic event details to complex cross-document narratives. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods delineate the current capability boundary and identify critical deficiencies, providing insights into the future improvement of LLMs in challenging event analysis tasks.

AI.tldr: MiGUE-Bench is a multi-granularity event analysis benchmark for LLMs, built using an LLM-driven self-correcting annotation pipeline, covering event detection, relation reasoning, structure induction, and future prediction across document granularities.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluations for event analysis are limited by narrow document granularity, constrained task designs, and restricted data sources, leaving a gap in comprehensive understanding of LLM capabilities in this domain.
AI.method: The authors introduce MiGUE-Pipeline, an LLM-driven self-correcting annotation framework for scalable, high-quality event data acquisition with automatic labels. They then design MiGUE-Bench with four core tasks — event detection, relation reasoning, structure induction, and future prediction — spanning atomic event details to cross-document narratives. Extensive experiments compare state-of-the-art LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) methods.
AI.result: Experiments delineate the current capability boundary of state-of-the-art LLMs and RAG methods, identifying critical deficiencies across the four tasks and various document granularities.
AI.conclusion: MiGUE-Bench provides a systematic framework for assessing LLMs in multi-granularity event analysis, revealing significant room for improvement and offering insights to guide future research in challenging event-centric tasks.

title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
summary: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current AI literacy frameworks, focused on technical competency and responsible use, reduce individuals to consumers. Drawing on Foucault and Freire, it proposes a critical AI literacy model centered on epistemic agency through contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance, while addressing structural inequities in AI access.
AI.motivation: Existing AI literacy frameworks are insufficient because they enforce a consumer orientation toward AI, failing to equip individuals with genuine epistemic agency to critically evaluate, resist, and shape AI systems. As generative AI becomes a dominant system of knowledge production, questions of access and participation in that production become urgent.
AI.method: The paper employs a theoretical-conceptual methodology, synthesizing Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and digital literacy scholarship to critique current AI literacy models and construct an alternative framework.
AI.result: A reconceptualized three-part framework for AI literacy is proposed: (1) contextual use — using AI tools with awareness of their situatedness; (2) critical interrogation — evaluating and resisting the structuring assumptions embedded in AI systems; and (3) participatory governance — engaging in the collective shaping and oversight of AI. The framework recasts literacy as the cultivation of epistemic agents rather than competent consumers.
AI.conclusion: AI literacy must be reimagined as a critical, emancipatory practice that addresses structural epistemic injustices reproduced by unequal AI access. A literacy framework oriented toward empowerment, not mere competency, is essential for fostering genuine democratic participation in AI-mediated knowledge production.

title: From Textual Requirements to Microservice Architectures - A Comprehensive Evaluation of LLM-Based Design Synthesis
summary: Microservice architectures have become dominant for modernizing monolithic systems, yet identifying appropriate services remains challenging and largely manual. Existing decomposition approaches are predominantly code-centric, limiting applicability in early design stages where only textual requirements are available. Despite advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), limited empirical evidence exists on their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures from natural-language requirements, including service definitions and inter-service interactions. This study investigates whether an LLM can bridge requirements engineering and architectural design, generating architectures solely from textual requirements and evaluating structural agreement and perceived quality of results. We conduct a mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), one execution per system/condition. Architectures are evaluated through (i) comparison with reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery, and (ii) a blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, plus open feedback synthesis. OpenAI o3 identifies services with higher agreement under FS prompting (F1 = 0.79 for ZS versus = 0.97 for FS). Communication recovery is more challenging: ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1 = 0.61), while FS improves agreement, reaching F1 = 0.82 and reducing unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation corroborates these results, with FS architectures perceived as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs. OpenAI o3 shows potential for requirements-driven synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. Results are model- and context-specific from two small systems, not model-independent proof.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates whether OpenAI o3 can generate microservice architectures directly from textual requirements. Using zero-shot and few-shot prompting on two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic), few-shot prompting achieves strong service identification (F1=0.97 vs. 0.79) and improved communication recovery (F1=0.82 vs. 0.61). Expert assessment confirms few-shot outputs are more modular, coherent, and plausible, demonstrating LLM potential for requirements-driven architectural synthesis when guided by exemplars—though results are model- and context-specific.
AI.motivation: Microservice decomposition remains manual and challenging. Existing approaches are code-centric, limiting their use in early design stages where only textual requirements exist. Despite LLM advances, little empirical evidence examines their ability to synthesize complete microservice architectures (services and inter-service interactions) from natural-language requirements alone.
AI.method: A mixed-method study using OpenAI o3 under zero-shot (ZS) and few-shot (FS) prompting, with one execution per system/condition across two systems (Bookstore, PetClinic). Evaluation combines: (i) quantitative comparison against reference architectures using precision, recall, and F1-score for service identification and communication recovery; and (ii) a blinded expert assessment of correctness, completeness, modularity, and plausibility, supplemented by open feedback synthesis.
AI.result: Few-shot prompting yields substantially higher service identification agreement (F1: FS=0.97 vs. ZS=0.79). Communication recovery is harder: ZS produces dense architectures with high recall but low precision (F1=0.61), while FS improves to F1=0.82 by reducing unsupported dependencies. Expert evaluation aligns with quantitative results, rating FS architectures as more modular, coherent, and plausible than ZS outputs.
AI.conclusion: OpenAI o3 demonstrates potential for requirements-driven microservice synthesis when guided by exemplar prompting. However, findings are model- and context-specific (two small systems) and do not constitute model-independent proof. Further research on broader systems and diverse LLMs is needed.

title: AskChem: Claim-Centered Infrastructure for Chemistry Literature Synthesis
summary: Chemistry literature synthesis often requires assembling specific findings scattered across many publications, yet existing literature-search systems primarily return ranked document lists. As a result, scientists and AI agents need to locate relevant information, verify their provenance, and assemble cross-paper answers manually. We present AskChem, a claim-centered infrastructure for cross-paper chemistry search. AskChem changes the unit of retrieval from the paper to the provenance-carrying claim: each paper is converted into atomic, typed claims, each grounded by a source DOI and a verbatim quote or an explicit evidence locator. Over this shared claim store, AskChem exposes complementary structures for search and synthesis: a stabilized faceted taxonomy for hierarchical retrieval and browsing, an evidence graph linking claims through relations, and an exploratory living taxonomy that situates indexed papers under scientific principles. AskChem currently indexes 2.4M claims from 147K papers and provides a web interface, as well as REST, SDK, and MCP access for AI agents. On AskChem-Bench, grounding a GPT-5.5 reader in AskChem yields 100% resolvable DOIs, compared with 88.3% without retrieval, and the highest citation density among five tested systems. AskChem is live at https://askchem.org.

AI.tldr: AskChem introduces a claim-centered retrieval infrastructure for chemistry literature, converting papers into 2.4M atomic, provenance-carrying claims across 147K papers, with faceted taxonomy, evidence graphs, and living taxonomy for cross-paper synthesis, achieving 100% resolvable DOIs when grounding a GPT-5.5 reader.
AI.motivation: Existing literature-search systems return ranked document lists, forcing scientists and AI agents to manually locate, verify, and assemble cross-paper answers. This is inefficient for chemistry literature synthesis where findings are scattered across many publications.
AI.method: AskChem changes the retrieval unit from papers to provenance-carrying claims. Each paper is decomposed into atomic, typed claims grounded by source DOI and verbatim quote/evidence locator. Three complementary structures are built: (1) a stabilized faceted taxonomy for hierarchical retrieval/browsing, (2) an evidence graph linking claims through relations, and (3) an exploratory living taxonomy situating papers under scientific principles. Access is provided via web interface, REST API, SDK, and MCP for AI agents.
AI.result: The system indexes 2.4M claims from 147K papers. On AskChem-Bench, grounding a GPT-5.5 reader in AskChem achieves 100% resolvable DOIs (vs. 88.3% without retrieval) and the highest citation density among five tested systems.
AI.conclusion: A claim-centered architecture with provenance grounding significantly improves cross-paper synthesis accuracy and citation fidelity for chemistry literature search, outperforming traditional document-ranked retrieval systems.

title: Checking Information Flow in Cloud-based IoT Access Control Policies (Extended Version)
summary: Many cloud providers for IoT technologies offer access control mechanisms whose proper configuration is critical for security. However, verifying permissions in isolation is insufficient in a setting where devices have different levels of trust or are compartmentalised in various subsystems. This work analyses IoT access control policies to identify potential security vulnerabilities from unwanted information flow between devices. To this end, we formally model AWS IoT Core's components and define an information flow graph to capture the communication among devices permitted by the access control policies. We build a finite representation of the graph by leveraging an SMT solver, thus enabling the verification of information flow between devices. We implement our approach in a tool called IOT:POKER, and assess it on a realistic scenario and several real-world policies.

AI.tldr: This paper presents IOT:POKER, a tool that formally models AWS IoT Core access control policies and uses SMT solving to detect unwanted information flow between IoT devices, addressing security vulnerabilities arising from cross-device communication in compartmentalised environments.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches verify IoT access control permissions in isolation, which is insufficient when devices operate across different trust levels or subsystems. Improperly configured policies can create indirect information flow paths between devices that should be segregated, leading to security breaches that isolated permission checks cannot detect.
AI.method: The authors formally model AWS IoT Core components, define an information flow graph capturing permitted device-to-device communication, and build a finite representation of this graph using an SMT (Satisfiability Modulo Theories) solver. This enables verification of whether information can flow between any pair of devices. The approach is implemented in the IOT:POKER tool.
AI.result: The approach was evaluated on a realistic IoT scenario and several real-world AWS IoT Core policies, demonstrating its ability to identify unintended information flow paths that isolated permission verification would miss.
AI.conclusion: Verifying IoT access control policies for information flow properties, rather than isolated permissions, is essential for security in compartmentalised environments. The IOT:POKER tool provides a practical, SMT-based solution for this verification on AWS IoT Core.

title: The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise
summary: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

AI.tldr: First convergence guarantees for plain vector-form Adam under heavy-tailed noise (bounded p-th moment, p∈(1,2]) are established using a generalized online-to-nonconvex framework. Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points but exhibits suboptimal iteration complexity that is p-dependent; optimal rates are recovered when domain radius is known.
AI.motivation: Adam's behavior under heavy-tailed stochastic gradients—where only a bounded p-th central moment exists for p∈(1,2]—is poorly understood despite this setting being common in deep learning. Prior work focused on bounded-variance assumptions or required Adam variants; plain Adam lacks convergence guarantees in the heavy-tailed regime.
AI.method: The authors generalize the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to handle heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. They then develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling, enabling convergence analysis under the weaker p-th moment condition.
AI.result: Adam converges to (ρ,ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise but with suboptimal, p-dependent iteration complexity—this suboptimality persists even when p=2 (bounded variance). When domain radius is known and used to control online-learner outputs, the convergence rate improves to match optimal complexity.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals both the robustness and limitations of plain Adam in heavy-tailed regimes: while convergence is guaranteed, inherent suboptimality exists unless additional structural knowledge (domain radius) is leveraged, providing new theoretical insight into Adam's behavior beyond the bounded-variance setting.

title: ICLE++: Modeling Fine-Grained Traits for Holistic Essay Scoring
comment: Accepted as a long paper to NAACL 2024
summary: The majority of the recently-developed models for automated essay scoring (AES) are evaluated solely on the ASAP corpus. However, ASAP is not without its limitations. For instance, it is not clear whether models trained on ASAP can generalize well when evaluated on other corpora. In light of these limitations, we introduce ICLE++, a corpus of persuasive student essays annotated with both holistic scores and trait-specific scores. Not only can ICLE++ be used to test the generalizability of AES models trained on ASAP, but it can also facilitate the evaluation of models developed for newer AES problems such as multi-trait scoring and cross-prompt scoring. We believe that ICLE++, which represents a culmination of our long-term effort in annotating the essays in the ICLE corpus, contributes to the set of much-needed annotated corpora for AES research.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ICLE++, a new annotated corpus of persuasive student essays with both holistic and trait-specific scores, designed to address the over-reliance on the ASAP corpus in automated essay scoring (AES) research. It enables evaluation of model generalizability, multi-trait scoring, and cross-prompt scoring.
AI.motivation: Most AES models are evaluated exclusively on the ASAP corpus, which raises concerns about generalizability to other datasets. The field also lacks annotated corpora for emerging AES tasks like multi-trait scoring and cross-prompt scoring. ICLE++ is introduced to fill these gaps.
AI.method: The authors annotated the existing ICLE corpus of persuasive student essays with both holistic scores and trait-specific scores through a long-term annotation effort, resulting in the ICLE++ corpus.
AI.result: ICLE++ serves as an evaluation benchmark that can test the generalizability of AES models trained on ASAP, and supports evaluation of models for multi-trait scoring and cross-prompt scoring tasks.
AI.conclusion: ICLE++ represents a significant contribution to AES research by providing a much-needed additional annotated corpus, mitigating the field's over-dependence on ASAP and enabling broader, more robust evaluation of AES models.

title: Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation
summary: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

AI.tldr: GPT-4 generates new product ideas that outperform human-created ones on purchase intent (7x more likely to be top-tier), but AI ideas are less novel and more similar to each other, especially with few-shot prompting.
AI.motivation: To empirically evaluate whether LLMs can effectively contribute to the front end of new product development by generating commercially viable product ideas, and to quantify the trade-offs between AI and human creativity.
AI.method: Three pools of product ideas (college-student-targeted, ≤$50) were compared: (1) human-generated ideas from a product design course, (2) GPT-4 zero-shot ideas, and (3) GPT-4 few-shot ideas. Purchase intent was measured via standard market research techniques; text mining assessed pairwise similarity; human raters scored novelty. Top-idea quality was also analyzed.
AI.result: AI-generated ideas achieved higher average purchase intent than human ideas (few-shot > zero-shot). However, AI ideas were rated less novel and showed higher pairwise similarity, especially under few-shot prompting, indicating reduced diversity. Critically, AI ideas were 7x more likely to rank in the top 10%, a conservative advantage given AI's higher productivity.
AI.conclusion: LLMs offer substantial, productivity-weighted advantages for high-quality idea generation in new product development, despite drawbacks in novelty and diversity. The 7:1 top-idea advantage likely underestimates AI's practical value.

title: Structural Validation of LLM-Generated Microservice Decompositions Using Source-Code Dependencies
summary: Decomposing monolithic systems into microservices is a key activity in software modernization. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate semantically plausible decompositions from textual requirements, it remains unclear whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies implemented in the source code. This paper evaluates the structural adherence of microservice decompositions generated by OpenAI o3 for the PetClinic and Bookstore systems. We propose an automated validation pipeline based on static dependency analysis and compare zero-shot and few-shot prompting using dependency preservation (TPD) and dependency violation (TVD) metrics. A robustness analysis was conducted to control for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage. After normalization, both prompting strategies produced equivalent structural adherence, achieving TPD values of 68.0% (PetClinic) and 83.3% (Bookstore). The findings demonstrate that structural evaluations of LLM-generated decompositions should explicitly control for mapping coverage, as apparent differences between prompting strategies may otherwise reflect methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.

AI.tldr: LLM-generated microservice decompositions show equivalent structural adherence across prompting strategies after controlling for mapping coverage, with TPD of 68% (PetClinic) and 83.3% (Bookstore). Apparent differences may stem from methodological bias rather than genuine architectural quality.
AI.motivation: While LLMs can generate semantically plausible microservice decompositions from textual requirements, it is unknown whether these proposals preserve the structural dependencies actually implemented in source code. The paper aims to fill this gap by quantitatively evaluating structural adherence.
AI.method: An automated validation pipeline using static dependency analysis was built to evaluate decompositions of the PetClinic and Bookstore systems generated by OpenAI o3. Zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies were compared using two metrics: True Positive Dependencies (TPD — preserved dependencies) and True Violation Dependencies (TVD — violated dependencies). A robustness analysis was performed to normalize for differences in class-to-service mapping coverage.
AI.result: Before normalization, prompting strategies appeared to differ in structural adherence. After controlling for mapping coverage, both strategies yielded equivalent results: TPD of 68.0% for PetClinic and 83.3% for Bookstore. The initial differences were attributable to methodological bias rather than genuine differences in decomposition quality.
AI.conclusion: Structural evaluations of LLM-generated microservice decompositions must explicitly control for mapping coverage to avoid conflating methodological artifacts with architectural quality. Both zero-shot and few-shot prompting can achieve comparable structural adherence when this factor is normalized.

title: Agent Harness Distillation: Inference-Time Harness Extraction and Exploitation in Autonomous Multi-Agent Systems
comment: This work is currently in progress
summary: Autonomous multi-agent systems (AMAS) built on large language models (LLMs), such as Hermes, increasingly rely on inference-time harnesses to coordinate reasoning and action. Constructing these harnesses requires substantial engineering effort and computational resources, as they are iteratively optimized over a combinatorial search space while co-evolving with the underlying LLM. Inference-time harnesses therefore constitute valuable intellectual property (IP). Although prior work has investigated IP leakage in static multi-agent systems with pre-configured architectures, it remains unclear whether similar risks arise in AMAS, where harness behavior emerges dynamically during inference. To address this gap, we introduce Agent Harness Distillation (AHD), a framework for studying the security risks arising from inference-time harness extraction in AMAS. We formalize harness extraction as a new security problem and develop an evaluation framework for quantifying such risks. AHD extracts inference-time harness capabilities from a target agent through black-box interactions and consists of two stages. In the pre-distillation stage, AHD infers inference-time harness behaviors from the responses of the target agent and constructs an initial harness. In the post-distillation stage, AHD iteratively refines the initial harness to align with the behavioral patterns of the target agent. Experiments on real-world AMAS across multiple backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of AHD and reveal substantial IP leakage risks. We further propose a deception-based defense that reduces harness extraction effectiveness while preserving the utility of the protected agent. Our findings uncover a previously underexplored security threat to AMAS.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Agent Harness Distillation (AHD), a framework for extracting inference-time coordination mechanisms from autonomous multi-agent systems (AMAS) via black-box interactions, revealing significant intellectual property leakage risks. The authors also propose a deception-based defense to mitigate extraction while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Autonomous multi-agent systems (AMAS) built on LLMs use inference-time harnesses for coordinating reasoning and action, which are costly to develop and constitute valuable IP. While IP leakage has been studied in static multi-agent systems, it is unclear whether similar risks exist in AMAS where harness behavior emerges dynamically during inference. This gap motivates the investigation.
AI.method: The authors formalize harness extraction as a security problem and propose AHD, a two-stage black-box extraction framework. In the pre-distillation stage, AHD infers harness behaviors from target agent responses and constructs an initial harness. In the post-distillation stage, the initial harness is iteratively refined to align with the target agent's behavioral patterns. A deception-based defense is also proposed to reduce extraction effectiveness.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world AMAS across multiple backbone LLMs demonstrate AHD's effectiveness in extracting inference-time harnesses, revealing substantial IP leakage risks. The proposed deception-based defense reduces harness extraction effectiveness while maintaining the protected agent's utility.
AI.conclusion: The findings uncover a previously underexplored security threat to AMAS: inference-time harness extraction via black-box access. The work highlights the need for defenses in dynamically coordinated multi-agent LLM systems.

title: FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize
summary: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

AI.tldr: FunL2O introduces a unified framework that automates feature function design for learning-to-optimize (L2O) pipelines using LLM-driven program evolution in a FunSearch-style loop, consistently outperforming hand-crafted features across continuous and discrete optimization tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing L2O methods rely on hand-crafted feature functions to map problem instances to ML model inputs — a manual, domain-specific, and largely overlooked bottleneck that limits generality and scalability across optimization tasks.
AI.method: FunL2O employs a FunSearch-style evolutionary loop where an LLM proposes executable feature functions, which are then evaluated by retraining the original L2O model and measuring downstream optimization performance. The best-performing features are retained and used as seeds for subsequent iterations.
AI.result: Evaluated on linear/quadratic programming (solution prediction, warm-starting) and mixed-integer optimization (GNN-guided backdoor branching, Predict-and-Search) across four LLMs, evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is established as a general, effective, and automatable approach to representation design in L2O, eliminating the manual bottleneck of feature engineering.

title: Recall Before You Rank: Similarity-Guided Top-$K$ Reuse for Efficient Long-Context Attention
summary: Top-$K$ sparse attention reduces the cost of Softmax and value aggregation by attending to only a small subset of key--value (KV) entries. However, identifying this subset still requires scoring the current query against the full KV cache and performing global Top-$K$ selection, leaving selector cost linear in context length and limiting the practical efficiency of sparse attention for long-context decoding. In this paper, we introduce ReTopK, a training-free method that accelerates dynamic Top-$K$ attention by reusing historical retrieval decisions. ReTopK builds on the observation that similar queries often attend to overlapping supports and that partially overlapping supports can still preserve most of the Exact Top-$K$ attention mass. For each attention head, it maintains a bounded cache of historical query--support pairs, retrieves the most similar cached queries for each new query, unions their stored supports with a recent window, and reranks only the resulting compact candidate set using exact current-query scores. A similarity-based fallback invokes full-history Exact Top-$K$ when reuse is unreliable, while periodic exact refreshes limit cache drift. ReTopK retains the complete KV cache and reuses only selected indices, rather than historical scores, attention weights, or outputs. Across 16K--128K contexts, ReTopK achieves the lowest PG19 perplexity and the highest NIAH and LongBench scores among the evaluated approximate methods. At 128K with $K=512$, ReTopK incurs only a 0.50\% perplexity increase over Exact Top-$K$ while accelerating attention computation by $3.07\times$.

AI.tldr: ReTopK accelerates dynamic Top-K sparse attention by reusing historical query-support pairs to avoid scoring the full KV cache, achieving 3.07× speedup at 128K context length with only 0.50% perplexity degradation over Exact Top-K.
AI.motivation: Top-K sparse attention reduces Softmax and value aggregation costs, but identifying the top-K KV entries still requires scoring against the full KV cache, making selector cost linear in context length and limiting practical efficiency for long-context decoding.
AI.method: ReTopK maintains a bounded cache of historical query–support pairs per attention head. For each new query, it retrieves the most similar cached queries, unions their stored supports with a recent window, and reranks only the resulting compact candidate set using exact current-query scores. A similarity-based fallback invokes full Exact Top-K when reuse is unreliable, and periodic exact refreshes limit cache drift. Only selected indices are reused, not historical scores or attention weights.
AI.result: Across 16K–128K contexts, ReTopK achieves the lowest PG19 perplexity and highest NIAH and LongBench scores among evaluated approximate methods. At 128K with K=512, it incurs only 0.50% perplexity increase over Exact Top-K while accelerating attention by 3.07×.
AI.conclusion: ReTopK demonstrates that reusing historical retrieval decisions is an effective, training-free approach to accelerate Top-K sparse attention, preserving near-exact attention quality while substantially reducing selector overhead in long-context decoding.

title: Demystifying Solana Bots: From GitHub Blueprints to On-Chain Fingerprints
summary: Solana is an emerging blockchain platform designed for high throughput and low transaction fees, making it inexpensive to submit transactions at scale and, consequently, increasing exposure to bot spamming and related financial exploitation. Solana bots are typically off-chain software systems that operate in a competitive on-chain execution environment by constructing and submitting transactions, and the bot-related transactions on the decentralized exchanges exceed 250 million dollars in daily trading volume in January 2026. Prior studies on Solana have examined system performance, smart-contract security, and specific on-chain phenomena. However, we still lack a systematic understanding of what Solana bots implement in practice and how these implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints. To address this gap, we performed a large-scale empirical study of Solana bots from two complementary views: (i) 586 bot repositories collected from GitHub, and (ii) 200 bot addresses on Solana, with over 44 million on-chain transactions. Our study derives an implementation-grounded taxonomy of Solana bots comprising 15 categories grouped into five domains (e.g., Trading Operations, MEV, and On-chain Analytics), identifies a largely shared five-stage operational pipeline manifested in bot implementations, and uncovers systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors of Solana bots across diverse trading platforms and assets. Based on our findings, we highlight future research directions, and provide recommendations for building and operating bots on the Solana blockchain.

AI.tldr: A large-scale empirical study analyzing Solana bots from 586 GitHub repositories and 200 on-chain addresses (~44M transactions), deriving a taxonomy of 15 bot categories across 5 domains, identifying a common five-stage operational pipeline, and characterizing systematic variations in on-chain trading behaviors.
AI.motivation: Solana's high throughput and low fees incentivize bot activity, with bot-related DEX transactions exceeding $250M daily. Despite prior work on Solana's performance, security, and specific on-chain phenomena, there is no systematic understanding of how Solana bots are actually implemented or how those implementations manifest as observable on-chain execution fingerprints.
AI.method: Dual-view empirical analysis: (1) mining 586 bot repositories from GitHub to analyze implementation patterns, and (2) collecting 200 bot addresses on Solana with over 44 million on-chain transactions to characterize runtime behavior. The study synthesizes these two views to derive a taxonomy and operational pipeline model.
AI.result: An implementation-grounded taxonomy of 15 bot categories organized into 5 domains (Trading Operations, MEV, On-chain Analytics, etc.). A largely shared five-stage operational pipeline was identified across bot implementations. Systematic variation in on-chain trading behaviors was uncovered across different trading platforms and asset types.
AI.conclusion: The study provides the first systematic characterization of Solana bots, bridging the gap between off-chain implementation and on-chain behavior. The authors propose future research directions and offer practical recommendations for building and operating bots on Solana.

title: Piggybacking on Perception: Stealthy Concurrent Audio Prompt Injections against Multimodal LLM Agents
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Limax666/AudioAgentSecurity
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-driven multimodal agents are increasingly deployed to execute autonomous tasks via continuous audio interaction. While this paradigm enhances interaction naturalness, it introduces a critical yet under-explored attack surface, as audio inputs inevitably contain environmental noise beyond user control. In this paper, we investigate concurrent audio prompt injection attacks targeting multimodal agents. Distinct from traditional acoustic attacks on voice devices, we propose novel techniques for instruction augmentation and scenario concealment. These methods allow malicious audio instructions to imperceptibly "piggyback" onto user speech, thereby hijacking agents to execute malicious actions. To systematically quantify this threat, we construct AudioAgentSecurity, the first comprehensive benchmark for audio instruction injection attacks, encompassing 8 real-world task scenarios and 10 distinct attack patterns. We evaluate 11 state-of-the-art agents, including Gemini 3 Pro and GPT-4o-audio. Notably, our methods achieve an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 69.10\% against the advanced Gemini 3 Pro. To counter this threat, we further introduce Cascaded Audio Decoupling and Verification (CADV), a defense mechanism based on source separation and consistency analysis. Compared with existing prompt-level defenses, CADV leverages acoustic source separation and cross-modal consistency analysis to detect audio instruction injections more robustly, achieving over 90\% detection success across diverse attack vectors. Finally, real-world experiments with human volunteers on Doubao AI Smartphone in diverse dynamic real-world scenarios confirm the attacks' high stealth and efficacy, while demonstrating that our defense reliably mitigates these vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates "concurrent audio prompt injection" attacks on LLM-driven multimodal agents, where malicious audio instructions are imperceptibly overlaid onto user speech to hijack agent behavior. The authors construct AudioAgentSecurity, a benchmark with 8 scenarios and 10 attack patterns, evaluate 11 state-of-the-art agents (achieving 69.10% ASR against Gemini 3 Pro), and propose CADV, a defense using source separation and cross-modal consistency analysis that achieves >90% detection success.
AI.motivation: LLM-driven multimodal agents increasingly rely on continuous audio interaction, but audio inputs inevitably contain environmental noise beyond user control. This creates a critical yet underexplored attack surface where adversaries can inject malicious audio instructions concurrently with legitimate user speech. Traditional acoustic attacks on voice devices do not address the unique challenges of this multimodal agent paradigm, motivating a systematic investigation of concurrent audio prompt injection.
AI.method: The authors propose two novel attack techniques: (1) instruction augmentation — crafting malicious audio prompts that semantically blend with benign user commands, and (2) scenario concealment — hiding attacks within plausible environmental sounds. A comprehensive benchmark, AudioAgentSecurity, is constructed with 8 real-world tasks and 10 attack patterns. For defense, they introduce Cascaded Audio Decoupling and Verification (CADV), which combines acoustic source separation (to isolate potential injection signals) with cross-modal consistency analysis (comparing audio-derived instructions against expected multimodal coherence).
AI.result: The proposed attack methods achieve an average Attack Success Rate (ASR) of 69.10% against Gemini 3 Pro, the most advanced agent tested. Across 11 evaluated agents, the attacks demonstrate broad effectiveness. The CADV defense achieves over 90% detection success across diverse attack vectors, outperforming existing prompt-level defenses. Real-world experiments on the Doubao AI Smartphone with human volunteers confirm both high attack stealth/efficacy and reliable defense mitigation in dynamic environments.
AI.conclusion: Concurrent audio prompt injection represents a serious and practical threat to LLM-driven multimodal agents, with attacks proving both highly stealthy and effective in real-world settings. The CADV defense, leveraging source separation and cross-modal consistency analysis, provides robust mitigation superior to prompt-level defenses. The AudioAgentSecurity benchmark establishes a foundation for future research on audio-based adversarial robustness in multimodal agent systems.

title: ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders
comment: Research paper. Includes supplementary material and publicly available source code
summary: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

AI.tldr: ECG-InterpBench is a benchmark that systematically evaluates the interpretability of ECG foundation model representations using sparse autoencoders with controlled capacity matching. It assesses six models across 450 experimental cells, measuring sparse reconstruction fidelity, clinical feature accessibility, and cross-seed reproducibility, revealing distinct interpretability profiles that differ from downstream performance rankings.
AI.motivation: Existing ECG foundation model benchmarks focus solely on downstream predictive performance, neglecting whether internal representations are decomposable, clinically interpretable, or reproducible. This gap hinders trust, transparency, and scientific independent verification.
AI.method: ECG-InterpBench employs sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments with capacity matched across models (dictionary width, encoder depth). Six frozen ECG foundation models are evaluated at five encoder depths, five dictionary widths, and three random seeds, yielding a 450-cell atlas. Three complementary dimensions are assessed: (1) sparse reconstruction fidelity, (2) single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinical ECG measurements, and (3) cross-seed feature reproducibility. Patient-sampling uncertainty, depth/seed-dependent variation, and sparsity sensitivity are also quantified.
AI.result: ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. Reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms this divergence, demonstrating that interpretability rankings do not simply mirror performance rankings.
AI.conclusion: ECG-InterpBench provides a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework that complements performance-centered benchmarks by enabling rigorous comparison of ECG foundation models along distinct interpretability dimensions. It includes executable code, standardized manifests, and reproducibility audits.

title: A Sparse Glimpse of the Whole: Train-Free Self-Speculative Decoding
summary: Speculative decoding alleviates the memory-bandwidth bottleneck in large language model inference, but its acceleration is jointly constrained by drafting overhead, token acceptance, and speculation length. We present a unified efficiency analysis showing that extending the speculation horizon can reduce rather than improve speedup when the marginal acceptance probability falls below the relative drafting cost. Guided by this analysis, we introduce SparseSpec-L, a training-free self-speculative decoding framework for long-context inference. SparseSpec-L generates lightweight drafts directly from the target model using a dynamically sparsified and recallable KV cache. It recycles per-head attention statistics produced during full-context verification as a no-extra-forward importance signal, allowing critical historical tokens to be recalled without permanently discarding the dense KV cache. An online entropy-based controller further selects the speculation length according to expected step-wise efficiency. Experiments across multiple long-context tasks and model scales show consistent end-to-end acceleration, with up to speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution.

AI.tldr: Speculative decoding speedup is bounded by a tradeoff between drafting cost and token acceptance; SparseSpec-L uses a dynamic sparse KV cache with entropy-based length control to accelerate long-context LLM inference training-free, achieving up to 2.71× speedup.
AI.motivation: Existing speculative decoding methods suffer from drafting overhead and fixed speculation lengths, which can hurt speedup when marginal acceptance probability drops below relative drafting cost—especially in long-context scenarios where KV cache management is critical.
AI.method: SparseSpec-L is a training-free self-speculative framework. It uses a dynamically sparsified, recallable KV cache for drafting, recycles per-head attention statistics from full-context verification as a cost-free importance signal to recall critical tokens, and employs an online entropy-based controller to adaptively select speculation length based on expected step-wise efficiency.
AI.result: Achieves up to 2.71× end-to-end speedup over autoregressive decoding across multiple long-context tasks and model scales while preserving the target model's output distribution.
AI.conclusion: Extending speculation length is only beneficial when marginal acceptance probability exceeds relative drafting cost. SparseSpec-L demonstrates that training-free, adaptive self-speculation with dynamic sparse KV cache management can yield substantial acceleration for long-context LLM inference without sacrificing output quality.

title: DeepResearch Agent System
summary: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

AI.tldr: A 30B-parameter sparse-activation LLM agent system for deep research achieves SOTA on multiple benchmarks via dual-mode reasoning, multi-tool coordination, GRPO-based RL optimization, and automated data synthesis — all open-sourced.
AI.motivation: To address the limitations of existing LLM agents in conducting deep, multi-step, autonomous research tasks requiring long-context reasoning, reliable tool use, and efficient inference — particularly the performance-efficiency trade-off in large dense models.
AI.method: (1) Sparse activation architecture: 30B total parameters, only 3B activated per token for 3.2× faster inference. (2) 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms. (3) Dual-mode reasoning engine: ReAct paradigm for basic tasks + IterResearch mode (up to 20 reasoning steps). (4) Multi-tool coordination integrating retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing. (5) GRPO-based reinforcement learning with token-level policy gradients. (6) Automated seed-based data synthesis pipeline.
AI.result: Hierarchical attention: +18.7% accuracy, +23.4% recall over standard long-context approaches. Dual-mode reasoning: +31.2% accuracy over single-pass baselines. Tool-use accuracy: 92.1%. GRPO-RL: +35% training stability, +42% convergence speed. Data synthesis: 92.5% usability rate. Benchmarks: 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, 91.2% on WebWalkerQA.
AI.conclusion: The DeepResearch Agent System demonstrates that a sparse-activation architecture combined with hierarchical attention, iterative multi-step reasoning, multi-tool integration, and GRPO-based RL optimization can achieve SOTA agentic research performance while maintaining inference efficiency. The system is fully open-sourced for applications in academia, business, R&D, and education.

title: Emerging Challenges in Threat Modeling for GenAI-Augmented Systems: A View from the Trenches
comment: Accepted at the 2026 International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM)
summary: Threat modeling remains a central task in secure software engineering, as it enables the identification of security issues from system architectures. As Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly pervasive across software systems, traditional threat modeling methods (e.g., STRIDE) are insufficient to assess emerging GenAI-specific risks. In this work, we present the first results from an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in a Small and Medium Enterprise (SME) setting. For this, we conducted a rapid literature review to select relevant techniques and systematically applied three shortlisted methods to an industrial case study involving a GenAI-augmented system. The results highlight differences in the threats identified by each technique and reveal limited support for certain GenAI-specific risk categories, particularly those related to software supply chains and human-centered security issues. We further report practitioners' perceptions of the usability and integration of these methods in SME development workflows, including their perceived effort and adoption challenges.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an exploratory assessment of GenAI-aware threat modeling methods in an SME context. Through a rapid literature review and an industrial case study, the authors applied three shortlisted techniques to a GenAI-augmented system, revealing gaps in coverage for GenAI-specific risks—particularly supply chain and human-centered threats—and capturing practitioner feedback on usability and adoption barriers.
AI.motivation: Traditional threat modeling methods like STRIDE are inadequate for addressing risks unique to Generative AI systems. As GenAI becomes pervasive in software, there is a pressing need to evaluate whether existing GenAI-aware threat modeling techniques are practical and effective, especially in resource-constrained SME environments.
AI.method: The authors conducted a rapid literature review to identify candidate GenAI-aware threat modeling methods, then shortlisted three. These were systematically applied to an industrial case study of a GenAI-augmented system within an SME. The study compared the threats identified by each method and gathered qualitative feedback from practitioners regarding usability, perceived effort, and integration challenges.
AI.result: The three methods produced notably different sets of identified threats, indicating inconsistency in coverage. All methods showed limited support for GenAI-specific risk categories, particularly software supply chain risks and human-centered security issues. Practitioners reported concerns about the effort required and challenges integrating these methods into existing SME development workflows.
AI.conclusion: Existing GenAI-aware threat modeling methods, while a step forward, exhibit significant gaps in coverage and face practical adoption hurdles in SME settings. The findings call for more comprehensive and usable threat modeling approaches tailored to GenAI-specific risks and the constraints of smaller organizations.

title: Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning on Clinical EEG Data
comment: 27 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. A version of this manuscript has been accepted for presentation at the International Workshop on Hot Topics at the Intersection of Distributed Machine Learning and Security (HotDiSec 2026), co-located with ESORICS 2026
summary: Federated learning enables multiple institutions to train shared models without exchanging raw clinical EEG data, but it does not fully prevent privacy leakage from individual model updates. This paper presents a privacy-preserving federated learning framework for clinical EEG data using masking-based secure aggregation as the core protection mechanism. The framework combines graph-based communication, threshold secret sharing, dropout-resilient aggregation, local update clipping, an optional Bloom filter-based privacy-preserving record-linkage initialization module, and auxiliary-notary-based verifiability. It supports both semi-honest and malicious aggregation settings and is implemented using the Flower federated learning framework. The secure-aggregation variants are evaluated in a simulated cross-silo healthcare setting using TUH EEG-derived data under different client configurations. Under the stated assumptions, the secure variants hide individual updates from the aggregation server. The results show that these variants remain compatible with federated model training, although malicious-setting safeguards and lightweight consistency-checking mechanisms introduce additional computation, communication, and round-duration overhead. The semi-honest variant provides the lowest overhead among the secure configurations, while malicious and auxiliary-notary variants offer stronger consistency, integrity, and lightweight verification support at higher cost.
