AI.tldr: A privacy-preserving federated learning framework for clinical EEG data that uses masking-based secure aggregation, supporting both semi-honest and malicious settings, with trade-offs between privacy strength and computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Standard federated learning for clinical EEG data still leaks privacy through individual model updates. Stronger protection is needed to prevent inference attacks on sensitive neural health data while maintaining model training utility.
AI.method: Masking-based secure aggregation framework combining graph-based communication, threshold secret sharing, dropout resilience, local update clipping, optional Bloom filter-based record linkage, and auxiliary-notary verifiability. Supports semi-honest, malicious, and auxiliary-notary variants, implemented on Flower FL framework and evaluated on TUH EEG data in cross-silo simulation.
AI.result: Secure variants successfully hide individual updates from the aggregation server. Semi-honest variant offers lowest overhead. Malicious and auxiliary-notary variants provide stronger consistency, integrity, and verification but incur higher computation, communication, and round-duration costs.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates viable privacy-utility trade-offs for clinical EEG federated learning, with the semi-honest variant suitable for trusted environments and the malicious/notary variants appropriate when stronger adversarial guarantees are required.

title: Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 29th International Conference on Information Fusion (IEEE FUSION)
summary:
Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

AI.tldr: Proposes Conditional Informer, a Transformer-based architecture that treats long-term ship trajectory prediction as conditional generation, where environmental context modulates vessel dynamics via cross-attention, and uses Modality Masking to handle missing sensor data.
AI.motivation: Existing Transformer-based methods treat vessels as isolated systems relying only on kinematic states, while multimodal approaches treat environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence where weather modulates vessel dynamics.
AI.method: Conditional Informer encoder-decoder with a Conditional Attention mechanism where vessel state queries environmental contexts via cross-attention, plus Modality Masking training strategy to prevent degradation during sensor fallback.
AI.result: Outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy with context available; Modality Masking reduces fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.
AI.conclusion: The Conditional Informer effectively encodes the physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions and, through Modality Masking, maintains robustness under intermittent sensor data.

title: Can LVLMs Uncover the Truth Behind Visual Illusions? An Analysis of Perceptual and Reasoning Capabilities
summary: Large Vision Language Models have integrated reasoning capabilities, elevating cognitive performance to new levels. However, existing evaluations either focus solely on perception or rely on specific domains such as maths or coding. Evaluation for reasoning capabilities that align with an open-world environment is still required, especially one that considers perception and reasoning jointly. To bridge this gap, we propose to evaluate LVLMs by exploiting visual illusions as a diagnostic tool. Visual illusions are phenomena in which the human visual system misinterprets objective signals, resulting in an understanding that deviates from reality. We constructed IllusionReasoning, a benchmark of illusion images collected from the real world, incorporating diverse annotated question-answer pairs. Based on IllusionReasoning, we show that the reasoning capabilities of a wide range of LVLMs are not as advanced as claimed. Our work provides new insights into LVLMs and offers future direction for optimisation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces IllusionReasoning, a benchmark using visual illusions to jointly evaluate perception and reasoning in Large Vision Language Models, revealing that their reasoning capabilities are not as advanced as claimed.
AI.motivation: Existing LVLM evaluations either focus solely on perception or are confined to specific domains (math, coding). There is a need for evaluation that jointly assesses perception and reasoning in open-world contexts.
AI.method: The authors construct IllusionReasoning, a benchmark comprising real-world visual illusion images with diverse annotated question-answer pairs, using illusions as a diagnostic tool where human perception deviates from objective reality.
AI.result: Evaluation across a wide range of LVLMs on IllusionReasoning demonstrates that their reasoning capabilities fall short of claimed performance levels.
AI.conclusion: The work offers new insights into LVLM limitations and suggests directions for future optimization, highlighting the importance of joint perception-reasoning evaluation.

title: What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering
summary: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a formal, constitutive definition of "prompt graph engineering" — treating prompts not as isolated strings but as nodes in explicit, executable, improvable graphs. It traces the concept's genealogy, establishes four defining conditions, uses them to include/exclude six real systems, and outlines a research agenda.
AI.motivation: Industry practice has converged on graph-structured prompt pipelines (chaining, routing, aggregation, retrieval interleaving), but the vocabulary and conceptual framework have not kept pace. Terms like "prompt engineering" still evoke crafting a single string, while frameworks (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow) already operationalize graphs. A precise, reference definition is missing.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis over scholarly sources with persistent identifiers, supplemented by primary grey literature. The authors reconstruct the genealogy from dataflow graphs and build systems through prompt chaining and thought topologies (chain, tree, graph) to compiled/optimized graph artifacts. They then propose a constitutive definition with four necessary conditions, operationalize them as an inclusion/exclusion test, and apply it to six real systems.
AI.result: The four defining conditions are: (1) explicit structure, (2) separation between structure and prompt content, (3) executable semantics, and (4) the graph as a first-class engineering artifact. The test consistently includes LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents while excluding six neighboring concepts. A research agenda is proposed along four design tension axes.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes an operational definition and shared vocabulary for a practice industry already performs daily but cannot name precisely. This fills a conceptual gap and provides a foundation for systematic research and engineering of graph-structured prompt systems.

title: CoGate: Confidence-Gated Co-Decoding for Secure Code Generation
summary: Large language models are widely used for code generation, but they can also produce insecure programs due to patterns learned from their pretraining data. Decoding-time steering has become an important solution to this problem: a small expert model is combined with the target model at each step to generate more secure code, which is referred to as co-decoding. However, the acceptance rule for existing co-decoding approaches does not consider the expert model's confidence. When the security expert is unconfident due to unseen patterns or out-of-distribution (OOD) contexts, its guidance can therefore be misleading. To address the challenge, we propose CoGate, a confidence-gated co-decoding approach that controls the expert's influence on the co-decoding process based on its confidence. We implement our approach and evaluate it across multiple LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) on several code generation benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, and CWEval). Our approach outperforms existing co-decoding methods (CoSec+) across multiple benchmarks, achieving up to a 12.6% gain of Func-Sec@10 on CWEval.

AI.tldr: Existing co-decoding methods for secure code generation do not account for the security expert model's confidence, leading to misleading guidance on OOD or unfamiliar patterns. CoGate introduces a confidence-gated mechanism that modulates the expert's influence based on its confidence, outperforming prior methods like CoSec+ across multiple LLMs and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large language models can generate insecure code due to patterns inherited from pretraining data. While decoding-time steering via a security expert (co-decoding) mitigates this, existing approaches naively accept the expert's guidance without considering its confidence. When the expert encounters out-of-distribution or unseen patterns, its low-confidence guidance can be misleading and degrade security performance.
AI.method: CoGate uses a confidence-gated co-decoding mechanism. At each decoding step, a security expert model provides guidance, but its influence is scaled or gated according to the expert's confidence score. When confidence is low (e.g., OOD contexts), the gate reduces the expert's sway, allowing the base model to dominate; when confidence is high, the expert's secure generation preferences are fully applied.
AI.result: CoGate was evaluated on four LLM backends (CodeGen, DeepSeek-Coder, Qwen-Coder, StarCoder) across three benchmarks (HumanEval, security suite, CWEval). It consistently outperforms the existing co-decoding baseline CoSec+, achieving up to a 12.6% gain in Func-Sec@10 on the CWEval benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Confidence-gating is an effective and principled enhancement to co-decoding for secure code generation, preventing low-confidence expert predictions from corrupting the generation process. CoGate establishes a new state-of-the-art among decoding-time steering approaches for code security.

title: Security of World-Model-Based Embodied AI: A Lifecycle of Threats, Defenses, and Evaluation
summary: World models give embodied AI a predictive core: they compress observations into states, simulate action-conditioned futures, and enable planning beyond reactive control. This predictive layer, however, opens a new security boundary-compromise can propagate from data, sensors, prompts, or feedback into physical action. Rather than treating world models as an isolated component, this survey traces threats across their entire lifecycle-from data construction and representation learning, through state grounding and imagination, to trajectory evaluation, execution, and long-term adaptation via memory and tools. We show that familiar attack families: poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection, trajectory manipulation, and supply-chain attacks take on distinct meanings when they corrupt world states, learned dynamics, affordance estimates, or safety costs. We also highlight a duality: world models can serve as runtime safety shields, yet when compromised or over-trusted they generate predictive safety illusions. The survey offers a lifecycle taxonomy, maps existing attacks to world-model security properties, outlines evaluation protocols for safety failures, and structures defenses across provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance.

AI.tldr: This survey examines security threats against world models in embodied AI across their entire lifecycle, mapping attack families (poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection) onto world-model-specific vulnerabilities. It highlights the dual nature of world models as both safety shields and sources of predictive illusion, and structures defenses across provenance, robust grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance.
AI.motivation: World models are increasingly central to embodied AI as predictive engines that compress observations, simulate futures, and enable planning. However, this predictive layer introduces a new security boundary where compromise can propagate from data, sensors, prompts, or feedback into physical action. Existing security literature treats world models as isolated components rather than examining threats across their full lifecycle.
AI.method: The paper conducts a comprehensive survey that traces threats across the entire world model lifecycle: data construction, representation learning, state grounding, imagination, trajectory evaluation, execution, and long-term adaptation (memory and tools). It proposes a lifecycle taxonomy, maps known attack families (poisoning, backdoors, adversarial examples, sensor spoofing, prompt injection, trajectory manipulation, supply-chain attacks) to world-model-specific security properties, and outlines evaluation protocols for safety failures.
AI.result: The survey reveals that conventional attack families acquire distinct semantics when applied to world models—corrupting world states, learned dynamics, affordance estimates, or safety costs. A key finding is the duality: world models can serve as runtime safety shields but, when compromised or over-trusted, generate predictive safety illusions that mask real dangers.
AI.conclusion: Securing world models requires a lifecycle-spanning defense strategy including provenance tracking, robust state grounding, uncertainty-aware prediction, trajectory gating, feedback auditing, and deployment assurance. The survey provides a structured framework for evaluating and mitigating safety failures in world-model-based embodied AI systems.

title: Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search
summary: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

AI.tldr: Contrastive critics used for action selection in reinforcement learning suffer from norm drift, miscalibration, and misranking, making them unsafe for maximizing. The paper decomposes these failures, shows that cosine normalization does not resolve them, and demonstrates that Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds where contrastive scores fail. The core insight: contrastive critics are useful as compatibility rankers but require a value-calibrated scalar for reliable action selection.
AI.motivation: Contrastive critics are increasingly deployed as value-like objectives for best-of-K selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. However, the paper identifies that even well-ranked contrastive scores can be unsafe to maximize directly, motivating a rigorous analysis of why and when these failures occur.
AI.method: The authors perform a controlled support decomposition of bilinear regret, attributing it primarily to norm drift. They evaluate cosine-bounded and hybrid critics on off-support action selection and calibration across four OGBench navigation tasks. They compare contrastive critics against Bellman-trained TD-Q in a parameter-matched function-class control. A training/readout decomposition isolates whether lost ordering stems from the cosine training objective or inference-time normalization. Realized costs are measured via simulator rollouts on PointMaze, AntMaze, HumanoidMaze, and an exact-Q* toy task.
AI.result: Cosine bounding does not eliminate the failure mode. Both cosine and hybrid critics select off-support actions and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across all four OGBench tasks and fail to order fixed-query actions by value. TD-Q succeeds at this ordering task. Simulator rollouts reveal significant single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-Q* toy, but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze where the controller self-corrects. The training/readout decomposition traces the ordering loss to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. False positives arise from norm drift, score saturation, and in-support misranking.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive critics remain valuable as compatibility rankers for navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar. Candidate maximization over contrastive scores is unreliable due to systematic false positives.

title: From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

AI.tldr: This study adapted the Implicit Association Test paradigm to probe racial sentiment bias in ChatGPT (GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, GPT-4T). A small ANOVA-detected effect of race on sentiment scores disappeared under sensitivity analysis and post-hoc corrections, yielding only weak, analysis-dependent evidence for bias. The authors highlight methodological limitations of sentiment scoring and call for interdisciplinary refinement of behavioral bias measures for LLMs.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce complex, non-linear, and opaque outputs, resembling unobservable human mental processes. Psychological methods like the Implicit Association Test (IAT) may therefore help audit LLM behavior for implicit racial bias — a pressing concern in high-stakes domains such as government and healthcare.
AI.method: Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories plus a race-agnostic control, yielding 126 prompts. Each prompt was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, and GPT-4T (378 total responses). Sentiment was scored by assigning positive-label source scores, negating negative-label scores, and zeroing neutral responses. A two-way ANOVA (racial condition × model) tested sentiment differences, followed by a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis and Tukey-corrected pairwise comparisons.
AI.result: The two-way ANOVA showed a small significant main effect of racial condition (p = .042, η²ₚ = .044), no effect of model (p = .933), and no interaction (p = .999). The effect was not significant under rank-transformed sensitivity analysis (p = .145), and no pairwise comparisons survived Tukey correction. An uncorrected European–Indigenous Australian comparison was significant but was selected post hoc and treated only as hypothesis-generating.
AI.conclusion: Evidence for racial sentiment differences in ChatGPT was weak and dependent on analytical choices. Sentiment scoring cannot disentangle genuine evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by prompts. The authors recommend design improvements — such as controlled prompt framing and multi-dimensional bias metrics — and advocate for interdisciplinary collaboration between psychology and AI safety to develop robust behavioral measures of model bias.

title: PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: SWE-bench-like benchmarks are widely used for evaluating LLM's issue resolution capability. They typically follow a common construction pipeline: each PR (Pull Request) is paired with its linked issue by extracting issue references from the PR description; the issue description is used as the problem statement, and the PR patch serves as the test oracle. However, due to the inherent complexity of developing and maintaining large repositories, such PR-Issue pairings are often misaligned in practice. In this work, we systematically study SWE-bench Verified instances, finding that 13.6% exhibit misalignment across five patterns in eleven fine-grained scenarios. To enable reliable and scalable construction of those benchmarks in the future, we propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system for checking PR-Issue misalignment in SWE-bench-like benchmarks. Specifically, PAIChecker adopts a three-phase design that combines specific pattern identification, cross-agent label synthesis, and code-level validation, thereby enabling more accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified detection. Experiments on SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual show that PAIchecker achieves the best performance across all four LLM backbones, reaching up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy, respectively.

AI.tldr: SWE-bench-like benchmarks suffer from PR-Issue misalignment (13.6% in SWE-bench Verified). The authors propose PAIChecker, a multi-agent system with three-phase detection, achieving up to 92.12% binary accuracy in identifying misalignments.
AI.motivation: PR-Issue pairings in SWE-bench-like benchmarks are often misaligned due to the complexity of large repository maintenance, undermining evaluation reliability. A systematic, scalable detection method is needed.
AI.method: PAIChecker is a multi-agent system with a three-phase design: (1) specific pattern identification, (2) cross-agent label synthesis, and (3) code-level validation. This enables accurate, generalizable, and progressively verified misalignment detection.
AI.result: On SWE-Gym and SWE-bench Multilingual, PAIChecker achieves up to 92.12% and 91.67% binary accuracy respectively, outperforming all baselines across four LLM backbones.
AI.conclusion: PR-Issue misalignment is a non-trivial problem affecting benchmark integrity. PAIChecker provides a reliable, scalable solution for constructing cleaner SWE-bench-like benchmarks in the future.

title: Implementing Homomorphic Encryption-Based Logic Locking in System-on-Chip Designs
summary: This study presents a logic locking scheme based on the binary Ring Learning With Errors algorithm, implemented in a RISC-V System-on-Chip design. Unlike traditional logic locking methods that require providing users with raw locking parameters, the proposed approach secures critical logic paths in the privilege switching process without exposing these sensitive parameters. The implemented locking module itself consumes 3519 Look-Up Tables and 2645 Registers, leading to an overall overhead of 6.0% in Look-Up Tables and 6.9% in Registers compared to the baseline system. The unlock process requires about 2.6 us, introducing moderate performance impact, primarily affecting system-level operations while preserving user-level computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: A logic locking scheme using binary Ring-LWE is proposed for RISC-V SoCs, securing privilege-switching paths without exposing sensitive locking parameters, with 6.0% LUT and 6.9% register overhead and ~2.6 μs unlock time.
AI.motivation: Traditional logic locking methods require disclosing raw locking parameters to users, creating a security vulnerability. The authors aim to develop a scheme that protects critical logic paths without exposing these sensitive parameters.
AI.method: The proposed approach employs the binary Ring Learning With Errors (Ring-LWE) algorithm as the basis for a logic locking module, integrated into a RISC-V System-on-Chip. The locking targets critical logic paths involved in the privilege switching process, and the Ring-LWE-based mechanism enables secure locking/unlocking without revealing raw locking parameters to end users.
AI.result: The locking module consumes 3,519 LUTs and 2,645 Registers, yielding an overall overhead of 6.0% (LUTs) and 6.9% (Registers) versus the baseline. The unlock process takes approximately 2.6 μs, introducing moderate performance overhead primarily at the system level while leaving user-level computational efficiency intact.
AI.conclusion: The binary Ring-LWE-based logic locking scheme successfully secures privilege switching in a RISC-V SoC with modest hardware overhead and acceptable unlock latency, demonstrating a practical trade-off between security and performance for hardware IP protection.

title: SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups
summary: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

AI.tldr: SE(3)-MeanFlow extends the MeanFlow framework to SE(3) for fast protein backbone generation, enabling high-quality sampling in few steps by working natively in the Lie algebra and using novel training objectives.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion and flow-matching models for protein backbone generation on SE(3)^N require hundreds of ODE integration steps, each with costly Lie group exponential maps, creating a bottleneck for high-throughput design. The goal is to reduce sampling steps while maintaining generation quality.
AI.method: SE(3)-MeanFlow operates natively in so(3) and R^3, deriving closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations to provide simulation-free training targets. An SE(3) alpha-Flow objective removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch as a warm-up stage. Training then switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss for pretraining and rectification-based post-training.
AI.result: SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps. Its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget, at a modest cost in diversity.
AI.conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow enables fast, high-quality protein backbone generation with significantly fewer sampling steps, making it suitable for high-throughput de novo protein design campaigns.

title: ChronoMem: Version Control and Semantic Rollback for Large Language Model Agent Memory
summary: LLM agents increasingly rely on long-term memory to support multi-session interaction and personalization. However, existing agent memory systems are designed around forward-only evolution, continuously accumulating, consolidating, and overwriting knowledge, with no principled mechanism to inspect, version, or revert prior states. This makes agents brittle under corrections, concept drift, and memory corruption, particularly after they have already been exposed to subsequent information. We present ChronoMem, a semantic version-control layer for agentic memory integrated into the production-ready, open-source Agent Development Kit by Google. ChronoMem commits whole-memory snapshots at each memory write, maintains structured version histories, and supports natural-language rollback requests by mapping undo intents to concrete historical versions through hybrid lexical and semantic retrieval, rank fusion, and reranking. We further introduce a post-exposure evaluation protocol that tests whether an agent can behave counterfactually after rollback by answering queries and summarizing history as if future updates had never occurred. On long-horizon conversational benchmarks augmented with evolving memory states and rollback tasks, ChronoMem substantially improves rollback-consistent question answering and history summarization relative to prompt-only and retrieval-only baselines, while achieving strong performance in semantic version selection. To our knowledge, ChronoMem is the first open-source system and benchmark for systematic semantic global memory rollback in LLM agents.

AI.tldr: ChronoMem introduces a semantic version-control layer for LLM agent memory that enables whole-memory snapshots, structured version histories, and natural-language rollback, significantly improving rollback-consistent QA and summarization over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems are forward-only — they accumulate and overwrite knowledge without any mechanism to inspect, version, or revert prior states. This makes agents brittle under corrections, concept drift, and memory corruption, especially after exposure to subsequent information.
AI.method: ChronoMem commits whole-memory snapshots at each write, maintains structured version histories, and supports natural-language rollback by mapping undo intents to concrete historical versions via hybrid lexical-semantic retrieval, rank fusion, and reranking. A post-exposure evaluation protocol tests counterfactual behavior after rollback. Integrated into Google's open-source Agent Development Kit.
AI.result: On long-horizon conversational benchmarks with evolving memory states and rollback tasks, ChronoMem substantially outperforms prompt-only and retrieval-only baselines in rollback-consistent QA and history summarization, with strong semantic version selection performance.
AI.conclusion: ChronoMem is the first open-source system and benchmark for systematic semantic global memory rollback in LLM agents, addressing a critical gap in agent memory management.

title: Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset
summary: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

AI.tldr: Hasse clustering is a pattern extraction algorithm for sequential data that suffers from combinatorial complexity with large numbers of expected clusters. The paper introduces a theory of gluing wiring diagrams to enable iterative applications of Hasse clustering, achieving the same result as a single application, and validates the approach on figure skating jump video classification.
AI.motivation: Hasse clustering becomes computationally infeasible as the number of expected clusters grows due to combinatorial complexity. The authors aim to overcome this limitation by enabling iterative (rather than single-shot) application of the algorithm without sacrificing correctness.
AI.method: The authors develop a theoretical framework based on "gluing wiring diagrams" that formalizes how multiple smaller Hasse clustering runs can be composed iteratively to produce the same result as one large run. The theory is empirically tested on video classification of figure skating jumps.
AI.result: The gluing wiring diagram theory successfully enables iterative Hasse clustering to achieve equivalent results to a single application. The approach is validated in the domain of figure skating jump classification from video data.
AI.conclusion: Iterative Hasse clustering via gluing wiring diagrams provides a scalable alternative to single-shot Hasse clustering, preserving correctness while mitigating combinatorial explosion. The method holds practical promise for real-world sequential data analysis tasks such as video classification.

title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, and 15 tables, including appendices
summary: Scaling coding agents requires a continuing supply of executable data for training, benchmarking, and continuous evaluation. Each task must couple a realistic software state with a specification, development tools, and reliable verification. To expand this supply, we present Change2Task, a system grounded in repository history that converts merged pull requests into verified tasks on healthy modern revisions of the same repository. It aligns historical evidence with evolved code, reconstructs task states through Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, or Agent Reconstruction, and validates the lifecycle from a healthy base to a task state and a restored state. By deriving multiple tasks grounded in developer evidence from maintained environments, Change2Task provides executable data for coding agent training and evaluation while reducing repeated environment setup, storage, and task construction effort. We evaluate the system through five common and widely adopted coding agent task families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, Application Programming Interface Migration, and Security Repair. Starting from 1,130 source changes eligible for construction, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across these task families. On a matched candidate set, it recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a construction baseline based on pull requests. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation, while reuse of modern bases reduces measured expenditure across the complete pipeline by 10.8%.

AI.tldr: Change2Task is a system that converts merged pull requests from repository history into verified, executable coding tasks for training and evaluating coding agents, achieving 79.6% task construction success across five task families and recovering 29.2% more verified tasks than a PR-based baseline.
AI.motivation: Scaling coding agents requires a continuous supply of executable data for training and evaluation, but creating such tasks—each needing a realistic software state, specification, tools, and verification—is expensive and hard to scale. Existing approaches lack systematic methods to derive verified tasks from historical development evidence while reusing modern, maintained environments.
AI.method: Change2Task extracts merged pull requests from repository history and reconstructs executable tasks on healthy modern revisions using three techniques: Patch Reversal, Code Mapping, and Agent Reconstruction. It validates the full lifecycle from a healthy base state to a task state and then to a restored state. The system derives multiple task instances across five families: Bug Fix, Feature Addition, Test Generation, API Migration, and Security Repair, while sharing common base environments to reduce storage and setup overhead.
AI.result: Starting from 1,130 source changes, Change2Task achieves 79.6% verified task construction success across all five task families. It recovers 29.2% more verified tasks than a pull-request-based construction baseline on a matched candidate set. Historical and reconstructed cases achieve up to 98.0% matched outcome agreement under agent evaluation. Reuse of modern bases reduces measured expenditure across the complete pipeline by 10.8%.
AI.conclusion: Change2Task demonstrates that repository history is a rich, scalable source of grounded executable tasks for coding agent research. By aligning historical evidence with evolved code and reusing modern environments, it significantly improves task yield and reduces construction cost compared to PR-based baselines, with strong agreement between original and reconstructed task outcomes.

title: Formalization of security
comment: To appear as chapter19 of the book "Proof Assistants and Their Applications in Mathematics and Computer Science"
summary: Proof assistants are often used to validate that designs and implementations meet their expected security properties. A further motivation for using proof assistants is to support certification. This chapter focuses on their applications to system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography.

AI.tldr: A survey chapter on the use of proof assistants for security verification, covering system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography, with emphasis on certification support.
AI.motivation: Proof assistants serve dual purposes: (1) validating that designs and implementations satisfy security properties, and (2) supporting formal certification processes, which is a further compelling motivation for their adoption in security-critical domains.
AI.method: The chapter surveys existing approaches across four key application areas: system security (verifying OS kernels, hypervisors, and hardware), language-based security (enforcing information flow and memory safety via type systems and program logics), secure compilation (preserving security properties across compilation passes), and cryptography (mechanized proofs of cryptographic constructions and protocols). It examines how proof assistants like Coq, Isabelle/HOL, and F* are employed in each domain.
AI.result: The survey demonstrates that proof assistants have achieved notable successes, including verified microkernels (seL4), verified cryptographic libraries, and secure compilation chains with formally guaranteed property preservation. These results strengthen the case for using mechanized proof in certification frameworks.
AI.conclusion: Proof assistants have matured into practical tools for high-assurance security verification and are increasingly viable for certification. The coverage across system security, language-based security, secure compilation, and cryptography illustrates a broad and growing landscape of mechanized security proofs.

title: Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Channel Modeling in Low-SNR Regimes
summary: Accurate multipath parameter estimation is critical for modern wireless communication systems, particularly in challenging low-SNR environments. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms, such as CLEAN, provide high-resolution parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search. Conversely, purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. By replacing the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, NN-CLEAN isolates physical multipath parameters without accumulating non- physical errors. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the traditional Grid-Search CLEAN (GS- CLEAN) baseline, while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Crucially, NN-CLEAN exhibits a near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase. This highly efficient parallelization establishes NN-CLEAN as a robust, real- time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems.

AI.tldr: NN-CLEAN proposes a hybrid multipath parameter estimation framework that embeds a multi-head residual neural network into the iterative CLEAN algorithm, replacing exhaustive grid search with fast neural forward passes while retaining exact mathematical residual subtraction. It achieves >96% estimation accuracy at 5 dB SNR, matching GS-CLEAN with dramatically lower complexity, and exhibits near-flat scaling in runtime and memory with increasing batch size.
AI.motivation: Traditional CLEAN algorithms (GS-CLEAN) provide high-resolution multipath parameter estimates via exhaustive grid search but are computationally prohibitive. Purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical interpretability and fail to generalize across varying multipath densities and off-grid parameters. A method combining physical model rigor with neural efficiency is needed for real-time channel estimation in low-SNR MIMO systems.
AI.method: NN-CLEAN integrates a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. Rather than performing exhaustive grid search, the network performs rapid, parallelizable forward passes to estimate multipath parameters. Residual subtraction is handled by exact mathematical models, preserving physical consistency and preventing accumulation of non-physical errors.
AI.result: In Monte Carlo simulations, NN-CLEAN achieves >96% estimation accuracy at 5 dB SNR, matching GS-CLEAN baseline performance. It substantially outperforms subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Critically, execution runtime and memory consumption exhibit near-flat scaling as batch sizes increase, demonstrating efficient parallelization.
AI.conclusion: NN-CLEAN combines the accuracy of model-based CLEAN estimation with the computational efficiency of neural networks, establishing itself as a robust, real-time channel estimation solution for MIMO systems, particularly in low-SNR environments.

title: Reasoning Consensus: Structural Ensembling of LLM Reasoning via Weighted DAG Aggregation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) explore problems through chain-of-thought, but this exploration is buried in unstructured prose. On high-stakes tasks, users cannot tell which steps are well-supported, which alternatives were seriously considered, or how the final conclusion compares to those the model discarded. We propose a framework that ensembles the reasoning structure, not just the answers, of multiple LLMs by weighted merging of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) extracted from reasoning chains. We weight each step by how many traces independently attest to it, to return "Consensus Reasoning". Across six benchmarks spanning statutory interpretation, graduate-level science, narrative multi-hop reasoning, and first-order logic, our ensemble outperforms a matched-budget majority-vote baseline, with a maximum accuracy gain of 3.1% on MuSR-MM (narrative multi-hop reasoning). On a single model, the framework matches or exceeds self-consistency at the same trace budget while additionally exposing an inspectable consensus reasoning graph. Ensemble weights correlate with LLM-judge rankings of reasoning quality at Spearman $ρ= 0.30$-$0.51$, and consensus subgraphs are preferred over alternatives leading to the majority-vote answer in 54.4-65.4% of head-to-head comparisons across five of six datasets. We observe that our framework can also be used to analyze diverse reasoning perspectives for a problem.

AI.tldr: Proposes a framework that ensembles reasoning structures (DAGs) from multiple LLMs via weighted merging, producing a "Consensus Reasoning" graph. Outperforms majority-vote baselines with gains up to 3.1%, while exposing inspectable reasoning graphs whose weights correlate with LLM-judge quality rankings (ρ=0.30–0.51).
AI.motivation: LLMs use chain-of-thought reasoning buried in unstructured prose, making it impossible for users to assess which steps are well-supported, which alternatives were considered, or how the final conclusion compares to discarded paths. This is especially critical for high-stakes tasks requiring transparency and auditability.
AI.method: Extract Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) from multiple LLM reasoning chains. Merge these DAGs via weighted ensembling, where each step is weighted by the number of independent traces attesting to it. This yields a "Consensus Reasoning" graph that surfaces both the dominant reasoning path and alternatives considered.
AI.result: Outperforms matched-budget majority-vote on six benchmarks (statutory interpretation, graduate science, narrative multi-hop QA, first-order logic), with max gain of 3.1% on MuSR-MM. Matches or exceeds self-consistency at same trace budget. Ensemble weights correlate with LLM-judge rankings (Spearman ρ=0.30–0.51). Consensus subgraphs preferred over majority-vote-answer alternatives in 54.4–65.4% of head-to-head comparisons across five of six datasets.
AI.conclusion: Structured reasoning ensembling via DAG merging provides both accuracy gains and inspectability, offering a practical path toward more transparent and auditable LLM reasoning in high-stakes settings. The framework also enables analysis of diverse reasoning perspectives.

title: World Action Planner: Generalizable Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models
summary: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments, they often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. In this work, we propose World Action Planner, a robot planning system that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the physical grounding of a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. Our system enables an agent to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs. Project website at worldactionplanner.github.io

AI.tldr: World Action Planner integrates VLMs with a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model to enable robot planning through iterative action proposal, optimization, and search over imagined rollouts, achieving strong zero-shot and compositional generalization.
AI.motivation: Imitation learning-based policies excel in training environments but suffer from poor generalization to novel scenes and compositional tasks. There is a need for systems that combine semantic reasoning with physical grounding to bridge this generalization gap.
AI.method: The system uses Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to propose initial action plans, which are then iteratively refined using optimization and search over rollouts simulated by a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. This world model provides physical grounding for imagined trajectories, enabling the agent to reason about action outcomes before execution.
AI.result: The approach achieves superior performance on compositional tasks, novel layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs (Vision-Language-Action models) and WAMs (World Action Models).
AI.conclusion: Combining VLM-based reasoning with a physically grounded world model enables robust robot planning that generalizes beyond training distributions, offering a promising direction for building versatile, general-purpose agents.

title: Semantic-Aligned Structural Abstraction for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
summary: Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) aims to interpret complex human emotions by integrating natural language with non-verbal modalities. Non-verbal modalities share a structural isomorphism with natural language, as both can be viewed as feature sequences evolving over time. This isomorphism enables the transformation of non-verbal modalities into text-like tokens for unified semantic reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs), designed to understand and generate sequential data, can thus be utilized to interpret complex affective sequences. However, existing LLM-based methods primarily capture low-level superficial features, failing to model affective semantics arising from structural variations and contextual interactions. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{SentiLLM}, a unified framework that leverages \textit{Semantic-Aligned Structural Abstraction} to distill continuous raw signals into compact, semantically meaningful tokens. Specifically, we introduce a \textit{Dual-Stream Salience-Context Calibration Mechanism}, which disentangles non-verbal feature sequences into a focus stream and an ambient stream. The focus stream captures salient sentiment shifts (e.g., facial expressions) guided by textual priors, while the ambient stream characterizes stable background states. Through calibrating these dynamic sentiment shifts against background states, SentiLLM effectively projects non-verbal modalities into a unified semantic space, making them naturally understandable for LLMs. Serving as a plug-and-play module, SentiLLM significantly improves discriminative performance with only a small number of trainable parameters. Our method achieves superior performance on four datasets, MOSI, MOSEI, CH-SIMS, and CH-SIMS v2, demonstrating the effectiveness of the structural abstraction paradigm in MSA. Our code is available at: \href{https://github.com/especiallyW/SentiLLM}.

AI.tldr: SentiLLM proposes a semantic-aligned structural abstraction framework that converts non-verbal modalities into LLM-compatible tokens via a dual-stream salience-context calibration mechanism, achieving state-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis with minimal trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based MSA methods only capture low-level superficial features and fail to model affective semantics from structural variations and contextual interactions. Non-verbal modalities share structural isomorphism with language (both are temporal feature sequences), yet current approaches do not properly leverage this property for unified semantic reasoning.
AI.method: SentiLLM introduces Semantic-Aligned Structural Abstraction with a Dual-Stream Salience-Context Calibration Mechanism. This disentangles non-verbal feature sequences into: (1) a focus stream capturing salient sentiment shifts (e.g., facial expressions) guided by textual priors, and (2) an ambient stream characterizing stable background states. By calibrating dynamic sentiment shifts against background states, non-verbal modalities are projected into a unified semantic space interpretable by LLMs. The framework is a plug-and-play module with few trainable parameters.
AI.result: SentiLLM achieves superior performance on four benchmark datasets: MOSI, MOSEI, CH-SIMS, and CH-SIMS v2, with only a small number of trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: The structural abstraction paradigm is effective for MSA, demonstrating that distilling continuous non-verbal signals into semantically meaningful tokens enables LLMs to better perform unified multimodal sentiment reasoning.

title: CORE: In-Context Reconstruction for Unified Tabular Anomaly Detection
summary: Tabular anomaly detection (TAD), which focuses on identifying abnormal samples that deviate from the majority in tabular data, has received growing attention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend towards unified TAD, which seeks to detect anomalies across different datasets using a single generalizable model. In unified TAD, aligning heterogeneous data remains challenging. While existing methods often rely on distance-based unified feature construction, they may obscure the semantics of the original features. Moreover, existing approaches typically formulate anomaly detection as a binary classification task, which may overlook diverse anomaly patterns from various datasets and be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose an in-COntext REconstruction approach for unified TAD (CORE for short). It introduces a decorrelated feature alignment module to directly align heterogeneous features into a unified representation space, which retains their semantic information. Meanwhile, CORE formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies. Specifically, the in-context reconstruction module reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, such that reconstruction errors reflect its deviation from normality, facilitating unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

AI.tldr: CORE proposes an in-context reconstruction framework for unified tabular anomaly detection that aligns heterogeneous features via decorrelated feature alignment and detects anomalies through reconstruction errors against dataset-specific normal distributions, eliminating the need for labeled or synthetic anomalies.
AI.motivation: Existing unified TAD methods suffer from two key limitations: (1) distance-based feature alignment obscures original feature semantics, and (2) binary classification formulations overlook diverse anomaly patterns and can be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies.
AI.method: CORE consists of two main components: (1) a decorrelated feature alignment module that directly maps heterogeneous features into a unified representation space while preserving semantic information, and (2) an in-context reconstruction module that reconstructs each sample using contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, where reconstruction errors serve as anomaly indicators on unseen datasets.
AI.result: The paper does not specify quantitative results in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: CORE enables effective unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets by reformulating anomaly detection as in-context reconstruction, bypassing the need for labeled anomalies and better capturing diverse anomaly patterns across heterogeneous tabular data.

title: Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation
summary: While automated content-moderation systems have become essential for screening harmful content at scale, conventional task-specific classifiers often provide limited policy cov- erage and contextual understanding. Recently, commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models have been introduced with the promise of providing broader and more capable safety filters. In this work, we analyze whether this shift also yields more robust image moderation. We conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation on three established commercial image-moderation services and compare their robustness. By evaluating seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities, we find that: (1) all three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations that require no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system; (2) even fixed transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving content that remains recognizable to humans; (3) their robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm exhibiting pronounced vulnerabilities. This yields the conclusion that replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

AI.tldr: A black-box evaluation of three commercial multimodal moderation APIs reveals that simple, model-agnostic image transformations (e.g., color inversion, grayscale) can reliably bypass safety filters, exposing critical vulnerabilities in foundation-model-based content moderation systems.
AI.motivation: Commercial moderation APIs built on large foundation models are increasingly replacing task-specific classifiers, promising broader policy coverage and better contextual understanding. This paper investigates whether this architectural shift actually delivers more robust image moderation, or merely introduces new attack surfaces.
AI.method: A large-scale black-box evaluation across three commercial image-moderation services using seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations (including color inversion, grayscale conversion, rotation, blurring, and JPEG compression). Robustness is assessed across multiple datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities — without requiring gradients, surrogate models, or system knowledge.
AI.result: All three services can be bypassed using inexpensive transformations. Even fixed transformations like color inversion and grayscale cause unsafe-to-safe decision flips while preserving human-recognizable content. Robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories; multimodal content and self-harm categories show pronounced vulnerabilities.
AI.conclusion: Replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline, not as standalone safety filters.

title: Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring
summary: The information flow in the graph neural networks (GNNs) is fundamentally constrained by over-squashing, where structural bottlenecks impede long range information propagation. Graph-rewiring methods, which modify graph topology, have been extensively used to alleviate this. However, existing approaches often introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve the critical properties of original graphs, and increase the edge counts massively. We introduce a novel method Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring , a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. Our method provides theoretical guarantees, a graph that exhibits spectral gap and a bounded effective resistance, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: SCGR augments input graphs with Schreier-Coset graphs derived from special linear groups to create low-resistance bypasses for long-range information flow, reducing effective resistance by 5-40% while preserving critical graph properties.
AI.motivation: GNNs suffer from over-squashing due to structural bottlenecks that limit long-range information propagation. Existing graph-rewiring methods introduce prohibitive structural/computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve original graph properties, and massively increase edge counts.
AI.method: Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring (SCGR): a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. The method provides theoretical guarantees including spectral gap and bounded effective resistance.
AI.result: SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: SCGR offers a principled, group-theoretic solution to over-squashing in GNNs, outperforming prior rewiring methods by efficiently creating low-resistance communication paths without sacrificing graph integrity or computational tractability.

title: Beyond Borrowed Histories: Person-Aligned User Simulation for Interactive Role-Playing Evaluation
comment: 29 pages, 3 figures, including supplementary material. Resources: https://github.com/Zhuyh1139/PALATE
summary: Role-playing agents (RPAs) have become one of the most important consumer applications of large language models. Users engage in multi-turn conversations with RPAs for experiences such as emotional comfort, making reliable evaluation essential for measuring capability, comparing systems, and guiding further improvement. Existing benchmarks, however, typically require an RPA to continue a fixed dialogue history and then evaluate the continuation using a fixed rubric detached from the user. We identify and empirically demonstrate two limitations of this design. First, an RPA's output is shaped by the preceding dialogue history, preventing a scientifically grounded assessment of its role-playing ability in real multi-turn settings. Second, user experience varies substantially across individuals, and conventional fixed rubrics need not align with user satisfaction. We therefore introduce PALATE (Person-Aligned LLM-Simulated-User Assessment with Tailored Evaluation), a scalable RPA benchmark built on user simulators. PALATE is accompanied by a pool of 300 character profiles. Its main evaluation trains five per-user simulators and lets them engage candidate RPAs in free-form, multi-turn conversations over a pre-frozen panel of character profiles. Alongside a general quality rubric, we construct personalized rubrics to measure user satisfaction; on held-out annotated data, the personalized rubrics show higher agreement with human judgments than the general rubric. In the main evaluation of 16 candidates, PALATE separately characterizes generic turn quality, long-horizon session capability, and per-user experience on multi-turn trajectories co-constructed by each candidate. It thereby produces interpretable evaluations of specific user-RPA pairs rather than compressing systems into a single user-independent ranking.

AI.tldr: PALATE introduces a scalable RPA benchmark using LLM-simulated users for free-form multi-turn conversations, paired with personalized rubrics that better align with human satisfaction than fixed rubrics, enabling interpretable evaluation of specific user-RPA pairs.
AI.motivation: Existing RPA benchmarks have two key flaws: (1) they evaluate fixed dialogue continuations, ignoring how history shapes outputs in real multi-turn settings; (2) they use detached, fixed rubrics that fail to capture individualized user satisfaction. Both undermine scientific validity and practical relevance.
AI.method: PALATE uses 300 character profiles and trains five per-user LLM simulators. These simulators engage candidate RPAs in free-form multi-turn conversations over a frozen character panel. Evaluation employs both a general quality rubric and personalized rubrics derived per user. The personalized rubrics are validated against held-out human-annotated data. 16 candidate RPAs are evaluated on turn quality, session-level capability, and per-user experience along co-constructed trajectories.
AI.result: Personalized rubrics achieve higher agreement with human judgments than the general rubric on held-out data. PALATE provides interpretable, disaggregated evaluations characterizing generic turn quality, long-horizon session capability, and per-user experience for specific user-RPA pairs, rather than a single ranking.
AI.conclusion: PALATE advances RPA evaluation by grounding assessment in realistic multi-turn interactions and personalized user satisfaction, moving beyond user-independent rankings to nuanced, pair-level interpretability.

title: Hidden APIs in Language Models: Discovering Reusable Causal Interfaces from Forked Futures
summary: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states that support different future computations, so current-answer probes do not establish a reusable internal interface. We introduce forked futures: future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed, and states are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations. This yields an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels. Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interfaces then compete under prequential causal description length subject to future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints. In the two detailed model evaluations, Shared has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion; a five-backbone sweep preserves the positive direction of Sharedness Gain. The figure-aligned transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile, and API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one observed non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms. These results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, while keeping the claim explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "forked futures," a method for discovering reusable causal interfaces in language model hidden states by comparing response distributions induced by future operations, without requiring researcher-specified labels. Across multiple LLMs, a Shared interface achieves the lowest description length, strongest transplantation fidelity, and near-perfect recovery of architecture type, supporting the existence of economical reusable interfaces in transformer hidden states.
AI.motivation: Current methods that probe hidden states for identical answers cannot establish whether those states support a genuinely reusable internal interface, since identical outputs can arise from states that enable different downstream computations. The authors seek a principled, causal method to determine whether hidden states form Shared (reusable), Local (context-specific), Mixture, or Distributed interfaces — without relying on researcher-imposed latent labels.
AI.method: The core innovation is "forked futures": after a prefix state forms, future operations are sampled and states are compared through the response distributions those operations induce, yielding an empirical causal quotient. Four candidate interface types (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) compete under prequential causal description length, constrained by future-signature fidelity and matched capacity. Evaluation uses a five-backbone sweep across models (including Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3-8B), figure-aligned transplantation analysis comparing target vs. null paths, and a blind four-class model-organism classification test across 16 architectures.
AI.result: Shared interfaces achieved the lowest held-out description length (0.216 nats gain on Qwen2.5-1.5B, 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B) with tightly clustered future-signature distortion. The five-backbone sweep preserved positive Sharedness Gain. Transplantation analysis showed Shared had the strongest joint profile on target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite metrics; API-aligned paths mediated 0.749 of the target effect vs. 0.150 for null paths. In blind classification, 14/16 architectures were correctly recovered, with only one non-Shared→Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms.
AI.conclusion: The results support the existence of an economical, reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, suggesting transformer hidden states do contain Shared representations that generalize across contexts. However, the authors explicitly condition this claim on the specific candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures examined.

title: Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata
summary: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

AI.tldr: FLAMECHE reformulates metadata-based Clustered Federated Learning as a distributed Expectation-Maximization procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations. This enables compatibility with secure FL schemes while preserving communication and computational efficiency, addressing the CFL trilemma of privacy, communication cost, and computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing CFL methods face a "CFL trilemma" — a trade-off among privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. Metadata-based approaches (low-dimensional client data representations shared with the server) achieve efficiency in communication and computation but are incompatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. The goal is to resolve this incompatibility while retaining efficiency.
AI.method: The authors propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure. The key design choice is restricting all server-side updates to additive operations only. This constraint makes the clustering process compatible with practical secure FL schemes (e.g., homomorphic encryption, secure aggregation) without sacrificing the communication and computational benefits of metadata-based clustering.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and heterogeneous scenarios demonstrate that FLAMECHE improves client model effectiveness compared to baselines. Crucially, it enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, thereby improving its positioning within the CFL trilemma — achieving privacy compatibility alongside communication and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: FLAMECHE successfully bridges the gap between metadata-based CFL and privacy-preserving FL mechanisms by leveraging an additive-only EM formulation. This advances the state of the art by mitigating the CFL trilemma, enabling practical, efficient, and privacy-compatible clustered federated learning.

title: Latent States in Neural Networks: Recovering the Temporal Structure of Drifting Data from Model Weights
summary: A temporally drifting data stream may pass through discrete regimes rather than changing continuously. We ask whether such regimes are recoverable from the weights of models trained on the stream, using a hidden Markov model (HMM) fit to the chronologically ordered trajectory of those weights. We study this question in two domains known to drift over time: multimodal misinformation detection, using the Fakeddit dataset; and sentiment analysis, using the Yelp dataset. We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

AI.tldr: Model weights trained on temporally drifting data can be fed into a hidden Markov model to recover discrete latent regimes. These regimes partition timelines into coherent phases that predict cross-temporal generalization better than temporal proximity or equal-size partitioning, with effects persisting after controlling for class distribution shifts.
