AI.motivation: The paper investigates whether discrete latent regimes underlying temporally drifting data streams can be recovered from the trajectory of model weights alone, rather than from raw data. This matters for understanding how models encode distribution shift and for improving transfer learning under non-stationary conditions.
AI.method: Classifiers are trained on consecutive temporal windows from two datasets (Fakeddit for multimodal misinformation detection; Yelp for sentiment analysis). The chronologically ordered, aligned weight vectors are then treated as emissions of a hidden Markov model (HMM), which is fit to infer latent states that partition each timeline into discrete phases. Transfer generalization is measured by evaluating a classifier on test windows sharing vs. not sharing the HMM-inferred state of its training window. Controls include temporal proximity, a contiguous-equal-size partition baseline, and residualization of class distribution divergence and temporal lag.
AI.result: Classifiers generalize better to within-state windows than across-state windows on both datasets. This within-state transfer advantage survives controls for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds a naive equal-size partition. HMM-inferred states correlate more strongly with shifts in class distribution than with weight-space geometry. Crucially, after residualizing out class divergence and lag, the within-state advantage remains above permutation nulls, indicating recovered structure beyond data distribution shifts. All effects replicate across both tasks but are attenuated on Yelp, which exhibits greater temporal label stability.
AI.conclusion: Discrete latent regimes in drifting data streams are recoverable from model weight trajectories via HMMs, and these regimes carry transfer-relevant structure irreducible to temporal proximity or class distribution shifts alone. The method provides a model-centric lens for detecting and exploiting temporal structure in non-stationary learning problems.

title: AutoSupervision: Closing the Feedback Loop in Scientific Workflows with Grounded Revision Verification
summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled AI systems to assist scientific research and peer review. However, an essential capability for reliable AI-assisted scientific workflows remains underexplored: verifying whether reviewer feedback leads to meaningful and evidence-supported manuscript improvements. We introduce AutoSupervision, which evaluates whether scientific manuscript revisions genuinely address reviewer concerns through grounded evidence. AutoSupervision leverages transparent peer-review records as a natural source of supervision, where reviewer comments specify scientific concerns, author responses describe claimed resolutions, and revised manuscripts provide evidence of changes. Given reviewer comments, author responses, and revised manuscripts, models must characterize reviewer concerns, determine whether concerns have been addressed, and identify supporting manuscript evidence. We construct AutoSupervision from 56,000 Nature Communications articles and corresponding review records. Then we conducted experiments on LLMs, the ablation study, and the case study. Our results show that while LLMs perform well in characterizing reviewer concerns, with GPT-5.5 achieving a score of 0.754, evidence-based verification remains the primary bottleneck, with the best-performing model reaching only 0.501.

AI.tldr: AutoSupervision is a benchmark that evaluates whether LLMs can verify if manuscript revisions genuinely address reviewer feedback using evidence from peer-review records. Using 56,000 Nature Communications articles, it finds LLMs characterize concerns well (GPT-5.5: 0.754) but struggle with evidence-based verification (best model: 0.501).
AI.motivation: Current LLMs can assist in scientific peer review, but a critical capability remains underexplored: reliably verifying whether reviewer feedback actually leads to evidence-supported manuscript improvements. This verification is essential for trustworthy AI-assisted scientific workflows.
AI.method: The authors construct the AutoSupervision benchmark from 56,000 Nature Communications articles with transparent peer-review records. The task provides reviewer comments, author responses, and revised manuscripts, requiring models to: (1) characterize reviewer concerns, (2) determine whether concerns have been addressed, and (3) identify supporting manuscript evidence. They evaluate LLMs on this benchmark and conduct ablation and case studies.
AI.result: LLMs perform relatively well at characterizing reviewer concerns, with GPT-5.5 achieving a score of 0.754. However, evidence-based verification remains the primary bottleneck — the best-performing model reaches only 0.501 on this subtask, revealing a significant gap in current capabilities.
AI.conclusion: While LLMs can reasonably understand and characterize reviewer concerns in scientific peer review, they remain insufficient at the more demanding task of verifying whether manuscript revisions are supported by grounded evidence. This highlights a key area for improvement in building reliable AI-assisted scientific review systems.

title: SCOPE: Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization
comment: 43 pages; Kiet, Duc, and Bang contributed equally
summary: Black-box combinatorial optimization requires systematically identifying high-quality solutions under a limited evaluation budget, yet the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where the search should explore next. We introduce SCOPE, a general framework for Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization. Rather than directly optimizing the inaccessible objective, SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on the accumulated search history, where each objective is designed to expose a distinct and potentially useful preference over candidate solutions. These objectives are then used to evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, whose true quality is subsequently assessed through black-box evaluations. The outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives according to how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions. In contrast, the inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to reduce the risk of relying on a single surrogate preference. This formulation reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a framework for black-box combinatorial optimization that learns synthetic objective functions from search history to guide policy evolution, enabling diverse and effective exploration under limited evaluation budgets.
AI.motivation: Black-box combinatorial optimization suffers from the fundamental challenge that the unknown objective function provides minimal guidance for directing search. Under a limited evaluation budget, deciding where to explore next becomes critical yet poorly informed, motivating the need for a principled mechanism to generate useful search guidance without access to the true objective.
AI.method: SCOPE operates in a bi-level loop: (1) the outer loop adaptively learns and selects a set of synthetic objective functions conditioned on accumulated search history, each encoding distinct preferences over candidate solutions; (2) the inner loop evolves search policies using these synthetic objectives to generate diverse candidate solutions, which are then evaluated via black-box queries; (3) the outer loop updates synthetic objectives based on how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions, maintaining a portfolio of top-performing policies to hedge against reliance on any single surrogate preference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.
AI.conclusion: SCOPE reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. The framework offers a robust, general-purpose approach to black-box combinatorial optimization.

title: A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation
summary: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

AI.tldr: NEXUS is a lightweight (~3M parameter) autoencoder-based foundation model pre-trained on unlabeled LHC collision data, enabling improved performance on downstream tasks (kinematic regression, event classification) with small labeled datasets, and demonstrating cross-domain transfer to gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity.
AI.motivation: To develop a computationally efficient foundation model for scientific data that leverages unsupervised pre-training on particle physics data and transfers effectively to out-of-domain scientific tasks, avoiding the heavy computational cost of transformer-based approaches.
AI.method: A fully connected autoencoder with ~3 million parameters is pre-trained without supervision on large-scale LHC charged particle track features. Downstream tasks are built on the pre-trained weights. Latent space interpretation is performed, and cross-domain applicability is tested on gravitational wave, flood forecasting, and neural activity datasets.
AI.result: The pre-trained NEXUS model achieves improved accuracy on collider physics downstream tasks compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch, especially when using small labeled datasets. The model also demonstrates effectiveness across multiple scientific domains and offers significant computational simplicity relative to transformer models at comparable scale.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight autoencoder-based foundation models like NEXUS can effectively transfer knowledge from particle physics to diverse scientific domains, enabling power-efficient, real-time, and edge-deployable foundation models for scientific experiments.

title: ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

AI.tldr: ReDiPPO improves PPO for mathematical reasoning by introducing a reference-guided critic that uses answer signals during training to provide better value estimates, and a discrepancy-aware mechanism that reweights token-level advantages based on the gap between standard and reference-guided critics.
AI.motivation: Standard PPO critics struggle with token-level credit assignment in mathematical reasoning due to long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, leading to noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates.
AI.method: ReDiPPO employs a dual-critic architecture: (1) a reference-guided critic trained with privileged reference answer signals for accurate value estimation, and (2) a standard critic. The token-level discrepancy between the two critics' value estimates identifies difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight token-level advantages during PPO optimization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong baselines including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO in final reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: ReDiPPO effectively addresses the credit assignment challenge in mathematical reasoning RL by leveraging reference-guided signals and discrepancy-based reweighting, yielding superior policy optimization outcomes.

title: HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution
summary: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

AI.tldr: HALO is a runtime protocol for agentic AI systems that selectively preserves supported components from heterogeneous responses when conditions change, rather than rejecting the entire response. It checks dependencies, rechecks actions before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced by fresh candidates, achieving perfect retention of unaffected components in tests.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems produce heterogeneous responses containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. When environmental conditions change before external use, components from the same response may no longer all be supported. Whole-response rejection discards useful components, while independent component checking risks leaving dependents without their prerequisites. A principled middle ground is needed.
AI.method: HALO operates as a runtime protocol with three key mechanisms: (1) it preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported (localized obligations), (2) it rechecks each exact action before dispatch to ensure validity under current conditions, and (3) it allows blocked actions to be replaced exclusively by fresh candidates rather than stale alternatives.
AI.result: HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.
AI.conclusion: HALO provides a robust admission-control protocol that maximizes retention of valid response components under changing conditions, outperforming both whole-response rejection and naive independent checking. Its correctness is validated through comprehensive testing and realistic simulation.

title: Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models
summary: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a chain-of-thought reasoning-enabled triage classifier for SOC alert fatigue, combining prompt optimization, self-training, and RL with verifiable rewards. A separate calibrator recovers confidence from reasoning traces, achieving 82.6% accuracy with substantial recall improvements over direct-label LLMs.
AI.motivation: Security Operations Centers face alert fatigue because the volume of detections exceeds analysts' triage capacity. Prior LLM-based approaches predict triage labels directly without explicit reasoning, limiting both accuracy and trustworthiness. The authors aim to train LLMs that reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat, improving both performance and calibrated confidence.
AI.method: The system combines three training stages: (1) automated prompt optimization to discover effective CoT reasoning patterns, (2) self-training on real human-labeled Windows endpoint detections to bootstrap reasoning traces, and (3) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards derived from ground-truth labels. Because CoT reasoning degrades label-token probabilities, a separate calibrator is trained to read the full reasoning trace and estimate the probability of a correct verdict. The final system uses a fine-tuned 30B model.
AI.result: The system achieves 82.6% test accuracy. At the high-confidence operating point for automated triage, it improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. The trained calibrator is essential: an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero. A fine-tuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, supporting targeted training over scaling.
AI.conclusion: CoT reasoning combined with a dedicated calibrator yields substantial gains in SOC alert triage accuracy and calibrated confidence. Targeted fine-tuning of mid-size models proves more effective than using larger general-purpose LLMs, and verifiable rewards provide effective supervision for reasoning traces in cybersecurity domains.

title: Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation
summary: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first rigorous theoretical analysis of identifiability in sparsity-constrained real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. A novel decomposition strategy transforms the three-factor problem into two coupled two-factor problems, enabling recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how sparsity affects convergence, error bounds, and structure preservation. Monte Carlo experiments validate the theory.
AI.motivation: Matrix tri-factorisation with sparsity constraints offers greater modelling flexibility and improved interpretability compared to two-factor models. However, while sparsity in two-factor matrix factorisation has been extensively studied theoretically, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. This gap motivates the authors to establish the first formal identifiability and recovery analysis for this setting.
AI.method: The authors introduce a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original three-factor problem into two coupled auxiliary two-factor factorisation problems, while preserving structural information needed to recover the original factor matrices from observations. Building on this decomposition, they derive recovery guarantees, structural consistency results, high-probability bounds, spectral approximation error analysis, and convergence behaviour characterisation—all as functions of coefficient sparsity. Validation is performed through comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments.
AI.result: The analysis yields recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that explicitly characterise how coefficient sparsity influences sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, and high-probability bounds. Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate close agreement between theoretical predictions and empirical observations.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes the first rigorous theoretical foundation for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, filling a significant gap in the literature. The proposed decomposition strategy provides a principled framework for analysing three-factor models, and the derived guarantees offer practical insights into how sparsity regularisation affects recovery performance.

title: FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework
summary: Powered by advances in LLMs and autonomous agents, deep research has become one of the most widely adopted agentic products. However, most deep research systems write general-purpose reports, which are inadequate for financial deep research. Financial research demands specialized knowledge to analyze historical patterns and forecast upcoming events. Automating financial deep research therefore requires both a layered harness to drive the research agent and a verifiable, point-in-time benchmark that prevents leakage of future information. We present FinanceHarness, a harness that runs finance-oriented tools and practitioner-guided workflows, automating financial deep research end to end: environment and data construction, the agent execution loop, and reward modeling. We further propose FinanceGym, comprising thesis-driven research questions and rubrics that combine pre-cutoff and post-cutoff criteria. Professional expert validation yields an 82% pass rate. Even leading LLMs and agents score below 40% on the rubrics, showing that FinanceGym is challenging and leaves substantial headroom. With the same open-weight backbone, FinanceHarness improves the overall rubric score from 25.3% to 32.4%. FinanceHarness is available at https://github.com/Yijia-Xiao/FinanceHarness.

AI.tldr: FinanceHarness is an end-to-end framework for automating financial deep research using specialized tools and practitioner-guided workflows, paired with FinanceGym, a point-in-time benchmark that prevents data leakage. The benchmark achieves 82% expert validation pass rate, while leading LLMs score below 40%, and FinanceHarness improves scores from 25.3% to 32.4% over the same open-weight backbone.
AI.motivation: Existing deep research systems produce general-purpose reports inadequate for finance, which demands specialized domain knowledge for historical analysis and event forecasting. A key challenge is preventing future information leakage in benchmarks, requiring verifiable point-in-time evaluation.
AI.method: FinanceHarness provides a layered harness with three components: (1) environment and data construction with finance-oriented tools, (2) an agent execution loop following practitioner-guided workflows, and (3) reward modeling. FinanceGym introduces thesis-driven research questions with rubrics combining pre-cutoff (historical) and post-cutoff (forecasting) criteria, ensuring temporal integrity via point-in-time data splits.
AI.result: Professional experts validated FinanceGym with an 82% pass rate. Leading LLMs and agents score below 40% on the rubrics. FinanceHarness raises the overall rubric score from 25.3% to 32.4% using the same open-weight backbone model.
AI.conclusion: FinanceGym presents a challenging, verifiable benchmark for financial deep research with substantial headroom above current state-of-the-art. FinanceHarness demonstrates meaningful improvements in automated financial research quality, and the open-source release facilitates further research.

title: HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data
summary: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

AI.tldr: HealthCAT is a Transformer-based framework that integrates an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to provide class-specific, time-step-level interpretability for wearable sensor data, outperforming baselines by up to 17% in F1-score while enabling individual-level behavioural pattern analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning methods for wearable sensor data prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their utility in health research where understanding when and how behavioural patterns occur is crucial. There is a need to move beyond aggregated summary metrics toward interpretable temporal pattern analysis.
AI.method: HealthCAT employs an Encoder-only Transformer architecture combined with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT). This mechanism generates class-specific, time-step-level interpretations that can be mapped onto domain-relevant behavioural cycles (e.g., time-of-day). The framework was evaluated on two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants total), with masking experiments used to validate the predictive informativeness of identified time steps.
AI.result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy (p<0.05). Masking experiments demonstrated that time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions (p<0.05), validating the interpretability mechanism.
AI.conclusion: HealthCAT successfully couples predictive performance with validated interpretability, enabling accurate health indicator prediction from wearable sensor data while revealing when and how physical activity patterns occur, thus supporting health monitoring, behavioural analysis, and intervention design.

title: Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning
summary: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model that mimics human decision-making by comparing new cases to a few representative examples. The method supports single pivots, pivot pairs (inspired by proximity/oblique trees), and ensembles, is data modality-agnostic via pre-trained networks, and achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art interpretable models while using minimal pivots.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretable machine learning methods often rely on opaque decision procedures. Since humans naturally make decisions through case-based comparison with a few representative examples, the authors aim to design a model that selects such "pivots" to build predictive models that are inherently interpretable by design, rather than requiring post-hoc explanations.
AI.method: A hierarchical pivot selection model based on similarity between pivots and input instances, inspired by decision trees. The method functions as both a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. It extends beyond single pivots to incorporate pivot pairs (used by proximity and oblique trees) and ensemble variants. The approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained neural networks for data transformation across diverse data types.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse datasets — tabular data, text, images, and time series — show the method outperforms alternative instance selection strategies and achieves competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach successfully bridges human-like case-based reasoning with machine learning, delivering an interpretable-by-design model that is effective, versatile across data modalities, and economical in its use of representative examples.

title: Memory Decoder at Scale: A Pretrained, Parametric Long-Term Memory
summary: Decoder-only language models entangle long-term memory and reasoning in a single parameter set, making it difficult to scale memory capacity independently. Memory Decoder introduces a parametric long-term memory module but only studies it at a relatively small scale. In this work, we present Memory Decoder at Scale, scaling memory models up to 6.9B parameters and pretraining them on 300B tokens. At this data scale, the combined cost of indexing and search makes a standard Faiss pipeline infeasible. We address this bottleneck with a distributed pipeline for Faiss indexing and retrieval, together with sparse, batch-wise loading of kNN distributions. Across model scales, we find that allocating more parameters to memory yields a better parameter-performance tradeoff than scaling the base model alone. On 17 benchmarks, pairing a 6.9B general memory with Pythia-410M raises its average score from 29.86 to 37.34, surpassing Pythia-12B (37.24) with 39% fewer total parameters. For Qwen3 Base models ranging from 0.6B to 14B, 1.7B domain memories improve the average score across the three domains by more than 9 points at every scale. Overall, our results demonstrate that independently scaling pretrained memory offers a more parameter efficient path to improving language model performance.

AI.tldr: Memory Decoder at Scale demonstrates that independently scaling a parametric long-term memory module is more parameter-efficient than scaling the base language model alone. The authors scale memory models to 6.9B parameters trained on 300B tokens, introduce a distributed Faiss pipeline to handle indexing/retrieval at scale, and show that a 6.9B memory paired with a small base model can match or exceed much larger standalone models across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Decoder-only LMs entangle long-term memory and reasoning in a single parameter set, making independent scaling of memory capacity difficult. Prior work (Memory Decoder) introduced parametric long-term memory but only at small scale. Scaling this approach requires overcoming the prohibitive combined cost of indexing and search that makes standard Faiss pipelines infeasible at large data scales.
AI.method: The authors scale Memory Decoder models up to 6.9B parameters, pretraining on 300B tokens. They address the indexing/retrieval bottleneck by: (1) building a distributed pipeline for Faiss indexing and retrieval, and (2) using sparse, batch-wise loading of kNN distributions. They evaluate by pairing general and domain-specific memories with base models (Pythia, Qwen3) across 17 benchmarks and three domains, comparing parameter-performance tradeoffs against scaling the base model alone.
AI.result: Key results: (1) Allocating parameters to memory consistently yields better parameter-performance tradeoffs than scaling the base model. (2) A 6.9B general memory paired with Pythia-410M achieves an average score of 37.34 across 17 benchmarks, surpassing Pythia-12B (37.24) with 39% fewer total parameters. (3) For Qwen3 Base models (0.6B–14B), 1.7B domain memories improve average domain scores by more than 9 points at every scale.
AI.conclusion: Independently scaling pretrained memory offers a more parameter-efficient path to improving language model performance compared to monolithic scaling of the base model. The distributed Faiss pipeline makes large-scale memory retrieval feasible, and the approach generalizes across model families and domains.

title: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation
summary: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

AI.tldr: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF) introduces a discrete flow-matching kernel that natively models correlated token updates through a mixture of factorized components sharing a single latent variable, enabling few-step text generation that surpasses distilled/rectified methods without inheriting a teacher's quality ceiling.
AI.motivation: Existing discrete diffusion and flow-matching models factorize transitions across positions, making independent token decisions at each step. This fails to capture inter-position dependencies (e.g., subject-verb agreement), forcing many function evaluations to repair mismatches. Current few-step solutions rely on distilling or rectifying a slow teacher model, thus inheriting its quality ceiling. The authors seek a model that can natively express correlated steps without a teacher.
AI.method: LKF is a flow-map kernel formulated as a mixture of M factorized components, all tied by a single shared latent variable. Per component, computation is cheap (factorized), but the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. A single latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory, enabling correlated completions with the same sampling complexity as a factorized model. MDLM is shown to be a special case at M=1.
AI.result: On LM1B and WikiText-103 benchmarks for unconditional text generation, LKF learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over likelihood baselines without sacrificing diversity. Performance improves with M; at M=8, LKF surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers.
AI.conclusion: LKF demonstrates that native correlated-step modeling in discrete flow maps is feasible and outperforms teacher-dependent few-step methods, offering a principled from-scratch approach to high-quality few-step text generation.

title: RepBench: Compiling Benchmarks into Capability Representations for Large Language Models
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, with appendices. Yanshi Li and Xueru Bai contributed equally
summary: Representation engineering reads and steers capability directions in large language models, yet methods are typically evaluated on paper-specific synthetic data. The resulting measurements are difficult to compare or reproduce and may reflect surface patterns rather than capabilities. We present RepBench, a benchmark-grounded data layer for capability-aligned representation probing. Crawling 13,427 benchmark papers yields a taxonomy of 182 capability clusters in 13 families; harvesting 353 public benchmark datasets yields 46,149 audited probe texts covering 94 capabilities, each supported by at least two independent benchmarks. This multi-benchmark design reduces dependence on any single source: raw per-text vectors exhibit no natural cluster granularity, whereas benchmark-pooled capability vectors show an interior clustering optimum at a small number of clusters on all 12 evaluated models, with low agreement to the human taxonomy. Under cross-benchmark transfer evaluation across twelve models completed by all four readouts, difference-in-means attains the highest model-level mean on ten models, while logistic regression wins the most capability-model cells. This disagreement shows that the readout method and aggregation criterion are meaningful evaluation dimensions. The pipeline, corpus, and evaluation code are released as a reusable closed-loop workflow.

AI.tldr: RepBench is a benchmark-grounded data layer for probing LLM capabilities via representation engineering. It aggregates 46,149 probe texts across 94 capabilities from 353 public benchmarks, revealing that raw vectors lack natural clustering, benchmark-pooled vectors cluster optimally at few clusters with low human-taxonomy agreement, and readout method choice significantly impacts cross-benchmark transfer performance.
AI.motivation: Representation engineering methods for LLMs are typically evaluated on paper-specific synthetic data, making measurements difficult to compare or reproduce. These measurements may capture surface patterns rather than genuine capabilities. RepBench addresses this by providing a standardized, benchmark-grounded data layer for capability-aligned representation probing.
AI.method: The authors crawled 13,427 benchmark papers to build a taxonomy of 182 capability clusters across 13 families. They harvested 353 public benchmark datasets, yielding 46,149 audited probe texts covering 94 capabilities, each supported by at least two independent benchmarks. They conducted multi-benchmark probing experiments across 12 models using four readout methods and evaluated cross-benchmark transfer, clustering behavior, and human-taxonomy alignment.
AI.result: Raw per-text vectors show no natural cluster granularity. Benchmark-pooled capability vectors exhibit an interior clustering optimum at a small number of clusters across all 12 models, with low agreement to the human-defined taxonomy. In cross-benchmark transfer, difference-in-means achieves the highest model-level mean on 10 of 12 models, while logistic regression wins the most individual capability-model cells. This reveals that readout method and aggregation criterion are meaningful evaluation dimensions.
AI.conclusion: RepBench provides a reproducible, multi-benchmark framework for representation probing that exposes the sensitivity of probing results to readout method and aggregation choices. The pipeline, corpus, and evaluation code are released as a reusable closed-loop workflow to facilitate rigorous and comparable representation engineering research.

title: Evaluating and Pricing Advertisements in AI-Generated Responses
summary: As search increasingly shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded within the generated response itself and should therefore be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is click-through intent: behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound, as principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, while generating such a signal presupposes supervision that is currently unavailable. We construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, and distil it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent, together with the three companion dimensions of ad quality, as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validated through sign-certain behavioural perturbations, the evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence. Upon its estimates we build the pricing layer directly, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on a best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations. The same differentiable signal stands ready as a training objective for ad generation.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the lack of reliable click-through intent signals for LLM-driven answer engine advertising. It constructs supervision via a psychologically grounded agent simulation, distills this into an efficient evaluator, and builds a truthful-bidding pricing mechanism atop its continuous intent estimates.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become the interface for search, ads are embedded in generated responses, but evaluating them is broken: behavioral click logs don't exist, human annotation is uncalibrated, and LLM judges conflate intent with fluency. Principled ad pricing requires a continuous intent signal, yet generating such a signal requires supervision that currently does not exist — a circular dependency the paper aims to break.
AI.method: The authors construct missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework simulating user click-through behavior. This supervision is distilled into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent plus three companion dimensions of ad quality as smooth, differentiable estimates. The evaluator is validated via sign-certain behavioral perturbations. On top of these estimates, the authors derive the unique payment rule that makes truthful bidding optimal (a Vickrey-style mechanism), demonstrate it on best-of-k allocation, and extend to non-monotone allocations.
AI.result: The evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% vs 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalizes without error to 103 fictional products, and achieves 86% agreement with human pairwise judgments across five annotators, with agreement rising as evaluator confidence increases.
AI.conclusion: The differentiable intent signal solves the supervision gap for LLM-embedded advertising evaluation and enables truthful pricing mechanisms. The same signal can serve as a training objective for ad generation, unifying evaluation, pricing, and generation within a single framework.

title: ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?
summary: Large language models can write, patch, and search code, but oncall root cause analysis (RCA) demands something different: reasoning over noisy metrics, logs, traces, and source code, starting from ambiguous user-facing reports, often hours after the incident began. We introduce ORCA-bench, a benchmark that puts general-purpose coding agents in a production-fidelity oncall setting. ORCA-bench pairs a live OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice system--exposing six days of metrics, logs, and traces through real telemetry interfaces (Prometheus, Jaeger, and OpenSearch via Grafana) and full source-code access--with 1,079 RCA tasks that systematically vary report specificity, time-to-detection, and co-occurring fault scenarios. Ground-truth symptoms are curated and signed off by expert SREs, and our LLM-as-judge is independently re-scored by humans (Cohen's $κ_w=0.90$). Across five frontier agents, the best RCA Accuracy is 25.3% on Medium-difficulty tasks (the realistic-input setting) and 10.0% on Hard--a gap that remains even with Claude Fable 5. The weakest model hallucinates an implausible root cause in 40% of incident reports, and removing source-code access degrades every metric. Crucially, these are performances on a curated 50 GB / six-day testbed with tasks investigated in isolation on a system whose code and instrumentation are public. Since real production systems are order of magnitudes larger, more dynamic, and more idiosyncratic, the gap we report is a lower bound on the engineering investment required before frontier coding agents can be safely entrusted with production reliability. We release the public set at https://hub.harborframework.com/datasets/orca-bench/ORCA-bench.

AI.tldr: ORCA-bench introduces a production-fidelity benchmark for evaluating coding agents on oncall root cause analysis (RCA), revealing that even the best frontier agents achieve only 25.3% accuracy on medium-difficulty tasks, with hallucination rates up to 40%.
AI.motivation: Existing code agent benchmarks fail to capture the unique demands of oncall RCA: reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous telemetry data (metrics, logs, traces) alongside source code, starting from ambiguous user-facing reports with variable time-to-detection. No prior benchmark provides a realistic, SRE-vetted environment for evaluating agents on this task.
AI.method: The authors built ORCA-bench, pairing a live OpenTelemetry-instrumented microservice system (6 days of data surfaced via Prometheus, Jaeger, OpenSearch/Grafana) with 1,079 RCA tasks that systematically vary report specificity, detection delay, and co-occurring faults. Ground-truth symptoms were curated by expert SREs, and an LLM-as-judge scoring pipeline was validated against human evaluators (Cohen's κ_w=0.90). Five frontier agents were evaluated under multiple difficulty tiers.
AI.result: Best RCA Accuracy reached only 25.3% on Medium and 10.0% on Hard difficulty. The weakest model hallucinated implausible root causes in 40% of reports. Removing source-code access degraded every metric, confirming its necessity for RCA. The performance gap represents a lower bound, as real production systems are far larger and more dynamic than the curated 50 GB testbed.
AI.conclusion: Frontier coding agents are far from trustworthy for production oncall RCA. Substantial engineering investment is needed before these agents can be safely deployed. ORCA-bench is publicly released to drive further research.

title: When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment
summary: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved. Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether multi-view graph-text retrieval models genuinely perform semantic routing — directing queries to appropriate specialized heads — or merely exhibit architectural channelization. Using controlled experiments with deterministic text segments, isolated encoders, and external labels/properties, the authors show that correct routing significantly improves retrieval on molecular benchmarks (BBBP, BACE). However, evidence is limited to explicit, externally grounded routing and does not extend to free-form semantic routing or consistent multi-view specialization.
AI.motivation: Prior multi-view graph-text retrieval models (e.g., MV-GTA) use multiple heads ostensibly to capture different semantic aspects (topology, labels, properties). However, the authors observe that retrieval behavior changes when queries are sent to different heads even with incorrect text, suggesting these heads merely provide architectural channelization rather than true semantic routing based on content. The paper aims to establish rigorous causal conditions to distinguish genuine content-based routing from spurious architectural effects.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled version of MV-GTA featuring: (1) deterministic, verifiable text segments (not free-form); (2) isolated text encoders for each view; (3) view-specific graph heads; and (4) relevance derived from external labels or RDKit molecular descriptors. They introduce a causal test using correct routing versus per-sample derangements (sending text to wrong heads). Experiments are conducted on BBBP and BACE molecular datasets across topology, label, and property views. They compare a single joint model against three separately trained specialists, and test property paraphrase augmentation against matched-exposure canonical controls, along with consistency and hard-template extensions.
AI.result: Correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305–0.685 over deranged training on BBBP and BACE. The expected graph head outperforms the best wrong head by 0.303–0.453 in nDCG. Topology does not specialize consistently across datasets. A joint model achieves mean topology/label/property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877 versus separately trained specialists at 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140–0.147 over canonical controls. However, consistency and hard-template extensions reduce canonical retrieval in some settings.
AI.conclusion: Evidence supports explicit, externally grounded label and property routing, along with multi-interface consolidation benefits. However, the study does not establish free-form semantic routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to separately trained specialists, or superior downstream prediction performance. The distinction between architectural channelization and genuine semantic routing requires the causal framework introduced here, and the positive results are bounded by these caveats.

title: LEEPS: Latent-Guided Explore-Exploit Prompt Sampling for Efficient RLVR in Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but prompt groups with identical rollout rewards consume generation budget without effective learning signals. Pre-rollout prompt selection can reduce this waste by screening prompts before rollout generation. However, existing pre-rollout methods struggle to balance exploitation and exploration: repeatedly exploiting historically informative prompts can narrow training coverage, whereas broader exploration can lower the fraction of informative prompts. To address these limitations, we introduce LEEPS, a Latent-Guided Explore--Exploit Prompt Sampler that adaptively balances the reuse of previously observed informative prompts with continued exploration of uncertain ones. LEEPS partitions candidates into exploit and explore portfolios and adaptively allocates rollout budget according to their recent non-trivial ratios. It further uses representation-space neighbors and historical rollout outcomes to prioritize uncertain prompts likely to yield non-zero reward variance, thereby making exploration more targeted without additional rollouts. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, LEEPS achieves the highest average score at both model scales, with relative gains of 2.6\% and 3.7\% over the strongest baseline for Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and 7B, respectively, and generally improves faster during the training process. It also achieves the highest average score across the three evaluated OOD general-reasoning benchmarks at both model scales and adds only about 2 seconds of online sampling overhead per training step. Code is available at https://github.com/ShuangLiangX/LEEPS.

AI.tldr: LEEPS is an adaptive prompt sampling method for RLVR that balances exploitation of historically informative prompts with targeted exploration of uncertain ones, using representation-space neighbors and historical outcomes to improve reasoning performance with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: In RLVR, many prompt groups yield identical rollout rewards, wasting computation without providing learning signals. Existing pre-rollout selection methods either over-exploit known informative prompts (reducing diversity) or over-explore (diluting informativeness). A method is needed that adaptively balances exploitation and exploration without requiring additional rollouts during screening.
AI.method: LEEPS partitions candidate prompts into exploit and explore portfolios. It adaptively allocates rollout budget based on recent non-trivial ratios (fraction of prompts yielding informative signals). For exploration, it leverages representation-space neighbors and historical rollout outcomes to prioritize uncertain prompts likely to produce non-zero reward variance, enabling targeted exploration without extra rollouts.
AI.result: On six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, LEEPS achieves the highest average scores, with relative gains of 2.6% (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B) and 3.7% (Qwen2.5-Math-7B) over the strongest baseline. It also attains the highest average across three OOD general-reasoning benchmarks at both scales, improves faster during training, and adds only ~2 seconds of online sampling overhead per training step.
AI.conclusion: LEEPS effectively addresses the exploitation-exploration trade-off in pre-rollout prompt selection for RLVR, delivering consistent improvements across model scales and benchmarks with negligible computational overhead.

title: Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch
summary: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

AI.tldr: LLM-based pre-execution judgment of code modifications in autoresearch loops degrades significantly over time (selective accuracy dropping from 82.8% to 56.9%), a phenomenon termed the "confidence cliff." The proposed Rehearse system counters this using focused outcome memory, restoring late-loop selective accuracy to 83.5% and improving results across multiple domains under fixed training budgets.
AI.motivation: Autoresearch agents that iteratively propose and test ML code modifications rely on pre-execution judgment to avoid wasting training runs on unpromising ideas. The authors observe that this judgment reliability collapses over the course of a trajectory, creating inefficiency. Understanding and mitigating this degradation is the central motivation.
AI.method: The authors construct a benchmark of 296 same-baseline modification pairs (expanded to 366) from 39 AutoSOTA tasks, where each pair contains one successful and one unsuccessful modification. They evaluate LLM judges' accuracy in discriminating helpful from unhelpful modifications, with and without strict consensus, at different trajectory depths. They then propose Rehearse, which adds a lightweight skill to the autoresearch loop: generate multiple candidate ideas, compare them pre-execution, run the most promising, and judge using a focused memory of similar past attempts and their outcomes.
AI.result: Public AutoSOTA logs show the fraction of helpful modifications drops from ~70% (iterations 1-2) to ~43% (iteration 6+). On the 296-pair benchmark, LLM judges with strict consensus achieve 79.5% accuracy. However, selective accuracy conditioned on consensus verdicts falls from 82.8% early in the loop to 56.9% late in the loop—the judge remains confident but becomes wrong. Rehearse's focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting tasks, Rehearse improves the endpoint metric under the same training-run budget.
AI.conclusion: The "confidence cliff" is a systematic failure mode in LLM-based autoresearch loops where pre-execution judgment reliability degrades as successful modifications accumulate. Focused outcome memory, as implemented in Rehearse, effectively mitigates this degradation by anchoring judgments in relevant past outcomes, leading to better research outcomes under fixed computational budgets.

title: Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory
summary: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

AI.tldr: Exact deletion from language models is achievable when memory representations are addressable (via algebraic decrement) or when entangled writes are replayed; the paper empirically validates this distinction across models ranging from 1B to 48B parameters, demonstrating bit-for-bit exact deletion in deterministic implementations.
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the practical and regulatory need to delete specific records from language model memory. It challenges the prevailing assumption that exact deletion is inherently difficult or approximate, instead arguing that the feasibility of exact deletion depends fundamentally on how the model represents and stores memory—specifically whether influence is addressable and subtractable versus entangled through recurrent state updates.
AI.method: The authors test their theoretical distinction through two empirical setups. First, they modify Gemma 3 by replacing global-attention layers with support-vector memory, applying low-rank recovery at 1B scale, and comparing algebraic decrement against retained-key refit via next-token KL divergence, perplexity, elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. They scale experiments to 4B and 12B. Second, they use a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid model to analyze three write mechanisms (additive writes, diagonal decay, delta rule), measure suffix-dependence of contributions, and implement checkpointed rewind-and-replay for exact deletion of clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, verified bit-for-bit in a deterministic MLX implementation.
AI.result: At 1B scale, decrement and retained-key refit agree to median KL divergence of 5.4×10⁻¹⁵ over 31 deletions, with only +2.0% perplexity increase relative to matched fine-tuning. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from never-ingested baselines across all evaluation methods. At 4B and 12B, exact deletion remains certified but utility cost rises to 11.2% and 44.3% respectively. In the 48B Kimi Linear model, additive writes and diagonal decay permit fixed/corrected decrements, but the delta rule renders 12–49% of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Rewind-and-replay achieves bit-for-bit identical logits and recurrent states to never-ingested models, and supports exact amendment via replaying corrections.
AI.conclusion: Exact deletion is a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes. The paper demonstrates that when memory is architecturally addressable, algebraic decrement suffices; when writes are entangled in recurrent state, checkpointed rewind-and-replay provides a deterministic path to exact deletion.

title: GGC: Selective Query Correction for Reliable Text-to-SPARQL Generation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in structured query generation, making them a natural choice for Text-to-SPARQL, which translates natural language questions into executable SPARQL queries over knowledge graphs. However, their initial outputs remain unreliable: generated queries may be executable yet semantically misaligned with input questions, leading to incorrect retrieval. To address this issue, we propose Generator-Gate-Corrector (GGC), a framework for reliable LLM-based Text-to-SPARQL generation. GGC first uses a Generator to produce an initial query, then applies a Gate to predict whether correction is needed, and finally invokes a Corrector only for selected high-risk queries. This selective correction mechanism avoids unnecessary modifications and reduces the risk of degrading originally correct queries. Experiments on MCQA show that GGC improves query-level accuracy from 90.23\% to 98.33\% while reducing inference overhead by 45\% compared with correcting all generated queries. Ablation studies show that the Gate is robust across thresholds and that Corrector training data composition affects correction effectiveness and stability. Overall, the results demonstrate that selective correction enhances the accuracy, reliability, and efficiency of LLM-based text-to-SPARQL generation.

AI.tldr: GGC is a framework that improves LLM-based Text-to-SPARQL reliability by selectively correcting only high-risk queries using a Generator-Gate-Corrector pipeline, achieving 98.33% accuracy while reducing inference overhead by 45%.
AI.motivation: LLMs generate SPARQL queries that may be syntactically executable but semantically misaligned with the input question, leading to incorrect retrieval. Correcting all queries is wasteful and risks degrading originally correct ones.
AI.method: The GGC framework consists of three stages: a Generator produces an initial SPARQL query from a natural language question; a Gate predicts whether the query requires correction; and a Corrector refines only those queries flagged as high-risk by the Gate, leaving low-risk queries untouched.
AI.result: On the MCQA benchmark, GGC improved query-level accuracy from 90.23% to 98.33% and reduced inference overhead by 45% compared to correcting all queries. The Gate proved robust across different thresholds, and Corrector training data composition significantly impacted correction effectiveness and stability.
AI.conclusion: Selective correction via the GGC framework effectively enhances accuracy, reliability, and computational efficiency in LLM-based Text-to-SPARQL generation, outperforming both uncorrected baselines and indiscriminate full-correction approaches.

title: Guiding Large Language Models with Genetic Programming-Evolved Heuristic Knowledge for Dynamic Multi-Mode Project Scheduling
summary: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, activities have alternative execution modes and uncertain durations, while precedence relations and limited resources constrain their execution. Heuristic priority rules support fast online decisions, but their design requires substantial domain expertise. Genetic programming (GP) hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve such rules. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, provide a flexible interface for interpreting scheduling information and explaining decisions. However, zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume many tokens, and vary across repeated queries. GP-evolved rules therefore provide a potential source of scheduling knowledge for guiding LLM decisions. Unlike existing LLM--GP hybrids that use LLMs to support heuristic evolution, we transfer knowledge in the reverse direction, using knowledge extracted from high-quality GP rules to guide an online LLM decision maker. We extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it through Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. These mechanisms are evaluated in terms of scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus expressed in generated rationales. GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but its representation matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, whereas Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using knowledge extracted from GP-evolved priority rules to guide LLM-based decision-making in dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, reversing the typical LLM→GP knowledge flow. Four guidance mechanisms (Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, Rule Follow) are evaluated on scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and rationale feature focus.
AI.motivation: While GP hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve effective priority rules for dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, LLMs offer flexible natural language interfaces for interpreting scheduling context and explaining decisions. Zero-shot LLMs, however, lack domain knowledge, are token-inefficient, and produce inconsistent outputs. GP-evolved rules contain valuable scheduling knowledge that could address these limitations, but existing hybrids only use LLMs to support evolution—not the reverse.
AI.method: The authors extract knowledge from high-quality GP-evolved scheduling rules and inject it into LLM decision-making via four mechanisms: (1) Feature Selection—reducing the feature set shown to the LLM to only those deemed important by GP; (2) Feature Hint—explicitly indicating which features are most important; (3) Rule Reference—providing the GP rule as a reference in natural language; and (4) Rule Follow—instructing the LLM to directly apply the GP rule's decision logic. These are evaluated against an unguided LLM baseline across multiple GP rule sources and problem configurations.
AI.result: GP-derived guidance generally improves scheduling performance over the unguided LLM. Feature Selection achieves the best token efficiency, while Rule Follow delivers the strongest scheduling performance but at higher token cost. Feature Hint and Feature Selection provide intermediate improvements. Rule Reference and Rule Follow significantly improve decision stability across repeated queries. Guidance also shifts the feature focus expressed in LLM-generated rationales, aligning them more closely with GP-identified important features. The representation of injected knowledge critically matters: simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit logic proves more effective than merely highlighting important features.
AI.conclusion: Transferring knowledge from GP-evolved rules to guide LLM decision-makers is effective, but the mechanism of knowledge injection significantly impacts outcomes. Simplification (Feature Selection) and explicit logic (Rule Follow) outperform mere feature highlighting (Feature Hint), and both token efficiency and decision stability improve. This reverse knowledge transfer direction—from evolved heuristics to LLMs—represents a promising paradigm for combining the complementary strengths of GP and LLMs in operational scheduling.

title: Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures Accepted at FMSD @ ICML 2026
summary: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates memory requirements for Tabular Foundation Models (specifically TabPFN) and demonstrates that model compression can reduce memory usage by up to 7.6× (nearly 87% reduction) while maintaining comparable performance.
AI.motivation: While Tabular Foundation Models like TabPFN have gained attention for strong in-context learning performance on tabular data, their practical deployment considerations—particularly memory requirements—have been largely overlooked. The authors aim to address this gap.
AI.method: The authors apply model compression techniques to Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN) and evaluate the trade-off between memory reduction and performance retention on in-context tabular machine learning tasks.
AI.result: Model compression achieves memory reductions of up to 7.6×, corresponding to an approximately 87% decrease in deployment requirements, while maintaining similar levels of predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Practitioners can substantially reduce the memory footprint of Tabular Foundation Models through compression without sacrificing performance, making efficient deployment in practical settings feasible.

title: Challenges in annotations by humans and LLMs: A case study of evaluative language
