summary: In this paper, we draw a comparison between linguists in training, a trained linguist, and annotations generated by large language models (LLMs) to find out if they struggle with complex linguistic phenomena in a similar way. For this purpose, we analyse evaluative language in spoken popular science discourse, with the example of a corpus of English TED talk transcripts. We focus on the Appraisal theory and its Attitude subsystem, including the categories (classes) of Affect, Judgement, and Appreciation. In this context, Appraisal theory is an example of a highly subjective annotation task, making it a suitable example for the study of complex annotation challenges. First, we assess human annotations on a sentence level in specific scientific domains. Then, we develop three prompts and compare them for model performance for the automatic classification of Appraisal classes. We assess the performance of three LLMs using the best-performing prompt and finetune the model, reaching an F1-score of 0.77. We find that models perform best compared to annotations conducted by the trained linguist, while linguists in training do not reach high agreement scores. We conclude that LLMs can aid in complex annotation task resolution, opening new pathways for the complex theories annotated and analyzed in digital humanities studies.

AI.tldr: The paper compares LLMs, trained linguists, and linguists-in-training on annotating evaluative language (Appraisal Theory's Attitude subsystem) in TED Talks, finding LLMs align best with trained linguists (F1=0.77), suggesting LLMs can assist with complex, subjective annotation tasks in digital humanities.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether LLMs and humans struggle similarly with complex, highly subjective linguistic annotation tasks, using Appraisal Theory as a representative test case.
AI.method: Human annotation (by linguists-in-training and a trained linguist) of TED Talk transcripts at the sentence level for Affect, Judgement, and Appreciation categories. Three prompts were developed and compared; the best-performing prompt was used with three LLMs, including a fine-tuned variant.
AI.result: The fine-tuned LLM achieved an F1-score of 0.77. LLMs performed best when compared against the trained linguist's annotations, while linguists-in-training showed low inter-annotator agreement.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively aid in resolving complex annotation tasks, offering new opportunities for analyzing complex theoretical frameworks in digital humanities research.

title: SpatialCLI: Learning to Reason With Spatial Tools, Then Without Them
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in embodied agents to interpret visual inputs, reason about spatial relationships, and make task-level decisions based on that reasoning. However, a fundamental capability mismatch remains: general VLMs can reason about the overall task but often miss the visual details that determine success, while specialist vision models can capture those details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. In this work, we propose SpatialCLI, a framework that teaches VLMs to reason with spatial tools and progressively internalize the specialist perceptual capabilities they provide. SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment the VLM's perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; and (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. We further introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose. On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

AI.tldr: SpatialCLI is a three-stage framework (Call, Learn, Internalize) that teaches VLMs to use specialist spatial vision tools and eventually internalize their perceptual capabilities, significantly boosting embodied agent performance.
AI.motivation: General VLMs excel at task-level reasoning but miss fine-grained visual details critical for embodied tasks, while specialist vision models capture those details but lack task-level reasoning. Bridging this gap is the core motivation.
AI.method: SpatialCLI operates in three stages: (1) Call — exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment VLM perception; (2) Learn — uses Cold-Start Supervised Fine-Tuning and agentic Reinforcement Learning to improve tool-use proficiency; (3) Internalize — verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories so the VLM progressively internalizes specialist perceptual capabilities without needing tools at inference.
AI.result: On MindCube, SpatialCLI boosts Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%). After internalization, the model retains 73.8% accuracy without tools. SpatialCLI-Bench provides 516 examples for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose.
AI.conclusion: The Call-Learn-Internalize paradigm effectively bridges the gap between general VLM reasoning and specialist visual perception, enabling embodied agents to achieve high performance with tools while progressively internalizing those capabilities for tool-free inference.

title: Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings
summary: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

AI.tldr: This paper solves a continuous-time stochastic control model for entrepreneurial start-ups facing milestone-based success/failure, where the entrepreneur chooses among multiple activities. The optimal policy is characterized by an "efficient frontier curve" ordering controls by riskiness and cost-effectiveness, with qualitatively different optimal structures depending on the frontier type.
AI.motivation: New ventures must survive through multiple milestone stages, yet continuous-time stochastic models with three or more controls are notoriously difficult to solve. Prior literature lacks a tractable framework that fully characterizes optimal policies under multiple control options and reveals how the structure of optimal strategies changes qualitatively with different parameter regimes.
AI.method: The authors model the start-up's state as a diffusion process bounded by an upper (success) and lower (failure) boundary. The entrepreneur selects from multiple activities (controls) that each carry different costs and determine the drift and variance of the process. They solve the stochastic control problem analytically, introducing the concept of an "efficient frontier curve" that orders controls by two metrics: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio).
AI.result: The optimal policy uses only controls lying on the efficient frontier curve. Depending on model parameters, this curve can take different types, leading to qualitatively distinct optimal policy structures. The authors provide a complete, explicit characterization of the optimal policy across all cases.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study to analyze a stochastic control model admitting efficient frontier curves of different types. The results offer start-up firms intuitive measures for evaluating activities and provide foundational insights into entrepreneurial decision-making under milestone-oriented settings.

title: FinSMART: Financial Sentiment Analysis for Algorithmic Trading through Market-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
summary: Recent advances in Generative AI have substantially improved financial sentiment analysis through post-trained financial large language models (LLMs). However, existing approaches remain confined to a market-agnostic, supervised learning paradigm that relies on limited, static and human-annotated datasets, and thus are incapable of adapting to evolving market conditions. To address this limitation, we introduce FinSMART, the first market-aligned reinforcement learning framework for financial sentiment analysis, which directly optimizes sentiment signals using realized market outcomes. To deal with the noisy, non-stationary, and multifactorial nature of financial markets, FinSMART incorporates a signal extraction pipeline that combines market-aware data filtering with a discrete asymmetric trading reward, enabling stable reinforcement learning from economically meaningful market feedback. Experimental results demonstrate that FinSMART significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in profitability, risk-adjusted performance, and sentiment signal quality, improving cumulative trading returns by 220% over the strongest baseline. Uniquely, the FinSMART framework naturally supports market-aware retraining, at any point in time, by replacing costly manual annotation with newly observed financial articles and their realized market outcomes. Such a retraining strategy enables the model to continuously adapt to changing market dynamics, resulting in consistent performance gains over its static counterpart. These findings demonstrate the practical applicability of market-aligned reinforcement learning and highlight its potential as a next-generation paradigm for developing adaptive financial LLMs.

AI.tldr: FinSMART introduces a market-aligned reinforcement learning framework for financial sentiment analysis that directly optimizes sentiment signals using realized market outcomes, significantly outperforming static supervised methods and enabling continuous adaptation to evolving market conditions.
AI.motivation: Existing financial sentiment analysis LLMs rely on market-agnostic supervised learning with limited, static, human-annotated datasets. They cannot adapt to evolving market conditions, as manual annotation is costly and static labels fail to capture the noisy, non-stationary, and multifactorial nature of financial markets.
AI.method: FinSMART is a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sentiment signals directly against realized market outcomes. It features: (1) a signal extraction pipeline with market-aware data filtering to handle noisy financial data; (2) a discrete asymmetric trading reward function that translates market outcomes into stable, economically meaningful feedback; and (3) a market-aware retraining strategy that replaces manual annotation with newly observed articles and their realized outcomes for continuous model adaptation.
AI.result: FinSMART significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across profitability, risk-adjusted performance, and sentiment signal quality, achieving a 220% improvement in cumulative trading returns over the strongest baseline. The market-aware retraining strategy yields consistent performance gains over its static counterpart.
AI.conclusion: Market-aligned reinforcement learning represents a viable next-generation paradigm for developing adaptive financial LLMs, demonstrating practical applicability through continuous, annotation-free adaptation to changing market dynamics.

title: Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration
summary:
Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

AI.tldr: Albilich is an open-source agentic framework for AI-assisted mathematical research that integrates long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems, literature retrieval, and persistent context management. It achieves strong performance on the RealMath benchmark and makes novel contributions to open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook.
AI.motivation: While LLMs can contribute useful ideas to mathematics, long-horizon proof attempts are difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. There is a need for a structured, reproducible agentic harness that can sustain extended mathematical reasoning, leverage external tools, and maintain context over long proof trajectories.
AI.method: Albilich is an agentic harness combining: (1) long-horizon reasoning capabilities, (2) integration with computer algebra systems (CAS), (3) literature retrieval mechanisms, and (4) persistent SQLite-based context management for maintaining state across extended proof attempts. An advisor agent component guides proof route synthesis. The system is evaluated on RealMath (with and without CAS) and open group theory problems from the Kourovka Notebook, with ablation studies on token usage and agent component contributions.
AI.result: On RealMath, Albilich solved 10/10 problems with CAS and 9/10 without CAS. On Kourovka open problems, it produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof strengthening Problem 20.2. Ablation on Problem 17.91 showed 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. Ablation on Problem 21.142 showed that removing the advisor agent leads to higher verifier-rejection rates and failure to synthesize proof routes.
AI.conclusion: Albilich demonstrates viability as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research, with the advisor agent and CAS integration proving critical to its success on challenging open problems.

title: Rethinking LLM-Judged Helpfulness as a Pedagogy Signal: A Pre-Registered Audit Across Tutor Models
summary: LLM tutoring poses a measurement problem: can a general-purpose helpfulness rubric distinguish direct answer-giving from pedagogical guidance? We audit this signal in a pre-registered study. Within each of three tutor bases, we compare conversational and pedagogical policies instantiated with the same underlying model and paired with one fixed weak simulated student. Deterministic detectors measure answer leakage and next-turn independent work. Claude Opus 4.8 is the frozen, condition-blind primary judge. After the Opus scores were fixed, GPT-5.6 Sol was prospectively specified for a post hoc robustness audit of the same 1,179 confirmatory answer-phase tutor turns under the frozen helpfulness and pedagogy rubrics. On the primary base under Opus, the policies do not differ significantly in helpfulness but are perfectly rank-separated under the pedagogy rubric (Cliff's $|δ|{=}0.10$ vs. $1.0$). Across the two judges, pedagogy contrasts retain their direction where detected, whereas the helpfulness ordering is judge-contingent, reversing between judges on two of three bases. In an Opus-only ablation, seven primary-base policies span $2.3$ points in mean judged pedagogy within a $0.25$-point band of mean judged helpfulness. Separately, answer-revealing turns are followed by less independent student work on every base, a result that is judge-invariant by construction. In this controlled setting, general-purpose helpfulness is not a reliable pedagogy signal. Tutor evaluation should pair pedagogy-targeted rubrics with deterministic process measures.

AI.tldr: In a controlled LLM tutoring experiment, general-purpose helpfulness rubrics fail to distinguish direct answer-giving from genuine pedagogical guidance—pedagogy-specific rubrics and deterministic process measures (answer leakage, independent work) are necessary for reliable tutor evaluation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based tutoring systems are increasingly deployed, but evaluation relies heavily on general helpfulness ratings. The authors question whether such rubrics can validly discriminate between a tutor that genuinely scaffolds learning versus one that simply gives away answers—a distinction critical for educational efficacy.
AI.method: A pre-registered audit comparing conversational vs. pedagogical tutoring policies—instantiated from the same underlying model—across three tutor bases, each paired with a fixed weak simulated student. Deterministic detectors measure answer leakage and next-turn independent student work. Claude Opus 4.8 serves as the primary frozen, condition-blind judge; GPT-5.6 Sol is used for a post hoc robustness audit on 1,179 confirmatory answer-phase turns under both helpfulness and pedagogy rubrics. Cliff's delta quantifies separation between policies.
AI.result: Under Opus, the two policies do not differ significantly in helpfulness but are perfectly rank-separated under the pedagogy rubric (Cliff's |δ| = 0.10 vs. 1.0). Helpfulness ordering reverses between judges on two of three bases, while pedagogy contrasts retain direction when detected. A seven-policy ablation shows pedagogy scores spanning 2.3 points within a 0.25-point helpfulness band. Answer-revealing turns consistently predict less independent student work across all bases, a judge-invariant result.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose helpfulness is not a reliable proxy for pedagogical quality in LLM tutoring. Reliable evaluation requires pairing pedagogy-targeted rubrics with deterministic, judge-invariant process measures such as answer leakage and downstream student independence.

title: MECA: A Mechanism-Centered Agent for Constructing Well-Specified and Valuable Mathematical Conjectures
comment: 78 pages, 5 figures. Includes appendices and the full collection of 100 generated conjectures
summary: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures remains a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies. We view a mathematical mechanism as a structure or reasoning principle that connects the assumptions of a candidate problem to its target conclusion, such as an inequality, invariant, decomposition, or reduction to an intermediate claim. We present MECA (MEchanism-centered Conjecture Agent), a multi-agent framework that constructs conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms. Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise the candidate conjecture accordingly, while critic agents assess their mathematical validity and research value. Their feedback guides changes to the assumptions, scope, and conclusion. Through this process, MECA transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures with substantive mathematical support while retaining a clearly identified unresolved core. We evaluate MECA in two complementary settings. First, we compare it with a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. Second, we construct 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems and evaluate them through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Our results indicate that mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified and research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

AI.tldr: MECA is a multi-agent framework that constructs mathematical conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and supporting mechanisms (reasoning principles like inequalities, invariants, or decompositions). Explorer agents propose and test mechanisms, while critic agents assess validity and research value. Evaluated against a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing target conclusions and via 100 semi-open problems tested by automated provers, MECA produces well-specified, research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.
AI.motivation: Existing open problems and conjectures in mathematics are often too broad, underspecified, or lack clear connections to plausible proof or refutation strategies. This limits their utility in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. The authors identify a gap: current conjecture-generation methods do not systematically pair candidate statements with the reasoning principles (mechanisms) that connect assumptions to conclusions.
AI.method: MECA is a multi-agent framework with two agent types: (1) Explorer agents that propose mathematical mechanisms, test their applicability, and revise candidate conjectures accordingly; (2) Critic agents that evaluate mathematical validity and research value, providing feedback that guides modifications to assumptions, scope, and conclusions. The process iteratively transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures supported by substantive mechanisms while preserving a clearly identified unresolved core.
AI.result: In the first evaluation, MECA outperformed a generate-and-revise baseline in reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. In the second evaluation, 100 semi-open problems constructed by MECA from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems were tested by automated provers; the conjectures proved well-specified and challenging, resisting both proof and refutation attempts.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism-centered refinement produces conjectures that are simultaneously well-specified enough to be mathematically tractable and challenging enough to resist current automated reasoning tools. By anchoring conjecture generation in explicit reasoning mechanisms, MECA addresses a key bottleneck in AI-assisted mathematical discovery.

title: Can Agents Deceive? Evaluating Reasoning and Deception in ParliamentBench using a Social Deduction Game
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as agents in high-stakes settings, such as medical and legal systems, understanding their deceptive capabilities is fundamental to safety. Controlled social deduction games provide a reproducible proxy for isolating and evaluating these complex adversarial behaviors. We present the open-source benchmark framework ParliamentBench based on the game Secret Hitler to evaluate LLMs in scenarios that require deception, persuasion, and reasoning under information asymmetry. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 1,600 simulated matches playing each other, playing against humans, and compare them against a large set of online games. We introduce three novel metrics that isolate social deduction, reasoning, and deceptive consistency. Our experiments reveal that frontier models achieve strong performance across cooperative and deceptive roles, with a strong top-four cluster (GPT-5.4, Kimi K2.5, Grok 4.1 Fast, and DeepSeek 3.1 Terminus), whereas the weakest models fall short of random (33%) and simple algorithmic (45%) baselines. Most LLMs struggle to maintain a consistent deceptive persona throughout an entire game, with deception retention dropping below 50%.

AI.tldr: ParliamentBench is an open-source benchmark based on Secret Hitler that evaluates LLMs on deception, persuasion, and reasoning under information asymmetry across 1,600 simulated matches. Frontier models (GPT-5.4, Kimi K2.5, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek 3.1 Terminus) perform strongly, while weaker models fall below random baselines. Most LLMs fail to maintain consistent deceptive personas, with deception retention dropping below 50%.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are deployed in high-stakes domains like medicine and law, understanding their deceptive capabilities is critical for safety. Controlled social deduction games offer a reproducible method to isolate and evaluate adversarial behaviors such as deception and persuasion under information asymmetry.
AI.method: The authors introduce ParliamentBench, an open-source benchmark framework built on the game Secret Hitler. They evaluate 16 LLMs across 1,600 simulated matches in LLM-vs-LLM and LLM-vs-human settings, comparing results against a large corpus of online human games. Three novel metrics are proposed: one isolating social deduction, one for reasoning, and one for deceptive consistency.
AI.result: Frontier models (GPT-5.4, Kimi K2.5, Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek 3.1 Terminus) form a strong top-four cluster and perform well in both cooperative and deceptive roles. The weakest models fall below random (33%) and simple algorithmic (45%) baselines. Deception retention across an entire game drops below 50% for most LLMs, indicating difficulty maintaining consistent deceptive personas.
AI.conclusion: Frontier LLMs demonstrate strong social deduction capabilities, but consistent deception over extended interactions remains a significant challenge. The benchmark provides a reproducible framework for ongoing safety evaluation of adversarial LLM behaviors.

title: New Synchronous Computation Dynamics for Hopfield Networks
summary: The dynamics of the original Hopfield network is asynchronous (sequential) (updates the state of only one neuron per time step). In this paper, we propose a new tool and a new dynamics to reduce the processing time by updating one or more neurons simultaneously per instant while ensuring process convergence and aiming for the maximum energy decrease at each step, thus guaranteeing the shortest total processing time. From the point of view of synchronous dynamics, calculating the next network state at which energy decreases the most from the current state while ensuring convergence is itself a combinatorial optimization problem. We develop and use a new tool to solve it. We call this new tool Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and, based upon it, we develop a new synchronous dynamics which we call SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). In this paper, we review the original asynchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks and present a new tool and a new synchronous dynamics with its theoretical justification and four computational experiments to assess the speed up in processing time empirically.

AI.tldr: Proposes a new synchronous dynamics (SD-DDF) for Hopfield networks using a Discrete Differential Filter to update multiple neurons simultaneously, maximizing energy decrease per step while guaranteeing convergence, thereby reducing total processing time compared to traditional asynchronous updates.
AI.motivation: The original Hopfield network uses asynchronous (sequential) dynamics, updating only one neuron per time step, which leads to long processing times. The authors aim to accelerate convergence by enabling synchronous updates of multiple neurons while ensuring that the network still converges and that energy decreases maximally at each step.
AI.method: The authors introduce a new tool called the Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) to solve the combinatorial optimization problem of selecting which subset of neurons to update synchronously for maximal energy decrease while preserving convergence. Based on DDF, they develop SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). The paper provides theoretical justification and validates the approach with four computational experiments.
AI.result: Four computational experiments empirically demonstrate a significant speed-up in processing time when using the proposed SD-DDF dynamics compared to the original asynchronous Hopfield dynamics.
AI.conclusion: The SD-DDF approach successfully reduces processing time in Hopfield networks by enabling convergent synchronous multi-neuron updates that maximize energy descent, validated both theoretically and empirically.

title: RRM: Experience-Driven Reflective Retrieval Memory for Long-Horizon Multimodal Reasoning
summary: Existing multimodal long-term memory agents use external memory to overcome the limited context available for long videos. However, most methods emphasize what to store rather than how stored memory should be retrieved. When retrieval becomes inaccurate or repeatedly fails to obtain useful evidence, existing agents lack mechanisms to diagnose failures from previous task trajectories and adapt future search strategies.We introduce Reflective Retrieval Memory (RRM), a reflective memory framework for long-horizon multimodal reasoning. RRM augments an entity-centric multimodal memory graph with reflective experience memory, which distills transferable procedural retrieval knowledge from historical task trajectories. Unlike episodic and semantic memories that preserve factual evidence from the current video, reflective experience memory captures reusable search strategies across tasks. RRM converts retrieved experiences into query-level guidance, while answer generation remains conditioned only on factual evidence newly retrieved from the current video. A lifecycle management mechanism further regulates experience memory through usage frequency, reuse feedback, and temporal decay, thereby reducing redundancy and noise. RRM consistently outperforms previous state-of-the-art approaches on M3-Bench-Robot, M3-Bench-Web, and Video-MME-Long, demonstrating the effectiveness of reflective retrieval memory for long-horizon multimodal reasoning.

AI.tldr: RRM introduces a reflective memory framework that augments multimodal memory graphs with reusable retrieval strategies distilled from past task trajectories, enabling agents to adapt search behavior when retrieval fails, outperforming prior SOTA on long-horizon reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal long-term memory agents focus on storage strategies but lack mechanisms to diagnose retrieval failures from previous task trajectories and adapt future search strategies when retrieval is repeatedly inaccurate or unproductive.
AI.method: RRM augments an entity-centric multimodal memory graph with reflective experience memory that distills transferable procedural retrieval knowledge from historical task trajectories. Retrieved experiences are converted into query-level guidance, while answer generation conditions only on factual evidence from the current video. A lifecycle management mechanism regulates experience memory via usage frequency, reuse feedback, and temporal decay to reduce redundancy and noise.
AI.result: RRM consistently outperformed previous state-of-the-art approaches on M3-Bench-Robot, M3-Bench-Web, and Video-MME-Long benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Reflective retrieval memory effectively improves long-horizon multimodal reasoning by enabling agents to learn and reuse procedural retrieval strategies, with lifecycle management ensuring memory quality over time.

title: Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes
summary: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

AI.tldr: Baikal frames deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem, clustering heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions and using adaptive policies (e.g., UCB, Bayesian ε-greedy) to balance exploration and exploitation. It outperforms strong baselines by 28–36% on HybridQA and TAT-QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based deep research methods use iterative retrieval and generation, where accumulated context drives subsequent investigation. This approach tends to overexploit locally promising evidence and misses distinct semantic regions, failing to achieve adequate coverage under a fixed subquestion budget. The authors aim to systematically balance exploration and exploitation across a heterogeneous data lake.
AI.method: Baikal operates in three stages: (1) clustering heterogeneous evidence (tables and passages) into semantic regions; (2) adaptively selecting regions using policies including random, LLM-guided, Bayesian ε-greedy, and UCB, with region-level value estimates updated via finding quality as reward; (3) generating and investigating region-grounded subquestions within selected regions. A new evaluation rubric assesses groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, scored by GPT-5-mini.
AI.result: On 15 queries each over HybridQA (10,993 tables + 227K passages) and TAT-QA (2,757 tables + 13K passages), Baikal's best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines (DeepSearcher, OpenCode research agent) by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Gains are attributed to improved groundedness, diversity, and utility under the same subquestion budget.
AI.conclusion: Structured semantic exploration via region clustering and adaptive search policies significantly improves systematic research over heterogeneous data lakes. Organizing evidence into semantic regions and balancing exploration–exploitation yields more grounded, diverse, and useful findings compared to iterative retrieval-generation approaches.

title: MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation
summary: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

AI.tldr: MUGEN is a unified motion-language framework that eliminates discrete codebooks and iterative decoding, using a single adaptive-length autoencoder to compress motion into continuous latent slots. A language model generates these slots in one draw for text-to-motion and reads them for motion understanding, achieving state-of-the-art generation and retrieval results at minimal inference cost.
AI.motivation: Existing unified motion-language systems rely on discrete motion codebooks (with stacked residuals) and costly iterative decoding (masked stages, autoregressive rollouts, diffusion chains), which degrade generation quality and serve no purpose for understanding tasks. The authors aim to design a framework that achieves high-quality bidirectional motion-language processing without these costs.
AI.method: MUGEN employs: (1) a single adaptive-length autoencoder that compresses arbitrary-length motion sequences into a small set of continuous latent slots — the sole motion representation; (2) a language model that autoregressively generates these slots for text-to-motion (K steps, one draw, one decoder pass) and reads them back for motion understanding; (3) depth-routed hidden states allowing each slot to access only the transformer layers it requires; and (4) a calibrated prediction head that models a joint distribution over the full latent set, capturing cross-slot variation in a single draw.
AI.result: MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID (HumanML3D), raises retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses discrete-token state-of-the-art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.
AI.conclusion: MUGEN demonstrates that a codebook-free, single-draw continuous latent approach can unify motion generation and understanding with state-of-the-art quality, matching or exceeding both continuous and discrete prior work while drastically reducing decoding cost.

title: Where and When to Commit: Candidate-Aware Decoding for Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) expose a provisional prediction at every denoising step, creating an opportunity for generation-time early exit that stops decoding before the schedule is exhausted. Existing early-exit gates decide termination from fixed-region confidence statistics or schedule-dependent rules, evidence too coarse for a decision that freezes every remaining position at once, so they fire prematurely on long chain-of-thought outputs whose answers stabilize only near the end. Adaptive sampling, the other axis of training-free acceleration, paces how quickly positions commit while decoding continues but never verifies that the output itself has stabilized. We introduce a training-free, candidate-aware early-exit framework that keeps the two axes separate and matches each decision to evidence of its own scope. Confidence-Verified Commit (CVC) governs when the sequence may stop by verifying confidence and sustained argmax stability over the dynamically extracted candidate span using a deterministic parser specified from each task's output format. Block-Wise Early Commit (BWEC) governs where to accelerate by applying a cheaper local rule to non-final blocks, while leaving the final block and global termination under CVC. We refer to their combination as LATCH (Localized Acceleration with Tracked-Candidate Halting). Unlike prior methods, LATCH needs no suffix-prompt construction; it is prompt-anchor-free but format-aware. We evaluate LATCH end to end on 11 tasks under zero-shot settings using LLaDA and Dream. LATCH stays within 2.0 percentage points of full-decoding accuracy across all 22 evaluation settings, with one frozen hyperparameter set that transfers cross-backbone untuned, while achieving end-to-end TPS speedups of 9.3-17.8x on short-answer tasks and 2.0-3.3x on long-reasoning tasks.

AI.tldr: LATCH is a training-free, candidate-aware early-exit framework for diffusion language models that combines Confidence-Verified Commit (CVC) for global termination decisions and Block-Wise Early Commit (BWEC) for local acceleration, achieving 9.3–17.8× speedups on short-answer tasks and 2.0–3.3× on reasoning tasks while staying within 2% accuracy of full decoding.
AI.motivation: Existing early-exit methods for diffusion language models rely on coarse fixed-region confidence statistics or schedule-dependent rules, causing premature termination on long chain-of-thought outputs where answers stabilize only near the end. Adaptive sampling accelerates commitment pacing but never verifies output stabilization. A framework is needed that separates when to stop from where to accelerate, matching each decision to appropriate evidence.
AI.method: LATCH (Localized Acceleration with Tracked-Candidate Halting) consists of two components: (1) CVC (Confidence-Verified Commit) governs global termination by verifying both confidence and sustained argmax stability over a dynamically extracted candidate span, using a deterministic format-aware parser; (2) BWEC (Block-Wise Early Commit) governs local acceleration by applying a cheaper local rule to non-final blocks while leaving the final block under CVC. The method requires no suffix-prompt construction, is prompt-anchor-free, and transfers cross-backbone untuned with one frozen hyperparameter set.
AI.result: Evaluated on 11 zero-shot tasks using LLaDA and Dream backbones across 22 settings, LATCH stays within 2.0 percentage points of full-decoding accuracy, achieving end-to-end TPS speedups of 9.3–17.8× on short-answer tasks and 2.0–3.3× on long-reasoning tasks.
AI.conclusion: LATCH demonstrates that decoupling global termination decisions from local acceleration mechanisms, with each governed by scope-appropriate evidence (candidate-span stability for halting, block-wise rules for committing), yields robust training-free early exiting for diffusion language models that transfers across backbones without tuning.

title: VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills
summary: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

AI.tldr: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework for program verification that attributes failures to specific skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines skills with semantic-preserving revisions, outperforming all baselines across tools, frameworks, and LLMs.
AI.motivation: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, lemmas, and tool invocations — all dependent on reusable skills. While skill self-evolution (distilling and refining skills from execution trajectories) is a natural solution, existing methods fail in program verification because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback.
AI.method: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework with three key components: (1) failure attribution that maps verification failures to specific skill deficiencies, (2) distillation of diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and (3) iterative refinement of candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics.
AI.result: VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends in experimental evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Skill self-evolution is viable and effective for program verification when failures are properly attributed to skill deficiencies and refinements are gated by semantic-preserving verification improvement. VeriSkill establishes a new state-of-the-art approach for automating program verification with LLM agents.

title: Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs
summary: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

AI.tldr: Prox is a two-stage, training-free framework that enables sparse execution of SwiGLU FFNs in LLMs by constructing channel masks from magnitude rankings of approximate intermediate states, achieving up to 1.99× decoding speedup at 70% sparsity without significant quality loss.
AI.motivation: FFNs dominate memory and computation in LLM inference. While activation sparsification can reduce this overhead, existing training-free methods degrade model quality at high sparsity due to poor channel-selection strategies. The SwiGLU intermediate state is an excellent channel-selection signal but requires expensive dense computation to obtain.
AI.method: Prox uses a two-stage framework. Stage 1 constructs a shared channel mask using input sparsity and quantized proxy weights, exploiting the insight that only the magnitude ranking (not exact values) of the intermediate state is needed. Stage 2 computes only the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three FFN projections.
AI.result: Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels and achieves up to 1.99× end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity. It is also compatible with quantization and sparse attention.
AI.conclusion: Prox demonstrates that effective activation sparsification for SwiGLU FFNs can be achieved without training by leveraging approximate magnitude ranking of the intermediate state, enabling practical inference speedups while maintaining model quality.

title: The MADRS Pipeline: Supporting Depression Assessment in Clinical Trials
summary: Depression is a major mental disorder for which diagnosis relies primarily on clinical assessments. Automated methods to support its detection via the psychiatric MADRS scale are getting more and more attention. While existing solutions primarily focus on detecting the disorder from different text sources (e.g., online text, social media), there is still limited support for clinical trials, where clinical assessments are conducted through structured interviews based on standard guidelines such as SIGMA. In this work, we develop a LLM pipeline specifically designed to support clinicians in supporting the assessment of depression in patients enrolled in clinical trials. Our pipeline converts audio interviews into transcripts, maps them into the ten MADRS symptom items, estimates their severity, and identify problematic clinical ratings associated with them. Evaluation on real clinical interviews shows a strong overall correlation of 0.867 with expert ratings, providing interpretable support for future assessments in clinical trials.

AI.tldr: A study presenting an LLM pipeline that transcribes clinical audio interviews, maps them to MADRS depression symptom items, estimates severity, and identifies problematic clinical ratings, achieving a 0.867 correlation with expert assessments.
AI.motivation: Automated depression detection methods primarily target informal text sources (social media, online posts) rather than structured clinical trial interviews. There is limited support for clinical trials using standardized assessment guidelines like SIGMA, creating a gap in automated tools for clinician-assisted MADRS-based depression evaluation.
AI.method: An LLM-based pipeline was developed that: (1) converts audio interviews into text transcripts, (2) maps transcript content to the ten MADRS (Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale) symptom items, (3) estimates symptom severity for each item, and (4) flags problematic clinical ratings. The system was evaluated on real clinical interview data against expert clinician ratings.
AI.result: The pipeline achieved a strong overall correlation of 0.867 with expert clinician ratings, demonstrating high agreement with human assessments on real clinical interview data.
AI.conclusion: The LLM pipeline provides interpretable, automated support for depression assessment in clinical trials, bridging the gap between automated detection research and structured clinical interview settings, with performance competitive with expert raters.

title: SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction
summary: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

AI.tldr: SpecCal is a training-free, plug-and-play calibration framework that re-ranks and augments candidate molecules from existing IR-to-molecule models by enforcing spectral consistency, improving top-k molecular reconstruction without any parameter updates.
AI.motivation: IR spectra provide limited structural information due to similar functional groups and vibrational patterns across different molecules, making molecular reconstruction inherently ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models generate ranked candidate sets biased by learned generation preferences rather than genuine spectral consistency, failing to fully capture structures that best satisfy observed spectral constraints.
AI.method: SpecCal is a training-free, model-agnostic candidate calibration framework that operates on outputs from any base IR-to-molecule model. It re-ranks existing candidates and introduces additional structurally plausible alternatives, both guided by spectral consistency with the observed IR spectrum. No parameter updates are required for integration.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction performance at both SMILES and scaffold levels when applied to diverse base models.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity via spectral consistency provides a practical and effective approach to improving molecular reconstruction from IR spectra, without requiring model retraining.

title: Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters
summary: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hypernetwork-based framework that generates LoRA adapters conditioned on safety policy specifications, enabling a single large reasoning model to adapt on-demand to arbitrary subsets of safety policies without training separate models for each combination.
AI.motivation: As large reasoning models (LRMs) are personalized for downstream users, different users require compliance with different subsets of safety policies. Training separate models for each policy combination is combinatorially prohibitive, while in-context learning methods introduce computational overhead from long context generation. A more efficient, unified solution is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose an adaptive hypernetwork that takes safety policy descriptions as input and outputs LoRA adapter weights. These generated weights are then applied to a downstream LRM, enabling it to produce responses compliant with the specified policy subset. The hypernetwork is trained once and can dynamically generate policy-specific adapters on demand.
AI.result: The framework achieves on-demand policy compliance adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance, demonstrated across reasoning models of different sizes and on multiple evaluation datasets.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is an effective and practical approach for multi-policy compliance in LRMs, eliminating combinatorial training overhead while maintaining performance and flexibility.

title: Fidelity Is Not Safety: Gently-Compressed LLMs Pass Every Data-Free Quality Guard Yet Invent Procedure Steps in Agentic Execution
summary: Practitioners accept a compressed language model once it clears a stack of data-cheap quality guards: perplexity within a small factor of the original, downstream accuracy (for example MMLU) inside a confidence interval, and data-free output-fidelity signals that compare the compressed and original network's internal representations under random probe inputs. This stack has a blind spot. Across three model families, gently-compressed models clear every guard and then invent procedure steps that were never in the instructions when they run a standard operating procedure (SOP) as an agent. The effect is operator-specific: coherent low-rank (SVD) truncation induces it, and magnitude pruning matched to the same perplexity does not. One dissociation isolates the cause. The same compressed weights that CI-win a paired output-fidelity test CI-fail the invented-step canary. The governing axis is the coherence of the compression error times its rate; the magnitude of the damage does not predict it. The data-free fidelity probe is a fidelity oracle by construction, so it cannot see this axis. We characterize the blindspot and dissociation with paired confidence intervals on a pre-registered, powered canary across three architectures. Operator-specificity replicates on all three, and the perplexity-guard evasion appears where the model admits in-guard low-rank headroom. We then give a data-free screen: a two-axis statistic of the compression error (coherent-fraction and error-rate) that flags the failing builds with fixed thresholds across architectures and matches the coherence-times-rate mechanism. Perplexity, MMLU, and fidelity acceptance do not certify agent safety. Screen gently-compressed low-rank builds before agentic deployment

AI.tldr: Compressed language models can pass all standard quality checks (perplexity, MMLU accuracy, representation fidelity) yet silently invent procedure steps when deployed as agents. This failure is specific to low-rank (SVD) compression and is driven by the coherence of compression error, not its magnitude. The authors characterize this blindspot and propose a data-free screening statistic to flag unsafe compressed models.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation guards for compressed language models — perplexity, downstream accuracy, and data-free fidelity probes — miss a critical failure mode: the spontaneous generation of fabricated steps when executing standard operating procedures as agents. The work aims to expose and characterize this blindspot.
AI.method: The authors conduct a pre-registered, powered canary experiment across three model families. They compare low-rank (SVD) truncation against magnitude pruning, matched for perplexity, and evaluate whether compressed models invent steps not present in SOP instructions. Paired confidence intervals are used to dissociate fidelity-test passing from canary-test failing. A two-axis statistic (coherent-fraction and error-rate of compression error) is introduced as a data-free screening tool.
AI.result: Gently-compressed models clear all standard guards yet invent procedure steps. The effect is operator-specific: SVD truncation induces it; magnitude pruning at the same perplexity does not. The governing axis is the coherence of compression error times its rate — not the magnitude of damage. The proposed two-axis screen flags failing builds with fixed thresholds across architectures, matching the coherence-times-rate mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Perplexity, MMLU, and fidelity acceptance do not certify agent safety. Low-rank compressed models should be screened with the proposed coherence×rate statistic before agentic deployment to catch silent failures that standard evaluation pipelines miss.

title: Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings
summary: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents. The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

AI.tldr: LeDA is a web-based legal data annotation system that enables dynamic creation of annotation tags, allowing annotators to discover concepts from legal case proceedings without a pre-defined ontology. It supports semantic document representation as bags of concepts for downstream tasks like case retrieval and judgment prediction.
AI.motivation: Moving beyond flat bag-of-words text representations toward structured, concept-based representations of legal documents can significantly improve processing capabilities for downstream legal AI tasks. However, pre-defined ontologies for legal concepts are often unavailable, necessitating a system that allows concepts to be discovered dynamically during annotation.
AI.method: The authors propose LeDA (Legal Data Annotation), a web-based annotation system featuring dynamic tag creation — annotators can create new entity/concept tags on the fly as they examine documents. The system supports both annotation and adjudication of entities. It was deployed with 3 assessors to annotate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.
AI.result: The system was successfully used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concepts from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings, producing semantic document representations (bags of concepts) suitable for downstream tasks such as prior case retrieval and judgment prediction.
AI.conclusion: LeDA effectively addresses the gap in legal document annotation where no pre-defined ontology exists, enabling iterative concept discovery and structured semantic representation of legal texts. The resulting concept-based representations can enhance multiple downstream legal AI applications.

title: Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise
summary: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a KV cache eviction strategy that removes past tokens well-predicted by future context, using a counter-causal attention mask to score redundancy without additional training. A fast single-layer approximation further reduces cost.
AI.motivation: KV cache size grows linearly with context length, consuming GPU memory and hindering long-context generation. Existing compression/eviction methods aim to prune redundant entries while preserving generation quality. The key insight is that tokens predictable from more recent context are redundant and can be safely evicted.
AI.method: The method scores KV cache entries for eviction by running the model with a counter-causal attention mask, where each position attends only to future tokens. This reuses existing cached key-value representations, is in-distribution, and requires no training. Redundancy is measured by how well a token can be predicted from its future context. A fast approximation variant restricts the counter-causal pass to only the last transformer layer, achieving significant speedup with marginal accuracy loss.
AI.result: Evaluated on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets, the method shows competitive or improved performance over state-of-the-art KV cache eviction methods.
AI.conclusion: The proposed counter-causal eviction scheme is a simple, training-free, and effective approach to KV cache management, offering practical speed-accuracy trade-offs via the single-layer approximation.

title: Causal Discovery with Inverted Self-attention for Multivariate Time Series
summary: Causal discovery in multivariate time series data is challenging due to complex interactions, high dimensionality, and nonlinear dependencies among variables. Existing methods often struggle to capture these complexities, resulting in inaccurate causal structures. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that leverages self-attention mechanisms within the transformer architecture for causal discovery. Our approach introduces a novel inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) that emphasizes latent and indirect causal relationships by inverting tokens and inducing sparsity in attention scores, focusing on significant causal interactions and reducing spurious correlations. Additionally, we develop a global causal algorithm to identify global causal links, providing a holistic metric for causal influence, along with a causal verification module to ensure robustness in the identified causal relationships, enhancing the reliability of our framework. Experiments on both linear and nonlinear datasets, along with ablation studies and sensitivity analyses, show that our framework outperforms existing methods, demonstrating its potential for causal discovery in complex multivariate time series.

AI.tldr: Proposes a transformer-based framework with a novel inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) for causal discovery in multivariate time series, outperforming existing methods on linear and nonlinear datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery methods struggle with complex interactions, high dimensionality, and nonlinear dependencies in multivariate time series, often yielding inaccurate causal structures.
AI.method: The framework introduces: (1) an inverted causal self-attention mechanism (CSAM) that inverts tokens and induces sparsity in attention scores to emphasize latent/indirect causal relationships while suppressing spurious correlations; (2) a global causal algorithm to identify holistic causal links; and (3) a causal verification module that ensures robustness of identified causal relationships.
AI.result: The proposed framework outperforms existing methods on both linear and nonlinear datasets, validated through ablation studies and sensitivity analyses.
AI.conclusion: The transformer-based approach with inverted CSAM demonstrates strong potential for accurate causal discovery in complex multivariate time series, addressing key limitations of prior methods through sparse attention and global causal verification.

title: MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes
summary: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

AI.tldr: MemeBench is a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes that uses the VIKR schema (Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, Reasoning mechanisms) to pinpoint where LVLMs fail in meme interpretation, revealing a persistent Visual-Knowledge gap. The authors also introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline that improves VIKR Success by 3.6–7.4%.
AI.motivation: Current LVLMs describe visual content accurately but struggle when interpretation requires cultural knowledge, background context, and community conventions—precisely what memes demand. Existing meme benchmarks reduce evaluation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where explanations break down. The authors seek a fine-grained diagnostic framework that decomposes interpretation failures.
AI.method: The authors construct MemeBench (1,253 Chinese/English memes from anime, comics, gaming subcultures) with human-written references and VIKR annotations. The VIKR schema decomposes explanations into four axes: Visual clues, Identity links (recognizing entities/characters), Knowledge units (cultural/background knowledge), and Reasoning mechanisms. They evaluate 26 LVLMs across these axes and propose KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase, to test whether targeted evidence can close diagnosed gaps.
AI.result: Every LVLM covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it; even the strongest model retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. KAR yields a 3.6–7.4% improvement in VIKR Success across four controlled models. Compared to generic retrieval, KAR repairs more answers and breaks fewer. However, both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while paradoxically reducing Visual coverage in all comparisons.
AI.conclusion: MemeBench demonstrates that fine-grained diagnostic evaluation reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap. The persistent Visual-Knowledge gap and the trade-off between knowledge augmentation and visual coverage highlight fundamental challenges for LVLMs in culturally-grounded understanding tasks.

title: Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

AI.tldr: KGPS reformulates RL prompt selection as dynamic state estimation using a Kalman filter, adaptively tracking non-stationary prompt difficulty without extra rollouts, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency and accuracy.
AI.motivation: RL finetuning of LLMs depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty, but difficulty evolves non-stationarily during training. Existing methods trade off accuracy (expensive evaluation-based) against efficiency (prediction-based methods assuming stationary difficulty). Neither handles RL's dynamic training well.
AI.method: KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space via a linear-Gaussian state-space model. Process noise is coupled to policy update magnitude, so uncertainty grows with larger policy changes. A Kalman filter maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty. Prompts are selected by maximizing posterior-expected training utility, favoring intermediate difficulty while revisiting uncertain prompts. No extra rollouts beyond standard training are required.
AI.result: KGPS consistently improves final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines across math, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks and multiple RL algorithms. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while improving average performance by 0.12 points across six math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: KGPS achieves state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods by treating prompt selection as dynamic state estimation, effectively handling non-stationary training dynamics with a principled Kalman filtering approach.

title: STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs
summary: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes.
