We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

AI.tldr: STEREODISCO is a framework that systematically discovers stereotypical semantic axes in LLM internal representations by constructing ~2,000 candidate axes from WordNet antonyms, recovering them geometrically via probing, and identifying stereotypical ones through statistical testing. Applied to LLAMA-3-8B and MISTRAL-7B, it reveals LLM stereotypes diverge from human social psychology findings and uncovers novel axes like humble/proud and cowardly/brave.
AI.motivation: Prior computational research on stereotypes in LLMs is limited to a narrow set of semantic axes from social psychology and operates on word embeddings rather than internal representations. This leaves two open questions: (1) which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs, and (2) how LLMs internally represent such axes. The work aims to broaden the systematic discovery of stereotypical content encoded in LLMs.
AI.method: The authors introduce STEREODISCO, which adapts Osgood et al.'s semantic differential method. It proceeds in three stages: (1) constructing approximately 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets; (2) recovering each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space using probing classifiers (linear probes trained on internal representations); and (3) identifying stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections, comparing how social group concepts project onto each axis relative to a null distribution.
AI.result: Applied to LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT, the framework reveals that the two LLMs agree more with each other on social group stereotype ratings than with human judgments from social psychology, indicating LLM-encoded stereotypes diverge from documented human stereotypes. The method also discovers stereotypical axes not previously studied, including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which were independently validated by human annotators.
AI.conclusion: LLMs encode a broader set of stereotypical semantic dimensions than previously studied, and their stereotype content diverges from human social psychology findings. STEREODISCO provides a scalable, principled method for auditing LLM internal representations for stereotypical associations, enabling more comprehensive stereotype discovery and model auditing.

title: Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning
comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE Real-Time Systems Symposium (RTSS)
summary: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes OCO-PAoI-Hard, a hard real-time scheduling framework for IoT systems that guarantees zero per-slot peak AoI deadline violations under adversarial conditions by reformulating the fractional deadline as an affine half-space constraint and solving it via time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set.
AI.motivation: Safety-critical IoT systems (industrial control, V2X, teleoperation) require hard per-slot peak AoI deadlines, not just average bounds. Existing approaches—Whittle-index (stochastic channels), DRL (simulator rollouts), or OCO with long-term constraints (sublinear cumulative violation)—fail to guarantee zero per-slot violation under adversarial conditions.
AI.method: The key insight is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector. The problem is then cast as time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility via one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. Closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds are established, along with a matching Ω(√T) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant for execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio.
AI.result: On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard achieved zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines missed between 1.65% and 64.0% of slots. Empirical normalized regret remained within the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.
AI.conclusion: OCO-PAoI-Hard provides the first hard per-slot peak AoI guarantee under adversarial conditions with provable O(√T) regret, outperforming existing stochastic, learning-based, and long-term-constrained approaches in both safety and regret.

title: Understanding Is Done Early: A Depth Division of Labor in Large Language Models and Its Use for Unbounded-Context Memory
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 27 tables. Submitted to ACL Rolling Review
summary: Transformer depth is not used uniformly: lower and middle layers build semantic representations, while upper layers increasingly specialize them for prediction. We turn this division of labor into CoMem (Comprehension Memory), which writes each context chunk only through an intermediate layer, retrieves a fixed number of cached residual states, and recomputes the query-conditioned upper layers over the resulting pack. For a fixed retrieval budget, model-side read compute and memory are independent of stored-context length. We evaluate a continued-trained Qwen3-8B base LM under a unified chat-template-free protocol. The backbone is frozen; the flagship trains only a rank-32 self-distillation LoRA on plain PG19, and we report an adapter-free arm separately. CoMem reaches 97.05 on RULER and 38.27 on LoCoMo versus 34.59 for full-context KV-Direct; the dialogue-memory advantage survives conversation-cluster resampling and an independent judge. Results on additional long-context and long-document tasks expose both the benefits of bounded retrieval and its in-window compression tax. Controlled depth sweeps show that deeper caching lowers per-query recomputation but incurs a fidelity loss that self-distillation substantially repairs. In a separate adapter-free efficiency control on an NVIDIA H20 at 128k, CoMem uses 18.26 GB rather than 89.36 GB and achieves a 7.83x prefill speedup. These results show that long-context memory can be organized along the layer axis, not only the token axis.

AI.tldr: CoMem leverages the layer-wise division of labor in Transformers by caching intermediate-layer representations of context chunks and recomputing only upper layers query-conditioned on a fixed-size retrieval pack, achieving memory and compute independent of context length with strong long-context performance.
AI.motivation: Transformer layers specialize: lower/middle layers build semantic representations, upper layers specialize them for prediction. Existing long-context methods compress along the token axis; this work proposes organizing memory along the layer axis instead, exploiting this division of labor to decouple memory and compute costs from total context length.
AI.method: CoMem (Comprehension Memory) writes each context chunk only through an intermediate layer, stores the residual states, and retrieves a fixed number of cached states per query. The query-conditioned upper layers are then recomputed over the resulting pack. The backbone is frozen; training uses a rank-32 LoRA with self-distillation on PG19. Evaluation follows a unified chat-template-free protocol. A separate adapter-free variant is also reported. Depth sweeps control the caching layer.
AI.result: CoMem achieves 97.05 on RULER and 38.27 on LoCoMo (vs. 34.59 for full-context KV-Direct). Gains persist under conversation-cluster resampling and independent judging. On an NVIDIA H20 at 128k context, CoMem uses 18.26 GB (vs. 89.36 GB) with 7.83× prefill speedup. Self-distillation substantially repairs fidelity loss from deeper caching, which lowers recomputation cost but degrades quality.
AI.conclusion: Long-context memory can be effectively organized along the layer axis, not only the token axis. CoMem provides a practical architecture for bounded retrieval with length-independent memory and compute, validated across both model quality and efficiency metrics.

title: Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding
summary: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA. Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA), a new task for evaluating semantic understanding of sign language videos beyond recognition and translation. The authors construct two benchmarks (SignQA) with automatically generated QA pairs across five categories, and propose a baseline model with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and knowledge transfer strategy that outperforms existing vision-language models.
AI.motivation: Existing sign language understanding tasks (continuous SL recognition, SL translation) are limited to fixed mappings (sign→gloss or sign→sentence) and fail to comprehensively assess whether models truly understand the semantic content of SL videos. The authors aim to fill this gap with a more flexible, reasoning-oriented evaluation paradigm.
AI.method: (1) Propose SLQA, a new task requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. (2) Construct two SignQA benchmarks from PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily using template-based automatic generation of QA pairs covering five categories: position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. (3) Propose a baseline with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module (for question-aware temporal feature modeling) and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy (leveraging existing SLU tasks).
AI.result: The proposed baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all five question categories on both benchmarks, establishing a strong reference for future SLQA research.
AI.conclusion: SLQA offers a more comprehensive and flexible framework for evaluating SL understanding, and the proposed baseline model with its specialized modules provides an effective starting point. The publicly released datasets aim to spur further research in this direction.

title: First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection
summary: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints and proposes F²CTO, the first distributed optimization method for solving such problems, achieving a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε⁻³/²) with empirical validation on reliable continual learning.
AI.motivation: With IoT generating massive data across distributed edge networks, training on full data is computationally prohibitive, and coreset selection is critical. However, existing approaches fail to simultaneously address (1) privacy-sensitive local data, (2) model robustness requirements, and (3) distributed optimization constraints. No prior work integrates these three aspects into a unified framework.
AI.method: The authors characterize hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, formulating the problem as a trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints. They propose F²CTO (Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization), which combines a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm to solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner.
AI.result: F²CTO achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε⁻³/²) for finding an ε-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning tasks demonstrate the method's effectiveness and efficiency compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: F²CTO is the first method for distributed robust coreset selection and the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel problems with level-wise constraints. It successfully bridges robust optimization, coreset selection, and federated/distributed learning in a theoretically grounded and empirically validated framework.

title: MORFES: A Benchmark for Productive Inflectional Competence in Modern Greek
summary: Modern Greek is a richly inflected language, yet the language models built for it are evaluated mainly on factual knowledge, and no benchmark is dedicated to their inflectional competence. We introduce MORFES (Morphological Open-class Recognition-and-Formation Evaluation Suite), a benchmark of 500 expert-verified items that tests the recognition and production of Greek inflected forms, favoring lower-frequency lemmas so that a correct answer reflects the rule rather than a memorized form. We make it publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/KIEFERSA/MORFES. We evaluate a range of open language models on MORFES, situating them within the rapidly scaling open-weight ecosystem from LLaMA to Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Magistral, and Kimi K2, where multilingual coverage grows but grammatical competence in morphologically rich languages remains under-measured. Among them, Sophea-Genesis-1, a model we developed and release as open weights at https://huggingface.co/KIEFERSA/Sophea-Genesis-1, leads on inflectional morphology while matching similarly sized models in general capability.

AI.tldr: MORFES is a 500-item benchmark evaluating Greek inflectional morphology in language models, favoring low-frequency lemmas to test rule-based competence. The authors also release Sophea-Genesis-1, an open-weight model that leads on this benchmark while matching peers in general capability.
AI.motivation: Modern Greek is morphologically rich, yet existing LM evaluations focus on factual knowledge with no dedicated benchmark for inflectional competence. As multilingual open-weight models scale rapidly, their grammatical capabilities in morphologically complex languages remain under-measured. The authors aim to fill this gap with a rigorous, expert-verified evaluation suite.
AI.method: The authors constructed MORFES, a benchmark of 500 expert-verified items covering both recognition and production of Greek inflected forms. Items deliberately favor lower-frequency lemmas to ensure correct responses reflect morphological rule application rather than rote memorization. They evaluated a range of open LMs — from LLaMA to Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Magistral, and Kimi K2 — and developed Sophea-Genesis-1, an open-weight model optimized for inflectional morphology.
AI.result: Sophea-Genesis-1 achieves the highest performance on MORFES among evaluated models while maintaining general capability comparable to similarly sized models. The benchmark reveals that morphological competence varies significantly across the open-weight model ecosystem, with multilingual coverage not guaranteeing strong performance on Greek inflection.
AI.conclusion: MORFES fills a critical evaluation gap for morphologically rich languages, and the results demonstrate that targeted attention to inflectional morphology can yield models like Sophea-Genesis-1 that excel on such tasks without sacrificing general performance. Both the benchmark and the model are publicly released.

title: MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory
summary: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

AI.tldr: MemTxn is a governance layer that provides transactional guarantees for persistent memory in LLM agents, using Ordered PatchTest for write validation, a Temporal Resolver for conflict resolution, and a durable snapshot journal for fault recovery.
AI.motivation: Persistent memory enables LLM agents to retain information across sessions, but erroneous writes can corrupt future behavior. Existing systems lack transaction boundaries for reliable updates and recovery, creating a need for a governance mechanism that ensures memory integrity.
AI.method: MemTxn operates as an external governance layer decoupled from the answer model. It employs three core components: (1) Ordered PatchTest — validates whether a memory update is supported by its source evidence; (2) Temporal Resolver — selects the correct visible version when conflicting facts arise; (3) Durable Snapshot Journal — restores application-visible state after faults without requiring knowledge of the physical write set.
AI.result: On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepted all 60 supported originals and rejected all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo, it fully restored the declared active map. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, it achieved the highest average F1 across all 12 answer-model configurations, outperforming Dense by 17.06–24.07 points in five representative settings.
AI.conclusion: MemTxn effectively provides transaction-like guarantees for persistent agent memory, ensuring that only source-supported updates persist, conflicts are correctly resolved, and state is recoverable after faults — all without modifying the underlying answer model.

title: Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation
summary: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

AI.tldr: OPAL is a framework that decides whether adaptive experimentation should be permitted at all, using a precommitted contract requiring non-trivial adaptation, controlled risk, and positive executed value. It establishes impossibility boundaries under unrestricted conditional outcome shift and demonstrates risk-controlled authorization on a large-scale Cell Painting dataset.
AI.motivation: Most adaptive experimental methods begin after adaptation is already permitted, but no existing framework addresses the prior question: should adaptation be enabled in the first place? Without such a gate, adaptive experiments risk false activations, negative executed value, and failure under distributional shift — particularly when source outcomes and unlabeled target covariates may not support reliable adaptation.
AI.method: OPAL introduces a precommitted contract with three requirements: (1) non-trivial adaptation, (2) controlled target risk below a specified limit, and (3) positive executed value after cost. The authors derive an impossibility boundary showing that unrestricted conditional outcome shift precludes uniform non-trivial authorization, then develop a target-calibrated recovery procedure. The frozen gate is evaluated on an 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition across six methods.
AI.result: On the unseen Cell Painting partition, OPAL's frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities, and maintained strictly positive executed value under least-favorable completion. The false-activation upper bound was 5.18%, below the 7.5% limit. Among six methods compared, only OPAL combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies further distinguished policy misalignment from non-certifiability.
AI.conclusion: Authorization constitutes a distinct and necessary layer for safe adaptive science, separate from adaptation method selection. OPAL demonstrates that pre-experimental risk-contracted gating is both feasible and essential, establishing that not all experimental contexts warrant adaptation — and providing a principled framework for making that determination.

title: (Towards) Scalable Reliable Automated Evaluation with Large Language Models
comment: 17 pages. Published in the Proceedings of the Fourth Workshop on Generation, Evaluation and Metrics (GEM2) at ACL 2025
summary: Evaluating the quality and relevance of textual outputs from Large Language Models (LLMs) remains challenging and resource-intensive. Existing automated metrics often fail to capture the complexity and variability inherent in LLM-generated outputs. Moreover, these metrics typically rely on explicit reference standards, limiting their use mostly to domains with objective benchmarks. This work introduces a novel evaluation framework designed to approximate expert-level assessments of LLM-generated content. The proposed method employs pairwise comparisons of outputs by multiple LLMs, reducing biases from individual models. An Elo rating system is used to generate stable and interpretable rankings. Adjustable agreement thresholds, from full unanimity to majority voting, allow flexible control over evaluation confidence and coverage. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through evaluating competency profiles extracted from scientific abstracts. Preliminary results show that automatically derived rankings correlate well with expert judgments, significantly reducing the need for extensive human intervention. By offering a scalable, consistent, and domain-agnostic evaluation layer, the framework supports more efficient and reliable quality assessments of LLM outputs across diverse applications.

AI.tldr: A scalable, domain-agnostic evaluation framework for LLM outputs that uses pairwise comparisons by multiple LLMs combined with an Elo rating system, yielding rankings that correlate well with expert judgments while reducing human annotation effort.
AI.motivation: Existing automated metrics for evaluating LLM-generated text fail to capture output complexity, rely on explicit reference standards, and are mostly limited to domains with objective benchmarks. There is a need for a scalable, reference-free method that approximates expert-level assessment.
AI.method: The framework uses multiple LLMs to perform pairwise comparisons of outputs, mitigating individual model biases. An Elo rating system converts these comparisons into stable, interpretable rankings. Adjustable agreement thresholds (from unanimity to majority voting) provide flexible control over evaluation confidence versus coverage.
AI.result: Demonstrated on competency profiles extracted from scientific abstracts, the automatically derived rankings show strong correlation with expert judgments, substantially reducing the need for human intervention.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a scalable, consistent, and domain-agnostic evaluation layer that enables more efficient and reliable quality assessments of LLM outputs across diverse applications.

title: Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration
summary: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

AI.tldr: LLM unlearning methods suffer from a universal "relearn attack" vulnerability where fine-tuning on just 20 forget examples restores forgotten knowledge. The authors identify a geometric phenomenon called the "margin cliff"—where per-token answer margins collapse into a narrow band—and propose Margin Calibration (MC), a plug-in polish that counters this by adding a non-saturating margin hinge loss. MC achieves consistent robustness gains across multiple models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM unlearning methods are fragile: knowledge ostensibly removed can be easily recovered via relearn attacks (fine-tuning on a small number of forget-set examples). The root cause of this fragility was not well understood, limiting progress toward robust unlearning.
AI.method: The authors first diagnose the fragility by analyzing the per-token answer margin across 14 post-hoc unlearning methods (spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families) on TOFU. They identify the "margin cliff" regularity and prove it arises when a "retain coupling" condition holds—where token-saturating losses keep forget content log-odds above a floor. To fix this, they propose Margin Calibration (MC): a plug-in polish that adds (1) a non-saturating margin hinge loss anchored at the reference model's per-token margin, and (2) a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure. They also provide theoretical analysis under a gradient-dominance condition to bound relearn attack success.
AI.result: MC with a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News (Llama-2-7B-hf), and a Phi-3.5 panel. Panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L drops from 0.41 to 0.18. MC also lowers raw membership inference AUC on 13/14 methods, at the cost of reduced retain-side utility. A deployment variant achieves similar gains without a retain-trained reference.
AI.conclusion: The margin cliff is a fundamental, geometry-rooted explanation for the brittleness of LLM unlearning. Margin Calibration provides a principled, reference-anchored fix that robustly resists relearn attacks across diverse models and settings, advancing the practical viability of machine unlearning in LLMs.

title: Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition
comment: 41 pages, 6 figures, 11 tables including supplementary information. Submitted to Applied Intelligence
summary: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

AI.tldr: This paper deconstructs EEG emotion recognition evaluation, showing that reported accuracy depends on the full evaluation pipeline—not just the classifier. Using a single DGCNN architecture on SEED/SEED-IV, the authors demonstrate that protocol-matched checks, checkpoint selection strategies, and subject-disjoint vs. subject-dependent splits yield dramatically different results, arguing that these should be reported as answers to fundamentally different questions.
AI.motivation: EEG emotion recognition literature suffers from inconsistent evaluation protocols, making reported accuracies difficult to compare and potentially misleading. The authors aim to systematically isolate how different components of the evaluation procedure—target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule—affect reported performance, using a fixed model architecture to eliminate classifier variability.
AI.method: The authors fix a single dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) architecture and systematically vary evaluation protocols on the SEED and SEED-IV datasets. They examine: (1) protocol-matched subject-dependent evaluation against public reference values; (2) checkpoint selection via repeated test-set evaluation across 30 subject-session trajectories; (3) five-fold subject-disjoint cross-validation with validation-selected checkpoints; and (4) evaluation on entirely held-out subjects. Supporting analyses include participant ranking consistency across representations/time scales and tail-risk ensemble evaluation. BCa bootstrap intervals are used for held-out subject accuracy.
AI.result: Protocol-matched subject-dependent SEED accuracy was within 1.47 points of the reference; SEED-IV showed a 3.40-point unresolved gap. Repeated test-set checkpoint selection inflated mean window accuracy from 0.7855 to 0.8892. Subject-disjoint validation yielded near-perfect training-participant accuracy (0.9990 SEED, 0.9920 SEED-IV) but held-out participant accuracy dropped to 0.5348 (SEED) and 0.3954 (SEED-IV). Participant rankings depended on representation and time scale; a tail-risk ensemble showed no positive gain in final evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results answer distinct questions and should be reported separately. The large train-to-held-out-subject accuracy gaps cannot be attributed solely to underfitting. The work advocates for transparent, protocol-explicit reporting that disentangles the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule in EEG emotion recognition research.

title: CACHE-UK: A Stability-Aware Memory Editor for Sequentially Updated Quantized LLMs in Finance
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) deployed in dynamic financial environments face a critical challenge: maintaining factual accuracy as market conditions, regulations, and corporate facts change continuously. While 4-bit quantization enables efficient deployment, it severely limits the viability of sequential memory editing: existing methods undergo catastrophic performance degradation under this "quantization stability crisis." We introduce CACHE-UK (Contextual Adaptive Continual Hybrid Editor for UK Finance), a stability-aware memory editing framework specifically designed for domain-specific, quantized LLMs. CACHE-UK integrates three components: a rank-1 LoRA perturbation mechanism that confines edits to the low-rank adapter subspace, a financial domain prioritization module for content-adaptive edit strength, and a closed-loop Stability Controller that tracks "degradation debt" to prevent catastrophic forgetting across sequential updates. Evaluated on a 4-bit quantized OpenLLaMA-3B model with a curated UK financial corpus of 88,021 documents, CACHE-UK reduces knowledge degradation by 11-17% relative to adapted baselines under identical 4-bit constraints -- its most robust effect -- while attaining the highest test success (generalization) rate observed in our setting (28%, a 6 percentage point improvement over the strongest adapted baseline). These results indicate that stability-aware editing can improve factual maintenance in resource-constrained financial LLM deployments, though absolute generalization rates remain low.

AI.tldr: CACHE-UK is a stability-aware memory editing framework for 4-bit quantized LLMs in UK finance, using rank-1 LoRA perturbations, domain-adaptive edit strength, and a degradation-debt tracking controller to reduce knowledge degradation by 11–17% and improve generalization by 6 percentage points over adapted baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed in dynamic financial environments must maintain factual accuracy amid continuously changing market conditions, regulations, and corporate facts. While 4-bit quantization enables efficient deployment, existing sequential memory editing methods suffer catastrophic performance degradation under these low-precision constraints — a phenomenon termed the "quantization stability crisis."
AI.method: CACHE-UK integrates three components: (1) a rank-1 LoRA perturbation mechanism that confines edits to a low-rank adapter subspace to preserve model stability; (2) a financial domain prioritization module that modulates edit strength based on content relevance; and (3) a closed-loop Stability Controller that tracks cumulative "degradation debt" across sequential updates to prevent catastrophic forgetting. The framework is evaluated on a 4-bit quantized OpenLLaMA-3B model using a curated UK financial corpus of 88,021 documents.
AI.result: Under identical 4-bit quantization constraints, CACHE-UK reduces knowledge degradation by 11–17% relative to adapted baselines. It achieves the highest generalization rate (test success) at 28%, representing a 6 percentage point improvement over the strongest adapted baseline. However, absolute generalization rates remain low overall.
AI.conclusion: Stability-aware editing can meaningfully improve factual maintenance in resource-constrained financial LLM deployments, but the low absolute generalization rates indicate that substantial challenges remain for reliable sequential memory editing under extreme quantization.

title: Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue
summary: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

AI.tldr: Proposes the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that captures workflow provenance for multi-stage manufacturing, enabling FAIR dataset access and distinction between datasets from individual workflow steps for downstream AI optimization.
AI.motivation: In multi-stage manufacturing, downstream AI-based optimization tasks require distinguishing between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. Existing catalogues lack explicit capture of both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance in a FAIR-compliant manner, motivating a Knowledge Graph-based solution.
AI.method: The authors develop three integrated components: (1) the VPD ontology as the semantic core of the catalogue; (2) a provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation directly into the production environment; and (3) a human-centered user interface for interacting with the VPD Knowledge Graph.
AI.result: The VPD system provides FAIR datasets with explicit prospective and retrospective workflow provenance, enabling downstream AI tasks to distinguish between datasets from different workflow steps. The ontology and code are publicly available on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: The VPD effectively combines a data catalogue with workflow provenance capture using Knowledge Graph technology, addressing a critical gap in multi-stage manufacturing where AI optimization requires fine-grained dataset distinction and provenance traceability.

title: Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution
summary: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

AI.tldr: SCSE is a novel recurrent formulation for Looped Transformers that enforces exact anchor invariance via a zero-deviation mask, ensuring a learned fixed-point anchor while allowing nonzero deviations to drive computation, thereby improving controlled recurrent quality across language modeling benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In additive-injection looped Transformers, the shared block must govern an entire trajectory of hidden states, but reintroducing an input-conditioned signal at each recurrent step can destabilize the reference state. The core tension is reconciling input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence — the shared transition applied at an input-conditioned reference can still perturb the hidden state, undermining the notion of a stable reference point.
AI.method: SCSE introduces three components: (1) a learned anchor derived from the input but treated as a one-step fixed point, (2) an initial deviation from that anchor which drives recurrent computation, and (3) a zero-deviation mask that maps zero deviation to zero, guaranteeing exact anchor invariance. The "zero-deviation forcing bias" — the next deviation produced from the anchor itself — is explicitly set to zero, eliminating spurious drift from the reference. SCSE frames this bias as a design degree of freedom (harmful, neutral, or beneficial) and selects the zero-setting for strict invariance.
AI.result: Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies attribute the primary gains to the learned anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence. A trained-model case study confirms that the anchor-response diagnostic aligns with observed recurrent motion.
AI.conclusion: SCSE successfully reconciles input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence in looped Transformers by enforcing exact anchor invariance. The zero-deviation forcing bias is identified as a tunable design choice, and setting it to zero yields consistent empirical improvements. The learned anchor and deviation recurrence are the key drivers of performance gains.

title: Fairness Pruning: Locating Demographic Bias in GLU-MLP Layers via Differential Activations
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Code and datasets publicly available
summary: This work presents Fairness Pruning, a lightweight structural intervention method designed for the management and future mitigation of demographic bias in large language models (LLMs). As a foundational empirical validation of this method, this work focuses on causal bias localization. Using minimally contrastive prompt pairs and inference-time activation capture, the method identifies neurons that react differentially when processing demographic attributes in GLU architectures, evaluating the signal at the down_proj input. Empirical evaluation was conducted on models of up to 3 billion parameters (Llama-3.2 family and Salamandra-2B), combining standardized benchmark evaluation with qualitative text generation experiments. Results demonstrate that zeroing the identified neurons alters how the model responds to associated demographic variables. However, rather than producing flat mitigation, the intervention causes bidirectional bias destabilization: because BiasScore is unsigned, candidate sets mix neurons that push toward and against the stereotype, and the net effect on aggregate bias depends on which sign dominates. The intervention is extremely surgical: zeroing at most 40 neurons in Llama-3.2-1B (less than 0.031% of total MLP width) achieves a mean retention of 99.49% in reasoning and general knowledge capabilities. These findings empirically confirm that demographic bias processing and model capabilities operate on dissociable circuits, establishing the methodological foundations for transitioning from blind zeroing toward directional behavior modulation.

AI.tldr: Fairness Pruning identifies neurons in LLMs (up to 3B parameters) that differentially respond to demographic attributes, then zeros them out. The intervention is extremely surgical (<0.031% of neurons) with 99.49% capability retention, but produces bidirectional bias destabilization rather than clean mitigation, demonstrating that bias and capabilities operate on dissociable circuits.
AI.motivation: To establish a lightweight, structural method for localizing and managing demographic bias in large language models, moving beyond surface-level debiasing toward precise, causal circuit-level intervention.
AI.method: Uses minimally contrastive prompt pairs to capture inference-time activations in GLU architectures, identifying neurons at the down_proj input that react differentially to demographic attributes. Candidate neurons are then zeroed out. Evaluated on Llama-3.2 family and Salamandra-2B using standardized benchmarks plus qualitative text generation. BiasScore (unsigned) is used to quantify differential activation.
AI.result: Zeroing at most 40 neurons (<0.031% of MLP width) achieves 99.49% retention of reasoning and general knowledge. However, bias mitigation is bidirectional rather than flat — candidate neuron sets mix stereotype-pushing and stereotype-opposing neurons, so net bias effect depends on which sign dominates. This constitutes bias destabilization rather than simple mitigation.
AI.conclusion: Demographic bias processing and general model capabilities operate on dissociable neural circuits. The work establishes foundations for transitioning from blind zeroing toward directional behavior modulation, where the sign and magnitude of each neuron's bias contribution is tracked to enable targeted, directional debiasing.

title: Simplifying Neural Networks During Training
summary: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

AI.tldr: Proposes an NC-inspired training framework that monitors Neural Collapse dynamics via the Inverse Fisher Criterion to identify when and where to truncate overparameterized networks, replacing trailing layers with a lightweight classification head for substantial parameter reduction with minimal accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Overparameterized deep networks are computationally expensive. While Neural Collapse reveals structured geometry in late training and the Tunnel Effect suggests only a subset of layers is essential, no existing method exploits these insights jointly to simplify networks dynamically during training.
AI.method: The framework monitors representation dynamics using the Inverse Fisher Criterion as a proxy for variability collapse. It identifies (1) the split point between feature extraction and classification layers, and (2) the training stage where simplification becomes viable. Trailing layers are then replaced with a lightweight classification head, and the reduced model continues training.
AI.result: Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures demonstrate substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to full models.
AI.conclusion: Combining Neural Collapse and Tunnel Effect perspectives enables principled, dynamic simplification of deep networks during training, yielding efficient reduced models without sacrificing performance.

title: Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective
summary:
Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a unified theoretical framework connecting Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) to classical concepts in representation learning. It characterizes how Total Information objectives capture intra-class structure and Mutual Information objectives capture inter-class structure, then validates these characterizations through controlled synthetic experiments.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) like the SCORE framework for supervised contrastive learning, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different SIMs remain poorly understood. There is a need for principled theoretical guidance on selecting and designing SIM-based objectives.
AI.method: The authors develop a unified theoretical framework that maps three SIM variants (Graph Cut, LogDet, Facility Location) across two measure types (Total Information and Mutual Information) to classical representation learning concepts. They characterize TI objectives as capturing intra-class structure (within-class variance, generalized variance, imbalance-aware separation) and MI objectives as capturing inter-class structure (centroid separation, Mahalanobis distance, nearest-mode overlap). Validation uses controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.
AI.result: The theoretical characterizations were validated empirically: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation favoring rare and confusable classes. For MI objectives, Graph Cut MI relates to centroid separation, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation via Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap. Empirical behavior closely matched theory across all synthetic experimental settings.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures, offering principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

title: LLMs struggle to simulate human belief updates in controlled environments
summary: LLMs are increasingly deployed as proxies for human study participants in social science experiments, yet the fidelity of this practice has rarely been tested directly. We test whether six LLMs can simulate individual human belief updates, comparing LLM outputs 1-to-1 against ground truth data from 391 UK participants on Prolific, who updated their stances on three discussion topics after reading Reddit comments. Each participant was simulated by an LLM conditioned on a persona derived from their demographic and personality trait data. We find that some LLMs (Qwen3-32B and GPT-5-Mini) can match the human post-stance distribution, but only when given participants' actual initial stances. All six models fail to simulate initial stances themselves and to produce faithful belief updates from self-generated stances. Three systematic biases emerge across all models: overrepresentation of neutral positions, more frequent but smaller belief shifts than humans, and a failure to rank comments by convincingness. Demographic and personality trait personas had no consistent effect on fidelity. LLM simulations of human belief dynamics are only reliable when grounded in realistic starting conditions, that current multi-round social media simulations rarely provide.

AI.tldr: LLMs fail to faithfully simulate human belief updating unless explicitly given real initial stances. Without this grounding, models exhibit systematic biases: neutrality overrepresentation, smaller-than-human belief shifts, and inability to rank argument convincingness. Persona conditioning on demographics/traits does not improve fidelity.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as proxies for human participants in social science experiments, but the validity of this substitution has rarely been empirically tested. The authors aim to directly assess whether LLMs can replicate individual-level human belief updating in a social media discourse context.
AI.method: Six LLMs (including Qwen3-32B and GPT-5-Mini) were each conditioned on demographic and personality trait personas derived from 391 real UK Prolific participants. The task involved updating stances on three discussion topics after reading Reddit comments. LLM outputs were compared 1-to-1 against ground-truth human data across three dimensions: initial stance generation, post-exposure belief shift magnitude/direction, and comment convincingness ranking.
AI.result: Only Qwen3-32B and GPT-5-Mini matched human post-stance distributions, and only when given actual initial stances. All models failed to generate realistic initial stances and could not produce faithful updates from self-generated stances. Three systematic biases were universal: overrepresentation of neutral positions, more frequent but smaller belief shifts, and failure to rank comments by convincingness. Persona conditioning had no consistent effect on simulation fidelity.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based simulation of human belief dynamics is unreliable unless grounded in externally provided realistic starting conditions—a requirement most current multi-round social media simulations do not meet.

title: Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs
summary:
Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

AI.tldr: Sampled-negative evaluation in continuous-time dynamic graphs introduces conditional biases: non-uniform negative distributions distort Bayes-optimal ranking, and finite candidate sets destabilize model comparisons and module-effect measurements. The authors advocate replacing sampled-negative benchmarks with all-entity ranking against a fixed destination catalog.
AI.motivation: Standard next-destination prediction benchmarks in CTDGs rely on ranking an observed interaction against a set of sampled negative destinations. The authors identify that this practice introduces two confounds: (1) the choice of negative sampling distribution changes the theoretical optimal ranking, and (2) finite candidate sets inject instability into both model rankings and measured module effects. The paper aims to quantify these issues and propose a remedy.
AI.method: The authors conduct a factorial evaluation crossing repeated vs. new positives with seen vs. unseen negatives. They employ a minimal scorer based solely on time-varying source-destination pair-history membership to isolate the transmission path of sampler influence. Controlled representation interventions are used to probe how model operations propagate negative-sampling artifacts. Six models are evaluated across four datasets (LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, Wikipedia), comparing expected Uniform-20 metrics against full-catalog ranking.
AI.result: On three of four datasets, at least one pair of models changes relative ranking order between Uniform-20 and full-catalog evaluation. Measured module effects vary in both magnitude and direction depending on candidate-set size and training objective. The sampler's influence propagates through models via time-varying source-destination history features and operations that exploit this information.
AI.conclusion: Model-superiority claims and ablation conclusions drawn from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the specific negative configuration. All-entity ranking, which evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, removes this degree of freedom and eliminates sampling variation while preserving the original CTDG scorer. The authors recommend it as the primary evaluation protocol for CTDG benchmarks possessing an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

title: FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning
summary: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

AI.tldr: FedOGL is a federated graph learning framework that combats catastrophic forgetting in multimodal graph streams through client-side semantic-structural memory preservation (replay, task-start distillation, structure-basis projection) and server-side compact prototype transfer, achieving a 42.67% reduction in forgetting-induced performance degradation.
AI.motivation: Federated multimodal graph learning faces a unique catastrophic forgetting challenge that goes beyond classifier drift: historical knowledge can be lost through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. Existing solutions do not jointly address these three intertwined forgetting mechanisms in a privacy-preserving decentralized setting.
AI.method: FedOGL operates on two levels. On the client side, it preserves historical decision behavior via replay and task-start distillation, and safeguards graph-propagation memory by projecting onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, it maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to enable cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that FedOGL reduces performance degradation from catastrophic forgetting by 42.67% compared with the best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving downstream task performance.
AI.conclusion: FedOGL effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning by addressing forgetting at both semantic and structural levels, with a prototype-based server mechanism that preserves privacy. The framework sets a new state-of-the-art for continual learning over decentralized, private graph streams.

title: Correlation between prosody and pragmatics: A case study of the discourse marker hālā `now' in Persian
summary: The Persian discourse marker hālā ('now') exhibits remarkable multifunctionality, extending far beyond its temporal adverbial role to encompass a variety of pragmatic functions. This study presents a pragmatic and acoustic analysis of hālā in spoken Persian, examining 267 instances from spontaneous conversations. While temporal uses were present, they were often combined with other discourse marker functions, indicating extensive multifunctionality, with 70% of tokens serving two or more pragmatic roles. Textual functions (topic shifting, signaling relationships, boundary marking, attention guidance, topic introduction, and topic emphasis) were most frequent, followed by interactive functions (turn management, listener engagement, and feedback regulation), and modal functions (epistemic stance, emotional expression, and attitudinal marking). Prosodic analysis revealed that duration and intensity are key cues for distinguishing hālā's functions. Textual uses were significantly shorter, while temporal uses showed a tendency toward longer realizations. Interactive functions correlated with higher intensity, while modal functions showed a weaker tendency toward lower intensity. These findings indicate that duration and intensity are the main prosodic cues associated with functional differentiation in hālā, especially in textual and interactive uses.

AI.tldr: Persian "hālā" (now) is highly multifunctional beyond temporal use. Analysis of 267 conversational tokens shows 70% serve dual pragmatic roles. Textual functions dominate, followed by interactive and modal. Duration and intensity are key prosodic cues distinguishing these functions.
AI.motivation: To systematically investigate the multifunctional pragmatic roles of the Persian discourse marker "hālā" in spontaneous conversation and identify the prosodic cues (duration, intensity) that differentiate its various functions.
AI.method: Pragmatic and acoustic analysis of 267 instances of hālā drawn from spontaneous Persian conversations. Functional categorization into textual, interactive, and modal domains was combined with prosodic measurements of duration and intensity.
AI.result: 70% of tokens served two or more pragmatic roles simultaneously. Textual functions (topic shifting, boundary marking, etc.) were most frequent, followed by interactive (turn management, engagement) and modal (epistemic stance, emotion). Duration significantly distinguished textual (shorter) from temporal (longer) uses. Intensity correlated with interactive functions (higher) and modal functions (weaker tendency toward lower).
AI.conclusion: Hālā exhibits extensive multifunctionality in Persian discourse. Duration and intensity serve as the primary prosodic cues for functional differentiation, particularly effective for textual and interactive uses.

title: Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time
summary: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

AI.tldr: Orca introduces a framework combining structural causal models with neural operator learning, enabling causal reasoning (interventions and counterfactuals) on systems that evolve continuously in time, are observed irregularly, and contain feedback loops. Each causal graph node is a function of time, and mechanisms are learned maps between function spaces.
AI.motivation: Standard structural causal models (SCMs) assume static variables measured once and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Real-world systems (patients, climates, economies) evolve continuously, are observed at irregular intervals, and contain feedback loops. Existing causal frameworks cannot handle this dynamic, continuous-time setting.
AI.method: The authors propose Orca, a framework where each node in a causal graph is a function of time and each causal mechanism is a learned map between function spaces using neural operators. Neural operator architectures are extended to: (1) compute a node's function value from several parent functions, (2) respect the arrow of time, and (3) treat latent exogenous noise as an inferable, reusable function for counterfactual reasoning.
AI.result: The framework is formalized as a model class and demonstrated on synthetic continuous-time examples, showing effective counterfactual reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for extending causal reasoning to continuous-time, irregularly-observed, feedback-loop systems. Orca operationalizes this insight, bridging SCMs and function-space learning for dynamic causal inference.

title: Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

AI.tldr: This paper establishes tight statistical guarantees for Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA): an upper bound of Õ(rd/n) and a matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n). It proves a rank-selection dichotomy: constrained ERM is harmed by over-ranking, while nuclear-norm-then-truncate adaptive estimators are not. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic and real NLP benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Prior work on LoRA generalization provided only upper bounds (Õ(√(rd/n)) or Õ(rd/n)) without matching lower bounds, and offered no formal guidance on how to choose the LoRA rank r. This paper aims to close both gaps by providing tight statistical characterization and a principled answer to rank selection.
AI.method: (1) A local Rademacher complexity argument yields an excess risk upper bound of Õ(rd/n) for the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, assuming the target adaptation has rank ≤ r. (2) A Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of ℝ^{d×d} establishes a matching minimax lower bound of Ω(rd/n) for any estimator in the rank-r LoRA class. (3) Analysis of constrained ERM versus nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators reveals a dichotomy in sensitivity to over-parameterization. (4) Empirical validation on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on DistilBERT/RoBERTa fine-tuning for SST-2 and MRPC.
AI.result: The upper bound Õ(rd/n) and lower bound Ω(rd/n) match, yielding tight characterization. Constrained ERM achieves optimal performance at r = r* (intrinsic rank) and degrades with over-ranking. Nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators are insensitive to over-ranking, with rate saturating at Θ̃(r*d/n). Experiments on SST-2 and MRPC confirm the predicted U-shape in validation loss; two configurations show statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (p = 0.016).
