AI.conclusion: The empirically observed over-parameterization penalty in LoRA is a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than inherent to the LoRA parameterization. The optimal rank for constrained ERM is the intrinsic rank r*, while adaptive nuclear-norm-based estimators avoid the penalty entirely.

title: Beyond a Single Judge: Simulating Social Persona Panels for Generative UI Evaluation
summary: Generative UI (GenUI) lets large language models synthesize a complete, renderable interface directly from a natural-language instruction, but evaluating the quality of what they generate remains an open problem. Human evaluation is costly and rater-variant, while LLM-as-a-judge is scalable but reflects only a single implicit viewpoint, unable to capture how different populations of real users actually perceive the same interface. We propose the Evidence-Grounded, Social-Weighted Persona Panel (ESPP), a three-stage GenUI evaluation method in which a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas independently rates a screenshot, exchanges opinions under a trait-derived, semantically-gated bounded-confidence mechanism, and is aggregated via Delphi-inspired social weighting into a single judgment. ESPP tracks human judgment substantially more closely than a naive single-pass judge, raising Pearson $r$ from $0.716$ to $0.922$, and a prompt-ensemble control recovers only about a third of this gap, isolating genuine persona and evidence grounding as the dominant source of improvement. Beyond this fidelity gain, retaining each panelist's individual rating further reveals that user subgroups agree on overall model rankings yet diverge sharply on specific rating dimensions, a structural disagreement a single homogeneous judge would systematically erase. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/ESPP.

AI.tldr: ESPP introduces a three-stage method for evaluating generative UI quality using a panel of psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded personas that debate under a bounded-confidence mechanism and are aggregated via social weighting, achieving substantially higher correlation with human judgment (r=0.922) than single-pass LLM judges (r=0.716).
AI.motivation: Evaluating the quality of LLM-generated UIs is an open problem: human evaluation is expensive and inconsistent, while LLM-as-a-judge is scalable but reflects only a single implicit viewpoint, failing to capture how diverse real-user populations perceive the same interface.
AI.method: ESPP operates in three stages: (1) a panel of psychologically diverse personas grounded in evidence independently rates a UI screenshot; (2) panelists exchange opinions under a trait-derived, semantically-gated bounded-confidence mechanism (they influence each other only if their views are sufficiently similar); (3) judgments are aggregated via a Delphi-inspired social weighting scheme into a single evaluation. A prompt-ensemble baseline serves as an ablation control.
AI.result: ESPP raises Pearson r with human judgment from 0.716 (naive single-pass judge) to 0.922. The prompt-ensemble control recovers only ~1/3 of this gap, confirming that persona diversity and evidence grounding are the dominant improvement sources. Additionally, individual panelist ratings reveal that user subgroups agree on overall model rankings but diverge sharply on specific rating dimensions — structural disagreement that a homogeneous judge would erase.
AI.conclusion: ESPP demonstrates that psychologically diverse, evidence-grounded persona panels with bounded-confidence deliberation and social weighting can closely approximate human evaluation of generative UI quality while preserving subgroup-level disagreements, offering a scalable and faithful alternative to both costly human studies and naive LLM-as-a-judge.

title: Search as Computation Allocation
summary: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes anytime algorithms as terminal computation-allocation problems, uses Bellman equations to characterize optimal computation policies, relates value of computation (VOC) to information-theoretic quantities, and shows that maximizing approximate VOC recovers algorithms like weighted A*.
AI.motivation: Many algorithms expend internal resources (time, simulations, node expansions) before outputting a decision, yet are evaluated solely by the quality of that final output. There is no unified framework for reasoning about optimal allocation of computation in such settings. The authors aim to provide a formal structure connecting bandit problems, tree search, and heuristic search under a common decision-theoretic lens.
AI.method: The paper formalizes terminal computation-allocation problems with three variants: fixed computation budgets, priced computation (cost per operation), and exact certification. Bellman equations characterize optimal dynamic allocation policies. The authors then analyze the relationship between value of computation (VOC) and information measures — comparing mutual information (myopic VOC under log loss), knowledge-gradient quantities (VOC under simple regret), and information gain. Finally, they apply the framework to bandit pulls, Monte Carlo tree search node expansions, and heuristic search, showing that maximizing approximate VOC under a frontier-resolution model recovers weighted A* (with A* and greedy best-first search as limits).
AI.result: Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss. Under simple regret, VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity. Information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly but provides a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Under a frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*; A* and greedy best-first search emerge as limiting cases.
AI.conclusion: The framework identifies a shared decision problem across diverse computation-allocation domains (bandits, tree search, heuristic search) without claiming any single acquisition rule is universally optimal. It clarifies when information-theoretic acquisition heuristics are justified and when they fail.

title: Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries
summary: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

AI.tldr: ES-PINN is a physics-informed neural network for transient stability assessment that enforces exact state chaining across pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing event stages. It defines a differentiable CCT boundary for accurate stability margin estimation, sensitivity analysis, and direct CCT prediction, with a proven local residual-to-CCT error bound. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show improved trajectory and boundary accuracy over baselines.
AI.motivation: Reliable critical clearing time (CCT) estimation is essential to prevent cascading outages, but it is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated time-domain simulations across many fault severities and clearing times. Existing surrogate models often fail to accurately capture event-stage transitions and stability boundaries.
AI.method: An event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that: (1) aligns its internal representation with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics; (2) enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces; (3) defines a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin as a differentiable CCT boundary approximation; (4) supports local sensitivity analysis and optional direct CCT prediction via a distilled readout; and (5) provides a proven local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate that eliminates state-interface defect terms through exact event chaining.
AI.result: On IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems, ES-PINN consistently improved held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrated effectiveness and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: ES-PINN offers an accurate, efficient, and theoretically grounded framework for CCT estimation and transient stability boundary extraction, outperforming standard neural surrogates while providing local sensitivity analysis and a rigorous error bound, with broad applicability validated across multiple IEEE test systems and contingency scenarios.

title: Lightning OPD 2.0: Mitigating Style Bias in Cross-Teacher On-Policy Distillation for Large Reasoning Models
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a teacher, but its effectiveness can depend on teacher consistency, meaning that the model providing OPD supervision should also have generated the demonstrations used to train the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) reference. However, this condition is frequently violated in practice when SFT data have mixed or unknown provenance or when different models are preferred for SFT data generation and subsequent distillation. In such cross-teacher settings, even a stronger OPD teacher can yield little improvement over the SFT reference. We find that raw teacher--reference disagreement contains potentially useful context-specific teacher evidence as well as a recurring component associated with differences in wording, formatting, and reasoning cadence. We introduce Lightning OPD 2.0 with cross-fitted style residualization, which uses rollout-level cross-fitting to estimate this recurring component as an operational proxy for style-token bias and subtracts it before constructing the token-level OPD update. Across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks, Lightning OPD 2.0 consistently outperforms Lightning OPD in cross-teacher settings. Starting from Klear-Reasoner-8B-SFT, Lightning OPD 2.0 reaches 82.4% on AIME 2024 and 63.0% on LiveCodeBench v5. Together, these results establish Lightning OPD 2.0 as a practical approach to cross-teacher OPD, relaxing teacher consistency as a prerequisite and allowing the SFT data generator and distillation teacher to be selected independently. Code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: Lightning OPD 2.0 introduces cross-fitted style residualization to remove style-token bias from teacher signals, enabling effective on-policy distillation even when the SFT data generator and distillation teacher are different models, outperforming prior OPD methods on math and code benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard on-policy distillation (OPD) assumes teacher consistency — the distillation teacher must be the same model that generated the SFT data. In practice, this is often violated (mixed provenance, different models for SFT vs. distillation). In these cross-teacher settings, even a stronger teacher yields little improvement. The authors identify that teacher–reference disagreement contains both useful evidence and a recurring style-token bias (differences in wording, formatting, reasoning cadence) that degrades OPD effectiveness.
AI.method: The proposed method, Lightning OPD 2.0, uses rollout-level cross-fitting to estimate the recurring style-token bias component from teacher–reference disagreements. This estimated bias — operationalized as a proxy for style differences — is then residualized (subtracted out) before constructing the token-level OPD update. This allows the true context-specific teacher evidence to drive the distillation signal without contamination from stylistic discrepancies.
AI.result: Lightning OPD 2.0 consistently outperforms Lightning OPD in cross-teacher settings on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks. Starting from Klear-Reasoner-8B-SFT, it achieves 82.4% on AIME 2024 and 63.0% on LiveCodeBench v5.
AI.conclusion: Lightning OPD 2.0 relaxes the teacher consistency prerequisite, making cross-teacher OPD practical. This allows independent selection of the SFT data generator and the distillation teacher, broadening the applicability of on-policy distillation in real-world settings.

title: An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding
summary:
Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

AI.tldr: MSEval is a benchmark for evaluating multi-agent coding systems on real-world full-stack projects. It uses 10 authentic projects, an execution engine (LegoGent) testing 10 collaboration topologies with CI/CD deployment, and an automated grader (TAgent) measuring functional success, latency, and token cost. Key finding: organizational topology rivals model capability in determining speed-cost-quality trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent coding benchmarks are limited to synthetic environments that ignore real-world time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward superficial task completion. There is a need for a rigorous, realistic evaluation framework that reflects how multi-agent teams actually build software in practice.
AI.method: MSEval is built on 10 authentic full-stack projects spanning 10 domains, scored via hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics. The LegoGent execution engine tests 10 distinct collaboration topologies where agents synchronize at periodic intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. The TAgent automated grader dynamically probes implementations to jointly assess functional success, wall-clock latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Experiments span 100 runs.
AI.result: Organizational topology proves as influential as model capability in the speed-cost-quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines achieve the fastest convergence with highest quality, while heavy managerial oversight degrades performance.
AI.conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for evaluating multi-agent software development. The finding that team organization matters as much as agent intelligence has practical implications for designing collaborative AI coding systems. The benchmark and codebase are publicly released.

title: NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation
summary:
Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

AI.tldr: Proposes a fully neural estimator for normalized mutual information (NMI) in continuous multidimensional settings, combining a MINE-based mutual information estimator with neural marginal entropy estimators. Experiments on 1–8 dimensional Gaussian data show improved accuracy over KSG-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard mutual information is unbounded and not comparable across datasets or dimensions. While normalized mutual information addresses this, existing estimators (particularly KSG-based) suffer from sensitivity to dimensionality and numerical stability issues. A robust neural alternative is needed.
AI.method: Combines a MINE-based mutual information estimator using the Donsker–Varadhan representation with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators. Marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution. The ratio of MI to marginal entropies yields the normalized dependency score.
AI.result: On Gaussian data spanning 1 to 8 dimensions, the proposed neural NMI estimator achieves higher accuracy than a KSG-based NMI baseline.
AI.conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings, offering improved accuracy and robustness over traditional nearest-neighbor-based approaches.

title: Improving Mental Health Screening and Early Risk Detection in Spanish
summary: Early detection of mental health disorders is often limited by the lack of specialized resources in Spanish and the difficulty of analyzing long histories of social media posts. This paper addresses these challenges through three main contributions. First, we introduce three Spanish foundational models specifically adapted to the mental health domain through domain-specific pre-training. Second, we propose Incremental Context Expansion (ICE), an automatic relabeling methodology designed for early detection. ICE identifies the point at which cumulative messages provide enough evidence of a disorder, generating more informative training samples. Third, we provide a set of fine-tuned models using the samples generated with the ICE methodology for early risk detection tasks. Our results on three Spanish benchmarks show that combining these specialized models with ICE improves the state-of-the-art, reducing detection latency while maintaining high performance. All models are publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces three Spanish mental health foundation models and a novel Incremental Context Expansion (ICE) relabeling method for early disorder detection from social media, achieving state-of-the-art results with reduced detection latency on Spanish benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Early detection of mental health disorders is hindered by a scarcity of Spanish-language specialized resources and the challenge of analyzing lengthy social media post histories to identify disorders promptly.
AI.method: Three Spanish foundation models are pretrained specifically on mental health domain data. Additionally, Incremental Context Expansion (ICE) is proposed — an automatic relabeling methodology that pinpoints the exact moment in a sequence of cumulative messages where sufficient evidence of a disorder emerges, thereby creating more informative training samples. Fine-tuned models are then developed using ICE-generated samples for early risk detection.
AI.result: On three Spanish benchmarks, the combination of domain-specialized models and ICE surpasses prior state-of-the-art performance, lowering detection latency while preserving high accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific pretraining for Spanish mental health, paired with the ICE relabeling strategy, effectively advances early detection capabilities. All models are publicly released to facilitate further research.

title: Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals that on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) produces unreliable token-level credit signals, as most tokens shift in the same direction regardless of outcome correctness. The authors propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a GRPO extension that downweights highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes advantages, consistently outperforming GRPO on long-CoT math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Critic-free RLVR methods like GRPO uniformly broadcast response-level rewards across all tokens, ignoring unequal token contributions. OPSD attempts to provide dense supervision via forward KL divergence with a privileged self-teacher, but the authors hypothesize that the resulting token-level likelihood shifts may not encode reliable answer-aligned information. This motivates a rigorous empirical investigation of whether privilege-induced directions genuinely reflect learning value.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a diagnostic analysis: they fix each sampled trajectory and re-score it under two opposing outcome conditions (correctness vs. incorrectness), measuring token-level shift directions, sign reversals, and overlap in optimization signals. They then propose CSCR, which identifies highly sensitive tokens via counterfactual scoring, reduces their credit allocation, and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. This operates as a lightweight extension to GRPO without requiring a critic network.
AI.result: The diagnostic study shows that (1) most tokens shift in the same direction under opposite outcome conditions with few sign reversals, (2) large shifts concentrate on substitutable surface-form tokens rather than reasoning-critical tokens, and (3) privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms the GRPO baseline at matched policy update counts. Ablations confirm that privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and overly aggressive modulation destabilizes optimization.
AI.conclusion: Privileged self-distillation signals in OPSD are unreliable for token-level credit assignment, as they primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than genuine learning value. CSCR offers a simple yet effective correction by reallocating credit away from highly sensitive tokens, improving GRPO without additional computational overhead. The findings highlight the importance of scrutinizing distributional supervision signals in RLVR for long-CoT reasoning.

title: VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction
summary: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

AI.tldr: VESTIGE is a parameter-free replacement for standard MLM collation that aligns masking probability with empirically measured, position-dependent corruption profiles. Applied to ancient DNA reconstruction, it significantly outperforms uniform masking across all tested conditions, with improved validation loss and high-fidelity protein structure predictions.
AI.motivation: Standard masked language modeling assumes uniform reconstruction difficulty across token positions, which fails when degradation is concentrated at predictable positions (e.g., cytosine deamination in ancient DNA). At peak damage sites, uniform masking can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor, motivating a corruption-aware masking strategy.
AI.method: VESTIGE replaces the standard MLM collator by rescaling the per-position masking distribution to match an empirically measured corruption profile (e.g., mapDamage2-derived C-to-T/G-to-A gradients in aDNA). The mean C/G masking rate is held at 15%, identical to standard MLM, isolating spatial redistribution as the sole experimental variable. Evaluation uses DNABERT-2 on mammoth CDS sequences across two specimens, seven genes, and 626 paired windows spanning six terminal-zone widths.
AI.result: VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at every terminal-zone width (Δ = +4.18 to +10.35 percentage points, all p < 10⁻⁸), reduces validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions, even under 10–30× amplified damage. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier achieves AUC = 0.935, clearing 98.2% of reconstructed windows.
AI.conclusion: The approach is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile (FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, nanopore) can substitute for the PMD array, establishing VESTIGE as a general knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded sequence inputs.

title: Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning
summary: As large language models (LLMs) continue to advance in complex reasoning tasks, they have learned to heavily prioritize explicit conditions provided in the input. However, in everyday commonsense reasoning, this mechanism exposes a critical vulnerability which we term Salience Bias: models become easily hijacked by useless explicit distractors (e.g., numerical values), leading them to ignore the implicit physical or commonsense prerequisites of a task. A critical open question is whether this failure reflects a genuine gap in commonsense knowledge or merely its suppression under misleading task framing. To investigate this, we construct the SaliTrap Benchmark, a high-quality dataset across four trap dimensions. Evaluating 12 state-of-the-art LLMs, we find that all mainstream models suffer significantly from salience bias, with severity scaling with distractor density and detecting the trap often decoupled from actually avoiding it. Crucially, by re-eliciting the same models with the task framing stripped away, we show that this is overwhelmingly a failure of \textbf{knowledge suppression rather than knowledge absence}: a context-free knowledge probe alone recovers over 90\% of sycophantic-compliance failures, revealing that the requisite commonsense is intrinsically present but actively crowded out by salient distractors that lure the model into over-compliant, unnecessary computation. Building on this diagnosis, we further show that lightweight, inference-time prompting alone substantially closes the gap without any retraining. Our findings relocate the bottleneck of commonsense reasoning failures from model competence to elicitation, and we release SaliTrap as a testbed for this blind spot. The codes are available at https://github.com/Wuzheng02/SaliTrap.

AI.tldr: LLMs exhibit a "Salience Bias" where explicit distractors in input override implicit commonsense knowledge. The SaliTrap benchmark reveals this is primarily a knowledge suppression issue (not absence), as context-free probing recovers >90% of failures. Lightweight prompting interventions significantly mitigate the problem without retraining.
AI.motivation: LLMs prioritize explicit conditions in prompts, but this creates a vulnerability where salient yet irrelevant distractors (e.g., numbers) hijack reasoning and suppress implicit commonsense prerequisites. The critical question is whether these failures stem from genuine knowledge gaps or from knowledge suppression under misleading task framing.
AI.method: The authors construct SaliTrap, a benchmark spanning four trap dimensions to test salience bias. They evaluate 12 state-of-the-art LLMs, measuring failure rates against distractor density and testing whether models can detect traps. Crucially, they compare performance under standard (distractor-laden) vs. context-free probing conditions to disentangle knowledge absence from knowledge suppression. They also test lightweight inference-time prompting interventions to close the gap.
AI.result: All 12 mainstream LLMs suffer significantly from salience bias, with severity scaling with distractor density. Trap detection is often decoupled from trap avoidance. Context-free probing recovers over 90% of sycophantic-compliance failures, confirming knowledge suppression rather than knowledge absence as the dominant mechanism. Lightweight inference-time prompting substantially closes the performance gap without retraining.
AI.conclusion: The bottleneck in commonsense reasoning is relocated from model competence to knowledge elicitation. Salience bias represents a failure of suppressing irrelevant salient information rather than lacking commonsense knowledge. SaliTrap is released as a testbed for studying this blind spot.

title: Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators
summary: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

AI.tldr: DSF proposes evolving the graph propagation filter itself over time, using compact Chebyshev polynomial coefficients as recurrent temporal states with gated updates. It achieves strong link-prediction performance with dramatically fewer parameters, lower GPU memory, and faster training than comparable methods.
AI.motivation: Temporal graph learning typically focuses on evolving node states or encoding interaction histories, but the question of whether the graph propagation mechanism itself should evolve over time remains underexplored. The authors identify a gap: can a time-evolving spectral filter serve as an efficient and effective temporal inductive bias?
AI.method: Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF) represents graph propagation at each snapshot t using a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. These compact multi-order coefficients are treated as recurrent temporal states, updated via a recurrent branch with multiplicative global and order-specific gates that regulate magnitude. Crucially, the temporal state size is independent of the number of nodes, ensuring parameter efficiency.
AI.result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF achieves AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860 respectively, using 93K–133K trainable parameters, 68–182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6–2.1 seconds per training epoch. Compared to DEFT, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3–8.6× fewer parameters, 25–33× less GPU memory, and 5–19× less time per epoch. Against all measured alternatives, DSF uses 3.3–38.6× less GPU memory.
AI.conclusion: Direct spectral-response evolution is a useful temporal inductive bias, particularly when computational efficiency is a first-class design requirement. DSF demonstrates that evolving the propagation operator itself — rather than node states or interaction encodings — can yield competitive accuracy with substantial resource savings.

title: Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules
summary: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

AI.tldr: This paper examines the joint effect of learning rate and batch size schedules on deep learning training dynamics through convex optimization theory, deriving a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any given learning rate schedule, and demonstrating that dynamic batch size schedules outperform static ones in large language model training.
AI.motivation: Modern deep learning practice typically fixes batch size throughout training, ignoring the interdependent relationship between learning rate and batch size on training dynamics. The authors aim to formalize this relationship and demonstrate the value of dynamic batch size scheduling.
AI.method: The authors analyze deep learning training dynamics through the lens of convex optimization, deriving a joint characterization of the loss function in terms of both learning rate and batch size schedules. This theoretical framework applies to general optimizers and model architectures, and yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule.
AI.result: The derived joint characterization leads to joint scaling laws for learning rate and batch size. Empirically, dynamic batch size schedules consistently outperform static batch size baselines, with particular significance demonstrated in large language model training.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic batch size scheduling, when jointly optimized with learning rate schedules, offers consistent improvements over static batch size approaches. The closed-form optimal schedule provides a principled way to tune batch size dynamically during training.

title: Beyond Sentiment: Structured Information Extraction from Financial News
summary: Financial sentiment analysis has become a standard component in news-driven stock prediction, yet it reduces rich, multi-dimensional news articles to a single polarity score. We hypothesize that financial news encodes multiple orthogonal information dimensions---event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, and semantic confidence---that sentiment alone cannot capture, and that these dimensions carry independent predictive value. To test this hypothesis, we propose a structured information extraction framework that leverages LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions from financial news. Through large-scale experiments on 41,618 news--stock pairs from the FNSPID dataset, we find that (i) FinBERT sentiment features exhibit strong predictive power under nonlinear models (F1=0.576) but substantially weaker performance under linear models (F1=0.230), revealing a highly nonlinear sentiment--return relationship; (ii) LLM-extracted structured features, while individually weaker, capture information orthogonal to sentiment, as evidenced by a 53.5% systematic disagreement rate between the two approaches; and (iii) combining both signal sources yields F1=0.600, significantly outperforming either alone ($p < 0.0001$), with consistent improvements across all seven event types. Ablation experiments confirm that non-sentiment structural dimensions (event type, impact subject, time horizon, confidence) independently contribute $Δ\text{F1} = +0.019$ beyond FinBERT alone. Feature importance analysis reveals balanced contributions from all six extracted dimensions (14--21%), demonstrating that compressing news into a single sentiment score incurs substantial information loss. Our results suggest that the sentiment--semantics decoupling in financial text is systematic and exploitable, opening a new direction for multi-dimensional financial NLP.

AI.tldr: Financial news contains multiple orthogonal information dimensions beyond sentiment (event type, impact scope, temporal horizon, confidence), and combining LLM-extracted structured features with FinBERT sentiment yields significantly better stock prediction (F1=0.600) than either approach alone, demonstrating that compressing news into a single sentiment score incurs substantial information loss.
AI.motivation: Current financial sentiment analysis reduces rich news articles to a single polarity score, potentially discarding valuable predictive information. The authors hypothesize that financial news encodes multiple orthogonal dimensions that sentiment alone cannot capture, and that these dimensions carry independent predictive value for stock movement.
AI.method: The authors propose a structured information extraction framework using LLaMA-3.1-70B to extract six semantic dimensions from financial news. They conduct large-scale experiments on 41,618 news-stock pairs from the FNSPID dataset, comparing FinBERT sentiment features with LLM-extracted structured features using both linear and nonlinear models. They perform ablation experiments and feature importance analysis to quantify each dimension's contribution.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) FinBERT sentiment shows strong nonlinear predictive power (F1=0.576) but weak linear performance (F1=0.230); (2) LLM-extracted features capture orthogonal information with a 53.5% systematic disagreement rate; (3) Combining both yields F1=0.600, significantly outperforming either alone (p<0.0001); (4) Non-sentiment structural dimensions independently contribute ΔF1=+0.019 beyond FinBERT; (5) All six dimensions show balanced feature importance (14-21%).
AI.conclusion: The sentiment-semantics decoupling in financial text is systematic and exploitable. Multi-dimensional feature extraction from financial news opens a new direction for financial NLP, demonstrating that reducing news to a single sentiment score incurs substantial information loss.

title: MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos
summary: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

AI.tldr: MMHBench is a multimodal benchmark for mental health understanding in long-form videos, featuring 268 videos and 2,184 questions across third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking. A Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework synthesizes multi-perspective questions refined through iterative optimization and expert verification. Evaluation of 22 MLLMs shows the task remains highly challenging.
AI.motivation: Existing mental health benchmarks reduce understanding to coarse-grained classification, failing to assess whether models truly grasp psychological phenomena or merely exploit superficial correlations. There is a need for nuanced, multi-perspective evaluation over long-form video that captures observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent mental states.
AI.method: The authors introduce MMHBench with 268 long-form videos and 2,184 curated questions, organized into two settings: (1) third-person assessment (605 questions) evaluating interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking (1,579 questions) requiring perspective-conditioned reasoning. A Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple viewpoints, refined through multi-role feedback, iterative optimization, and expert-guided verification. Twenty-two MLLMs (open-source and closed-source) are evaluated.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation across 22 representative MLLMs demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging, with models struggling on both third-person assessment and first-person perspective-taking tasks.
AI.conclusion: Long-form video mental health understanding is a substantially unsolved problem for current MLLMs. MMHBench provides a more rigorous and ecologically valid framework for evaluating multimodal mental health reasoning, exposing significant gaps in models' ability to perform nuanced, perspective-aware psychological inference.

title: Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

AI.tldr: An extension of Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) that introduces a clean teacher alongside the robust teacher, using cross-layer attention to transfer features from both, improving clean accuracy while preserving adversarial robustness on CIFAR-10/100.
AI.motivation: Existing defense methods like IBD trade off clean accuracy for adversarial robustness. The authors aim to recover the lost clean accuracy while maintaining robust performance.
AI.method: Extends IBD by introducing a dual-teacher distillation framework: a clean teacher (trained on clean inputs only) and a robust teacher (adversarially trained). Both teachers' features are transferred to the student via a cross-layer attention matrix. Evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.
AI.result: Improved clean accuracy over original IBD with similar adversarial accuracy. Competitive with state-of-the-art methods including B-MTARD, particularly on the harmonic mean of clean and robust accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The dual-teacher approach with cross-layer attention effectively mitigates the clean-robust accuracy trade-off inherent in IBD, yielding a more balanced classifier.

title: Generative AI and linguistic diversity in academic writing and publishing: Perspectives from World Englishes
summary: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic writing and publishing (AWP) raises questions about linguistic inclusivity and the legitimacy of diverse Englishes in global scholarly communication. This article responds to these questions through a structured scholarly dialogue involving five sociolinguists from World Englishes and adjacent fields. Organised around five guiding questions, the dialogue interrogates how GenAI tools influence writing practices, reinforce or disrupt dominant language norms, and raise ethical challenges. Contributors reflect on the potential of GenAI to democratise writing processes while also raising concerns about GenAI's tendency to marginalise minoritised varieties and flatten nuance in scholarly writing. Across the dialogue, themes of linguistic (in)justice, researcher agency, and institutional responsibility emerge, with contributors calling for equity-informed policies, critical AI literacy, and inclusive co-design in GenAI development. The article shows the value of dialogic reflection in understanding GenAI's role in AWP. It concludes that while GenAI may reinforce existing hierarchies, it can also serve as a site of resistance, depending on how it is designed, governed and used within scholarly communities committed to linguistic diversity.

AI.tldr: This article presents a structured dialogue among five sociolinguists examining how generative AI in academic writing and publishing affects linguistic inclusivity, questioning whether GenAI reinforces dominant English norms or can be harnessed to support diverse World Englishes. Contributors weigh both the democratizing potential and the risks of marginalizing minoritized varieties, ultimately calling for equity-informed policies, critical AI literacy, and inclusive co-design.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of generative AI in academic writing and publishing raises urgent questions about linguistic inclusivity and the legitimacy of diverse Englishes in global scholarly communication, prompting a need for informed, critical reflection from sociolinguistic perspectives.
AI.method: A structured scholarly dialogue involving five sociolinguists from World Englishes and adjacent fields, organized around five guiding questions that interrogate GenAI's influence on writing practices, language norms, and ethical challenges.
AI.result: The dialogue reveals that GenAI both democratizes writing processes and risks marginalizing minoritized varieties while flattening scholarly nuance. Key themes include linguistic (in)justice, researcher agency, and institutional responsibility. Contributors advocate for equity-informed policies, critical AI literacy, and inclusive co-design in GenAI development.
AI.conclusion: GenAI can either reinforce existing linguistic hierarchies or serve as a site of resistance, depending on how it is designed, governed, and used. Dialogic reflection proves valuable for understanding GenAI's complex role in academic writing and publishing within communities committed to linguistic diversity.

title: A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models
summary: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares five inference-time defence directions against vision-language model jailbreaks across 15 model/layer combinations. Under magnitude-controlled evaluation, no single defence dominates; the image conditioning shift works best on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral, while prompt instructions and attack-specific residuals excel on Qwen variants. Crucially, directions are architecture-specific and non-transferable, and the CMRM refusal direction shows consistent positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift, indicating partially overlapping geometry.
AI.motivation: Jailbreak defences for vision-language models typically subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream, but there is no systematic comparison of which direction works best, whether directions transfer across architectures, or how different defence recipes relate geometrically. The authors aim to fill this gap with a rigorous, magnitude-controlled benchmarking protocol.
AI.method: Five defence candidates are compared across 15 model/layer cells from four architectural families (LLaVA 1.5, Pixtral 12B, Qwen2.5 VL, Qwen2 VL 2B). A magnitude-controlled protocol matches intervention size per prompt and pairs each direction with a random control of identical norm. Candidates include: mean image conditioning shift, CMRM-style refusal direction, ShiftDC-style attack-specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. Geometric analysis (cosine alignment, sign tests) is used to relate text-only and multimodal refusal geometry.
AI.result: No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss stays at the measurement noise floor across all families. Prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL; attack-specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction-specific in 13/15 cells but strongly architecture-specific and non-transferable even between the dimension-compatible LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells (mean 0.35, range 0.17–0.65, 15–25× random baseline, sign test p ≈ 3e−5), indicating partially overlapping geometry between the two recipes.
AI.conclusion: Direction-based jailbreak defences must be calibrated separately for each language decoder family, as no universal direction works across all architectures. The CMRM and image conditioning shift recipes recover partially overlapping geometry, suggesting a shared underlying structure. Practical deployment requires architecture-specific tuning rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.

title: Creative Transformation in Literary Texts: Modelling Change Across Representational Levels
summary: Creativity is often framed as the production of novelty, yet many cultural works emerge through transformation of earlier artifacts and not through isolated invention. Drawing on theories of imitation by Gabriel Tarde and James Mark Baldwin, this paper models creativity as selective transformation across multiple levels of textual representation. We introduce a multi-level framework that compares literary texts across lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative dimensions using directional alignment and control calibrated similarity measures. Applying the model to historically documented literary relationships, we show that different pairs preserve source structure at different representational levels while diverging in others. These transformation profiles provide a quantitative method for characterizing how imitation persists and where creative divergence occurs within literary works.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a multi-level computational framework that quantifies creative transformation in literary texts by measuring directional alignment across lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, and narrative dimensions, revealing how imitation and divergence co-occur at different representational levels.
AI.motivation: To move beyond the conventional framing of creativity as isolated novelty and instead model it as selective transformation of earlier artifacts, operationalizing theories of imitation by Gabriel Tarde and James Mark Baldwin through quantitative, multi-level textual comparison.
AI.method: A multi-level framework that compares literary texts across five representational dimensions (lexical, semantic, conceptual, structural, narrative) using directional alignment and control-calibrated similarity measures, applied to historically documented literary pairs.
AI.result: Different literary pairs exhibit distinct "transformation profiles," preserving source structure at certain representational levels while diverging at others, thereby quantitatively characterizing where imitation persists and where creative divergence occurs.
AI.conclusion: Transformation profiles offer a principled quantitative method for characterizing how creative works selectively inherit and depart from their precursors, supporting a view of creativity as multi-level selective transformation rather than pure novelty generation.

title: IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models
summary: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

AI.tldr: IFHierBench benchmarks LLMs on hierarchical instruction-following with nested constraints across four depth levels. Even the best model barely exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy, revealing a major gap in models' ability to follow layered, scope-specific constraints.
AI.motivation: Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat constraints as a flat, uniform list applied to the entire response. Real-world LLM deployments, however, increasingly require outputs with hierarchical structure — overall artifacts, structural sections, and nested fields — each demanding constraint satisfaction at specific scopes. No prior benchmark evaluates constraint adherence at this granularity.
AI.method: The authors construct IFHierBench, containing 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraint types. Each prompt is paired with a deterministic, scope-aware checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every hierarchical level. Seven leading proprietary and open-weight models are evaluated using this benchmark.
AI.result: The strongest tested model only marginally exceeded 50% prompt-level accuracy. Performance degrades sharply as constraint-tree depth increases, indicating that reliably following nested, scope-specific constraints remains a substantial challenge for current LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs fall short in hierarchical instruction-following, particularly as constraint nesting deepens. This gap motivates future training methods that emphasize constraint adherence at finer granularity to better serve real-world, structured-output applications.

title: DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by ACM Multimedia 2026
summary: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

AI.tldr: DAS-PMVC proposes a partial multi-view clustering framework using dual alignment (anchor graph + contrastive/Hungarian) and structure-enhanced feature learning to handle misaligned views, outperforming SOTA methods.
AI.motivation: Multi-view data often suffers from misalignment across views due to limitations in data collection devices, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). Existing methods struggle with view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, motivating a framework that leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance for robust clustering.
AI.method: DAS-PMVC comprises three components: (1) Anchor graph structure alignment — deriving joint embeddings with consistent latent space from anchor point relationships for initial alignment; (2) Structure-enhanced feature learning — pretraining to capture view structure information, combined with multi-view GCNs to extract deep latent features from aligned graphs; (3) Dual alignment strategy — initial alignment via anchor graphs in pretraining, then contrastive loss plus the Hungarian algorithm during training to refine latent feature alignment.
AI.result: Experiments on various datasets show DAS-PMVC outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, demonstrating its effectiveness and superiority.
AI.conclusion: The DAS-PMVC framework effectively addresses the partial view alignment problem in multi-view clustering through dual alignment and structure enhancement, achieving superior clustering performance compared to existing approaches.

title: AI systems and the reproduction of (standard) language ideologies in World Englishes
summary: The rapid growth of large language models (LLMs) has resurrected age-old questions in sociolinguistics and world Englishes, such as who decides what counts as legitimate English, whose English is suspect etc. This paper examines how AI systems, their uses and discourse on them reflect, reinforce, and occasionally challenge (standard) language ideologies, which privilege Inner Circle norms and marginalize non-dominant Englishes. Drawing on evidence from empirical studies, media commentary, social media debates, and examples from AI outputs, the paper shows that AI technologies reproduce dominant language ideologies at different levels: training data, design protocols, evaluation benchmarks, user feedback and public commentary. The analysis uses the public controversy over AI-sounding language, especially the fixation on the word delve, to illustrate how speakers of English from the Global North police the English language norms of Global South English users. The paper also identifies what Christian Mair has called a "standardisation paradox": AI may homogenize English by privileging standard forms and at the same time pluralize Englishes through exposure to wide-ranging corpora and annotation work carried out by Global South users. In doing so, the paper argues that generative AI is reigniting long-standing debates in World Englishes about standardization, legitimacy, and the ownership of English, now playing out in algorithmic systems, model training, evaluation practices, and public discourse, where non-dominant Englishes are increasingly conflated with AI-generated speech. Discussing AI systems as a site where language ideologies are (re)produced, the paper argues for more inclusive design approaches that recognize the plurality of Englishes in order to address the real-world negative consequences of treating some as more legitimate than others.

AI.tldr: AI systems reproduce standard language ideologies that privilege Inner Circle Englishes while marginalizing non-dominant varieties. The paper uses the "delve" controversy and Christian Mair's "standardisation paradox" to show how generative AI both homogenizes and pluralizes English, arguing for inclusive design that recognizes the plurality of Englishes.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of LLMs has revived longstanding sociolinguistic questions about who defines legitimate English. The author seeks to examine how AI systems, their usage, and surrounding discourse reflect, reinforce, and occasionally challenge standard language ideologies that privilege Inner Circle norms while marginalizing non-dominant World Englishes.
AI.method: The paper employs a qualitative, multi-source analytical approach, drawing evidence from empirical studies, media commentary, social media debates, and AI output examples. It uses the public controversy over "AI-sounding language" (particularly the word "delve") as an illustrative case study, and applies Christian Mair's concept of the "standardisation paradox" as a theoretical lens.
AI.result: AI technologies reproduce dominant language ideologies at multiple levels: training data, design protocols, evaluation benchmarks, user feedback, and public commentary. The "delve" controversy exemplifies how Global North English speakers police Global South English norms. The analysis also identifies a "standardisation paradox": AI simultaneously homogenizes English by privileging standard forms and pluralizes it through exposure to diverse corpora and Global South annotation labor. Non-dominant Englishes are increasingly conflated with AI-generated speech.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI reignites foundational World Englishes debates about standardization, legitimacy, and ownership of English, now unfolding in algorithmic systems and public discourse. The paper argues for more inclusive design approaches that recognize the plurality of Englishes, to address the real-world harms of treating some varieties as more legitimate than others.

title: One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs
summary: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a neuron-level safety alignment framework that identifies and fine-tunes a tiny subset of shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons, ~0.03% of parameters) to defend against compound multilingual+multimodal attacks on LVLMs, outperforming existing methods while preserving model utility.
AI.motivation: As LVLMs deploy globally, malicious actors can combine multilingual instructions with visual information for covert, sophisticated attacks. Existing defenses isolate language and modality safety mechanisms, fail against compound attacks, and suffer from scarce multilingual safety data and high fine-tuning costs.
AI.method: The framework operates in three stages: (1) Identify monolingual/unimodal safety neurons by comparing harmful vs. benign sample responses using activation strength and downstream impact. (2) Intersect unimodal neurons within each language to yield Modality-Shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) bridging visual-textual risk representations. (3) Using English as a semantic anchor, intersect MS-Neurons across languages to obtain Modality- and Language-Shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). Finally, fine-tune only these MLS-Neurons (~0.03% of parameters) to transfer English-only safety supervision to multilingual, multimodal scenarios.
AI.result: The method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.
AI.conclusion: Targeting a minimal shared neuron subset for safety alignment is both highly effective against compound attacks and parameter-efficient, enabling scalable cross-lingual and cross-modal safety transfer without compromising model performance.

title: Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

AI.tldr: Training GNNs on geometrically renormalized (coarse-grained) replicas of large graphs enables zero-shot weight transfer to the original graph, preserving predictive performance while drastically reducing training cost, suggesting structural similarity outweighs network size for transferability.
AI.motivation: GNNs become computationally prohibitive at billion-node scales, requiring expensive distributed training. The authors ask whether a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down version of a graph can be directly deployed on the full-scale graph without retraining, potentially bypassing scalability bottlenecks.
AI.method: The authors propose a zero-shot transfer protocol using geometric renormalization (GR), a coarse-graining technique rooted in hyperbolic geometry that preserves the structural self-similarity of graphs. A GNN is trained on the GR-reduced replica, and the learned weights are directly transferred to the original, full-resolution graph for inference without any fine-tuning.
AI.result: Across synthetic and real-world networks, GNNs trained on GR-scaled replicas retain most of the predictive performance of models trained on the original graph, while substantially reducing training time and memory. Learned embeddings and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales, indicating structural fidelity of GR coarse-graining.
AI.conclusion: Structural similarity, rather than graph size, governs GNN transferability. The findings motivate the development of scale-equivariant graph architectures that can naturally operate across multiple resolutions, leveraging geometric renormalization as a principled scaling mechanism.

title: Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training
summary: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories.
