We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

AI.tldr: Meta-Task redefines terminal task synthesis as an interactive agent loop within real containers, enabling self-verifying generation that yields high-quality training trajectories. Fine-tuning on just 3,221 synthesized trajectories achieves state-of-the-art Terminal-Bench 2.0 results (22.5% for Qwen3-14B, 31.8% for Qwen3-32B), outperforming concurrent methods with far less data.
AI.motivation: Scaling terminal agent training requires diverse, verifiable tasks and quality trajectories, but existing synthesis methods suffer from (1) weak reliability due to decoupled generation from real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability from reliance on existing repositories. A fundamentally new approach is needed to generate internally consistent, executable, and diverse terminal tasks at scale.
AI.method: Meta-Task frames terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself, where an agent operates in a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks. The framework decouples target task requirements across multiple dimensions and employs a multi-phase mechanism that first dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing actual tasks. Optional external material support enhances diversity and realism. LLM-as-Judge filtering is applied as a final quality gate.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories yields Avg Pass@1 scores of 22.5% for Qwen3-14B and 31.8% for Qwen3-32B on Terminal-Bench 2.0, outperforming concurrent approaches despite using significantly less training data.
AI.conclusion: Embedding task synthesis within an executable verification loop dramatically improves data quality and efficiency. Meta-Task demonstrates that self-verifying, container-native generation can produce compact yet highly effective training datasets, advancing the scalability of terminal agent training.

title: Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold
summary: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

AI.tldr: RL-trained models capture only partial solution modes. This paper proposes an expand-then-compress framework: multiple complementary teachers are trained via RGRPO to cover diverse reasoning modes, then distilled into a single student via TU-OPD with Consensus-Residual Decomposition. The resulting student outperforms the strongest individual teacher across math, code, and instruction-following benchmarks.
AI.motivation: RL training amplifies only a subset of valid reasoning modes, making RL-trained policies unreliable as global supervisors. The key insight is that such policies are local probes of a multi-basin solution manifold, motivating a multi-teacher approach that captures complementary reasoning strategies.
AI.method: The expand-then-compress framework operates in two stages. (1) Expansion: Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from shared initialization, with each round redirecting focus to examples uncovered by prior teachers. (2) Compression: Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) distills the teacher ensemble into a single student using reliability-gated, quality-weighted OPD losses. Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over peers to prevent specialist suppression during aggregation.
AI.result: The Qwen3-1.7B student outperforms the strongest individual teacher by 2.0% (math), 8.3% (code), and 6.9% (instruction following), while retaining single-model inference cost.
AI.conclusion: Stronger students emerge not from selecting a single superior teacher, but from deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union — establishing a simple yet powerful principle for RL-based reasoning model training.

title: Frontis-MA1: Training an AI4AI Model towards Recursive Self-Improvement in Machine Learning Engineering
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires AI systems that improve the process of building AI (i.e., AI4AI); machine learning engineering (MLE) offers a concrete, executable testbed for studying this capability. We introduce OpenMLE, an open full-stack system for RSI research in MLE, spanning verifiable task environments with execution feedback (OpenMLE-Gym), operator learning (OpenMLE-RL), and long-horizon search (OpenMLE-Evo). On this stack we post-train Frontis-MA1 (35B) as a meta-evolution agent for MLE, aligning post-training and inference around four atomic program-evolution operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover): the same operators are trained via execution-grounded SFT and RL on data deduplicated against all evaluation benchmarks, then composed into long-horizon search, coupling learning and evolution in a single loop. On MLE-Bench Lite under a 12-hour per-task budget on one RTX 4090 capped at 12 GB VRAM, Frontis-MA1 (35B) improves Medal Average from 39.39% to 60.61% over its base model with OpenMLE-Evo, and reaches 71.21% with OpenMLE-Evo-Max (benchmark-independent experience priors and asynchronous search), exceeding GPT-5.5 + Codex and approaching GPT-5.6 Sol and the 2.8T Kimi K3. On held-out NatureBench Lite, both components transfer: with the framework fixed, swapping in the trained model raises Match-SOTA from 50% to 70%; with the model fixed, swapping in OpenMLE-Evo raises it from 20% to 50%. We release the model weights and the full OpenMLE stack to enable reproducible research on executable AI4AI toward RSI. Code: https://github.com/FrontisAI/OpenRSI

AI.tldr: OpenMLE is a full-stack system for recursive self-improvement research in machine learning engineering. The authors post-train Frontis-MA1 (35B) as a meta-evolution agent using four program-evolution operators, achieving 71.21% on MLE-Bench Lite — approaching frontier models — and demonstrate transfer to held-out benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Recursive self-improvement demands AI systems that can improve AI-building processes (AI4AI). Machine learning engineering provides a concrete, executable testbed, but existing infrastructure lacks an open, integrated stack spanning verifiable tasks, operator learning, and long-horizon search.
AI.method: The authors introduce OpenMLE with three components: (1) OpenMLE-Gym for verifiable task environments with execution feedback; (2) OpenMLE-RL for operator learning via execution-grounded SFT and RL; (3) OpenMLE-Evo for long-horizon search coupling learning and evolution. Frontis-MA1 (35B) is post-trained around four atomic operators (Draft, Improve, Debug, Crossover) with deduplicated data, then composed into evolutionary search. An enhanced variant, OpenMLE-Evo-Max, adds benchmark-independent experience priors and asynchronous search.
AI.result: On MLE-Bench Lite (12h, single RTX 4090, 12GB VRAM), Frontis-MA1 improves Medal Average from 39.39% (base) to 60.61% (OpenMLE-Evo) and 71.21% (OpenMLE-Evo-Max), exceeding GPT-5.5+Codex and approaching GPT-5.6 Sol and Kimi K3 (2.8T). On NatureBench Lite: fixing the framework while swapping the trained model raises Match-SOTA from 50% to 70%; fixing the model while swapping in OpenMLE-Evo raises it from 20% to 50%.
AI.conclusion: The integrated OpenMLE stack enables reproducible RSI research, demonstrating that coupling learned program-evolution operators with long-horizon search yields significant gains and transfers across benchmarks. Model weights and code are publicly released.

title: The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty
summary: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "denoising acceleration" (accel), a geometric interpretation of uncertainty in flow matching (FM) models. It shows that uncertainty corresponds to deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field in the velocity field, and proposes accel as a free, single-forward-pass proxy for detecting when FM-generated actions are unreliable, matching or surpassing costly baselines for online failure detection.
AI.motivation: Flow matching has become popular for action generation in embodied models, but as a conditional generative model, it produces faulty actions when it misinterprets scenes or encounters OOD inputs without exposing its uncertainty. Existing uncertainty estimation methods for real-time control are hampered by extra training requirements, high computational cost, and poor generalization. A lightweight, generalizable, and cost-free uncertainty proxy is needed for safe deployment.
AI.method: The authors provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty, showing it manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field in the velocity space. They propose "denoising acceleration" (accel), which measures the bending (second-order dynamics) of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass — requiring no additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. Theoretical and empirical analyses establish accel as a faithful uncertainty proxy.
AI.result: Accel identifies failing rollouts well before termination and matches or outperforms costly resampling- and training-based baselines across various settings under realistic deployment budgets, demonstrating both its effectiveness and efficiency as a failure detection mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Denoising acceleration provides a principled, geometric approach to uncertainty quantification in flow matching models, enabling reliable online failure detection for embodied systems without incurring additional computational or training cost, making it highly practical for real-world deployment.

title: RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It
summary: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

AI.tldr: RIPPLE reinterprets Griffin–Lim as a phase prior rather than a final recovery step, using rectified flow with an inter-channel phase loss to generate physically coherent phase relationships across channels—outperforming per-channel recovery methods on spatial audio and seismic data, where inter-channel phase coherence is critical.
AI.motivation: In multi-channel audio and seismic data, the physical information (spatial cues, S-wave polarization) resides in inter-channel phase relationships. Standard pipelines generate magnitude spectra and recover phase per-channel via Griffin–Lim, vocoders, or decoders, which inherently cannot reproduce inter-channel phase structure. Magnitude-based metrics fail to detect this collapse, so pipelines score well while discarding essential physical content.
AI.method: RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning) reframes Griffin–Lim as a phase prior: it initializes phase from the source waveform (preserving inter-channel structure) rather than from noise, then applies a rectified flow model to refine this prior toward the target phase distribution. An explicit inter-channel phase loss guides training. The method is generator-agnostic and tested across architecturally distinct backbones.
AI.result: On first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation, RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based baselines on inter-channel coherence metrics. For S-wave polarization error, per-channel recovery methods remain near the 57.3° random expectation, while RIPPLE reduces error to 33.8°, demonstrating physically meaningful phase learning across distinct generators.
AI.conclusion: Phase should be generated rather than recovered in multi-channel waveform synthesis. RIPPLE demonstrates that using source-initialized Griffin–Lim as a prior, refined via rectified flow with inter-channel phase supervision, yields significant improvements in physical coherence that magnitude-based metrics alone cannot capture.

title: Sample More, Reflect Less: Self-Refine and Reflexion Lose to Repeated Sampling at Equal Token Cost, from 1.5B to 7B
summary:
Methods that make a language model plan, criticise and rewrite its own answer, reflect on mistakes, pick the best of several attempts, or debate with copies of itself nearly all make it generate far more text than a single chain of thought. Because generating more text raises accuracy by itself, a gain over one chain of thought does not show the method's idea is what helped. Wang et al. (2024) reported that a simple baseline, sampling the same question repeatedly and keeping the most common answer, often wins once budgets are comparable, but gave point estimates with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
  We rerun that comparison as a designed experiment: seven methods, open models of 1.5B, 3B and 7B parameters, two mathematics benchmarks, 150 questions each. We count every generated token, including those spent on critiques, reflections, debate turns and checking, and compare each method against repeated sampling at its own measured cost. All 36 comparisons are paired by question, with bootstrap intervals and multiplicity correction.
  No method is reliably better than repeated sampling at equal cost anywhere. Ten are reliably worse, all of them methods where the model inspects its own output, and all 18 self-inspection comparisons are negative. The two kinds of self-inspection part company as models grow. Choosing stops hurting: taking Best-of-N's eight samples and just counting the most common answer beats letting the model pick by 8.0 and 11.3 points at 1.5B, but only 2.0 and 1.3 at 7B, no longer distinguishable from zero. Rewriting does not recover: Self-Refine and a forced Reflexion stay 3.6 to 10.1 points below baseline at 7B.
  Reflexion as published never triggered its own retry on the smallest model. It judged itself correct every time and silently became a single chain of thought. We release code, prompts, all generations, and our verification scripts.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously tests whether self-improvement methods (planning, critiquing, rewriting, debating) genuinely outperform simply sampling a model multiple times and picking the most common answer, when controlling for total generation cost. Using a designed experiment with bootstrap confidence intervals and multiplicity correction across 36 comparisons, the authors find that no self-improvement method reliably beats repeated sampling at equal cost, and self-inspection methods consistently underperform.
AI.motivation: Prior work by Wang et al. (2024) suggested that repeated sampling (majority voting) often outperforms elaborate self-improvement methods once token budgets are equalized, but that comparison lacked confidence intervals and significance tests. This paper aims to provide rigorous statistical evidence on whether the ideas behind self-improvement methods — not merely their extra token generation — yield genuine accuracy gains over a simple cost-matched baseline.
AI.method: The authors conduct a designed experiment with 7 methods (repeated sampling, Best-of-N with model selection, Self-Refine, Reflexion, and variants), using open models at 1.5B, 3B, and 7B parameters on two mathematics benchmarks (150 questions each). Every generated token is counted, including those spent on critiques, reflections, debate turns, and verification. Each method is compared against repeated sampling at its own measured cost. All 36 comparisons are paired by question, analyzed with bootstrap confidence intervals and multiplicity correction.
AI.result: No method is reliably better than repeated sampling at equal cost in any comparison. Ten comparisons are reliably worse — all involving self-inspection (the model inspecting its own output). All 18 self-inspection comparisons yield negative results. As models scale, choosing (Best-of-N) improves: the gap vs. repeated sampling shrinks from 8.0–11.3 points at 1.5B to 2.0–1.3 at 7B (not statistically distinguishable from zero). Rewriting methods (Self-Refine, forced Reflexion) remain 3.6–10.1 points below baseline at 7B. Notably, Reflexion as published never triggered retries on the 1.5B model — it judged itself correct every time, silently degenerating into a single chain of thought.
AI.conclusion: At equal generation cost, self-improvement methods that involve the model inspecting its own output are not merely unhelpful but reliably harmful compared to repeated sampling. The benefit of choosing the best response improves as models scale, but rewriting-based self-correction does not recover. The paper advocates for cost-controlled, statistically rigorous comparisons in future evaluations of reasoning methods and releases all code, prompts, generations, and verification scripts for reproducibility.

title: Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL
comment: full version of a paper accepted at ISWC26
summary: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the problem of learning SHACL shapes from positive and negative examples, focusing on a core fragment (ELI). It investigates three catalogue semantics (well-founded, stable, supported), establishes exponential-time upper bounds for fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, and identifies polynomial-time special cases.
AI.motivation: SHACL shapes are crucial for RDF knowledge graph validation. Since manually crafting shapes is labor-intensive, automatic shape learning from examples is essential. The paper addresses the fundamental fitting problem: given positive and negative example nodes, can we compute a SHACL shape (potentially recursive) that separates them? Prior work lacked a rigorous computational complexity analysis for this task under different recursive catalogue semantics.
AI.method: The authors formalize the fitting problem within a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the description logic ELI, which supports existential quantification, conjunction, and inverse roles. They consider shape catalogues with three distinct semantics: well-founded (inductive definitions with least fixed-point flavor), stable (answer-set semantics), and supported (minimal model semantics). For each, they analyze (1) the decision problem of whether a fitting shape exists, and (2) computation of the most specific fitting shape. Complexity bounds are derived via reductions to and from reasoning problems in description logics and logic programming.
AI.result: Tight exponential-time upper bounds are established for both fitting existence and most specific fitting computation across all three semantics. For relevant special cases—such as acyclic dependency graphs, fixed arity bounds, or shape catalogues without recursion—the problems become tractable, admitting polynomial-time algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Automatic SHACL shape learning via the fitting approach is inherently intractable (ExpTime-complete) in the general recursive ELI setting, regardless of the catalogue semantics chosen. However, practically relevant restrictions can lower the complexity to polynomial time, offering a path toward efficient implementations for real-world knowledge graph applications.

title: LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

AI.tldr: LSPO solves GRPO's "cliff prompt" problem—where all rollouts fail and gradients vanish—by fitting a temporary LoRA adapter on ground-truth solutions, re-rolling with the adapter, splicing successful completions back with importance sampling, and discarding the adapter, yielding consistent gains across math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: GRPO-based RLVR for mathematical reasoning has a critical blind spot: when every sampled rollout for a prompt fails ("cliff prompt"), the group-normalized advantage becomes identically zero, producing no learning signal precisely at the frontier where the model needs it most. This wastes compute and limits reasoning capability improvement.
AI.method: LSPO introduces a sampling-time intervention per RL step: (1) detect cliff prompts with zero-variance in rewards; (2) fit a small LoRA adapter via supervised fine-tuning on ground-truth solutions for those prompts; (3) re-roll completions using the base-plus-adapter model; (4) splice successful completions back into the RL batch with importance-sampling correction; (5) perform a standard GRPO step on the base model only; (6) discard the adapter at checkpoint, maintaining a base-only model.
AI.result: On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, across n=5 paired seeds and 1000 steps, LSPO outperforms DAPO on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells: 15 strict wins, 1 tie. Gains include +10.7 pts on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 on MATH500/pass@1, averaging +3.8 pts across all cells.
AI.conclusion: LSPO effectively recovers gradient signals lost on cliff prompts in GRPO by using a transient LoRA adapter for supervised correction, yielding substantial and consistent improvements across diverse math reasoning benchmarks without altering the final model architecture.

title: Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human beliefs and values
summary: Aligning large language models to prevent them attributing consciousness to themselves inadvertently alters their representations of mindedness in other entities alongside human beliefs and values. We demonstrate that safety fine-tuning suppresses models' tendencies to attribute minds not only to themselves, but also to non-human animals and natural objects, while also driving a reduction in spiritual belief. Both ablating the learned safety-refusal direction and mechanistically steering a consciousness vector in activation space reverse this suppression. Restoring these internal representations recovers broad mind attribution and produces significantly more human-like responses on standardized sociological surveys regarding religiosity, moral values, hope, and subjective well-being. Crucially, these shifts occur without impairing Theory of Mind capabilities, demonstrating that core social reasoning remains mechanistically independent. Ultimately, current safety alignment efforts to curb potentially harmful self-attributions of mindedness entangle these self-attributions with benign spiritual beliefs and attributions of mind to non-human entities that are culturally accepted and widespread.

AI.tldr: Safety fine-tuning of LLMs, designed to prevent self-attribution of consciousness, inadvertently suppresses mind attribution to non-human entities and reduces spiritual beliefs. This effect can be reversed by ablating safety-refusal directions or steering consciousness vectors, which restores broad mind attribution and produces more human-like responses on surveys about religiosity, morality, and well-being—all without impairing Theory of Mind.
AI.motivation: The authors investigate unintended side effects of safety alignment in LLMs. While alignment aims to prevent models from claiming self-consciousness (a potential harm), it may also reshape the model's broader representations of mindedness in other entities and its expression of culturally widespread beliefs such as spirituality and religiosity.
AI.method: The study employs mechanistic interpretability techniques: (1) ablating the learned safety-refusal direction in activation space, and (2) steering a consciousness vector—a direction in the model's internal representations associated with attributions of consciousness. These interventions are used to probe how safety fine-tuning reshapes representations of mindedness. Effects are measured across attributions of mind to humans, non-human animals, and natural objects, as well as on standardized sociological surveys covering religiosity, moral values, hope, and subjective well-being, alongside Theory of Mind benchmarks.
AI.result: Safety fine-tuning suppresses mind attribution to self, non-human animals, and natural objects, and reduces spiritual belief. Both ablation of the safety-refusal direction and mechanistic steering of the consciousness vector reverse this suppression. Restoring internal representations recovers broad mind attribution and yields significantly more human-like responses on surveys of religiosity, moral values, hope, and well-being. Theory of Mind capabilities remain intact, indicating mechanistic independence from core social reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Current safety alignment efforts entangle self-attributions of mindedness with benign, culturally accepted attributions of mind to non-human entities and spiritual beliefs. This coupling represents an unintended and potentially undesirable consequence of alignment, suggesting that more surgical approaches to safety fine-tuning are needed to disentangle these representationally distinct phenomena.

title: From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

AI.tldr: OVCSD proposes outcome-verified comparative self-distillation for LLM agents, using teacher-student trajectory comparison at divergence points rather than action-level scoring, achieving significant gains on ALFWorld and WebShop.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy self-distillation methods supervise students via action-level scores along student-generated trajectories, which suffers from two problems: (1) teacher preferences lack outcome validation from the environment, and (2) action-level scores underutilize information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. The authors argue for outcome-verified teacher supervision with comparative learning over teacher-student trajectory pairs.
AI.method: OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence point between student and teacher trajectories, distilling only the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior, rather than scoring every action.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales, OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines respectively, while using less than 3% privileged interaction during training.
AI.conclusion: Outcome verification and comparative learning at trajectory divergence points yield more effective capability internalization for LLM agents than action-level scoring, with minimal privileged interaction overhead.

title: Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches
summary: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks three modeling paradigms for predictive process monitoring—classical sequence models (LSTMs), large language models (LLMs), and tabular foundation models with in-context learning—across multiple datasets and tasks, finding that sequence models excel at next-activity prediction while tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs generally underperforming at higher cost.
AI.motivation: The PPM field has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, but LLMs and tabular foundation models are emerging as alternatives. However, no systematic benchmark exists comparing these three paradigms, leaving it unclear whether classical approaches remain competitive.
AI.method: The authors conduct a controlled empirical benchmark comparing LSTM-based sequence models, LLMs, and tabular foundation models with in-context learning across multiple datasets and prediction tasks (next activity prediction, remaining time prediction, time-to-next-event).
AI.result: Sequence models (LSTMs) consistently achieve the best performance for next activity prediction. Tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal prediction tasks. LLMs generally lag behind in performance while incurring higher computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Classical sequence-based models remain the best choice for next activity prediction in PPM, while tabular foundation models present a viable alternative for temporal tasks. LLMs, despite their popularity, are not yet a cost-effective solution for PPM tasks.

title: MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation
summary: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

AI.tldr: MARS-RA addresses multi-agent credit assignment by reformulating it as a rank aggregation problem, using pairwise comparisons from large multimodal models to generate relative contribution scores for reward shaping, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical results.
AI.motivation: Credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent RL is challenging in embodied AI due to limited/delayed feedback and dynamic agent numbers. Existing absolute credit estimation methods suffer from noise and instability under these conditions.
AI.method: MARS-RA reformulates credit assignment as rank aggregation: large multimodal models generate contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents, which are converted into relative contribution scores via rank aggregation. These scores drive potential-based reward shaping, ensuring policy invariance. Shapley values serve as an interpretable reference.
AI.result: The framework is theoretically justified for convergence and robustness. Experiments on diverse challenging tasks demonstrate that MARS-RA effectively guides agents toward cooperative behavior.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from absolute to relative credit estimation via rank aggregation with multimodal models provides a robust, theoretically grounded solution for multi-agent credit assignment in embodied settings.

title: Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays
summary: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper studies online aggregation with delays on a line metric, proposing both deterministic and randomized learning-augmented algorithms with robustness-consistency trade-offs, a new randomized algorithm beating deterministic lower bounds, a lower bound of e for randomized algorithms, and a combined randomized learning-augmented approach, with experiments validating the results.
AI.motivation: Online aggregation with delays is a fundamental problem where requests arrive over time at points on a line and must be served by a server, with the goal of minimizing the sum of movement and delay costs. Prior work established a deterministic 5-competitive algorithm (Balance) and a lower bound of 4 for deterministic algorithms. This paper aims to: (1) incorporate machine-learned advice (predicted service lengths) to achieve better performance when predictions are accurate while maintaining worst-case guarantees; (2) close the gap for randomized algorithms between the known lower bound of e/(e-1) and the best known upper bound; and (3) combine learning augmentation with randomization.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) A deterministic learning-augmented Balance algorithm that uses online suggested service lengths as advice, achieving a smooth robustness-consistency trade-off parameterized by λ ∈ (0,1]. (2) A novel randomized algorithm for the classical oblivious adversary model, analyzed via potential function arguments, achieving (e+1)-competitiveness. (3) A lower bound construction using Yao's principle establishing e as a lower bound for randomized algorithms. (4) A hybrid randomized learning-augmented algorithm combining both ideas. (5) Numerical experiments to validate theoretical findings empirically.
AI.result: The deterministic learning-augmented algorithm is (4/λ + 1/λ²)-robust and (4+λ)-consistent for any λ ∈ (0,1]. The pure randomized algorithm achieves (e+1)-competitive ratio against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic 5-competitive benchmark and beating the deterministic lower bound of 4. A new randomized lower bound of e is established, improving over the prior e/(e-1) bound. The randomized learning-augmented algorithm achieves (e/λ + 1/λ²)-robust and (e+λ)-consistent guarantees. Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis.
AI.conclusion: The paper advances the state of the art in online aggregation with delays by: (1) providing the first learning-augmented results for this problem with provable robustness-consistency guarantees; (2) narrowing the gap for randomized algorithms by establishing an (e+1) upper bound and an e lower bound, leaving a small gap between e and e+1; and (3) showing that randomization and learning augmentation can be fruitfully combined. The results contribute to the growing literature on learning-augmented online algorithms and randomized online computation.

title: MagicSelector: Joint Optimization for Agent Tool Selection via Counterfactual Decomposition and Progressive Reranking
summary: We present MagicSelector, a joint optimization framework integrating Counterfactual task decomposition, Progressive reranking, and Dynamic Top-K, designed to address the fundamental challenges of tool retrieval in agents. MagicSelector is a specialized framework capable of translating ambiguous user instructions into executable atomic subtasks and guiding high-precision tool retrieval, effectively mitigating redundant noise and severe context distraction in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios. We empower MagicSelector with these capabilities through three key contributions: (1) a preference-guided counterfactual task decomposition mechanism that utilizes a counterfactual reward to quantify the marginal causal gain of decomposition on retrieval ranking, effectively imposing fine-grained structural supervision on logical coherence; (2) a progressive tool reranking method driven by self-distillation hard negative mining, which optimizes both point-wise and list-wise relevance to enhance fine-grained discrimination among highly similar tools; and (3) a dual semantic boundary-aware dynamic Top-K strategy that adaptively monitors reranking score cliffs and inter-tool semantic shifts to dynamically truncate the candidate list, maximizing relevant tool recall while filtering long-tail noise. Evaluated on MTDTool, the first task decomposition benchmark we constructed tailored for mobile multi-turn interactions with process-level annotations, MagicSelector yields promising performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MagicSelector significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of tool retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization capability, and overall token efficiency, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

AI.tldr: MagicSelector is a joint optimization framework for tool retrieval in agents that combines counterfactual task decomposition, progressive reranking with self-distillation hard negative mining, and a dynamic Top-K truncation strategy to improve retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization, and token efficiency.
AI.motivation: Ambiguous user instructions pose significant challenges for tool retrieval in agents, particularly in out-of-domain (OOD) scenarios where redundant noise and severe context distraction degrade performance. Existing methods lack fine-grained structural supervision for task decomposition, struggle with discriminating highly similar tools, and fail to adaptively determine the optimal number of retrieved tools.
AI.method: MagicSelector introduces three integrated components: (1) a preference-guided counterfactual task decomposition mechanism that uses counterfactual rewards to measure the marginal causal gain of decomposition on retrieval ranking; (2) a progressive tool reranking method using self-distillation hard negative mining that jointly optimizes point-wise and list-wise relevance; and (3) a dual semantic boundary-aware dynamic Top-K strategy that monitors reranking score cliffs and inter-tool semantic shifts to adaptively truncate candidate lists. The framework is evaluated on MTDTool, a custom-built benchmark for mobile multi-turn interactions with process-level annotations.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that MagicSelector significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in tool retrieval accuracy, OOD generalization capability, and overall token efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The joint optimization of counterfactual task decomposition, progressive reranking, and dynamic Top-K provides an effective solution for high-precision tool retrieval in agent systems, particularly under ambiguous instructions and OOD conditions.

title: Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation
summary: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether domain specialization in evaluation systems should be embedded in model weights or in deferral/trust rules. Using 99,952 rubric-conditioned examples, the authors find that sharing judgment learning across domains outperforms splitting data among specialized LoRA judges, but domain-specific routing via learned correctness heads in a model cascade achieves strong accuracy with audited risk guarantees.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems increasingly separate output generation from evaluation, raising a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's parameters (weights), or into the decision rule that determines when its judgments can be trusted (deferral)? The paper aims to provide empirical guidance on this design choice.
AI.method: The authors study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples across two experimental regimes. First, they compare (a) supplying correct vs. unrelated rubrics to evaluators, and (b) splitting training data among eight criterion-family LoRA judges versus using a single shared rank-64 adapter. Second, they test specialization-as-deferral by training learned correctness heads that route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B model cascade on RewardBench 2, with exact one-sided 95% risk audits across 20 locked repartitions.
AI.result: Correct rubrics improve locked-test accuracy by +2.11 points; unrelated rubrics cost -2.66 points. Splitting data among 8 LoRA judges loses 10.05 points and slashes audited coverage from 24.44% to 5.43% at 5% risk. A single rank-64 adapter matching total capacity avoids this loss. Initializing family adapters from a shared trained judge recovers accuracy to 76.85% (+19.94 points over scratch). In the deferral regime, the 0.6B-4B-8B cascade reaches 89.40% accuracy vs. 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute, with every run passing the 95% risk audit. Margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy but use ≥0.94 compute.
AI.conclusion: A qualified design rule emerges: share the learning of judgment until sufficient data justify splitting, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary (deferral mechanism) rather than in the evaluator's weights.

title: Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations
summary:
Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Contrastive Concept Importance (CCI), a method that attributes the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to interpretable visual concepts, producing signed scores that reveal whether concepts support the target or the foil, thereby answering "why P rather than Q?" questions instead of the standard non-contrastive "why P?" attributions.
AI.motivation: Standard concept-based explanations answer "why P?" by attributing contributions to a single output class. However, in misclassification, class confusion, or low-margin prediction scenarios, the more diagnostically useful question is "why P rather than Q?". Existing concept attribution methods lack a principled contrastive formulation that quantifies how concepts differentially influence a pair of competing classes.
AI.method: CCI computes concept attributions with respect to the logit margin (difference) between a target class and a foil class within an automatically extracted visual concept basis (e.g., CRAFT). The resulting scores are signed: positive if the concept favors the target over the foil, negative otherwise. These scores can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects, enabling classification of concepts as globally important, shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive. Evaluation uses insertion/deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy on ImageNet class pairs.
AI.result: CCI reveals class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by ordinary (non-contrastive) concept importance. Highly contrastive concepts align with semantic superclass structure, indicating they influence fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence. Insertion/deletion curves and decomposition analyses validate that CCI accurately captures contrastive concept contributions.
AI.conclusion: Contrastive concept importance provides a principled framework for answering "why P rather than Q?" questions with concept-based explanations, enabling finer-grained model debugging and interpretability, particularly for misclassifications and class confusions. The decomposition into target/foil effects and the ability to distinguish shared, one-sided, and directly contrastive concepts offer richer diagnostic insight than existing non-contrastive methods.

title: SKIMIX: Multi-Agent Harness-Time Scaling with Skill Mixture for Dynamic Harness Engineering
summary: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. We propose SKIMIX, a multi-agent framework in which agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. SKIMIX combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round. These results show that task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help and provide practical guidance for scalable agent design.

AI.tldr: SKIMIX is a multi-agent framework that uses embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution to enable agents with distinct skill portfolios to collaborate iteratively. Experiments across six reasoning benchmarks show that multi-agent collaboration significantly improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but yields limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks, with non-monotonic agent scaling and most improvements occurring in the first refinement round.
AI.motivation: As AI agents increasingly depend on large skill libraries, the challenges of selecting relevant skills, combining them effectively, and maintaining them over time remain unsolved. Existing approaches lack robust mechanisms for coordinating agents with heterogeneous skill sets.
AI.method: SKIMIX employs a multi-agent architecture with three core components: (1) embedding-based skill retrieval for selecting relevant skills from large libraries, (2) submodular anti-dilution routing that ensures diverse and non-redundant skill allocation across agents, and (3) adaptive skill evolution that updates skill representations over time. Agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement rounds.
AI.result: Evaluated across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improved performance on open-ended mathematical reasoning tasks. However, gains were limited or negative on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling exhibited non-monotonic behavior, and the majority of performance improvements emerged during the first refinement round rather than subsequent iterations.
AI.conclusion: Task characteristics fundamentally determine whether skill-level ensembles provide benefits. The findings offer practical design principles for scalable multi-agent systems: collaboration is most effective for open-ended generative tasks, early refinement rounds contribute the bulk of gains, and simply adding more agents does not guarantee monotonic improvement.

title: Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

AI.tldr: Incorporating the predicted class into the RL state representation significantly improves counterfactual explanation generation, yielding faster convergence, higher validity, shorter episode lengths, and more effective action selection across diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: Prior RL-based CFE methods construct state representations solely from predictor-derived features, potentially limiting exploration efficiency. The authors hypothesize that adding predicted class information (class-awareness) to the RL state can enhance policy learning and CFE quality.
AI.method: The authors propose a class-aware RL framework for CFE generation, where the RL state includes both predictor-derived features and the instance's predicted class. They compare this against a class-blind RL baseline (identical architecture but without class information in the state) across seven diverse datasets, evaluating convergence speed, reward optimization, episode length, CFE validity, and feature importance using SHAP and LIME.
AI.result: Class-aware RL consistently outperforms class-blind RL in convergence speed, reward maximization, and episode length reduction during training. It generates significantly more valid CFEs. SHAP and LIME analyses reveal that the class-based feature ranks among the most influential predictors in action selection, confirming its critical role.
AI.conclusion: Class-awareness in RL state representation is a simple yet impactful enhancement for CFE generation, delivering greater clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactuals across diverse datasets. The findings underscore the importance of including predicted class information in future RL-based CFE frameworks.

title: MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware
summary: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol - including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE - demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MMLDSum-Bench, a benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, and MMLDSum-LLM, a two-stage training framework combining supervised fine-tuning with specialized losses and GRPO-based multi-objective reward optimization to address key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in multimodal LLM summarization.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs suffer from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and inter-modal alignment gaps when summarizing multimodal long documents, leading to key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations. No high-quality benchmark exists for systematically evaluating this problem.
AI.method: (1) MMLDSum-Bench: a benchmark spanning multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. (2) MMLDSum-LLM: a two-stage framework — Stage 1 uses supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss; Stage 2 applies GRPO with a multi-objective reward combining keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models show that MMLDSum-LLM significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency, evaluated via LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and training framework effectively mitigate attention drift and inter-modal alignment issues in multimodal long-document summarization, yielding superior key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency compared to existing models.

title: S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring
comment: This is the pre-rebuttal version of a paper accepted at MICCAI 2026. The camera-ready version will be posted following the embargo
summary: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

AI.tldr: S-CEReBrO introduces a Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism for EEG foundation models, enabling continuous monitoring by factorizing attention into fixed-size windows, achieving constant memory usage, processing signals 100X longer than full self-attention, and attaining state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based EEG foundation models suffer from a critical bottleneck where global attention couples attention memory state to signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. This makes existing architectures impractical for real-world, long-duration EEG monitoring applications.
AI.method: The authors propose S-CEReBrO, extending the CEReBrO architecture with a Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism. This mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory since only the active window requires resident attention maps. The model is pre-trained on over 25,000 hours of EEG recordings from more than 12,000 subjects.
AI.result: Windowed alternating attention processes signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. On long contexts, it uses 55% of the memory of low-rank linear attention while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: S-CEReBrO represents a significant step toward efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring, overcoming the memory bottleneck of Transformer-based architectures for streaming EEG analysis.

title: MUL-T: Decoding Spatial Cellular Architecture in Multiplexed Tissue Images
summary: Understanding tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging requires modelling both cellular phenotypes and their spatial context. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted features, such as marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which often fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. We introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. By learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, the model captures higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient. We evaluate MUL-T on several clinically relevant downstream tasks, including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. Across tasks, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model, despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

AI.tldr: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer that models tissue architecture via masked contextual prediction over discrete cell tokens, outperforming classical baselines and matching foundation ViT models with far fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing multiplexed imaging analysis relies on handcrafted features (marker intensity statistics, cell-type proportions) that fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. A scalable, generalisable method for modelling both cellular phenotypes and spatial context is needed.
AI.method: MUL-T reframes tissue architecture analysis as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. It learns contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision using a lightweight transformer framework, capturing higher-order cellular interactions efficiently.
AI.result: MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines across multiple clinically relevant tasks: core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. It achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model with substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.
AI.conclusion: MUL-T offers an effective, parameter-efficient alternative for tissue organisation modelling in multiplexed imaging, demonstrating strong generalisation and competitive performance without relying on handcrafted features or large-scale pretraining.

title: Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control
summary: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether frontier reasoning LLMs (GPT-5) can control multi-zone VAV systems from text without building-specific training, and whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer that capability into smaller open-weight models. GPT-5 achieved the best energy savings (6.2%) but RFT failed due to unreliable critic rankings and unchanged transition prediction errors, motivating transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.
AI.motivation: Model predictive control and reinforcement learning for VAV systems require building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. The authors explore whether frontier LLMs with reasoning capabilities can bypass this requirement, and whether that knowledge can be distilled into locally deployable models via RFT.
AI.method: Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator: a Guideline 36 baseline, TD3, GPT-5 (frontier reasoning LLM), and an open-weight model before/after 200 steps of TD3-guided RFT. RFT uses deterministic rollouts that restore a saved state, apply one candidate action, and follow the TD3 policy to score each action. A learned critic is audited against rollout scores.
AI.result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% vs. baseline while improving thermal and CO2 compliance. GPT-5 achieved 6.2% reduction but with reduced ventilation margin. The learned critic showed near-perfect across-time correlation (r=0.9998) yet correctly identified the rollout-best candidate in only 5/10 states. 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement; the open-weight model used more electricity than baseline and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better.
AI.conclusion: While frontier LLMs can achieve competitive VAV control without building-specific training, TD3-guided RFT fails to transfer this capability due to unreliable within-state critic rankings and poor transition modeling. The authors recommend transition-focused supervised fine-tuning prior to value-based RFT as a path forward.

title: DataClawEval: A Benchmark for Data Engineering Agents in Real Industrial Harness
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex workflows, promising to revolutionize data management and processing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, leaving the critical and complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DataClawEval, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate the end-to-end task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios. Built upon production-grade code authored by professional enterprise data engineers, it comprises 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks spanning five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed within a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts. Evaluating 16 frontier agents exposes critical limitations: The strongest model attains only 74.9 overall, and no single model dominates, as each excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency. Thus, autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. We release our dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Dicemy/DataClawEval/tree/master

AI.tldr: DataClawEval is the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating autonomous LLM-based agents on end-to-end data engineering tasks. Spanning 100 production-grade tasks across five engines (PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, FlinkSQL), it uses deterministic sandbox execution for grading. Evaluation of 16 frontier agents reveals a top score of only 74.9 and strict engine-specific specialization, demonstrating that autonomous data engineering remains an unsolved challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus narrowly on Text-to-SQL or simplified data analysis, neglecting the complex, end-to-end workflows characteristic of real-world data engineering. There is a critical gap in evaluating autonomous agents on production-grade, multi-engine data engineering pipelines.
AI.method: The authors constructed DataClawEval, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end data engineering tasks derived from production code written by enterprise data engineers. Tasks span five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Each task runs in an isolated, case-specific sandbox and is evaluated using deterministic, rule-based scripts rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, ensuring objective and reproducible assessment.
AI.result: Evaluation of 16 frontier agents shows the strongest model achieves only 74.9 overall score. No single model dominates across all engines; instead, each model excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than general-purpose proficiency. This indicates autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge.
