AI.conclusion: Autonomous end-to-end data engineering is far from solved. Current frontier agents exhibit significant limitations and engine-specific specialization rather than omnipotent capability. The benchmark, along with its dataset, containerized environments, and evaluation scripts, is publicly released to catalyze further research.

title: ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow
summary: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

AI.tldr: PT-Flow and ODEWorld propose a continuous-time latent world model that uses an ODE-governed velocity field in latent space, enabling arbitrary temporal resolution, backward prediction, and high-quality long-horizon video generation while supporting downstream policy learning for robotics.
AI.motivation: Physical space and time are fundamentally continuous, yet existing world models rely on discrete-time prediction, which is inefficient for capturing real-world dynamics and suffers from representation collapse over long horizons.
AI.method: The authors introduce Physical-Time Flow (PT-Flow), which learns a continuous latent velocity field parameterized by an ODE in a structured representation space. Future prediction is recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver. ODEWorld is then built on PT-Flow, incorporating time-variant feature extraction and ODE property enforcement on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field to prevent representation collapse.
AI.result: ODEWorld achieves high-quality image reconstruction after long-horizon prediction, supports arbitrary temporal resolution and backward prediction, and provides planning-oriented information for downstream policy learning. It excels in both video generation and robotic control tasks.
AI.conclusion: ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, demonstrating that continuous-time latent world models can overcome key limitations of discrete-time approaches in world modeling.

title: SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents
summary: Skill-based prompting has become a practical mechanism for improving large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing skill acquisition methods often treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations. This creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: when a student fails because it lacks task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory may not contain enough evidence to infer the missing behavior, while the teacher trajectory may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance. We propose SKILL-KD, a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent repeated local updates from causing skill drift, SKILL-KD further maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped. Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

AI.tldr: SKILL-KD is a contrastive skill distillation framework that extracts actionable "skill patches" from teacher-student trajectory discrepancies, iteratively refines them through re-execution, and uses Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation to maintain skill quality, consistently improving frozen student agents across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing skill acquisition methods treat skills as experience summaries or direct demonstration summaries, creating a mismatch for weaker student agents: their failed trajectories lack evidence of missing behaviors, while teacher trajectories are too implicit to internalize as reusable guidance.
AI.method: SKILL-KD contrasts student failure trajectories against teacher success trajectories to distill actionable discrepancies into textual skill patches. These patches are evaluated by re-running the student and iteratively refined on failure. To prevent skill drift from repeated local updates, it maintains trace-linked edit histories and applies Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, which decides whether each patch should add, delete, modify, or skip a rule.
AI.result: SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines across five agent benchmarks and two student settings.
AI.conclusion: Skill distillation framed as contrastive discrepancy extraction with drift-aware consolidation offers an effective mechanism for transferring capabilities from stronger to weaker LLM agents without modifying model parameters.

title: Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting
summary: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Bayesian domain weighting method that infers optimal pre-training data domain weights from a Dirichlet distribution with Gamma priors, achieving stable, efficient, and data-efficient weight optimization compared to proxy-fitting and direct optimization approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing domain weighting methods either rely on strong structural assumptions (e.g., rank invariance, scaling laws) that introduce estimation bias, or suffer from unstable optimization and prohibitive computational costs when directly optimizing weights. A method is needed that combines stability, efficiency, and data efficiency without restrictive assumptions.
AI.method: A Bayesian framework that models domain weights as a Dirichlet distribution, incorporating Gamma prior information learned from observations. The method infers optimal domain weights through Bayesian inference, avoiding both the structural assumptions of proxy function-fitting approaches and the instability of direct optimization.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves stable and efficient domain weight learning, identifies optimal domain mixtures, and consumes substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods.
AI.conclusion: The Bayesian domain weighting approach revitalizes optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications by overcoming the limitations of both proxy-fitting and direct optimization paradigms.

title: IndustryForge-27B: A Domain-Enhanced Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial CAD
summary: Automating industrial CAD design and manufacturing places distinctive demands on multimodal foundation models: the model must see engineering drawings and 3D geometry screenshots, write correct parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and cover the full range from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fall short on these tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support the diverse calls that upper-layer agents issue. We build IndustryForge-27B on top of Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totalling $\sim$52k multimodal samples---CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor / SolidWorks (com_2d / com_3d / com_assembly)---and training with a unified multi-task SFT recipe. Across four CAD-domain benchmarks IndustryForge-27B lifts the base model by $+33.65$~pp on average and outperforms the strong closed-source model GPT-5.4 on all four; across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains, and slightly improves upon, the base model ($+1.56$~pp mean, no catastrophic forgetting). IndustryForge-27B will serve as the common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for a full-stack industrial agent that spans from CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

AI.tldr: IndustryForge-27B is a multimodal foundation model built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B, fine-tuned on ~52k industrial CAD samples across six sub-corpora. It improves CAD-domain performance by +33.65 pp on average, surpasses GPT-5.4, and retains general capabilities with no catastrophic forgetting.
AI.motivation: Industrial CAD automation demands multimodal models that can interpret engineering drawings and 3D geometry, generate parametric-modelling scripts and COM API code, and handle both single parts and assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fail on these specialized tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support diverse agent workflows.
AI.method: The authors build IndustryForge-27B on the Qwen3.5-VL-27B backbone. They curate six industrial-CAD sub-corpora (~52k multimodal samples): CAD-VQA, text2cadquery, text2cadquery-assembly, com_2d, com_3d, and com_assembly (targeting Inventor/SolidWorks). Training uses a unified multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) recipe.
AI.result: On four CAD-domain benchmarks, IndustryForge-27B improves over the base model by +33.65 pp on average and outperforms GPT-5.4 across all four. On eleven general-capability benchmarks, it retains and slightly improves upon the base model (+1.56 pp mean), demonstrating no catastrophic forgetting.
AI.conclusion: IndustryForge-27B serves as a unified substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, enabling a full-stack agent spanning CAD design to industrial-software operation, parts to assemblies, and single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

title: TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement
summary: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

AI.tldr: TriShield is a three-layer defense that completely blocks NeuroImprint-style privacy backdoor attacks on federated LLM fine-tuning with zero utility loss, using parameter artifact detection, stateful virtual iteration to entangle gradients, and SVD-based orthogonal projection to eliminate private memorization components.
AI.motivation: Existing defenses against the NeuroImprint attack—where a malicious parameter server reconstructs client training data via dedicated memorization neurons in PEFT adapters—either fail (LDP, gradient clipping) or severely degrade model utility. There is a pressing need for a defense that guarantees privacy against such reconstruction while preserving model performance.
AI.method: TriShield employs three complementary layers: (1) Parameter Artifact Detector scans distributed model parameters for memory-neuron signatures before local training; (2) Stateful Virtual Iteration exploits Adam/AdamW momentum to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, breaking NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; (3) Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection uses SVD to project gradients onto the main-task semantic subspace, removing gradient components linked to private memorization. The authors prove that after Layers 2 and 3, mutual information between uploaded gradients and any individual sample is zero.
AI.result: On GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B, TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to 0% across all attack variants while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with under 5% additional GPU computation overhead.
AI.conclusion: TriShield provides a deterministic, zero-utility-loss defense against NeuroImprint-style privacy backdoors in federated LLM fine-tuning, formally guaranteeing zero mutual information leakage and empirically eliminating reconstruction attacks with negligible computational cost.

title: SemPIC: Learning Semantic Position-Independent KV Caches
summary: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Our diagnostics show that a learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries but leaves interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself. We present \emph{SemPIC}, which trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. We further introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing, which reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

AI.tldr: SemPIC trains a LoRA-based Writer to compile position-independent document KV caches via behavioral distillation, achieving near-Full-Recompute performance while preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path.
AI.motivation: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads exhibit repeated document reuse under varying instructions, yet prefix caching fails to exploit this, and existing position-independent caching (PIC) is unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they'll be consumed. A diagnostic analysis reveals boundary-conditioned baselines reduce attention deviation near block boundaries but leave interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself.
AI.method: SemPIC employs a LoRA-enabled Writer that compiles native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation, while the pretrained decoder remains an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is restricted to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. The method also introduces KV Gradient Checkpointing to reduce peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs.
AI.result: Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.
AI.conclusion: SemPIC demonstrates that learned document representation adaptation via behavioral distillation can effectively bridge the gap between position-independent caching and full recomputation, offering a practical approach for efficient long-context retrieval and agentic workloads.

title: AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
summary: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

AI.tldr: AutoPref is an LLM-guided framework that automatically discovers programmatic preference objectives for neural combinatorial optimization, factorizing the objective into a pairwise loss program and a set-aware weighting program, and using staged conditional search to outperform hand-designed baselines across multiple COP benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing preference-based NCO methods rely on manually specified, one-size-fits-all objective formulations that conflate two design choices: (1) what learning signal to extract from each solution pair, and (2) how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. This manual design limits performance and adaptability across diverse combinatorial optimization problems and scales.
AI.method: AutoPref factorizes the preference objective into a composable pair of programs: a pairwise loss program (defining the learning signal) and a set-aware weighting program (determining pair contribution). Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space. To make search tractable, the authors introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. An LLM guides the program generation and search process.
AI.result: Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across various problem scales, demonstrating both effectiveness and scalability.
AI.conclusion: Automated objective discovery via programmatic search, guided by LLMs and constrained by behavioral gates, is a viable and superior alternative to manual preference-objective design in neural combinatorial optimization.

title: Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale
summary: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

AI.tldr: Echoverse is a pipeline that generates stateful, database-backed synthetic environments for training computer-use agents. It introduces a co-evolution loop where environment quality and model capability improve together. A 9B model trained on 12 Echoverse environments reaches 67.1% accuracy, approaching frontier-model performance. The paper demonstrates that environment depth, targeted failure repair, and co-evolution are key drivers of agent improvement.
AI.motivation: Training computer-use agents requires interactive applications they can act on, but critical real-world applications are login-gated and stateful, making them impractical for training at scale. Synthetic environments are used as proxies, but existing bulk-generation pipelines shift the bottleneck from quantity to quality — specifically, the behavioural depth, failure targeting, and adaptability of each environment. The authors aim to systematically improve these three properties.
AI.method: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications with database-backed task grading. It introduces a co-evolution loop: after each rollout, the system reads results twice — once to repair and improve the environment (its tasks, verifier, and rendering) and once to generate training signal for the model. This loop continuously aligns environment difficulty with model capability. A grounded verifier combined with a dense per-step reward judge enables reinforcement learning within the same environments.
AI.result: A 9B model trained on 12 Echoverse environments improves from 36.5% to 67.1% across 14 evaluation splits, within 14 points of the larger frontier teacher model. Deep environments lift live-site accuracy (80.0→85.0; 48.0→65.0), while shallow ones degrade it below baseline (80.0→75.0). Drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widgets and the open web. Repairing a single environment lifts a model from 16.2% to 38.5%. RL with the combined reward raises held-out score from 58.8% to 68.0%.
AI.conclusion: Environment depth, targeted failure repair, and co-evolution are critical properties for training effective computer-use agents. Echoverse demonstrates that relatively few (12) high-quality, co-evolving environments can drive substantial gains, rivaling frontier-model performance. The authors release four environments as a benchmark with applications, seed data, and grounded graders.

title: What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models
summary: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

AI.tldr: Proposes SliGFM, a Graph Foundation Model that uses topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction to unify heterogeneous node features across graph domains, guided by four desiderata: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility.
AI.motivation: Existing Graph Foundation Models project heterogeneous node features into fixed-dimensional spaces, but dimensional uniformity alone does not guarantee preservation of informative semantics or capture of transferable patterns for cross-domain knowledge transfer. There is a conceptual gap between dimensional alignment and meaningful feature unification.
AI.method: SliGFM introduces topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding: (1) feature dimensions are reordered by topological smoothness, (2) a shared sliding-window encoder scans the reordered features to produce ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens, (3) a smoothness-aware transformer captures transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, and (4) a generative reconstruction objective preserves original feature information.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper proposes the framework and design principles but does not report quantitative experimental results within the abstract text provided.
AI.conclusion: Dimensional uniformity is insufficient for effective cross-domain feature unification; the four proposed desiderata (formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, backbone compatibility) provide a principled framework, and SliGFM operationalizes these principles through smoothness-based reordering and generative reconstruction.

title: Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

AI.tldr: GRSD improves RLVR for LLM agents by extracting capability-aligned, outcome-discriminative guidance from on-policy rollouts. The policy reflects on successful and failed trajectories within a group, contrasts these reflections for privileged guidance, and uses a self-teacher to refine turn-level credit assignment while preserving verifier-determined learning direction. It consistently outperforms baselines across environments and scales.
AI.motivation: Terminal rewards in RLVR provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, entangling successful behaviors, mistakes, and incidental choices. Existing self-distillation methods that retrieve externally or extract skills from single trajectories by stronger models suffer from capability mismatch, path-specificity, and misalignment with current policy experience.
AI.method: GRSD operates in three stages: (1) For each prompt, the policy generates an on-policy group of rollouts and reflects on each verified trajectory. (2) A stop-gradient snapshot contrasts reflections from successful vs. failed trajectories to produce group-level privileged guidance that is both capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative. (3) A self-teacher uses this guidance to refine turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages, while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction.
AI.result: GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines across multiple agentic environments and model scales, and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.
AI.conclusion: GRSD provides an effective approach for enriching sparse RLVR signals by deriving fine-grained, capability-aligned guidance directly from the policy's own verified rollouts, enabling better credit assignment and stronger generalization without reliance on external or mismatched supervisory sources.

title: Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how reward design affects machine unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. The authors propose two new reward functions — an exponential reward based on forbidden-concept occurrence counts and a PageRank-inspired reward weighted by semantic importance — that consistently outperform binary rewards, achieving up to 3× faster forgetting while preserving model utility on the RWKU benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing machine unlearning methods formulated as RLVR problems rely on sparse binary rewards that only indicate whether forbidden content was avoided, providing minimal learning signal and limiting convergence speed. The authors aim to improve unlearning efficiency through better reward design.
AI.method: The authors introduce a reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, then propose two new reward functions: (1) an exponential reward providing graded penalties proportional to the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and (2) a PageRank-inspired reward that weights penalties by the semantic importance of forbidden concepts. These are evaluated within the RUL framework on the RWKU benchmark.
AI.result: Both proposed reward functions consistently outperform the binary reward baseline, achieving similar forgetting performance up to 3× faster while preserving general model utility.
AI.conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency, offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning without full retraining.

title: Distilling Answer Set Programming Theories from Large Language Models
summary: Writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch is a difficult and time-consuming task. We take a neurosymbolic approach to study whether a model can distill complete and correct theories, given a fixed agent harness with the solver in the loop. The protocol is dataset-agnostic: with a single prompt and an empty file as the starting point the model is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete theory. We chose VQA as the application domain, three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), as these are publicly available and non-trivial. In order to study the model scale required for solving this task we nine different models: four frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), two mid-tier (DeepSeek V4 Flash, gpt-oss-120b), and three open-weights (qwen3.6-27b, gpt-oss-20b, qwen3.5-9b). Three of four frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and to 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether large language models can autonomously distill complete and correct Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch within a 1-hour time limit, using a solver-in-the-loop neurosymbolic approach. Evaluated on three VQA benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER) across nine models, three of four frontier models achieve near-perfect or strong results, while GPT-5 shows fragility on GQA and when given reference theories.
AI.motivation: Writing ASP theories manually is difficult and time-consuming. The authors aim to explore whether neural models can automate this process by generating complete, correct theories through interaction with a solver, reducing human effort and enabling scalable neurosymbolic reasoning.
AI.method: A dataset-agnostic neurosymbolic protocol: models start with a single prompt and an empty file, then iteratively refine ASP theories within a 1-hour time budget, with an ASP solver providing feedback in the loop. Nine models spanning frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), mid-tier, and open-weights categories are tested on three VQA benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER). An ablation studies the effect of providing handwritten reference theories from other datasets.
AI.result: Three frontier models (Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro) reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%–98.8% on GQA, and 92.7%–95.3% on CLEVRER. GPT-5 achieves 98.7% on CLEVR but drops sharply to 41.8% on GQA and 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding reference theories alters the other frontier models by at most ±3.4 pp, but degrades GPT-5 by 3–19 pp.
AI.conclusion: Sufficiently capable frontier models can autonomously distill correct ASP theories from scratch in a solver-in-the-loop setup. However, not all frontier models are equally robust: GPT-5 exhibits significant brittleness, particularly on GQA and when exposed to reference theories. Model scale and architecture matter for reliable neurosymbolic theory distillation.

title: TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents
summary: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

AI.tldr: TAPO is a training framework that augments standard RL for LLM agents by adding auxiliary supervision on predicting next observations (transition dynamics) from rollout data, improving task performance without extra data, sampling, or inference cost.
AI.motivation: Existing RL methods for post-training LLM agents rely on sparse task rewards and neglect dense supervisory signals from environmental feedback. Theoretical work suggests that predictive knowledge of environmental dynamics is critical for generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks. TAPO addresses this gap by exploiting transition information already present in online interactions.
AI.method: TAPO alternates between standard policy optimization (any RL algorithm) and transition supervision: using rollout data to train the shared backbone model to predict next observations conditioned on actions. This is a plug-and-play module requiring no additional expert data, sampling, or inference overhead.
AI.result: Experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld across different foundation model scales and policy optimization algorithms show that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging action-conditioned transition prediction as an auxiliary objective during RL post-training enhances LLM agents' understanding of environmental dynamics, yielding consistent performance gains in interactive tasks.

title: Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization
summary: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

AI.tldr: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline that generates research directions from fine-grained researcher profiles, then selects them to balance individual fit with community-level diversity, reducing redundancy in AI research ideation.
AI.motivation: Current AI-assisted research ideation systems suffer from two blind spots: (1) coarse researcher representations produce mainstream, under-grounded suggestions, and (2) independent recommendations cause a community's research portfolio to cluster around recurring high-probability themes, stifling diversity.
AI.method: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline: (1) extraction of fine-grained researcher profiles, (2) generation of profile-conditioned candidate research directions, (3) scoring along three alignment dimensions — Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential, and (4) selection that surfaces researcher-local directions while de-duplicating across the community portfolio. Evaluation uses a benchmark of 95 AI researchers across five subfields.
AI.result: DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy significantly: average pairwise similarity drops from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608 versus coarse single-shot ideation. Against the independent top-choice variant, nearest-neighbor similarity decreases from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of researcher-direction fit.
AI.conclusion: DivAlign demonstrates that fine-grained researcher profiling combined with alignment-aware community-level de-homogenization can preserve individual fit while substantially increasing the diversity of AI research directions, offering a scalable path toward more varied scientific exploration.

title: Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness
summary: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper derives finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers by reformulating training as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem over measure-valued states. Using quantization and concentration inequalities on finite metric spaces, explicit bounds are obtained and transferred to the base model, with a further connection drawn to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of Transformers, rigorous finite-sample generalization guarantees remain scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by leveraging a measure-valued, dynamic programming perspective to obtain explicit, non-asymptotic bounds on generalization error.
AI.method: The paper adopts a doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, treating datasets as probability laws over pairs of empirical input-output measures. Training is cast as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. A quantized model is then constructed by discretizing state, action, and measure-state spaces. Finite-sample generalization bounds are derived via concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces combined with Lipschitz stability estimates for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the original (base) model with an explicit approximation error term. The same framework is shown to yield a distributionally robust control formulation linked to Wasserstein DRO.
AI.result: Explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers are obtained, expressed in terms of the quantization granularity, horizon length, and sample size. The approximation error from transferring bounds back to the base model is explicitly characterized. The framework also establishes a formal connection between Transformer generalization and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.
AI.conclusion: Transformers admit rigorous finite-sample generalization bounds when analyzed through a measure-valued dynamic programming lens. The quantized control approach provides a principled pathway to such bounds and reveals an intrinsic link to distributionally robust optimization, offering both theoretical insight and a potential framework for designing robust training algorithms.

title: PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses
summary: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

AI.tldr: PerturbMap predicts missing perturbation effects in unseen cellular contexts by combining a recipient-local low-rank base model with transported source-context responses weighted by route reliability, achieving improved MSE and specificity over baselines on a Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma dataset.
AI.motivation: Single-cell perturbation atlases are inherently incomplete — a query perturbation may be measured in some source contexts but missing in the target recipient context. Existing approaches either discard this query-specific evidence or naively copy/calibrate it across contexts, risking signal distortion. A method is needed to selectively transport measured source responses to unobserved recipient contexts while controlling for transfer reliability.
AI.method: PerturbMap uses a two-component architecture: (1) a recipient-local low-rank base model that captures context-specific structure, and (2) accepted proposals that transport a perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge regression experts trained on paired training perturbations. Proposal weights are determined by route reliability, estimated via validation anchor perturbations. This gated transfer mechanism selectively incorporates cross-context information only when reliable.
AI.result: On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1% over the recipient-local low-rank base alone. It outperforms FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. MSE remains within 2.82×10⁻⁶ of a centralized token-matched pooled reference that uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine similarity improves from 74.5% (low-rank base) to 80.5% (PerturbMap).
AI.conclusion: PerturbMap demonstrates that selective, reliability-weighted transport of measured source responses can effectively fill gaps in single-cell perturbation atlases, outperforming naive transfer and purely local baselines while approaching the performance of a centralized pooled reference.

title: It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations
summary:
Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

AI.tldr: The paper introduces einx, a universal tensor notation based on vectorization that reduces complex framework APIs to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and provides a clean, readable syntax embedded in Python.
AI.motivation: Existing tensor notations suffer from two main problems: (1) Numpy-like notation is verbose, error-prone, and inconsistent across operations, frequently leading to shape errors; (2) alternatives like einsum and einops, while more readable, are restricted to a narrow set of operations and lack generality. A universal, consistent, and expressive notation for tensor programming is needed.
AI.method: The authors revisit vectorization as a fundamental function that transforms tensor operations. Vectorization serves a dual role: it lifts lower-order operations to higher-order ones and conceptually decomposes higher-order operations into lower-order operations plus their vectorization. Building on this, einx is introduced as a declarative, pointful notation defined by analogy with loop notation, representing the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation unifies diverse tensor operations under a small set of elementary primitives with consistent rules.
AI.result: The einx notation successfully reduces the large APIs of existing tensor frameworks to a compact set of elementary operations. It applies uniform rules across all supported operations, eliminating the inconsistencies that cause shape errors in traditional notations. The accompanying Python implementation integrates seamlessly with existing frameworks and is publicly available on GitHub.
AI.conclusion: Vectorization provides a universal foundation for tensor operation notation. By building on this principle, einx offers a cleaner, more consistent, and fully general alternative to both Numpy-style APIs and restricted notations like einsum/einops, enabling more readable and less error-prone tensor programming.

title: An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale
summary:
This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

AI.tldr: A framework for transparent, multidimensional analysis of AI governance proposals using expert-informed rubrics and computational methods, surfacing policy tradeoffs rather than prescribing outcomes, with benchmarking of LLMs for rubric-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: AI policy debates tend to collapse into binary positions that conceal underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions, making systematic and transparent assessment difficult in a contested regulatory landscape.
AI.method: Mixed-methods approach integrating qualitative expert feedback with computational text analysis to construct policy attribute rubrics; quantification of policy objective emphasis; comparative visualizations; benchmarking commercial LLMs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicit analytical assumptions.
AI.result: A jurisdiction-agnostic framework that surfaces policy tradeoffs through multidimensional, empirically grounded rubrics; a transparent hybrid methodology combining SME input with computational validation; and benchmark comparisons of general-purpose LLMs against a rubric-calibrated model.
AI.conclusion: By making analytical assumptions explicit — including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes — the framework enables users to assess alignment between embedded priorities and their own normative commitments, supporting policymakers, analysts, and researchers in complex AI governance environments.

title: Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web
summary: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

AI.tldr: This paper presents a user foundation model for open-web RTB advertising, where user identity is fragmented and history is sparse. Using self-supervised pre-training (masked language modeling + contrastive objective) on browsing sequences with an LLM-in-the-loop optimization pipeline, the model achieves significant lifts on production bid win-rate (+1.197% RIG), CTR ranking (+1.354% RIG), and a live A/B test (+2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC).
AI.motivation: Open-web RTB environments differ fundamentally from traditional e-commerce/social recommendation settings: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across sessions, browsing history availability depends on privacy choices, and many requests carry no historical data. Existing industrial systems rely on coarse aggregated counters and recency buckets, discarding the sequential structure of user behavior. The authors aim to exploit this unused sequential signal via self-supervised representation learning.
AI.method: The approach consists of three core components: (1) A Transformer encoder pre-trained with masked language modeling (MLM) and a sequence-level contrastive objective on user browsing histories; (2) Fine-tuning the pre-trained encoder on click prediction; (3) An LLM-in-the-loop optimization pipeline that searches over a curated catalog of code-level edits ("lifters") to optimize the pre-training pipeline, operationalizing the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial context. The resulting encoder representations are then integrated into production bid win-rate and CTR ranking models.
AI.result: The pre-trained encoder delivers +1.197% relative improvement gain (RIG) on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker. A 7-day online A/B test validates these offline gains with +2.13% CTR lift and -1.13% eCPC reduction, both statistically significant at 80% CI.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised user foundation models are viable for open-web RTB despite fragmented, non-persistent user identities. Sequential modeling of browsing histories, combined with LLM-guided pipeline optimization, yields meaningful downstream improvements in both offline metrics and live production KPIs. This challenges the prevailing assumption that aggregated historical features are sufficient in this domain.

title: SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring
summary: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Deep Scientific Data Exploration, where LLM agents navigate hierarchical scientific repositories, interpret heterogeneous files, execute analyses, and integrate cross-file evidence. The authors present SciDataSailor, a framework using MCTS with four task-specific mechanisms to synthesize tool-interactive trajectories, and construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for training and SciDataSailor-Bench (627 summarization + 586 QA tasks across 27 datasets) for evaluation.
AI.motivation: Scientific datasets are organized as hierarchical repositories with heterogeneous, interdependent files, making inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive. While LLM agents excel at planning and reasoning, existing work has overlooked their capacity to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. There is a need for agents that can autonomously navigate, interpret, and derive conclusions from complex scientific data repositories.
AI.method: The authors propose SciDataSailor, a trajectory synthesis framework built on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) augmented with four mechanisms: (1) difficulty-stratified exploration seeds to ensure diverse starting conditions, (2) dual-feedback first-play urgency balancing exploration and exploitation, (3) hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation for structured decision-making, and (4) entropy-guided branching to prioritize informative search paths. The framework synthesizes tool-interactive trajectories used to build SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation.
AI.result: The resulting SciDataSailor-Bench contains 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets covering life sciences, earth sciences, and physical sciences. The framework and benchmarks operationalize the Deep Scientific Data Exploration paradigm for evaluating LLM agents on real scientific data interaction.
AI.conclusion: SciDataSailor demonstrates that MCTS-driven trajectory synthesis can effectively equip LLM agents for deep scientific data exploration, bridging the gap between agent reasoning capabilities and practical scientific data analysis. The released benchmarks provide a standardized testbed for future research in this domain.

title: Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts
summary: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

AI.tldr: Flux-OPD introduces a novel distillation paradigm that leverages evolving contexts as in-training supervision for open-ended domains. By decomposing the reverse KL objective, the authors reveal that the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, with a conflict term measuring inter-teacher disagreement. Flux-OPD uses contextual difference signals as corrections to a context-free teacher anchor, weighted by the conflict indicator, achieving superior performance over existing OPD methods.
AI.motivation: Training LLMs in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preference supervision difficult to formalize. While contexts can convey preferences, they provide diminishing supervision once distilled. Evolving contexts could address this, but direct use creates unstable distillation targets and conflicting distributions. The paper aims to understand and resolve these issues through a principled decomposition of the reverse KL objective.
AI.method: The authors decompose the reverse KL divergence objective for multi-teacher distillation, showing the student converges to the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers and identifying a conflict term measuring inter-teacher disagreement. Based on this, Flux-OPD computes contextual difference signals (the divergence between context-conditioned and context-free teachers), injects them as corrections into a context-free teacher anchor, and weights these corrections using the conflict term as a reliability indicator, stabilizing the distillation target while downweighting conflicting signals.
AI.result: Experiments on open-ended tasks demonstrate that Flux-OPD consistently outperforms existing OPD (Online Preference Distillation) paradigms, validating the effectiveness of combining teacher supervision with evolving contexts through the proposed decomposition and conflict-weighted correction mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Flux-OPD successfully addresses the instability and conflict challenges of using evolving contexts as in-training supervision. The reverse KL decomposition provides both theoretical insight and a practical mechanism — conflict-weighted contextual corrections — enabling effective preference capture in open-ended domains where verifiable rewards are absent.

title: MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck
summary: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

AI.tldr: MIND is a lightweight defense against memory injection attacks on LLM agents that uses an Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck to extract compact intent-behavior representations, enabling efficient detection of poisoned memories while avoiding redundant LLM auditing.
AI.motivation: Memory-augmented LLM agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks where poisoned memories divert agent behavior from user intent. Existing defenses are either computationally expensive or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn settings.
AI.method: MIND uses an Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck (IB) to extract compact representations capturing relationships between initial user intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information. A lightweight detector then classifies memories as benign or malicious based on these representations.
AI.result: On ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3% respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency. Broader experiments confirm MIND preserves task accuracy and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: MIND effectively mitigates memory injection attacks with minimal computational overhead, successfully addressing both the cost and information redundancy limitations of prior defenses.

title: Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation
summary: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

AI.tldr: CRPO reformulates on-policy self-distillation for LLMs as contrastive learning, using predictive entropy to separate reflective exploration (positive) from exposure bias (negative) positions, enabling group-wise contrast that outperforms RLVR and OPSD baselines on reasoning and deep-search benchmarks.
AI.motivation: On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) suffers from exposure bias due to privileged teacher information, causing reasoning route convergence and loss of clear optimization directions in multi-turn agentic settings. Existing RLVR approaches lack the dense, fine-grained supervision that OPSD provides, creating a need for a method that retains dense signals while mitigating exposure bias.
AI.method: CRPO (Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization) reframes agentic OPSD through a contrastive learning lens. It employs predictive entropy as a mechanism to differentiate positive positions (representing reflective exploration) from negative positions (representing exposure bias), and conducts group-wise contrastive optimization to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks show CRPO consistently outperforms existing RL and self-distillation baselines, with significant improvements in training stability and generalization during long-horizon interactions.
AI.conclusion: CRPO offers a novel contrastive formulation that addresses the exposure bias inherent in OPSD while retaining dense supervision signals, yielding superior performance and stability in multi-turn agentic LLM post-training compared to both RLVR and conventional self-distillation methods.

title: Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training
summary: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis.
