On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

AI.tldr: Synthetic textbooks improve LM pre-training not just from content quality, but from organizing related content into coherent book-level documents. A pipeline creates 686K textbooks via retrieval, clustering, TOC planning, and section assembly. Controlled experiments isolate "document packaging" as the key factor, yielding consistent gains (+1.09 avg) over content-matched but unorganized baselines.
AI.motivation: Prior work attributes gains from synthetic textbook data to generated content quality or local rewriting style, overlooking a structural factor: whether semantically related content is organized into coherent, book-length documents. This paper investigates whether book-level organization itself matters for pre-training.
AI.method: The authors build a scalable synthesis pipeline: (1) retrieve source material from a pre-training corpus, (2) cluster into topical units, (3) plan hierarchical tables of contents, (4) assemble source-grounded sections into complete books ("Full" setting). This yields 686K textbooks (32B tokens, 15K+ disciplines). Controlled comparisons include: a "Split" condition (same content, each section as independent document), a "RandomConcat" control (sections from different books joined, matching length), and a "Rephrase" condition (independent rewriting of retrieved documents without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly). Experiments replace natural books in a mid-training mix and evaluate downstream performance.
AI.result: Replacing natural books with the Full synthetic corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons isolate each factor: Full beats Split by +1.02 (document packaging effect), Full beats RandomConcat (ruling out length-alone explanations), and Full beats Rephrase by +1.17 (value of structured synthesis over independent rewriting). On Llama3-8B, Full also outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books.
AI.conclusion: Book-level document organization is a significant and previously overlooked axis for synthetic pre-training data design. Structured synthesis—clustering, TOC planning, and coherent assembly—yields gains beyond what content quality or rewriting style alone can explain.

title: Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework
summary: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

AI.tldr: WrapFlow is a continuous-time forecasting framework for irregular multivariate time series that combines continuous-time tokenization with a Transformer backbone and a simulation-free Residual Flow Matching training paradigm, achieving state-of-the-art performance without relying on discretization preprocessing or ODE solvers.
AI.motivation: Irregular multivariate time series (asynchronous observations, non-uniform intervals) are common in healthcare, activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Existing methods either use discretization (interpolation, imputation) which destroys continuous-time semantics, or ODE-based continuous models that incur heavy computational costs from numerical solvers. A framework is needed that preserves continuous-time structure while remaining computationally efficient.
AI.method: WrapFlow has three key components: (1) Continuous-Time Tokenization that encodes raw observation events with gap-aware tokens to explicitly model unobserved intervals; (2) a standard Transformer backbone processing these tokens to capture long-range dependencies; and (3) a simulation-free training paradigm based on Residual Flow Matching that learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions, avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training, requiring only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art forecasting performance compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: WrapFlow effectively bridges the gap between continuous-time modeling and computational efficiency, showing that continuous-time tokenization paired with simulation-free flow matching can outperform both discretization-based and ODE-based approaches for irregular time series forecasting.

title: BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints
summary: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

AI.tldr: BlueprintRepair introduces a typed, schema-checked repair interface for LLM-based Lean proving that edits blueprint dependency graphs through ten local operations. On the BlueprintTrace benchmark of 142 controlled failures, typed edits match the solve rate of free-form patching and rewriting but are significantly cheaper (1.30x vs. patching, 2.06x vs. rewriting) and reach final coverage faster.
AI.motivation: LLM-based Lean proof systems use blueprints (dependency graphs of formal statements) to organize proofs, but existing repair approaches rely on free-form source patches or full module rewrites. These lack structural guarantees: the target theorem can be inadvertently changed, and the dependency structure between lemmas is not enforced. The authors seek a repair interface that operates at the blueprint level, preserving structural integrity while enabling targeted, efficient fixes.
AI.method: BlueprintRepair provides ten schema-checked local operations that modify a blueprint's dependency graph. Each operation names the specific node it edits, preventing changes to the target theorem. Lean verifies every applied change, and an accepted repair must explicitly declare every blueprint lemma its proof depends on. The authors also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failure scenarios with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. They compare three interfaces — typed edits (BlueprintRepair), exact source patches, and complete module rewrites — under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, with one episode per state. Evaluation uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash.
AI.result: All three interfaces solve nearly the same number of localized failures on BlueprintTrace with DeepSeek-V4-Flash. However, typed repair is the cheapest per solved state: patching costs 1.30x more, rewriting 2.06x more. Within 10,000 completion tokens per task, typed repair reaches almost all its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces lag substantially behind. With Qwen3.6-Flash, typed repair remains cheapest, outperforms on proof-authoring states, and replicates the localized coverage pattern.
AI.conclusion: Typed, schema-checked blueprint repair matches the solve rate of free-form approaches while being substantially more cost-efficient and faster to converge. The structural guarantees — fixed target theorem, explicit dependency declarations, Lean verification of every change — do not sacrifice capability and instead yield efficiency gains. The BlueprintTrace benchmark provides a reusable resource for future work on structured proof repair.

title: Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers
summary: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

AI.tldr: A two-stage strategy for accelerating Newton's method is proposed: first, a regression model predicts a surrogate initial guess from learned feature spaces; second, a GMRES-based residual-minimizing correction refines it. This reduces Newton iterations and CPU time for large-scale nonlinear PDE problems.
AI.motivation: Newton's method converges faster when initialized close to a root, but obtaining good initial guesses for large-scale nonlinear systems (e.g., PDEs) across varying parameters is challenging. Existing surrogate-based initialization alone may be insufficient, motivating a complementary correction step to further improve the starting point.
AI.method: The approach has two stages: (1) Offline, discrete Newton trajectories from parameter-space sampling are decomposed into two reduced spaces — a solution feature space (converged states) and a corrective search direction feature space (Newton increments). A regression model maps parameters to a surrogate solution approximation. (2) Online, for a new parameter, the surrogate prediction is corrected via a GMRES-based residual-minimizing least-squares solve, yielding an improved initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton solver. The method is weakly intrusive, requiring only residual evaluations and scripting access.
AI.result: The two-stage strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and overall CPU time compared to standalone surrogate initialization. Quantifiable speedups are demonstrated on representative PDE problems, with significant gains observed.
AI.conclusion: The generic, weakly intrusive methodology effectively accelerates Newton convergence for large-scale nonlinear problems by combining learned feature spaces with a lightweight corrective step, and is broadly applicable across PDE-based applications.

title: ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs
summary: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

AI.tldr: ConMem is a contribution-aware memory framework that uses Shapley-style estimation to prioritize high-value inspection evidence under a memory budget, enabling early-risk screening in long-horizon steel-equipment inspection with LLM assistance.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG systems treat historical inspection logs as static corpora without estimating diagnostic value, causing them to miss early risk signals across repeated inspection cycles. There is a need for a memory mechanism that can identify and retain weak degradation signals for proactive maintenance.
AI.method: ConMem operates in three stages: (1) functional-role-aware segmentation of inspection logs into evidence units, (2) Shapley-style contribution estimation to quantify each unit's diagnostic value, and (3) retention of high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget, integrated into a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system.
AI.result: ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy on a real-world dataset, surpassing the strongest comparable baseline. Compared to naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablations confirm that both functional-role segmentation and contribution-based valuation help prioritize weak degradation signals. Practical deployment retains early seal-wear signals across three inspection cycles.
AI.conclusion: ConMem effectively addresses the gap in long-horizon equipment inspection by prioritizing diagnostically valuable evidence under memory constraints, enabling early-risk alerts that traditional static RAG systems miss.

title: ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents
summary:
As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

AI.tldr: ClawTrack is a dual-assessment benchmark that evaluates LLM agents on both final outcomes (Task Score) and reasoning quality (Process Score) across 320 tasks in 8 domains. Using 12,541 rubric items across four dimensions, it reveals that process scores can attribute failures, filter lucky successes, and improve post-training through trajectory filtering.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent benchmarks only evaluate final outcomes, failing to distinguish between genuine reasoning and lucky success, and cannot attribute failures to specific process deficiencies in long-horizon, multi-step tasks.
AI.method: ClawTrack introduces a dual-assessment framework with 320 tasks across 8 domains using 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader evaluates each reasoning turn on four dimensions — goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification — using 12,541 task-specific rubric items. The framework was tested across 21 models in over 16,000 trials.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) process scores effectively attribute successes and failures to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification emerging as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust across different judge LLMs; (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.
AI.conclusion: Process-based evaluation is essential for reliable assessment of LLM agents in complex workflows. ClawTrack demonstrates that measuring how agents reason — not just what they achieve — enables better failure attribution, filters spurious successes, and provides actionable signals for improving agent capabilities through post-training.

title: CDAE: Enhancing Perturbation Robustness in Pretrained Language Models with Contrastive Denoising
comment: Submitted to 16th International Conference on Computer and Knowledge Engineering (ICCKE 2026)
summary: Pre-trained language models have significantly improved sentence representation learning, yet their embedding remain sensitive to semantic preserving textual perturbations such as synonym substitution, masking and word dropout. This work proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embedding by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objective to learn perturbation-invariant representation. We evaluate the proposed framework using multiple perturbation strategies with varying strengths and compare it against the original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. Experimental results show that CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations, with the improvements becoming more pronounced as framework effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantic information, highlighting perturbation-invariant learning as a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ComputationIASBS/CDAE

AI.tldr: CDAE is a lightweight contrastive denoising autoencoder that refines BERT embeddings to be robust against semantic-preserving perturbations (synonym substitution, masking, word dropout) by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objectives.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained language model embeddings are sensitive to semantic-preserving textual perturbations, undermining their reliability for downstream tasks. There is a need for perturbation-invariant sentence representations that maintain stability without sacrificing semantic fidelity.
AI.method: A Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that jointly optimizes a contrastive objective (to pull perturbed embeddings close to original embeddings) and a reconstruction objective (to preserve semantic content). Evaluated across multiple perturbation strategies at varying strengths, benchmarked against original BERT embeddings and SimCSE.
AI.result: CDAE consistently achieves higher embedding similarity under perturbations compared to baselines, with gains becoming more pronounced as perturbation strength increases. The framework effectively balances representation stability with semantic preservation.
AI.conclusion: Perturbation-invariant learning is a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings. CDAE offers an effective, lightweight approach to enhancing embedding robustness while retaining semantic information.

title: AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach
summary: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent. AgenticASR implements this task through an ASR--Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. We also introduce AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics. Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR attains the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human--AI agreement study shows that rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality--latency trade-off between online and offline inference. Together, these results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech. Code, AASR-Bench, and a demo will be released at https://github.com/AnXMuy/AgenticASR.

AI.tldr: AgenticASR introduces a streaming audio-to-clean-text system that removes disfluencies and resolves self-corrections in real time via an ASR–Refiner architecture, supported by a new bilingual benchmark (AASR-Bench) and validated through human–AI agreement studies.
AI.motivation: Standard ASR produces verbatim transcripts containing disfluencies (fillers, repetitions, false starts, self-corrections) that increase cognitive load and degrade downstream task performance. Existing spoken-to-written methods operate on completed utterances and cannot retroactively revise earlier output when later speech recontextualizes it. This motivates a streaming, agentic approach that emits clean, intent-preserving text and can revise prior spans as new audio arrives.
AI.method: The authors formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR) as an audio-to-clean-text task. Their system, AgenticASR, uses an ASR–Refiner architecture: an ASR front end produces preliminary transcripts, and a Refiner module iteratively transforms a bounded active context window, replacing corresponding output spans as streaming audio arrives — enabling continual emission and revision over arbitrary-duration streams. They also construct AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics for evaluation.
AI.result: AgenticASR achieves the highest AASR-Bench scores across multiple ASR front ends compared to other evaluated systems. A human–AI agreement study confirms rubric-based evaluations align with independent expert judgments. Ablation studies characterize the effects of Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality–latency trade-off in online vs. offline inference.
AI.conclusion: AgenticASR establishes a practical framework for intent-preserving, clean transcription during ongoing speech, enabling real-time disfluency removal and self-correction resolution for streaming audio. The accompanying AASR-Bench and human-validation results strengthen the contribution.

title: GVR-Coder: A Visual-Feedback Framework for Structured SVG Generation in Complex Document and Meeting Scenarios
summary: In demanding professional environments and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text often imposes a high cognitive load. To facilitate efficient information communication, transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential. Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) provide an effective representation for this purpose due to their editability and resolution independence. However, current research on Text-to-SVG generation remains hindered by three major challenges: (1) the scarcity of datasets for complex, logic-rich diagrams; (2) the absence of explicit layout priors, which leads to chaotic spatial arrangements; and (3) the lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. To address these challenges, at the data level, we introduce DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset tailored for document authoring and meeting review scenarios. At the model level, we propose GVR-Coder, a novel framework designed to generate high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Specifically, we adopt a curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance the model's capability in modeling complex structures, while explicitly incorporating layout constraint knowledge during training. In addition, we introduce reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, a mechanism that provides implicit feedback through reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics. Furthermore, we design a generate-verify-repair agent loop, which improves generation quality through explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CurryaNa/GVR-Coder.

AI.tldr: GVR-Coder introduces DocMeetSVG-100K dataset and a novel framework for generating logically structured SVG diagrams from lengthy professional text, using curriculum-driven fine-tuning, layout constraints, and dual rendering feedback to produce coherent and aesthetically refined outputs.
AI.motivation: Lengthy professional texts impose high cognitive load in meetings and document authoring. Transforming them into logical diagrams (SVGs) aids comprehension, but existing Text-to-SVG methods suffer from scarce complex diagram datasets, lack of layout priors causing disordered spatial arrangements, and absence of fine-grained visual feedback for aesthetic correction.
AI.method: (1) DocMeetSVG-100K: a large-scale SVG dataset for document/meeting scenarios. (2) GVR-Coder framework with three components: curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively model complex structures with explicit layout constraints; reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback using reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics; and a generate-verify-repair agent loop providing explicit fine-grained feedback for targeted refinement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines, reliably producing logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams.
AI.conclusion: GVR-Coder effectively addresses the three core challenges in Text-to-SVG generation through data curation, layout-constrained training with curriculum learning, dual rendering feedback RL, and an agent-based repair loop, enabling high-quality logical diagram generation from lengthy professional texts.

title: Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Informed Framework for Trustworthy Chemical Property Prediction
summary: Chemical property prediction plays a critical role in accelerating scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and drug development. However, existing benchmarks often suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it challenging to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models. In this work, we introduce Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, covering various properties including density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. Chem World provides a unified platform for evaluating AI models across multiple property prediction tasks. Furthermore, we propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network based prediction framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning, improving the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of chemical property prediction. Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with existing methods. By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: Chem World is a large-scale benchmark integrating 17 datasets and 800K+ molecules for chemical property prediction, paired with Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network that leverages chemical priors to improve prediction accuracy and robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for chemical property prediction suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, hindering systematic assessment of AI model reliability and generalization.
AI.method: The authors introduce (1) Chem World, a unified benchmark aggregating 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples covering properties like density, conductivity, and solubility; and (2) Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network framework that embeds chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning for property prediction.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate that Mixture-PINN outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, robustness, and reliability across multiple chemical property prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: Chem World, combined with physics-informed learning, establishes a foundation for trustworthy AI systems in computational chemistry and advances AI-driven scientific discovery through standardized, large-scale evaluation.

title: WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning
summary: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

AI.tldr: WIDE is a token-level dynamic width pruning framework for LLMs that enables fine-grained, differentiable pruning at the neuron-block level (attention heads and FFN channels), achieving superior quality retention and practical speedups via a pruning-kernel co-design.
AI.motivation: Existing static structured pruning is hardware-friendly but input-agnostic, causing accuracy loss under aggressive sparsity. Dynamic sparsity methods improve quality but are limited to coarse-grained (layer-level) decisions and struggle with practical inference acceleration. There is a gap between fine-grained dynamic sparsity and real-world throughput gains.
AI.method: WIDE introduces an end-to-end differentiable framework for token-level dynamic width pruning. Each token dynamically selects attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups (neuron-block granularity). A two-stage training pipeline learns token-wise sparse patterns. For practical acceleration, a pruning-kernel co-design framework decomposes dynamic sparsity into: (1) mask reordering, (2) hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and (3) hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across granularities.
AI.result: At 50% sparsity, WIDE achieves a 55.1% performance boost over SOTA dynamic depth pruning (calibration-only). For inference: up to 1.98x (prefill) and 4.95x (decoding) kernel-level speedups; 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained token-level dynamic width pruning, combined with a co-designed kernel framework, can simultaneously achieve high quality retention and practical, near-theoretical inference speedups across both prefill and decoding phases of LLM inference.

title: Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report: Toward Next-Generation Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents
summary:
GUI agents have the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing digital devices. To advance them toward real-world use, we envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve their capabilities with minimal human effort. Guided by this vision, we present Qwen-UI-Agent, a real-world centric foundation GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. Qwen-UI-Agent combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. Its unified action space interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn. An AutoResearch-style data flywheel uses agents to construct tasks and environments, diagnose failures, and plan subsequent iterations. Online RL supports training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, with over 10,000 concurrent environments accelerating rollout. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer.
  Across a broad suite of evaluations, Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks while delivering competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models, including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol. On mobile use, it achieves 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. On computer use, it achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2. On browser use and GUI grounding, it achieves 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, respectively.

AI.tldr: Qwen-UI-Agent is a foundation GUI agent that operates across mobile, computer, web, and search environments, combining GUI and CLI actions with batched execution. It uses a data flywheel for autonomous improvement and online RL training on 100+ turn trajectories across 10,000+ concurrent environments, achieving SOTA on mobile benchmarks and competitive results against frontier models like Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
AI.motivation: The authors envision GUI agents as general-purpose executors on real devices that can: (1) operate reliably on actual hardware, (2) execute cross-platform workflows, (3) combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, (4) complete long-horizon tasks, (5) proactively initiate services, and (6) autonomously self-improve with minimal human intervention. Current agents fall short of these real-world requirements.
AI.method: Qwen-UI-Agent integrates: (1) diverse sandbox environments plus a large-scale real-device mobile runtime; (2) a unified action space interleaving GUI operations and CLI execution with batched actions per model turn; (3) an AutoResearch-style data flywheel where agents construct tasks/environments, diagnose failures, and plan iterative improvements; (4) online RL training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, scaled via 10,000+ concurrent environments; and (5) a lightweight harness layer enabling proactive service initiation and stateful cross-platform workflows.
AI.result: Mobile-use SOTA: 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, 97.5% on AndroidDaily. Computer-use: 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified, 40.0% partial-progress on OSWorld-v2. Browser/GUI grounding: 73.6% on WebArena, 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro. Competitive against frontier models Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol.
AI.conclusion: Qwen-UI-Agent demonstrates that a unified, real-world-centric foundation GUI agent can achieve state-of-the-art performance across mobile, computer, and browser environments by combining unified action spaces, large-scale real-device deployment, data flywheel self-improvement, and online RL at scale, representing a significant step toward practical general-purpose GUI agents.

title: From Expert Reduction to Behavioral Divergence: Tracing Numerical State through Sparse MoE Inference
summary: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders can produce observably different sparse-MoE executions. We isolate this effect in native DeepSeek-V4-Flash by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics. Four schemes separate operand representation from accumulator precision. At one layer-5 fork, 720 A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins; 720 B-mode orders form 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, the B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates 12, 24, and 36 of 50 prompts by 8, 16, and 32 tokens. Across 192 persistent trajectories per scheme, P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts. A separate 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE, post-mHC, next-router, and LM states bitwise. For one controlled B branch, exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction reproduces the measured downstream trajectory. At the next decode boundary, exact FP64 reconstruction of the branch's full persistent state yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, 301 persistent-state checkpoints, 301 routes, predictions, and text over seven steps, given the same naturally generated next input. These controls identify post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state: divergence can survive a token boundary and become visible later. These results make expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order part of a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. They establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence; C's order invariance is limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

AI.tldr: Different mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders in sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models produce observably divergent executions. The authors isolate this effect in DeepSeek-V4-Flash, showing that aggregation semantics (operand representation, accumulator precision, reduction order) create distinct continuation basins. Crucially, they identify the post-mHC state as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary, demonstrating that identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state.
AI.motivation: To rigorously characterize how numerically equivalent but operationally distinct reduction orders in sparse-MoE layers lead to divergent autoregressive trajectories, thereby establishing that expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order must be part of the numerical compatibility contract for MoE runtimes and hardware backends.
AI.method: The authors freeze local MoE state in DeepSeek-V4-Flash and systematically vary only aggregation semantics. Four schemes (P32, A, B, C) separate operand representation from accumulator precision. They trace 192 persistent trajectories per scheme, measure continuation basins at a layer-5 fork, classify structural classes under Chinese prompts, perform maximum-L-infinity branch selection, and conduct bitwise state comparisons (post-mHC, next-router, LM states). For one controlled B branch, they perform exact FP64 reconstruction of full persistent state and verify downstream agreement over seven decode steps.
AI.result: At the layer-5 fork: 720 A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins; 720 B-mode orders form 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates 12, 24, and 36 of 50 prompts by 8, 16, and 32 tokens. Schemes P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory; scheme C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts, and matches native MoE bitwise. Exact FP64 reconstruction of a B branch reproduces the downstream trajectory, yielding agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, persistent-state checkpoints, routes, predictions, and text over seven steps.
AI.conclusion: Post-mHC is an intra-token boundary; full persistent state is a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens do not guarantee identical autoregressive state — divergence can survive token boundaries and emerge later. Expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order constitute a numerical compatibility contract for MoE runtimes. Results establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence; scheme C's order invariance is limited to the evaluated six-term states and schedules.

title: Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States
summary:
What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes that hidden states encode two structural properties — aggregator (text-level consolidation) and differentiator (token transport into subspace) — that track a token's relational place within a specific text, validated against independent ground truths, and dissociate from type-level measures like surprisal and attention.
AI.motivation: To investigate what language model hidden states reveal about the organization of a single text, moving beyond type-level (essentialist) measures toward a relational, token-in-context understanding that operationalizes pre-existing literary/psychoanalytic theory.
AI.method: From a single forward pass without training, every token position is scored on two frozen properties: the aggregator (whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration) and the differentiator (whether other tokens transiently enter its subspace). Validation uses an engineered register (6/6 boundary cells), a psychoanalyst's pre-existing clinical transcript markings (34/36 cells), and a matched base/instruct pair transfer test.
AI.result: As a signifier repeats, surprisal and attention drain while aggregator score holds, marking token place rather than type. The aggregator tracks an engineered register across boundaries (6/6 cells) and aligns with a psychoanalyst's markings (34/36 cells, graded increment above lexical controls). The model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads singular discourse worst; instruction tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Dissociations appear that no type-level measure reproduces.
AI.conclusion: Structural value is a relational property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone. Hidden states operationalize a non-essentialist, place-based theory of textual organization that predates the instrument itself.

title: Information Bottleneck Learning for Faithful Time Series Forecasting Explanations
summary: As forecasts increasingly drive decisions in fields such as energy, transportation, and healthcare, understanding the historical data behind these predictions has become as crucial as the predictions themselves. Although existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal their internal structures, they offer no guarantee that these structures faithfully reflect the underlying evidence driving the predictions. In contrast, while faithfulness-oriented methods explicitly verify model behavior, they are almost exclusively designed for post-hoc classification tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose IB-Forecast, an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework. It decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. With a budget-constrained information bottleneck, end-to-end optimization enables users to directly control explanation sparsity. With a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol, extensive experiments demonstrate that IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Furthermore, under a matched sparsity budget, these native explanations consistently surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. Ultimately, whereas the native explanations of existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity, requiring only 14-20% of the observations to deliver low-error predictions.

AI.tldr: IB-Forecast is an interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework that decomposes predictions into periodic and residual components using explainable masks, optimized via an information bottleneck to control sparsity. It matches black-box forecasting accuracy while providing faithful, sparse explanations that outperform existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretable forecasters reveal internal structures but lack guarantees of faithfulness—their explanations may not reflect the true evidence behind predictions. Meanwhile, faithfulness-oriented methods are designed for post-hoc classification, not forecasting. There is a gap for a forecasting model that is both inherently interpretable and demonstrably faithful.
AI.method: The authors propose IB-Forecast, which decomposes multivariate time-series forecasting into: (1) a learned periodic component and (2) a residual component computed using explainable masks over input tokens. An information bottleneck with a budget constraint is employed for end-to-end optimization, allowing direct user control over explanation sparsity. A rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol is introduced to assess explanation quality.
AI.result: IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Under matched sparsity budgets, its native explanations consistently surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. It requires only 14–20% of observations to deliver low-error predictions. Existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor faithfulness by comparison.
AI.conclusion: IB-Forecast successfully bridges the gap between interpretable-by-design forecasting and faithfulness guarantees, delivering black-box-level accuracy with high-fidelity, sparse explanations. This enables trustworthy deployment in critical domains like energy, transportation, and healthcare where understanding the evidence behind forecasts is essential.

title: SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute
summary: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

AI.tldr: SVR is a multi-turn RL framework that trains a language model to use self-verification (correctness verdict + confidence score) as an internal control signal for adaptive test-time compute. It matches or exceeds fixed-budget and oracle-guided baselines while using far fewer inference turns.
AI.motivation: Uniform test-time compute budgets waste computation on easy problems, and verifier-guided refinement depends on external feedback. The authors aim to develop a method where the model learns to decide when to stop refining based on its own self-assessment, without oracle access at inference.
AI.method: SVR uses GRPO to train on fixed-horizon trajectories. At each turn, the model outputs a solution, a discrete correctness verdict (Correct/Incorrect), and a confidence score. An answer is retained only when verdict=Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold; otherwise refinement continues. Training rewards promote solution correctness, calibrated self-verification, and stop-ready correct states. Adaptive stopping is only applied at inference.
AI.result: On seven math reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves 0.563 macro-average accuracy with 2.99 average inference turns. It outperforms standard GRPO, multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference, while using substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.
AI.conclusion: Learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation, eliminating the need for external verifiers or uniform budgets.

title: AI and Authenticity in Islamic Research: A Critical Evaluation of Generative AI Reliability, Hallucination, and Source Fidelity in Quranic, Hadith, and Fiqh Knowledge
summary:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used by Muslims for religious guidance, Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith explanation, jurisprudential rulings, and Islamic education. Despite its growing adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on whether current AI systems provide authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge suitable for high-trust religious contexts. This study evaluates six leading generative AI systems using fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions covering Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Responses were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analysed using a mixed-method framework examining domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.
  The study addresses four research questions: (1) How accurate and authentic are AI-generated responses across major Islamic knowledge domains? (2) To what extent do AI systems produce hallucinations, incomplete citations, or unverifiable religious references? (3) How consistently do models handle jurisprudential disagreement, Madhhab diversity, and uncertainty? (4) Are current AI systems sufficiently reliable for religious guidance, Islamic education, and scholarly research?
  Overall, current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise. This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community.

AI.tldr: An empirical evaluation of six leading generative AI systems on 50 Islamic knowledge questions reveals they are useful for introductory learning but insufficiently reliable for authoritative religious rulings without human scholarly verification, due to issues with hallucinations, citation accuracy, and inconsistent handling of jurisprudential diversity.
AI.motivation: Despite growing Muslim reliance on generative AI for religious guidance—spanning Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, and Islamic education—there is a critical lack of empirical evidence assessing whether these systems deliver authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge in high-trust religious contexts.
AI.method: Fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions were posed to six leading generative AI systems under real-world conditions with participants in Australia and the UK. A mixed-method framework evaluated responses across seven dimensions: domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation. Four research questions structured the inquiry.
AI.result: Current generative AI systems function adequately as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but exhibit significant limitations: hallucinations, incomplete or unverifiable citations, inconsistent handling of Madhhab diversity and jurisprudential disagreement, and variable uncertainty acknowledgment. These shortcomings render them unsuitable as standalone authoritative sources for religious rulings or scholarly research.
AI.conclusion: Generative AI should be positioned solely as a supplementary aid in Islamic knowledge contexts. Any output must be cross-verified against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise before acceptance. The study offers the first comprehensive empirical benchmark of AI reliability in this domain and provides actionable guidance for researchers, educators, developers, and the Muslim community.

title: LM-GRASP: Instance-Specific Language Models for Combinatorial Construction via Online Imitation Learning
summary:
Machine learning for combinatorial optimization typically relies on neural constructors trained via reinforcement learning on large offline datasets for a fixed problem class-incurring high pretraining costs and generalizing poorly outside the training distribution. We propose an alternative: a metaheuristic framework that reformulates the randomized constructive phase of GRASP as an online imitation learning task, trained from scratch on each problem instance. A local search procedure acts as an expert oracle, while a decoder-only Transformer serves as the constructive policy. Unlike classical GRASP, which relies on static, myopic heuristic rules based on localized scalar costs, our approach is fully data-driven: the construction policy emerges from high-quality solutions discovered during the search itself, with no problem-specific feature engineering required.
  We instantiate this as LM-GRASP, a hybrid metaheuristic following an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories-no external data or offline pretraining needed. The pipeline interfaces with the domain solely through the objective evaluator used by local search.
  Evaluated on the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), the most discriminating block due to half its optima being unknown, LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average-comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations. This suggests instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising, practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

AI.tldr: LM-GRASP replaces the hand-engineered greedy construction phase in GRASP metaheuristics with an online-trained decoder-only Transformer, using local search solutions as expert demonstrations for behavioral cloning on each problem instance. It outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on the hardest Taillard PFSP instances.
AI.motivation: Standard ML-for-combinatorial-optimization approaches require expensive offline pretraining on large datasets and generalize poorly outside the training distribution. The authors aim to eliminate pretraining costs and hand-crafted heuristics by learning a constructive policy online from scratch per instance, using only the objective function evaluator.
AI.method: LM-GRASP is a hybrid metaheuristic with an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle. The randomized construction phase of GRASP is reformulated as online imitation learning: a local search procedure serves as an expert oracle generating elite solutions, and a decoder-only Transformer is trained via behavioral cloning on a dynamically maintained archive of elite trajectories. No problem-specific feature engineering or external data is used.
AI.result: On the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60) — the most discriminating subset where half the optima are unknown — LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by an average of 28.4 makespan units. This gain is comparable to the improvement from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though standard deviations overlap.
AI.conclusion: Instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising and practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors for combinatorial optimization, particularly on fitness landscapes where classical greedy construction fails.

title: Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation
comment: 15 pages, 1 figure, 6 tables. Reproducibility artifacts (frozen manifests, token IDs, per-item scores, analysis harnesses) described in Section 3.9
summary: Stage-replay diagnostics reconstruct intermediate token prefixes and treat fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix. We audit that assumption at a whole reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens and places an exact replica on both sides. In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; the accuracy difference is only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). A fixed-prefix 2x2 holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction and precision. The BF16 disagreements recur, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows; an all-200 saved-ledger audit reproduces every retained trajectory and comparison fingerprint. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor, both on a selected set at the primary checkpoint (24/24) and an outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint (43/43). Exact-token replay can therefore be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression.

AI.tldr: The paper audits the assumption that stage-replay diagnostics (reconstructing token prefixes and continuing from decoder states) faithfully reproduce live decoding behavior. Experiments on a Qwen2.5-derived system show that KV cache is causally sufficient for divergent trajectories, but numerical precision (BF16 vs. FP32) moderates behavioral expression, with BF16 introducing disagreements absent in FP32.
AI.motivation: Stage-replay diagnostics rely on the untested assumption that reconstructing intermediate token prefixes and continuing generation from the decoder state that originally produced the prefix yields faithful reproduction. The authors seek to audit this assumption at whole reasoning-stage boundaries, questioning whether exact-token replay preserves live-state fidelity.
AI.method: A matched 200-item experiment comparing retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens, with exact replicas on both sides. A fixed-prefix 2×2 design holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction (live vs. reconstructed) and precision (BF16 vs. FP32). Bidirectional K/V cache transplantation across all 48 layers tests causal sufficiency, with outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint.
AI.result: In BF16, replicas remain exact but constructions differ on 166/200 suffixes and 20 correctness labels (accuracy difference only 1 point; 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). FP32 eliminates all decoded disagreements (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). Token-by-token incremental and retained live caches achieve bit-exactness on 12/12 rows. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 K/V layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor (24/24 at primary checkpoint; 43/43 at later checkpoint).
AI.conclusion: Exact-token replay can be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of divergent trajectories, while numerical precision (BF16 vs. FP32) moderates behavioral expression. The findings validate stage-replay diagnostics under FP32 but reveal precision-dependent brittleness under BF16.

title: Operationally Guided Placement-Aware Learning for Industrial Online 3D Bin Packing
summary: The online three-dimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP) is a longstanding challenge in logistics and industrial palletizing. Recent learning-based methods use a learned policy to select among feasible candidate placements. Performance depends on the candidate generator and representation, especially in industrial settings where packings must be space-efficient, stable, compact, and balanced. However, prior work has mainly optimized the policy, while candidate generation and representation remain largely geometry-driven. We address this gap with OPAL, an operationally guided placement-aware learning framework for industrial online 3D-BPP which combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator (OG-EMS), an operational representation for each candidate placement, and a masked ranking policy trained with proximal policy optimization. OG-EMS evaluates multiple anchors within each free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements. An xLSTM-based Placement Encoder models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes, while a lightweight recurrent core combines the resulting embeddings with the current item and pallet state to rank feasible actions. On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, with improvements of 15.1% from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

AI.tldr: OPAL introduces an operationally guided, placement-aware learning framework for online 3D bin packing that combines a novel empty-maximal-space candidate generator, an xLSTM-based placement encoder, and a masked PPO-trained ranking policy, achieving 0.49 mean space utilization on BED-BPP with 15.1% improvement from candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking.
AI.motivation: Prior work on online 3D-BPP has focused primarily on optimizing the selection policy, while candidate generation and placement representation remain largely geometry-driven. Industrial settings require packings that are not only space-efficient but also stable, compact, and balanced — constraints poorly addressed by purely geometric approaches.
AI.method: OPAL consists of three components: (1) OG-EMS, an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator that evaluates multiple anchors per free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements; (2) an xLSTM-based Placement Encoder that models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes; and (3) a lightweight recurrent core that fuses placement embeddings with item and pallet state, trained via proximal policy optimization with masked action ranking.
AI.result: On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49. The operationally guided candidate generation contributes a 15.1% improvement, while the learned ranking policy adds a further 6.3% improvement, all while maintaining robust inference-time performance.
AI.conclusion: Integrating operational constraints directly into candidate generation and representation — rather than relying solely on geometry-driven heuristics — yields substantial gains in online 3D-BPP performance. OPAL demonstrates that jointly designing the candidate generator, placement representation, and ranking policy is a promising direction for industrial palletizing applications.

authors: Jacobus G. M. van der Linden
title: Search Strategies for Optimal Classification and Regression Trees
summary: Optimal decision trees (ODTs) are compact, interpretable machine learning models that globally optimize a given objective, but their scalability remains challenging. While recent work has proposed a variety of search strategies to improve scalability, the precise contribution of each strategy remains unclear. To address this gap, we introduce a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that instantiates previously used search strategies and enables the definition of new ones. This provides a common lens through which to understand and compare different strategies, which we use to empirically investigate the effect of 18 search strategies. Compared to the state of the art, the best strategy in our evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a unified algorithmic framework for optimal decision trees (ODTs) that systematizes existing search strategies and enables new ones. Through empirical evaluation of 18 strategies, the best one substantially outperforms prior art in anytime classification performance and achieves over an order-of-magnitude speedup for regression.
AI.motivation: Optimal decision trees offer global optimality and interpretability, but scalability is a persistent challenge. Although many search strategies have been proposed to improve scalability, their individual contributions and interactions are poorly understood, hindering systematic progress in the field.
AI.method: The authors develop a general algorithmic framework that abstracts and instantiates previously disparate search strategies under a common lens. This framework also supports defining novel strategies. They then empirically evaluate 18 distinct search strategies within this unified framework to isolate and compare their effects.
AI.result: The best strategy identified in the evaluation significantly improves anytime performance for classification over the state of the art, and reduces runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression tasks.
AI.conclusion: A unified framework for ODT search strategies enables rigorous comparison and reveals that careful strategy selection yields dramatic gains in both anytime performance and runtime efficiency across classification and regression tasks.

title: LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search for Constraint Model Reformulation to Improve Solver Efficiency
summary: Combinatorial problems appear in numerous industrial applications. A common approach is to formulate these problems as declarative constraint models that can subsequently be compiled to and solved by a range of back-end solvers. Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce correct models from natural language, but even a correct model can be expensive to solve because performance remains sensitive to modelling choices. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented model reformulation. Inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), we use an evolutionary framework in which an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against the user-defined baseline model. We compare AHD-adapted search strategies that control which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback enter each prompt. Existing retention strategies prioritize recency or performance, but do not explicitly diversify the context. To cover this gap, we introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviourally diverse attempts. We systematically evaluate the strategies on eight CSPLib problems using validation-based final model selection. The results show that: (i) iterative reformulation can produce substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies that keep the retained context diverse outperform those that retain only recent or the fastest attempts; and (iii) validation-based selection improves the held-out speedup of every strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates using LLMs within an evolutionary framework to automatically reformulate constraint models for better solver performance. It introduces Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), a strategy using Maximal Marginal Relevance on runtime vectors to maintain diverse reformulation attempts in the prompt context, and shows that diversity-aware retention combined with validation-based selection yields superior held-out speedups on CSPLib problems.
AI.motivation: Even when LLMs produce correct constraint models from natural language, solving performance is highly sensitive to modeling choices. Manual performance-oriented reformulation is expert-intensive, motivating the need to automate this process using LLMs.
AI.method: An evolutionary framework inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD) where an LLM iteratively proposes candidate reformulations. These are verified and benchmarked against a user-defined baseline. The authors compare various search strategies (retention policies) controlling what prior attempts, instructions, and feedback enter each LLM prompt, and introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviorally diverse attempts. Validation-based final model selection is also employed.
AI.result: Evaluated on eight CSPLib problems: (i) iterative reformulation produces substantial held-out speedups; (ii) diversity-retaining strategies outperform those retaining only recent or fastest attempts; (iii) validation-based selection improves held-out speedup across all strategies.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven automatic model reformulation is viable and effective. Maintaining behavioral diversity in the retained context is key to performance, and validation-based model selection further enhances results.

title: Multi-channel Uplift Policy Learning
summary: E-commerce platforms must allocate fixed marketing budgets across multiple channels to maximize business utility. However, standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in this compositional space due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation. We formulate this challenge as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and propose ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework. Specifically, an agile Orthogonal Teacher extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, while an Explanation-Guided Student distills them into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons. This design enables support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions. Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income.

AI.tldr: ReAlloc is a fast-slow causal framework for multi-channel marketing budget allocation that uses an Orthogonal Teacher for unbiased gradient estimation and an Explanation-Guided Student for long-term policy distillation, achieving simultaneous lifts in pay orders and income on Taobao.
AI.motivation: Standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) approaches fail in multi-channel budget allocation due to observational confounding (channels are not assigned independently) and severe extrapolation (data sparsity under budget constraints). A causal uplift framework is needed that respects the simplex constraint (fixed total budget) and captures cross-channel substitution effects.
AI.method: ReAlloc employs a fast-slow architecture: (1) an Orthogonal Teacher uses short-term randomized log data to extract unbiased local gradients via orthogonalization, mitigating confounding; (2) an Explanation-Guided Student distills these gradients into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons, enabling support-aware conservative decisions that account for cross-channel substitution under simplex constraints.
AI.result: Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on the Taobao platform show ReAlloc achieves significant simultaneous lifts in both pay order volume and overall income compared to baseline allocation strategies.
AI.conclusion: The ReAlloc framework effectively addresses the compositional causal inference challenge in marketing budget allocation, providing a practical solution that bridges short-term unbiased estimation with long-term structured decision-making under simplex constraints.

title: MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed
summary: Retrieving past experiences has become a common strategy to enhance large language model agents. However, most existing memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records to be replayed verbatim, injecting them into the context regardless of whether they align with the agent's current situation. This ``replay'' paradigm ignores the gap between the abstract, general nature of stored experience and the concrete, ever-changing states encountered at decision time, frequently causing negative transfer.
