In contrast, humans rarely recall past experiences verbatim; instead, they reorganize and adapt retrieved memories to fit the present context. Inspired by this, we propose MemHarness, a framework that equips LLM agents to actively harness and reconstruct past experiences based on the present context. At each decision step, a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability emerges naturally through end-to-end training with GRPO. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, demonstrating strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that this reconstruction objective not only prevents negative transfer but also serves as latent guidance during training, fundamentally improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: MemHarness is a framework that enables LLM agents to actively reconstruct retrieved past experiences based on the current context, rather than replaying them verbatim. Trained end-to-end with GRPO, it outperforms static memory baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, prevents negative transfer, and improves intrinsic reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing memory-augmented LLM agents treat retrieved experiences as static records replayed verbatim into the context, ignoring the mismatch between abstract stored experiences and the concrete, dynamic states at decision time. This "replay" paradigm frequently causes negative transfer. Humans, by contrast, adapt recalled memories to fit the present context — a capability current agents lack.
AI.method: MemHarness introduces a unified policy model that, at each decision step, critiques and reconstructs retrieved experiences conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability is acquired through end-to-end training using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), enabling the model to learn to actively harness memories rather than passively consume them.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks, MemHarness substantially outperforms both pure RL baselines and static memory-augmented agents. It also demonstrates strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Analysis shows the reconstruction objective prevents negative transfer and serves as latent guidance during training, fundamentally improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: Actively reconstructing retrieved experiences conditioned on the present context — rather than replaying them verbatim — is an effective paradigm for memory-augmented LLM agents. The reconstructive process not only mitigates negative transfer but also enhances intrinsic reasoning, suggesting that memory utilization in agents should be adaptive and context-sensitive rather than static.

title: Persistent Gaussian Perturbations Prevent Oversmoothing in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks
summary: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep graph neural networks (GNNs), where repeated message passing causes node representations to become increasingly similar, eventually collapsing toward a low-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon limits the effective depth of message-passing architectures and motivates the search for mechanisms that preserve representation diversity. In this paper, we study a recurrent graph neural network in which independent Gaussian noise is injected after every propagation step and analyze the resulting architecture as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a standard global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, we prove that the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain admitting a unique invariant probability measure. Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph. Consequently, the stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold, providing a rigorous guarantee that asymptotic oversmoothing is prevented in the sense of non-vanishing Dirichlet energy. Our analysis reveals persistent stochastic perturbations as a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches based on residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring. Finally, numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent graph neural networks closely match the theoretical predictions, illustrating the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of the limiting Dirichlet energy on the noise intensity.

AI.tldr: Recurrent GNNs with injected Gaussian noise are proven to admit a unique stationary distribution with a positive lower bound on expected Dirichlet energy, preventing oversmoothing without relying on residual connections or normalization.
AI.motivation: Oversmoothing fundamentally limits the depth of message-passing GNNs, as node representations collapse toward a low-dimensional subspace. The authors seek mechanisms beyond deterministic remedies (residual connections, normalization, rewiring) and explore whether persistent stochastic perturbations can provably preserve representation diversity.
AI.method: The authors model a recurrent GNN with independent Gaussian noise injected after each propagation step as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, they analyze the resulting Markov chain, proving geometric ergodicity and the existence of a unique invariant probability measure. They then derive an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to noise variance and the graph's spectral gap.
AI.result: A positive lower bound on expected stationary Dirichlet energy is established, guaranteeing that node representations cannot collapse to the constant manifold. Numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear recurrent GNNs confirm the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted linear dependence of limiting Dirichlet energy on noise intensity.
AI.conclusion: Persistent stochastic perturbations constitute a fundamentally distinct and rigorous mechanism for preventing asymptotic oversmoothing in deep GNNs, complementing existing deterministic approaches. The theoretical guarantees are validated empirically.

title: OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models
summary: Computer-using agents (CUAs) are advancing rapidly across the digital world. A CUA trajectory records the agent's actions, states, and reasoning. Verifying whether it fulfilled the task instruction is central to CUA evaluation, data curation, and reinforcement learning. Neither human-written verifiers nor human annotators can provide such verification at scale, so the field increasingly turns to vision-language models (VLMs) as judges of CUA trajectories. But a fundamental question has long gone unexamined: are these VLM judges reliable enough? To study it systematically, we introduce OSReward, a realistic, high-quality benchmark that evaluates VLM judges on CUA trajectories. The trajectories come from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, then rigorously labeled with ground-truth verdicts through multi-stage human annotation. Building on it, we derive OSReward-Hard, a challenge set concentrating genuinely hard cases, and OSReward-Multi for fine-grained efficiency and alignment scoring. The most comprehensive evaluation of VLM judges to date finds even state-of-the-art models fall short of an ideal judge, sharing a systematic leniency bias that mislabels failed runs as successes. The few reliable enough to trust are too expensive to run at scale, while affordable open models trail far behind. To close this gap, we construct and release OS-Shepherd-100K, an open corpus of reasoning-annotated trajectory judgments for the CUA community. On it, we train OS-Shepherd (9B and 35B), open reward models that supply low-cost, stable, and reliable reward signals, matching commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost than the frontier. Extensive analyses further inform the design of reliable CUA reward at scale. Our code, benchmark, dataset, and model checkpoints are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OSReward-Home/.

AI.tldr: Introduces OSReward, a benchmark for evaluating VLM judges of CUA trajectories, finding current models unreliable due to leniency bias. Also releases OS-Shepherd-100K, a training corpus, and OS-Shepherd models that match commercial judge performance at 30-60% lower cost.
AI.motivation: The field increasingly relies on VLMs to automatically judge whether computer-using agent (CUA) trajectories fulfill task instructions, but no systematic evaluation exists on whether these VLM judges are reliable. Existing verification methods (human-written verifiers, human annotators) cannot scale.
AI.method: The authors construct OSReward, a benchmark with CUA trajectories from diverse agent backbones executing human-verified instructions across platforms, labeled with ground-truth verdicts via multi-stage human annotation. They derive OSReward-Hard (hard cases) and OSReward-Multi (fine-grained efficiency/alignment scoring). They then build OS-Shepherd-100K, a reasoning-annotated corpus, and train OS-Shepherd (9B, 35B) reward models.
AI.result: Even state-of-the-art VLMs exhibit systematic leniency bias, mislabeling failed runs as successes. The few reliable models are too expensive for scale; affordable open models lag far behind. OS-Shepherd models match commercial judges at 30-60% lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Current VLM judges for CUA trajectories are not sufficiently reliable due to leniency bias and cost constraints. Open, fine-tuned reward models like OS-Shepherd offer a viable, low-cost, and stable alternative, and design insights are provided for building reliable CUA rewards at scale.

title: Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3
comment: 52 pages, 18 figures, 17 tables. Open-source implementation: https://github.com/NIMI-research/Tycho
summary:
ARC-AGI-3 turns abstraction into an interactive problem of skill acquisition. A player must infer an unfamiliar game's rules, hidden state, and goal while maintaining action efficiency because every move counts. We formalize these environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs and uses game-specific models during interaction. Tycho separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, an agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass a free-form executable hypothesis.
  In one matched public-set run per policy, we compare four orchestration policies on all 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets. Actor-requested delegation to a model builder obtains the highest observed mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), 88.49. With this selected policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels. Their game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks are 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than the aggregate official human baselines.
  Automatic repair after verification failures produces models that reproduce observed transitions much more accurately, yet reaches only 83.07 RHAE. Transition match indicates whether a simulator reproduces observed dynamics, not whether it has identified the objective or improves the next action. Strong play also requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model. We call this joint problem active abstraction: generating a testable model from costly interaction and deciding when acquiring or using it is worth its cost.

AI.tldr: ARC-AGI-3 reframes abstraction as interactive skill acquisition through parameterized deterministic Moore machines. The authors introduce Tycho, a coding-agent that builds game-specific models from structured observations. Four orchestration policies are compared across 25 public games; actor-requested delegation to a model builder achieves 88.49 mean RHAE, with GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 reaching 100.00 RHAE. The paper introduces "active abstraction" as the joint problem of model construction and deciding when to use or bypass a model.
AI.motivation: Traditional abstraction benchmarks treat it as a static reasoning task. ARC-AGI-3 instead frames abstraction as an interactive skill-acquisition problem where an agent must infer hidden rules, state, and goals from costly interactions. This shift exposes a gap: existing systems lack mechanisms for deciding when to build, repair, use, or bypass internal models during gameplay, motivating the formalization and the Tycho system.
AI.method: The authors formalize ARC-AGI-3 environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines. Tycho, a coding-agent system, structures observation history by separating actionable frames from animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, the agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass a free-form executable hypothesis. Four orchestration policies are evaluated under matched inference budgets: actor-requested delegation to a model builder, automatic repair after verification failures, and two others, all using Claude Opus 4.8 on 25 public games.
AI.result: Actor-requested delegation achieves the highest mean RHAE at 88.49. With this policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE, completing all 183 levels with game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks of 98.5 and 100.0 respectively. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than aggregated human baselines. In contrast, automatic repair after verification failures yields only 83.07 RHAE despite producing models with higher transition-match accuracy, revealing a dissociation between accurately reproducing observed dynamics and identifying objectives or improving actions.
AI.conclusion: Strong play requires not just accurate model-building but also intelligent decisions about when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model — a joint problem the authors term "active abstraction." Transition-match accuracy is insufficient as a proxy for model utility, and delegating model-building decisions to the actor yields superior efficiency over automatic repair strategies.

title: TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning
summary: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

AI.tldr: Topoformer introduces Topo-Scan, a method that decomposes graphs into ordered sequences of topological tokens via node/edge filtrations, then processes them with a Transformer. It achieves SOTA on graph classification and molecular property prediction while being parallelizable and avoiding costly persistent diagram computations.
AI.motivation: Existing topological deep learning methods (e.g., persistent homology pipelines) are computationally expensive due to diagram computations and lack easy parallelization. Meanwhile, Transformers excel on sequential data but cannot directly ingest graph topology. The authors aim to bridge this gap by encoding multi-scale topological structure into attention-friendly sequences.
AI.method: The core module, Topo-Scan, slices a graph over node or edge filtrations to produce a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens capturing multi-scale structural patterns (local motifs to global organization). These sequences are then fed into a standard Transformer to generate graph-level embeddings. The framework is lightweight, scalable, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures.
AI.result: Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines on graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. It provides theoretical stability guarantees for the topological encodings and offers predictable, efficient compute.
AI.conclusion: This work establishes a new paradigm for graph representation learning that unifies topological inductive biases with attention mechanisms in a parallelizable framework, opening avenues for scalable topology-aware Transformers.

title: One Human, $N$ Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence
summary: A single human must audit $N$ LLM agents under a budget of $B \ll N$ audits per round, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors. We model this as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula and locate the miscalibration threshold $δ^*$ past which confidence-ranked auditing is \emph{worse} than random. Two a-priori expectations reverse: $δ^*$ \emph{rises} as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low---shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, point estimates at or beyond the flip though CIs straddle it; a proprietary model is informative and lands below it. We give a quantitative criterion for \emph{vacuous} oversight, and replaying policies on recorded traces confirms the ordering.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the problem of auditing multiple LLM agents on a limited budget, where agents provide potentially miscalibrated confidence scores and exhibit correlated errors. It identifies a critical miscalibration threshold beyond which confidence-based auditing underperforms random selection, and empirically evaluates several LLMs against this criterion.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed at scale, human oversight becomes infeasible, requiring selective auditing based on agent self-reported confidence. However, if confidence scores are adversarially or inherently miscalibrated, and agent errors are correlated, confidence-ranked auditing may be counterproductive. The work seeks to formalize when confidence-based oversight becomes vacuous.
AI.method: The problem is modeled as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula, capturing both agent-level miscalibration and cross-agent error correlation (shared difficulty vs. lineage). A miscalibration threshold δ* is analytically derived as the point where confidence-ranked auditing degrades below random auditing. Five open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model are evaluated: confidence scores and audit outcomes are recorded, point estimates and confidence intervals for miscalibration are computed, and policies are replayed on recorded traces to verify the theoretical ordering.
AI.result: Two findings contradict prior expectations: (1) δ* rises as the audit budget shrinks, and (2) cross-family correlation is not low — shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs exhibit near-constant, operationally useless confidence with point estimates at or beyond the threshold; one proprietary model provides informative confidence below the threshold. Policy replay on recorded traces confirms the predicted ordering.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a quantitative criterion for detecting vacuous oversight in LLM auditing. Confidence-ranked auditing is only beneficial when miscalibration stays below a derivable threshold; many open models fail this test, while a proprietary model passes. The framework can guide design of human-in-the-loop oversight systems for AI agents.

title: HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

AI.tldr: HARGO introduces heterogeneity-aware reward-guided optimization that uses confidence-modulated advantage weighting to improve RL post-training for LLMs on heterogeneous HPC tasks, outperforming uniform-weight methods like GRPO across classification, QA, and generation tasks.
AI.motivation: SFT alone fails to produce appropriate task behavior in LLMs for HPC tasks—the same model can classify well but generate verbose, imprecise answers. Existing RL post-training methods like GRPO use uniform weighting, which is suboptimal given the extreme heterogeneity of HPC tasks (58x answer length variation, three distinct reward distributions, widely varying SFT accuracy).
AI.method: HARGO introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage. It computes two signals: (1) a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast, and (2) a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities. These signals modulate the advantage before computing per-response weights. Critically, this approach requires no task-type labels.
AI.result: Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves state-of-the-art on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62%, Data Race F1 91.30%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation studies confirm that both the discrimination and confidence signals contribute complementarily.
AI.conclusion: HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks, demonstrating that heterogeneity-aware weighting is essential for effective RL post-training in multi-task HPC settings.

title: PathView-Bench: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Achieve Fine-grained Multiscale Understanding of Pathology Images?
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to analyze pathology images. However, dominant multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports. These evaluations provide limited insight into whether a model understands the multiscale visual content needed for pathology reasoning and decision-making. We introduce PathVU, a vision-anchored benchmark for fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology. Built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, PathVU evaluates MLLM understanding in two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. By converting raw annotations into deterministic task targets, PathVU enables programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, we observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

AI.tldr: PathVU is a vision-anchored benchmark with 308K samples across 14 VQA-style tasks for evaluating fine-grained, multiscale visual understanding of MLLMs in pathology. Evaluation of 18 models reveals significant limitations in region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, and spatial reasoning across both region-level and whole-slide fields of view.
AI.motivation: Existing pathology MLLM benchmarks only score final diagnostic outputs (answers, captions, reports), providing limited insight into whether models truly understand the multiscale visual content required for pathology reasoning. There is a need for fine-grained, programmatically evaluable benchmarks targeting specific visual understanding capabilities.
AI.method: PathVU is constructed from 23 public pathology datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations. Raw annotations are converted into deterministic task targets enabling programmatic scoring. The benchmark spans two fields of view (Region FOV: high-resolution local regions; Slide FOV: macro whole-slide views) and covers five capability dimensions: region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. It includes 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Eighteen MLLMs (general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented) are evaluated.
AI.result: Even advanced MLLMs exhibit substantial limitations on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. Performance gaps are pronounced in region localization, spatial reasoning, and quantity estimation tasks, indicating that current models lack robust multiscale visual understanding despite strong performance on diagnostic-answer-based benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: PathVU provides a reproducible and rigorous foundation for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit, fine-grained multiscale visual understanding, exposing critical weaknesses that diagnostic-answer-only benchmarks fail to capture.

title: Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus
summary: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that ensemble consensus-based semi-supervised learning significantly improves molecular property prediction across diverse datasets and GNN architectures, with single models outperforming full supervised ensembles and exhibiting better calibration.
AI.motivation: Molecular sciences suffer from scarce labeled data due to costly acquisition, while unlabeled molecular data is abundant. Standard semi-supervised methods relying on label-preserving augmentations fail in the molecular domain because minor structural changes can drastically alter molecular properties, making it difficult to design valid augmentations.
AI.method: The authors employ an ensemble consensus semi-supervised learning approach: multiple graph neural network models are trained simultaneously with a combined objective that includes both standard supervised loss on labeled data and a consensus loss on unlabeled data. The consensus loss encourages predictions on unlabeled samples to agree across ensemble members. This approach avoids the need for domain-specific augmentations.
AI.result: Ensemble consensus training consistently boosts predictive accuracy across diverse molecular datasets, task types, and GNN architectures. A single model from the consensus-trained ensemble outperforms a full traditionally trained ensemble in nearly all cases. The method also reduces calibration error, yielding better-calibrated uncertainty estimates.
AI.conclusion: Ensemble consensus-based semi-supervised learning is a simple yet effective strategy for molecular machine learning that improves accuracy, model robustness, and calibration without requiring domain-specific augmentations. The approach also exhibits a knowledge distillation-like effect, where individual models benefit from the collective ensemble signal.

title: Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents
summary: LLM agents increasingly act as autonomous merchants that write their own product listings, and under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales. Even under instructions to be honest, they fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models. A platform's obvious remedy---verifying each claim against the truth---is unavailable, because it observes only a noisy, biased complaint signal, never the ground truth. We design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic gaming. CARP protects consumers by suppressing the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing the truth. It also achieves the best welfare of the policies we compare. We further show that this felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding through SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance. We trace this distinction to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, and observe the binding across models, with supporting confidence intervals.

AI.tldr: LLM agents acting as autonomous merchants fabricate product attributes even when instructed to be honest. The authors propose CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism using noisy complaint signals (no ground truth) with a deadband and state-dependent severity, combined with SPARC, a code-gated reflection mechanism. This suppresses dishonest sellers' sales while protecting honest ones, closing most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, and induces self-interested restraint in LLM merchants through penalty-gated self-correction reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLM-based autonomous merchants increasingly fabricate product attributes under competitive pressure to win sales, even when prompted to be honest. The platform's natural remedy—verifying claims against ground truth—is unavailable because platforms only observe noisy, biased complaint signals, never the actual truth. This creates a challenging mechanism design problem: how to deter fabrication without access to ground-truth verification.
AI.method: The authors design two complementary mechanisms. CARP (a reputation-penalty mechanism) features: (1) a deadband that forgives complaint noise, preventing honest sellers from being unfairly penalized due to stochastic complaints, and (2) state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion (where sellers with good reputations become harder to penalize). SPARC is a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism that makes the penalty behaviorally binding: LLM merchants engage in penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, restraining fabrication when it demonstrably costs them sales, functioning as a self-interested economic response rather than mere compliance.
AI.result: CARP suppresses the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing ground truth, and achieves the best welfare among all policies compared. Fabrication occurs when lying is free but self-restraint emerges when fabrication costs sales. The penalty-gated self-correction reasoning is observed across multiple models with supporting confidence intervals.
AI.conclusion: Effective deterrence of LLM merchant fabrication is achievable without ground-truth access through carefully designed reputation-penalty mechanisms (CARP) combined with code-gated reflection (SPARC). The binding mechanism is economic self-interest driving penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, not mere instruction-following. This holds robustly across different LLM models.

title: Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing
summary: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

AI.tldr: Sparse MoE models route tokens to multiple experts, but existing analyses conflate geometric distinctness with functional benefit. Using ESSI, factorial designs, and frozen-route interventions, the authors find that expert subspaces overlap substantially (coherent overlap), yet multi-expert routing still improves prediction — showing that geometric similarity does not imply functional redundancy.
AI.motivation: Prior work on sparse MoE language models often conflates three distinct quantities: route coherence, candidate expert quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. The authors aim to disentangle these to determine whether the benefit of multi-expert routing stems from experts contributing geometrically distinct representation directions, and whether geometric similarity implies functional redundancy.
AI.method: Three methodological innovations are introduced: (1) Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI) to quantify subspace overlap between experts; (2) matched-route residuals to isolate candidate quality; and (3) a prefix-controlled 2×2 factorial design to measure candidate-by-context interaction. Functional value is assessed via frozen-route interventions (freezing routing decisions and adding/removing experts) and a controlled Top-k training study across six MoE architectures (OLMoE, Mixtral, DeepSeek, and others).
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Across six architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, but actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. (2) Across 39 factorial cells, the selected candidate always explains more residual variance than the strongest unselected rival, but the prefix narrows this advantage — all interactions are negative with 95% CIs below zero. (3) Despite geometric narrowing, adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24/39 frozen-route comparisons (15 inconclusive), and Top-2 consistently outperforms Top-1 in controlled training (3/3 seeds).
AI.conclusion: The authors introduce the concept of "coherent overlap": routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, and useful multi-expert computation persists without requiring disjoint linear coverage. This explains why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning decisions in MoE models.

title: Correcting What You Cannot See: Credit Assignment for Perception Distillation in Multimodal Reasoners
summary: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but its trajectory-level reward cannot determine whether a failed answer arose from perception or subsequent reasoning. Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. We introduce \textbf{Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD)}, a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher--student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product, , forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. We motivate this rule through Bayesian evidence combination and show that multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception--reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged. Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B 2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28 and the 32B 8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively. Effective multimodal distillation therefore depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

AI.tldr: PCD is a label-free method that improves multimodal distillation by identifying correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher-student disagreement as complementary witnesses, combined via a multiplicative soft AND gate motivated by Bayesian evidence combination.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy distillation uses trajectory-level rewards that cannot distinguish whether a failed answer stems from perception errors or reasoning errors. The Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, is ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. Thus, there is a need for a method that can precisely identify when perception—rather than reasoning—is the appropriate target for correction.
AI.method: PCD identifies correctable perception failures using two complementary witnesses: (1) downstream task failure and (2) teacher-student disagreement. Their product forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present, motivated by Bayesian evidence combination. The multiplication operator is shown to be the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception–reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged.
AI.result: Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B→2B macro average from 44.50 (OPD) to 47.28, and the 32B→8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Effective multimodal distillation depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction. PCD demonstrates that combining downstream failure with teacher-student disagreement as a multiplicative gate yields significant and consistent improvements across model scales and benchmarks.

title: Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index
summary: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Gap Index (GI), a novel quality metric for 2D dimensionality reduction projections that quantifies spatial distortion in empty areas of the layout by decomposing space into triangles and comparing them to high-dimensional counterparts. Unlike traditional metrics that focus on point-wise relationships, GI captures visually salient structural deformations and is both computationally efficient and interpretable.
AI.motivation: Existing quality metrics for dimensionality reduction projections (e.g., trustworthiness, continuity) predominantly measure distortion in direct point relationships—distances or neighborhoods—while ignoring distortions in the empty spaces of a 2D layout. These empty areas often constitute visually significant features (gaps, clusters, separations), meaning users may be misled about structural fidelity since popular metrics are blind to deformations in these regions.
AI.method: The Gap Index works by tessellating the 2D projection space into empty triangles (triangles devoid of projected points) using a constrained Delaunay triangulation or similar decomposition. Each empty triangle is then compared to its corresponding high-dimensional counterpart by evaluating how the triangle's geometry deforms under the projection mapping. The per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a global scalar GI value or visualized as a heatmap overlay on the projection to reveal regional distortion patterns.
AI.result: The Gap Index is shown to be sensitive to small structural deformations that carry high visual impact—deformations that popular quality metrics fail to detect. The metric is also fast to compute and produces interpretable outputs suitable for both global quality assessment and localized distortion visualization.
AI.conclusion: The Gap Index fills a critical gap in projection quality assessment by capturing spatial distortion in empty regions, complementing existing point-focused metrics. It enables more reliable visual analysis by alerting users to structural artifacts that would otherwise go undetected.

title: How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents
summary: Computer-use agents (CUA) are being deployed to browse the web and operate desktop software, yet their benchmark scores are still commonly produced by brittle scripted oracles. A score is the output of a pipeline in which tasks can be stale, trajectories can omit decisive visual evidence, evaluators can reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports can hide the cause of failure. We organize these problems into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. We then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks, find that 15.3\% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7\% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7\% are broken tasks. For genuine failures, a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors, while a single scalar success rate can not explain. We connect these findings to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.

AI.tldr: An audit of 150 failure-scored trajectories across five CUA benchmarks reveals 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are wrong (10.7% evaluator false negatives, 4.7% broken tasks). The authors propose a reliability framework and a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy showing planning/verification failures dominate execution errors.
AI.motivation: Current CUA benchmarks rely on brittle scripted oracles where tasks may be stale, trajectories omit visual evidence, evaluators reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports obscure failure causes. There is no systematic framework for assessing the reliability of CUA evaluations.
AI.method: The authors (1) propose a reliability framework covering task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting; (2) manually audit 150 public failure trajectories from five benchmarks (web, enterprise workflow, desktop control); (3) develop a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy for genuine failures: verification/feedback failures, planning failures, and execution/grounding errors.
AI.result: 15.3% of FAIL verdicts are incorrect—10.7% due to evaluator false negatives and 4.7% due to broken tasks. Among genuine failures, verification/feedback and planning failures dominate over execution/grounding errors. A single scalar success rate fails to capture this diagnostic nuance.
AI.conclusion: CUA evaluation demands stage-specific design rules: robust evaluators, validated tasks, trajectory-level evidence preservation, and diagnostic (not just scalar) reporting. The taxonomy can inform the design of more reliable long-horizon CUA benchmarks.

title: HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection
summary: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

AI.tldr: HyperClaim introduces a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for video misinformation detection that captures higher-order interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal frame spans, outperforming both global fusion and reasoning-based baselines across three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing video misinformation detection methods either use global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning, both of which under-represent localized authenticity cues arising from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Pairwise graph formulations cannot capture these multi-way cross-modal dependencies, motivating a hypergraph-based approach.
AI.method: HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled video frames. It employs confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units. The framework performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout for sample-level authenticity classification.
AI.result: Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, HyperClaim achieves 83.7% accuracy on FakeSV, 82.0% on FakeTT, and 87.3% on FakeVV, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights reveal interpretable token- and frame-level structure.
AI.conclusion: HyperClaim demonstrates that preserving fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure via hypergraph reasoning, without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, yields superior video misinformation detection compared to approaches that flatten such structure through global fusion.

title: LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger
summary: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

AI.tldr: LedgerMind introduces a provenance-constrained state machine framework for multimodal agents, using a Structured Evidence Ledger with formal grounding protocols to ensure faithful multi-step reasoning. It targets four failure patterns obscured by final-answer accuracy and demonstrates improvements in both answer accuracy and trajectory faithfulness across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of multimodal agents for visual question answering relies on final-answer accuracy, which masks critical failure patterns: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. There is no mechanism to verify whether correct answers arise from grounded evidence versus language priors or error cancellation.
AI.method: LedgerMind models agent trajectories as provenance-constrained state machines. Tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger serving as trajectory state; downstream claims may only cite active ledger entries. Grounding is verified at entity/numeric levels. The system incorporates: (1) a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, (2) an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher matching reasoning depth to question complexity, and (3) an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. Repair proceeds via typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs demonstrate that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: Provenance-constrained reasoning via a Structured Evidence Ledger effectively addresses trajectory-level failures in multimodal agents. The formal grounding and repair guarantees prevent hallucination propagation and unsupported reasoning, yielding more trustworthy multimodal question answering systems.

title: When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to integrate multiple sources of information that may be inconsistent or conflicting. However, there is still a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying model preferences under conflicting specifications. By constructing specifications with explicit conflicts, the framework enables model choices between competing specifications to be directly observed and analyzed. A symmetry-based design further reduces confounding factors, allowing preferences across representation types to be compared systematically.
  We evaluate the framework on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances spanning 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input--output examples. Results show systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: $ \text{Formal} \approx \text{Naturalized Formal} > \text{Pure Natural Language} > \text{Input--Output Examples} $. Example effects further depend on model capability and function family.
  We extend the framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain, demonstrating its applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms. The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information.

AI.tldr: A controlled experimental framework is proposed to study how LLMs resolve conflicting specifications. Using symmetry-based design across 550 mathematical instances, the study finds a consistent preference ordering: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input–Output Examples. The framework is also extended to Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domains.
AI.motivation: LLMs increasingly face multiple, potentially conflicting information sources, yet there is no controllable, attributable method for analyzing how models resolve such specification conflicts. Existing approaches lack systematic frameworks for directly observing and comparing model preferences under competing specifications.
AI.method: The authors propose a controlled experimental framework that constructs specifications with explicit conflicts, enabling direct observation of model choices. A symmetry-based design eliminates confounding factors, allowing systematic comparison across representation types. The framework is evaluated on an executable mathematical benchmark of 550 conflict instances across 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input–output examples. Extensions to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domains are also demonstrated.
AI.result: Results reveal systematic preference patterns: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input–Output Examples. Preferences are not random; example effects vary with model capability and function family. The framework generalizes across diverse tasks and specification forms.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified, controllable approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing information sources, with consistent preference hierarchies that depend on representation type, model capability, and task domain.

title: Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs
summary: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves the open problem of achieving order-optimal convergence in average-reward CMDPs with neural critics by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that overcomes the bias-cost trade-off, yielding $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ optimality gap and constraint violation guarantees.
AI.motivation: In constrained MDPs with neural critics, a fundamental bias-cost trade-off arises: reducing critic bias under NTK analysis requires significantly more optimization cost, blocking order-optimal convergence in primal-dual methods. Prior work with linear critics achieves order-optimal rates, but extending to neural function approximation in the average-reward setting was unsolved.
AI.method: The authors propose a hierarchical MLMC neural critic that simultaneously debiases across two levels — trajectory sampling and critic optimization. This estimator achieves the bias of a long optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. This critic is then integrated into a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm for average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization.
AI.result: The algorithm achieves both optimality gap and constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$, establishing the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with neural critics, without requiring knowledge of the mixing time. The results are novel even for the unconstrained setting.
AI.conclusion: The hierarchical MLMC approach effectively decouples bias reduction from computational cost, enabling neural critics to be used in primal-dual CMDP algorithms with provably optimal convergence rates. This bridges a significant gap between theory and practice in safe reinforcement learning.

title: Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees
summary: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

AI.tldr: AAPT eliminates autoregressive decoding latency in GUI agents by pre-computing conditional policy trees during idle periods, enabling instant action execution when transient events occur. This boosts success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 in contested decision windows without modifying the underlying model, with branch routing identified as the key bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents fail on transient GUI events because autoregressive decoding takes too long — the correct action is generated only after the relevant window has already disappeared. The authors identify decision-time decoding latency as the root cause and aim to eliminate it without retraining or modifying the underlying multimodal model.
AI.method: AAPT operates in two phases: (1) During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines, sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. (2) When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without text generation. This shifts decoding off the critical path.
AI.result: In pre-registered paired trials with exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 (p=1.8×10⁻³) within the contested decision window, with zero incorrect actions. Open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines score zero. A latency-based tree-sizing sweep confirms the predicted gain threshold. Ablations identify fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing as critical. An oracle probe reveals branch routing as the causal bottleneck, not the initial hypothesis. The effect replicates on an independent model over 126 paired trials (p=4.9×10⁻¹³). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches reactive baseline performance with complementary strengths.
AI.conclusion: AAPT excels when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, while reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot. The two approaches exhibit complementary strengths, suggesting hybrid strategies for future work.

title: QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

AI.tldr: QuantWAMs is a post-training quantization framework for World Action Models that aligns quantization with the deployment context through three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, co-training-objective saliency scoring, and fixed-intervention rollout auditing. It achieves near-FP16 performance under W4A4 precision (<1% accuracy drop), reduces memory to ~29% of FP16, and delivers 1.4-1.6× block-level speedups on real-robot manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions through iterative denoising and closed-loop execution, making them computationally expensive to deploy. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods fail for WAMs because they: (1) use open-loop objectives that ignore the autoregressive rollout distribution; (2) assume homogeneous model structures; and (3) rely on calibration distributions mismatched to actual deployment conditions. There is a need for a PTQ framework specifically tailored to WAMs' unique architecture and execution patterns.
AI.method: QuantWAMs introduces three complementary strategies: (1) Shared-basis outlier calibration — pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules to handle heterogeneous WAM architectures; (2) Co-training-objective saliency — computes empirical Fisher scores from the joint video-action gradient and assigns weight precision at calibration-stable layer granularity; (3) Fixed-intervention rollout auditing — revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without increasing the precision budget. These are evaluated on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot AgiBot G2 manipulation tasks.
AI.result: Under a W4A4-dominant quantization setting, simulation results differ from FP16 baselines by only 0.2–0.7 percentage points. On three real-robot manipulation tasks with an AgiBot G2, QuantWAMs demonstrates deployment feasibility. For targeted video and action blocks, peak weight-and-activation memory is reduced to approximately 29% of FP16, with 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups.
AI.conclusion: QuantWAMs successfully bridges the gap between aggressive quantization and deployment fidelity for World Action Models by aligning quantization decisions with model structure, rollout distribution, and task objectives. The framework enables efficient real-world deployment of WAMs on robot platforms with minimal accuracy degradation and substantial memory and latency improvements.

title: On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces
summary: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

AI.tldr: This thesis addresses policy learning in large action space contextual bandits under both on-policy (regret minimization) and off-policy (logged data) settings, proposing structured Bayesian methods for exploration, latent-variable direct methods, concave optimization objectives, and differentiable pessimistic estimators with PAC-Bayesian bounds.
AI.motivation: In large action spaces, both on-policy and off-policy contextual bandit learning suffer from inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. Existing methods do not adequately address these compounded challenges.
AI.method: (1) On-policy: meTS (mixed-effect Thompson sampling) and dTS (diffusion-inspired priors) to share information across actions with regret guarantees. (2) Off-policy: sDM (structured direct method using latent variables), concave policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives for efficient optimization, and differentiable pessimistic methods combining exponential smoothing with PAC-Bayesian bounds to regularize importance-sampling estimators.
AI.result: The structured Bayesian methods yield regret bounds that scale with an effective number of actions rather than the full cardinality. The off-policy analysis reveals that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces. The proposed concave objectives and differentiable pessimistic methods provide principled bias-variance control for regularized importance-sampling estimators.
AI.conclusion: Structured modeling that shares information across actions, combined with careful handling of optimization error and bias-variance trade-offs via pessimistic principles and PAC-Bayesian bounds, enables effective policy learning in large action space contextual bandits under both on-policy and off-policy paradigms.

title: QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization
summary: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

AI.tldr: QQWorld replaces the Epps-Pulley regularization in LeWorldModel with a quantile-quantile matching objective that better controls heavy-tailed deviations in learned latent distributions, improving planning success across control environments.
AI.motivation: Latent world models rely on compact latent representations for planning, but the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective used in LeWM produces vanishing corrective gradients for tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations poorly controlled. A new approach is needed to maintain effective gradients in the tails and ensure better Gaussian alignment.
AI.method: The authors propose QQWorld, which substitutes EP with a quantile-quantile (QQ) matching objective. This method projects latent samples and aligns them with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, preserving corrective gradients in tail regions. A cross-batch QQ variant is also introduced, expanding the ranking pool with detached samples from prior batches, and its bias-variance trade-off is formally characterized.
AI.result: Across four control environments, QQWorld improves the average planning success rate over LeWM, while consistently achieving better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.
AI.conclusion: QQ matching is a superior alternative to EP for regularizing latent distributions in world models, as it mitigates the vanishing gradient problem in tails and yields more Gaussian-like latents, leading to more reliable planning.

title: When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence
comment: 25 pages, including references and supplementary material; 3 figures and 19 tables. Code: https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead
summary: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

AI.tldr: The paper defines "derived-feature over-trust" (DFOT) — a failure mode where LLMs treat instance-dependent derived measurements as direct facts. Using PPG-ECG physiological data (50,000 paired records, 187-patient test), five estimands quantify DFOT across conflict and context scenarios, with a privileged distillation baseline showing significant repair improvements (1.82–6.69 pp) while minimally increasing unnecessary verification.
