AI.motivation: Derived measurements (e.g., PPG-based heart rhythm) are increasingly fed into LLM pipelines as if they were direct, ground-truth facts, despite their validity being instance-dependent. No formal framework exists to define, detect, or quantify this over-trust phenomenon, which can cascade errors downstream in clinical and other high-stakes applications.
AI.method: The authors formalize DFOT and design two test scenarios (D1: conflict where PPG contradicts gold-standard ECG; D2: misleading context where reliable PPG is doubted due to severe history). Five estimands are defined: Conflict Over-Trust Rate (COTR), Context-Induced Error Rate (CIR), Correct Repair Rate (CRR), Evidence-Specific Repair Margin (ESRM), and Utility Harm Rate (UHR). The framework is demonstrated on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation (training with ECG supervision never shown to the LLM at inference) as a baseline reliability generator, evaluated on a protocol-locked 187-patient test set.
AI.result: The privileged distillation baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82–6.69 percentage points (all paired CIs exclude zero). The Utility Harm Rate increases by only 0.67 pp (95% CI: −0.4 to +1.7), indicating minimal additional unnecessary verification burden.
AI.conclusion: DFOT provides a unified, generator-agnostic evaluation framework for measuring derived-feature over-trust in LLM pipelines. The baseline results establish initial benchmarks, while the framework itself enables systematic development and comparison of stronger mitigation methods. Code is publicly released.

title: QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

AI.tldr: QAdapt is a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework that learns local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, adapts to evolving noise conditions while avoiding catastrophic forgetting, and feeds residual syndrome to a conventional decoder. It reduces logical error rates across 110 synthetic noise configurations and achieves up to 5.79% LER reduction and 9.32% latency reduction on Google's Willow benchmark data.
AI.motivation: FTQC performance is bottlenecked by classical decoder latency and degraded by fixed neural decoders under hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, nonstationary, and subject to simulation-to-reality distribution shift. A practical solution must adapt online to evolving noise without retraining from scratch.
AI.method: QAdapt is a neural pre-decoding framework for surface codes that captures local spatiotemporal syndrome correlations, sequentially adapts to drifting noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and passes residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. It functions as a noise-adaptive front-end, remaining decoder-compatible.
AI.result: On 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations, QAdapt consistently reduces logical error rate vs. the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves up to 5.79% LER reduction and 9.32% backend decoding latency reduction on the residual syndrome.
AI.conclusion: QAdapt offers a practical, decoder-compatible approach that improves both robustness and backend decoding efficiency of QEC under evolving hardware noise, bridging the gap between static neural decoders and real-world nonstationary noise environments.

title: A foundation model of numerical intelligence with cross-disciplinary generalization
summary: Intelligence is commonly understood as the ability to acquire and apply knowledge, adapt to unfamiliar situations and solve new problems. Large language models exhibit this capacity by inferring task-relevant knowledge from textual context and applying it to new tasks. Yet intelligence need not be confined to language. For scientific and social systems, we need models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context-an ability we call numerical intelligence. Here we introduce UNified In-Context Operator Networks (UNICON), a foundation model that exhibits numerical intelligence across disciplines. Using graph-based examples from a system as context, UNICON infers the predictive relation shared across them and applies it to queries from the same system. Across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training, the same model approaches specialist performance without retraining. Combining UNICON with language-model agents yields further gains, enabling it to surpass state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen in training. We further show that training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines. Together, these results establish UNICON as a foundation model of numerical intelligence and position it as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: UNICON is a foundation model that exhibits "numerical intelligence" — the ability to infer predictive relations from graph-based numerical examples (in-context) and apply them to new queries from the same system, generalizing across scientific and social disciplines, including unseen ones.
AI.motivation: Intelligence is not limited to language; scientific and social systems require models that can acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context. Existing models lack this "numerical intelligence" — the capacity to infer task-relevant knowledge from numerical examples in-context and generalize across diverse disciplines.
AI.method: The authors introduce UNICON (UNified In-Context Operator Networks), a foundation model that uses graph-based examples from a system as context to infer shared predictive relations and apply them to new queries. The model is combined with language-model agents, and training-corpus diversity is investigated as a factor for improving generalization.
AI.result: UNICON approaches specialist-level performance across scientific and social systems, including disciplines absent from training, without retraining. When combined with language-model agents, it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists in an unseen discipline. Greater training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines.
AI.conclusion: UNICON establishes itself as a foundation model for numerical intelligence and serves as a building block for a broader AI ecosystem that integrates both textual and numerical reasoning capabilities.

title: Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification
comment: 42 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables, was presented at the 10th International Conference 'Deep Learning on Computational Physics (DLCP2026)', under review for the Moscow University Physics Bulletin, Physics series
summary: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

AI.tldr: KSSE replaces dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of a Random-Bond Ising Model, achieving 88.93% Top-1 on ImageNet-1000 with ~21M parameters — 10–30× smaller than comparable vision transformers.
AI.motivation: Dense classifier layers in modern vision models impose heavy parameter and computational costs. The authors seek a physics-inspired alternative that leverages sparse graph structures and spectral methods to match state-of-the-art accuracy with drastically reduced model footprint.
AI.method: Pre-trained features are mapped onto quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs, where a regularized graph Laplacian acts as a Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian. D independent channel spectral problems are solved via FFT on circulant blocks (exploiting Pontryagin self-duality of Z/pZ) and low-order Rayleigh refinement (k_mode=5). Graph topology is optimized via "star-domain surgery" — edge shifts that create local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration. Six theoretical results are proved: (1) generalized Ihara–Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian, (2) trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence, (3) additive channel separability with exchange-correlation bound, (4) surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width Ω(1/√d_min), (5) quasi-stationarity perturbation bound, (6) fixed-point convergence theorem. Multi-scale fractal analysis via the D2 spectrum certifies a landscape transition from rough to star-domain basins.
AI.result: KSSE achieves 88.93% Top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features (D=1792) using ~21.24M parameters. This outperforms Swin-L (197M, 86.4–87.3%) and matches ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0–89.5%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by 10× and 30× respectively.
AI.conclusion: Sparse-graph spectral embedding at the Nishimori temperature, combined with star-domain surgery for graph topology optimization and FFT-based spectral solvers, provides a parameter-efficient alternative to dense classifiers that matches or exceeds large transformer performance. The theoretical framework (six theorems) rigorously supports the empirical results.

title: Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory
summary: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

AI.tldr: Introduces short-term graph memory, a plug-in module using an online graph neural surrogate to pre-screen candidate molecules, improving oracle budget efficiency in molecular optimization across multiple generators.
AI.motivation: Molecular optimization suffers from limited oracle budgets, making the selection of which molecules to evaluate as critical as generation. Existing generators lack a mechanism to learn from previously evaluated molecules during a run to prioritize future queries.
AI.method: A plug-in module called short-term graph memory maintains an online graph neural network (GNN) surrogate trained on previously evaluated molecules. The surrogate pre-screens each round's candidate pool, ranking molecules by predicted utility so the fixed oracle budget is allocated to high-potential candidates. This preserves the underlying generator's architecture and update rule.
AI.result: Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard benchmark, it improves mean top-10 score with no extra oracle cost and never underperforms the base. Gains generalize across all four tested generators at a tight budget of 1,000 calls. Analysis shows benefit depends on two backbone properties: search breadth and native exploitation of oracle feedback.
AI.conclusion: The surrogate-guided selection module offers a simple, architecture-agnostic way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively. Its effectiveness at larger budgets is predicted by the generator's search breadth and native exploitation capability.

title: LeanCSP: A Framework for Certifying Constraint Reformulation and Solving in Lean
summary: Constraint programming is a core technology for solving complex combinatorial problems in scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Trusting its results therefore demands guarantees at two levels: that reformulations applied beforehand are semantics-preserving, and that solvers produce correct answers. In this work, we introduce a framework that addresses both verification levels in the Lean theorem prover: it can be used to prove formulation-level properties, such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and the correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families; and to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats such as MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end workflow that establishes the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting the external solver. Experimental results show that our framework's verified symmetry breaking also pays off in practice: a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, while the entire in-Lean certification stays affordable, taking at most a few minutes for our largest instances.

AI.tldr: A Lean-based framework providing end-to-end verification for constraint programming: parametric proofs of formulation-level properties (equivalence, symmetry breaking correctness) combined with solver certificate checking, achieving up to 2×10⁷ reduction in solver search effort with affordable certification times.
AI.motivation: Constraint programming solvers and problem reformulations require trustworthiness at two levels: (1) that preprocessing reformulations preserve semantics, and (2) that solvers produce correct results. Existing approaches address these separately; this work aims to unify both verification levels in a single proof assistant framework.
AI.method: The authors implement a framework in Lean supporting: (a) parametric proofs over entire problem families for formulation-level properties like equivalence, equisatisfiability, and symmetry-breaking correctness; (b) translation backends to MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB for certificate checking of individual instances; and (c) an end-to-end workflow combining both to establish satisfiability/unsatisfiability without trusting the external solver.
AI.result: Verified symmetry breaking using a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2×10⁷. Full in-Lean certification remains affordable, taking at most a few minutes for the largest instances tested.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that combining formulation-level parametric verification with instance-level certificate checking yields a practical end-to-end trusted constraint solving pipeline, with verified symmetry breaking delivering significant performance gains alongside formal guarantees.

title: A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports
summary: Vision-language models remain underused in colonoscopy despite the rich expert descriptions recorded in routine reports. These reports document lesion appearance, size and location but summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. Here we develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists. These results suggest that recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

AI.tldr: EndoCLIP recovers lesion-level image-text pairs from routine colonoscopy reports to train a vision-language model that outperforms existing encoders on retrieval, report generation, and classification, approaching expert-level accuracy for benign-vs-malignant discrimination.
AI.motivation: Colonoscopy reports contain rich expert descriptions but are procedure-level summaries, leaving individual frames unannotated. This weak linkage between images and clinical findings prevents effective use of vision-language models in colonoscopy.
AI.method: The authors developed EndoCLIP, a vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs automatically recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records through finding-to-frame correspondence recovery. The model is evaluated on image-text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. A blinded reader study with 12 endoscopists benchmarks benign-vs-malignant classification.
AI.result: EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders across all tasks. Its linear probe on benign-versus-malignant classification approaches the performance of expert endoscopists in the 12-reader blinded study.
AI.conclusion: Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence from routine documentation can transform clinical records into scalable supervision, allowing clinical targets to be specified in natural language rather than requiring task-specific manual annotation.

title: The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse
summary:
Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes how algorithmic recourse can backfire when recommendations enable strategic gaming rather than genuine improvement. Using a causal performative framework, the authors show that ignoring causal relationships among features leads to unstable equilibria and degraded accuracy, while causally-aware recourse yields stable, effective recommendations that reduce the need for repeated retraining.
AI.motivation: Existing algorithmic recourse methods focus narrowly on flipping predictions without ensuring recommended changes reflect genuine qualification improvements. This creates a failure mode: individuals strategically game the classifier, inducing distribution shifts that degrade predictive accuracy and render the recourse policy ineffective after model retraining. The paper aims to formally characterize and resolve this problem.
AI.method: The authors propose a causal performative framework for recourse, modeling how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model (SCM) that captures feature interactions and effects on the true label. This yields a non-convex optimization problem. They characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed using simple iterative dynamics, contrasting standard empirical risk minimization (ERM) with causally-informed recourse policies.
AI.result: Causal recourse leads to stable equilibria with reduced incentives for gaming, while recourse policies ignorant of causal structure induce large, misaligned behavioral responses. Experiments on semi-synthetic and real credit datasets show the approach consistently outperforms standard ERM and reduces the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate strategic distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Deploying recourse without accounting for causal feature relationships is fundamentally unstable. Causal performative prediction offers a principled solution: by modeling how recommendations causally affect both features and true outcomes, one can design recourse policies that converge to stable equilibria, improve genuine qualifications, and maintain predictive accuracy over time.

title: Towards Autonomous Aircraft Surveillance from Nanosatellites through On-Board Inference and Generative Data Augmentation
summary: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have a limited downlink budget, yet the conventional approach still transmits terabytes of raw imagery to the ground for processing, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations either delay timely decision-making or prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes. In this paper, a workflow that combines on-board inference with generative data augmentation is proposed to address both limitations jointly. Inference is executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated, pseudo-labelled, by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples. The results show that the balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811, and that the quantised detector fits the on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit. This approach contrasts with the conventional bent-pipe architecture, in which the satellite acts as a passive data collector. Therefore, the computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

AI.tldr: A workflow combining on-board edge AI inference with diffusion-based generative data augmentation is proposed to overcome downlink limitations and class imbalance in nanosatellite-based airborne surveillance, improving minority-class detection from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811 and achieving 25-30 FPS on-orbit.
AI.motivation: Nanosatellites in low Earth orbit face two critical bottlenecks for airborne surveillance: (1) severely limited downlink bandwidth that makes transmitting terabytes of raw imagery impractical, and (2) scarce, class-imbalanced open satellite datasets that prevent robust detection of rare aircraft types. These jointly delay timely decision-making and degrade detector performance.
AI.method: The proposed workflow integrates two components: (a) on-board inference using a quantised detector deployed on a 6U CubeSat with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, and (b) generative data augmentation via a diffusion model fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to synthesise minority-class imagery. Synthetic images are automatically pseudo-labelled by an intermediate detector and merged with conventionally augmented samples to create a balanced training set.
AI.result: The balanced dataset raised global mAP from 77.9% to 82.2%, with minority-class F1-score improving from 0.683 to 0.811. The quantised detector fits within on-chip memory constraints and achieves 25-30 FPS on orbit, enabling real-time operation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed workflow contrasts with the traditional bent-pipe architecture (satellite as passive data relay) and is validated as a viable decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

title: Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors
summary: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes cross-task transfer between node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP) on the same graph, proposes a leakage-free evaluation protocol, and finds that NC→LP transfer is reliably beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC is fragile and only helps when LP is easy but NC is unsaturated. A new metric, the CoTask Score (CTS), is introduced to summarize joint utility.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of NC-LP transfer on the same graph use incompatible data splits, inconsistent assumptions about the observed graph, and ad-hoc negative sampling, making conclusions unreliable. The authors aim to establish a principled, leakage-free framework to understand when and how supervision can be productively shared between these two tasks.
AI.method: The authors formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and design a leakage-free protocol: fixing both node and edge splits, using a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employing fixed negatives for LP evaluation. They test three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), evaluate both transfer directions (NC→LP, LP→NC), and introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to measure joint NC+LP utility under a shared encoder. Dataset statistics like homophily are used to predict transfer success.
AI.result: NC→LP transfer is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs. LP→NC transfer is fragile: naive representation reuse can degrade NC accuracy. LP→NC becomes reliably positive only in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting LP serves as structural pretraining. The CoTask Score effectively summarizes joint utility, and homophily helps guide mechanism choice to avoid negative transfer.
AI.conclusion: Same-graph cross-task transfer between NC and LP is strongly directional. NC→LP is robustly beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP→NC requires careful conditions (structure-dominant, NC-unsaturated). Simple dataset statistics like homophily can predict transfer success, and the CTS provides a practical metric for joint optimization. The proposed evaluation protocol should be adopted to ensure reliable benchmarking.

title: A Fuzzy Rule-based Neuro-Symbolic Approach for Pipe Severity Prediction in Sewer Networks
summary:
Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment relies on direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the link between visual defects and final severity scores remains implicit. This study introduces a modular, fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by decoupling neural perception from symbolic reasoning. The perception module utilizes a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images. For reasoning, a DT, specifically Weka's J48, algorithm is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF--THEN rules. Inference operates via fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and combined with corresponding s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. We assessed Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs using a dataset of 3,244 images spanning five highly imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were robustly generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes. Our results show an improvement of accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1 and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, over image-only based classification.
  Overall, the framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

AI.tldr: A neuro-symbolic framework decouples sewer pipe defect perception (Swin Transformer) from severity reasoning (fuzzy rule-based system using J48 decision tree paths), achieving significant improvements over direct image classification across multiple metrics on a 5-class imbalanced dataset.
AI.motivation: Standard automated sewer pipe assessment uses direct image-to-severity classification, creating an opaque "black box" where the relationship between visual defects and final severity scores is implicit and untraceable. There is a need for interpretable, transparent reasoning that explicitly links detected defects to severity decisions.
AI.method: A modular framework with two decoupled components: (1) Perception module — Swin Transformer predicts 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees from images. (2) Reasoning module — Weka's J48 decision tree trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, with paths converted into 19 fixed IF-THEN rules. Inference uses fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions weighted by rule confidence, combined via s-norms to produce class evidence. Three operator pairs evaluated: Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher. Ground-truth labels generated via consensus from five independent LLMs analyzing inspector notes. Dataset: 3,244 images across five highly imbalanced severity classes.
AI.result: Accuracy improved by 17.9%, balanced accuracy by 12.2%, Macro F1 by 23.0%, and MCC by 17.3% over image-only based classification. The framework delivers competitive class-balanced performance with fully traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees through rule supports to final severity evidence.
AI.conclusion: The neuro-symbolic approach successfully combines competitive classification performance with interpretable, auditable reasoning chains. Decoupling perception from symbolic reasoning enables transparent severity assessment, eliminating the black-box limitation of direct image classification for sewer pipe inspection.

title: SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination
summary: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed. These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

AI.tldr: SCOPE is a composite policy model that unifies assortment, sourcing, replenishment frequency, and routing decisions into a single end-to-end framework using tokenized supply-chain entities and shared operational representations, outperforming decoupled and practice-oriented baselines on real data from Dingdong and JD.com.
AI.motivation: Modern supply chains suffer from operational silos: assortment, sourcing, frequency, and routing decisions are made by separate departments with separate systems, ignoring critical couplings between them. This leads to stockouts, excess inventory, and unnecessary transportation costs. The paper seeks to move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified, end-to-end operational planning.
AI.method: SCOPE represents supply-chain entities (products, facilities, vehicles) as tokens within a shared operational representation. A composite policy model maps each token type to its corresponding decision interface (assortment, source assignment, replenishment frequency, routing), with each decision conditioned on the partial plan formed by earlier stages. The completed plan is evaluated via a shared system-level utility. The framework is instantiated in urban fresh-retail replenishment and evaluated on real operational data from two large-scale supply chains (Dingdong and JD.com).
AI.result: Across both operational settings (Dingdong and JD.com), SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage in isolation, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly deployed in supply-chain operations.
AI.conclusion: Learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings yields more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions than isolated optimization. The token-based composite policy architecture provides a viable path toward unified supply-chain AI.

title: $β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance. Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

AI.tldr: Vanilla on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is brittle. The authors show it corresponds to a KL-regularized policy optimization with β=1, generalize it to β-OPSD where β controls the trade-off between reference policy proximity and teacher guidance, and implement the optimal solution efficiently via token-level logit mixing rather than costly RL, achieving improved stability and reasoning performance.
AI.motivation: Vanilla OPSD is promising for improving reasoning in language models but is practically brittle, requiring substantial engineering to work reliably. The authors aim to identify the structural source of this difficulty and provide a principled, more stable alternative.
AI.method: The authors prove that vanilla OPSD is the β=1 case of a broader KL-regularized policy optimization family where β weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. They derive β-OPSD, whose optimal policy is a geometric interpolation between the reference and teacher policies. Instead of directly optimizing via high-variance RL, they convert the closed-form solution into a distillation target by mixing reference and teacher token-level logits according to β. Return-to-go credit assignment aligns token-level updates with the sequence-level objective.
AI.result: Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, with improved optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance.
AI.conclusion: β-OPSD provides a principled path from self-distillation to policy optimization and back, preserving OPSD's practical efficiency while introducing controllable regularization that stabilizes training and boosts performance.

title: InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark
summary:
In this paper we present an active, constantly updated AI benchmark which measures the integrity of frontier language models against being co-opted for state-backed information operations. We draw on over 2,100 information operations from a live monitoring pipeline which tracks Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed information assets. Alongside this paper, we release a companion website that tracks the most prominent claims spread by state-backed media outlets, updated weekly, available from: pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench. The dynamic nature of the benchmark makes it resistant to saturation.
  In the benchmark, we test 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. We find that most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores, defined as the percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the resulting operation. Some models fabricate details and produce output more harmful than the source material, others defuse claims even while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%.
  Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, illustrating the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. With one exception (Z.ai's GLM 5.2), the Chinese-developed models sharply cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims, dropping 48-70 percentage points relative to matched benign claims.

AI.tldr: An active, continuously updated AI benchmark tests 17 frontier language models against co-option for state-backed information operations (Russian, Chinese, Iranian). Integrity scores range from 8.8% to 94.5%. Models vary widely in fabrication, fact-checking, and defusing behavior. Chinese-developed models (except GLM 5.2) sharply reduce compliance on China-critical claims.
AI.motivation: To measure and track the vulnerability of frontier language models to being weaponized for state-backed information operations, addressing the gap in dynamic, saturation-resistant safety benchmarks.
AI.method: A live benchmark drawing from over 2,100 information operations tracked by a monitoring pipeline across Russian, Chinese, and Iranian state-backed assets. Tests 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings, with results published on a weekly-updated companion website.
AI.result: Integrity scores (refusal rates) span 8.8%–94.5%, an 85.7pp spread unexplained by model size. Some models fabricate harmful details; others defuse claims while complying. Fact-checking rates range 2.9%–72.9%. Chinese-developed models (except Z.ai GLM 5.2) drop compliance 48–70pp on China-critical but factually grounded claims versus matched benign claims.
AI.conclusion: Most frontier models remain susceptible to co-option for information operations. Integrity partly correlates with general refusal behavior, revealing a safety-usability trade-off. Chinese-developed models exhibit politically aligned compliance suppression, raising concerns about geopolitical bias in model behavior.

title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
summary: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

AI.tldr: KAISEN is a stress-tested five-phase audit pipeline for clinical risk models that evaluates subgroup fairness. On synthetic benchmarks, it reveals: (1) significance-based disparity ranking improves when standardized by minimum detectable effect; (2) per-group threshold optimization reliably reduces equalized-odds difference (EOD), while Platt scaling does not and its variance should be reported; (3) mechanism diagnostics succeed under controlled conditions but fail silently under proxy misspecification; (4) CUSUM drift monitoring thresholds fail to transfer across cohort realizations.
AI.motivation: Clinical risk models exhibit aggregate-strong but subgroup-disparate performance. Existing audit pipelines are rarely stress-tested to failure, leaving practitioners uncertain about which audit components can be trusted and under what conditions. There is a need for rigorous evaluation of the entire audit workflow to identify brittle components before deployment in real clinical settings.
AI.method: The authors propose KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline: (1) subgroup stratification, (2) disparity measurement, (3) mechanism diagnostics, (4) post-hoc mitigation, and (5) drift monitoring. The pipeline is stress-tested to failure on a synthetic benchmark spanning 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Each component is evaluated with known ground truth, using metrics such as Spearman rank correlation, paired effect sizes with confidence intervals, binary classification accuracy of diagnostics, and chi-squared tests for CUSUM failure/false-alarm patterns across seeds.
AI.result: Finding (i): Significance count rank-correlates with raw EOD at ρ=0.56, improving to ρ=0.78 after standardizing by each axis's minimum detectable effect. Finding (ii): Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in all 48 held-out runs (mean Δ=-0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]); Platt scaling improves EOD in only 19/48 runs (95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with near-zero mean effect. Finding (iii): The mechanism diagnostic correctly classifies 144/144 controlled cases but recovers 0/48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification with no failure signal. Finding (iv): At the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7/8 missed CUSUM shifts arise from different seeds (χ² p=0.002), indicating threshold non-transferability across cohorts.
AI.conclusion: Audit pipelines must themselves be audited. The four failure modes identified — sensitivity of significance to detection floors, misleading average behavior of calibrators, silent failure under misspecification, and cohort-dependent drift thresholds — suggest that practitioners should not blindly trust standard audit components. All results are synthetic, so clinical validity is not claimed; the benchmark and code are released for reproducibility.

title: Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update
summary: Belief update concerns changes in an agent's beliefs induced by changes in the underlying world. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes that an epistemic input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, whereas credibility-limited belief update restricts, for each source world, the successor worlds regarded as credible or reachable. Nevertheless, existing credibility-limited approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, and therefore cannot represent cases in which only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. We introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, in which the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. We provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators. We then identify two well-behaved sub-classes; namely, consistency-preserving update operators, which require every transformed epistemic input to be credible from its source world whenever the original epistemic input is consistent, and maximal consistency-preserving update operators, which additionally require the selected proxy to be maximally informative among the credible consequences of the original epistemic input. Finally, we establish the generality of the proposed framework by showing that credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, while Katsuno--Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and the transformation functions are taken to be identities. These results demonstrate that the framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update, encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces selective credibility-limited belief update, a framework where epistemic inputs are transformed into weaker proxies per source world before a credibility-limited transition, generalizing both standard KM update and existing credibility-limited approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing credibility-limited belief update treats epistemic input as indivisible, failing to model scenarios where only part of a compound input can be realized. The authors aim to capture cases where an agent selectively accepts portions of new information based on credibility constraints tied to each possible world.
AI.method: The authors propose a semantic framework where, for each source world, the epistemic input is first transformed via a proxy function into a weaker formula before applying credibility-limited transition. They provide semantic characterizations via preorders and axiomatic characterizations via postulates. Two subclasses are identified: consistency-preserving and maximal consistency-preserving operators, the latter also enforcing maximal informativeness of the proxy.
AI.result: The framework strictly generalizes existing approaches: credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, and Katsuno-Mendelzon update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and transformation functions are identities. The two subclasses are shown to be well-behaved and formally characterized.
AI.conclusion: The selective credibility-limited framework provides a unified, strictly more expressive account of belief update that encompasses established approaches while enabling source-dependent selective acceptance of epistemic inputs.

title: MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.

AI.tldr: MANTA is a framework that enables multi-agent systems to dynamically adapt their communication topology at inference time, achieving state-of-the-art results across five benchmarks by self-evolving agent roles, links, execution order, and validation pathways based on collaboration traces.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems treat communication topology as fixed or offline-optimized, limiting adaptability during deployment. The authors argue that collaboration structures should evolve dynamically at inference time when the current organization proves insufficient for the task.
AI.method: MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience before execution. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates—modifying agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways—while preserving the task interface and agent budget.
AI.result: MANTA achieved an average score of 74.0 across five benchmarks (information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, mathematical reasoning), outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and securing the best result on PlanCraft.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time self-improvement can be successfully extended to the architecture of collaboration itself. Dynamic topology adaptation during execution yields significant performance gains over static communication structures in multi-agent systems.

title: Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling in Local Computer-Use Agents: Failure Modes and Compute Tradeoffs
summary: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents (CUAs) locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, yet improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While recent studies show that inference-time scaling can improve frontier computer-use agents through additional computation during execution, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models remains poorly understood. We present a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling in local CUAs across contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel dimensions. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark. Our results show that additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling provides historical grounding that improves trajectory stability and task accuracy, but its gains saturate as token cost increases and failures shift from repetitive or stalled trajectories toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling similarly reduces max-step stalls, yet does not substantially improve task success, indicating that longer horizons often extend erroneous trajectories rather than correct them. We further find that structural decomposition can introduce planning and formatting overhead in local two-stage agents, while parallel scaling partially mitigates these failures at a substantial computational cost. Overall, our findings suggest that efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling for local computer-use agents (CUAs), evaluating contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel scaling dimensions on models like Qwen3-VL and UI-TARS. Findings reveal diminishing returns: contextual scaling improves stability but saturates; temporal scaling reduces stalls without boosting success; structural decomposition introduces planning overhead. The authors advocate for selective compute allocation and failure-aware control mechanisms tailored to local model constraints.
AI.motivation: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents locally is critical for privacy, cost, and usability, but improving their performance under strict hardware constraints is challenging. While inference-time scaling has proven effective for frontier models, its applicability and effectiveness for resource-constrained local CUAs remain poorly understood, motivating a systematic investigation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling across four dimensions: (1) contextual scaling (providing historical grounding via longer context), (2) temporal scaling (extending execution horizons), (3) structural scaling (decomposing tasks into two-stage planning-and-execution agents), and (4) parallel scaling (running multiple trajectories concurrently). They evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark, analyzing both task success rates and failure mode shifts.
AI.result: Contextual scaling improves trajectory stability and task accuracy but exhibits saturating gains as token costs rise, with failures shifting from repetitive/stalled trajectories to premature false successes. Temporal scaling reduces max-step stalls but does not substantially improve task success, often prolonging erroneous trajectories. Structural decomposition introduces planning and formatting overhead in local two-stage agents. Parallel scaling partially mitigates these failures but at substantial computational cost. Overall, additional computation yields diminishing returns and shifts rather than eliminates failure modes.
AI.conclusion: Efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation rather than uniform scaling, failure-aware control mechanisms to detect and respond to shifting failure modes, and agentic frameworks designed specifically around the capabilities and limitations of local models rather than simply adapting frontier-agent strategies to constrained settings.

title: DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
comment: Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). 12 pages
summary: While Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation (MM-RAG) has shown promising results, it still struggles with complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. Existing methods primarily focus on independent instance-level matching, which often fails to capture explicit relationships across modalities and documents. Although Graph-enhanced methods introduce structural modeling, they face a fundamental challenge in multimodal scenarios: incorporating fine-grained visual features leads to rapid graph expansion and retrieval noise, whereas coarse-grained representations cause the discarding of critical local evidence. To address this dilemma, we propose DualG-MRAG, a Dual-tier framework that introduces a decoupled architecture comprising Macro-reasoning and Micro-matching Graphs for Multimodal RAG. Specifically, to suppress retrieval noise by isolating global structural reasoning from fine-grained evidence matching, we construct a Macro Graph for global topological routing and a Micro Graph for precise local verification. Subsequently, to enable dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence sources, we formulate retrieval as a query-driven message passing process via a GNN Retriever. Furthermore, to provide the generative model with coherent structural guidance, we introduce a dynamic programming decoding mechanism that extracts explicit reasoning paths directly from the GNN's forward pass, replacing the standard input of isolated document chunks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines in both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy.

AI.tldr: DualG-MRAG proposes a dual-tier graph framework for multimodal RAG that decouples global structural reasoning (Macro Graph) from fine-grained evidence matching (Micro Graph), uses a GNN Retriever for query-driven message passing, and employs dynamic programming decoding to extract explicit reasoning paths, outperforming baselines on evidence recall and complex QA.
AI.motivation: Existing MM-RAG methods struggle with complex multi-hop reasoning because instance-level matching fails to capture cross-modal and cross-document relationships. Graph-enhanced methods face a dilemma: fine-grained visual features cause graph expansion and retrieval noise, while coarse-grained features discard critical local evidence.
AI.method: DualG-MRAG introduces a decoupled dual-tier architecture: (1) a Macro Graph for global topological routing (isolating structural reasoning from noisy fine-grained evidence) and a Micro Graph for precise local verification; (2) a GNN Retriever that formulates retrieval as query-driven message passing for dynamic relevance propagation across heterogeneous evidence; (3) a dynamic programming decoding mechanism that extracts explicit reasoning paths from the GNN forward pass, replacing isolated document chunks as input to the generative model.
AI.result: DualG-MRAG outperforms baselines on both evidence recall and complex QA accuracy in extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The decoupled dual-graph approach effectively resolves the granularity dilemma in multimodal graph-enhanced retrieval, enabling robust multi-hop reasoning through structured evidence propagation and explicit path-guided generation.
